title: Embodied Neuro-symbolic AI: Making Robot Behavior Auditable, Safe, and Scalable
summary: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) end-to-end systems have driven major progress in robot learning, yet they still face persistent barriers to dependable real-world deployment. In practice, these models often exhibit brittle generalization under distribution shift (i.e., novel objects, layouts, lighting, or contact conditions), limited physical and causal reasoning, and inconsistent fine-grained motor control. Critically, many VLA pipelines offer limited ways to express and audit what a robot must not do, making it difficult to provide assurance in safety-critical settings. These limitations constrain scalability, maintainability, and trust when robots move beyond controlled demonstrations. We propose Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI: a deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning and control with explicit, machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints. By combining knowledge-guided perception, constraint-aware symbolic planning, and hybrid learning, Embodied NeSy AI enables robots to reason about their environment, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements, thus supporting scalable, trustworthy robot deployment.
full_text: Embodied Neuro-symbolic AI:\ Robot Behavior Auditable, Safe, and Scalable Ruwan Wickramarachchi , Jonathan Francis , Alessandro Oltramari Bosch Center for Artificial Intelligence, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA.\\ \ ruwan.wickramarachchi, alessandro.oltramari, jon.francis\ @us.bosch.com Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) end-to-end systems have driven major progress in robot learning, yet they still face persistent barriers to dependable real-world deployment. In practice, these models often exhibit brittle generalization under distribution shift (i.e., novel objects, layouts, lighting, or contact conditions), limited physical and causal reasoning, and inconsistent fine-grained motor control. Critically, many VLA pipelines offer limited ways to express and audit what a robot must not do, making it difficult to provide assurance in safety-critical settings. These limitations constrain scalability, maintainability, and trust when robots move beyond controlled demonstrations. We propose Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI: a deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning and control with explicit, machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints. By combining knowledge-guided perception, constraint-aware symbolic planning, and hybrid learning, Embodied NeSy AI enables robots to reason about their environment, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements, thus supporting scalable, trustworthy robot deployment. Neurosymbolic AI, Robot Learning, Embodied AI, Physical AI, Hybrid Learning Introduction The next generation of reliable, auditable, and scalable robot intelligence will require moving beyond the limitations of current end-to-end neural systems. While deep learning and VLA models have enabled robots to learn complex sensorimotor skills from demonstration and large-scale data, they remain fundamentally limited in their ability to generalize, reason about physical and causal structure, and provide verifiable guarantees for safety and compliance. These limitations are especially acute in open-world, safety-critical, or rapidly changing environments, where implicit statistical regularities are insufficient for robust deployment. Embodied NeSy AI addresses these challenges by integrating neural perception and control with explicit, machine-readable knowledge and formal constraints. Rather than relying solely on implicit statistical regularities, Embodied NeSy makes key domain structure—task semantics, operational procedures, hardware/product metadata, and safety requirements—explicit and actionable inside the decision loop. This knowledge is represented using ontologies, knowledge graphs, and constraint specifications, capturing site and use-case configurations, robot and tool capabilities/limits (e.g., payload, workspace envelopes, calibration, speed/force bounds), subject-matter expertise, standard operating procedures, and formal safety rules (e.g., restricted zones, proximity constraints, permitted contact regimes). Central to this framework are three tightly integrated components: (1) knowledge-guided semantic perception that grounds symbolic predicates in sensor data while tracking uncertainty; (2) constraint-aware symbolic planning that generates machine-checkable action sequences satisfying task goals and formal safety requirements; and (3) hybrid learning that updates both neural skills and symbolic knowledge from experience under safety envelopes. By combining these elements, Embodied NeSy AI enables robots to reason about their environment, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements—supporting compositional adaptation, continual learning, and clearer governance for trustworthy, large-scale robot deployment in diverse domains. The need for such integration becomes evident when considering the shortcomings of single-paradigm approaches. Purely neural embodied systems lack interpretability, offer no guarantees of constraint satisfaction, generalize poorly to novel task compositions, and require extensive retraining for new scenarios. Classical symbolic approaches, in contrast, can face challenges in grounding symbols in noisy sensor data, learning and adapting from experience, scaling to complex state spaces, and representing uncertainty. Embodied NeSy AI bridges these weaknesses by combining data-driven learning with structured reasoning. Embodied NeSy AI Framework: Components and Integration Embodied NeSy AI is built on three tightly integrated components (see Figure fig:embodied-nesy-framework ), each leveraging explicit knowledge representation for robust, auditable, and adaptive robot behavior. Knowledge representation is central to this framework: ontologies, knowledge graphs, and constraint specifications encode site and use-case configurations, robot and tool capabilities/limits (e.g., payload, workspace envelopes, calibration, speed/force bounds), subject-matter expertise, standard operating procedures, and formal safety rules (e.g., restricted zones, proximity constraints, permitted contact regimes). By making these elements structured and auditable, Embodied NeSy AI supports compositional adaptation, continual learning, and clearer governance during deployment. The three core components of this framework are explained below.\\ Semantic perception (knowledge-guided grounding with uncertainty): Perception modules employ Vision-Language Models (VLMs) or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems, guided by ontologies and knowledge graphs, to ground symbolic predicates in sensor streams (e.g., object identity, affordances, zones, human proximity) and estimate task-relevant properties (e.g., pose, fragility cues, graspability), while tracking uncertainty/confidence. The output is an uncertainty-aware, queryable belief state—comprising knowledge graph triples and logical predicates—that encodes entities, properties, geometry, and relations. This structured representation enables downstream symbolic planners to validate goals, decompose tasks, and enforce constraints by querying the current state of the world, supporting robust operation under ambiguity and novelty.\\ Constraint-aware symbolic planning (specification to plans): Symbolic planners generate only those action sequences that satisfy task goals, symbolic/task specifications, safety rules, and temporal logic constraints before execution. This pre-execution enforcement ensures that plans are filtered for reachability, forbidden states, restricted zones, tool/process prerequisites, and correct ordering of actions. The planner checks each candidate plan against formal constraints—such as state/action bounds, temporal safety rules, and process dependencies—so that only compliant plans are produced. VLA plan priors (e.g., likely action sequences or skill policies suggested by Vision-Language-Action models) can also be incorporated to guide or bias the symbolic planner, improving efficiency and leveraging learned experience. All plans are machine-checkable with respect to the abstract model and stated assumptions, providing explicit, auditable guarantees of constraint satisfaction at the planning level. This enables robots to reason about safety, compliance, and operational requirements in a transparent and verifiable manner, reducing the risk of unsafe or invalid behavior before any action is taken.\\ Hybrid learning (continual updates across perception, planning, and knowledge): Hybrid learning in Embodied NeSy AI operates at three levels: (1) Perception: Neural modules improve grounding accuracy and adapt thresholds for symbolic predicate extraction based on feedback and uncertainty; (2) Planning: Heuristics and plan priors are tuned from experience to improve efficiency and robustness of symbolic planners; (3) Knowledge: The symbolic layer is continually refined through knowledge graph completion, rule learning, and rule refinement, enabling the system to expand and update its knowledge base over time. Unlike conventional systems that keep symbolic knowledge static, Embodied NeSy AI continually refines the symbolic layer via rule learning, knowledge graph completion, or program synthesis under invariant-preserving safeguards. These continual updates allow rapid adaptation to new tasks and environments without full-stack retraining, supporting scalable and robust deployment. Related Work Neurosymbolic AI aims to unify subsymbolic learning with symbolic reasoning, addressing the limitations of classical symbolic approaches and the opacity of end-to-end neural policies garcezneurosymbolic2023,shethneurosymbolic2023 . We organize related work along three dimensions central to our Embodied NeSy AI framing: knowledge-guided perception and grounding, constraint-aware planning and verification, and hybrid learning and adaptation.\\ -guided perception and grounding. Explicit knowledge representations complement neural models with structured information about entities, relations, physical properties, affordances, and domain constraints. Ontologies such as KNOWROB support action-centered representations and reasoning about objects, actions, and affordances bessler2020formal , while knowledge graphs support hybrid modeling and neural-symbolic reasoning rudolph2024hybrid,tran2025reasoningneurosymbolicai . Recent approaches further combine neural perception with explicit symbolic relations for tasks such as spatial reasoning and object localization jahangard2025multi . Foundation models such as VLMs and VLAs provide powerful semantic priors but do not inherently maintain explicit, machine-queryable representations of task-relevant entities, constraints, and uncertainty. Our framing therefore emphasizes an uncertainty-aware symbolic belief state that connects learned perception, structured knowledge, and downstream reasoning.\\ -aware planning, safety, and verification. Neurosymbolic architectures increasingly combine learned models with symbolic planning and formal constraints. Modular approaches pair LLM-based reasoning with neural controllers ali2025control , while systems such as PFEA use vision-language planning, execution feedback, and replanning for robotic manipulation ding2025pfea . Safety-oriented approaches introduce specification-driven architectures and verification against explicit safety constraints zheng2025neurostrata,yang2025repv , with related work addressing reasoning shortcuts and assurance in neural-symbolic systems richards2025promise,marconato2025prototypical . These methods demonstrate the value of explicit reasoning and verification, particularly for safety-critical embodied systems. Our framing integrates these capabilities by placing constraint-aware symbolic planning directly between grounded perception and robot execution, enabling plans to be checked against task, operational, and safety constraints before execution.\\ learning and adaptation. Recent work also investigates tighter integration of neural learning and symbolic reasoning. Imperative Learning couples neural modules with classical solvers and model-based optimization wang2025imperative,li2025ikap ; Neurosymbolic Imitation Learning learns symbolic abstractions for decomposing tasks and sequencing neural skills keller2025nsil ; and Symbolic Imitation Learning uses Inductive Logic Programming to induce interpretable rules sharifi2025sil . Simulation-based approaches further support generalization through large-scale pretraining and synthetic data interndata2025 . While these approaches provide mechanisms for joint learning, abstraction, and generalization, adaptation often centers on individual components. Our framing instead treats learning as continual adaptation across perception, planning, and explicit knowledge, allowing the system to incorporate experience without requiring full-stack retraining while preserving safety

title: Hi3R-VLA: Grounding Semantics and Actions in 3D
summary: While recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate 3D geometry, how to effectively exploit it for precise and generalizable action prediction remains a central challenge. We introduce Hi3R-VLA, a 3D policy that grounds heterogeneous modalities - vision, language, and action - in explicit 3D geometry for robotic manipulation. Our model integrates spatially-aligned visual features and language conditioning into point cloud representations, enriching scene geometry with fine-grained, task-relevant semantics. It then anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D coordinate frame and uses 3D-RoPE enhanced action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine point features to model geometric relationships between action targets and observed points. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of semantic fusion within 3D and spatial alignment between observations and actions. With fewer than 250M trainable parameters, Hi3R-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa, RLBench, RoboTwin2, DexJoCo and DexSuite across diverse manipulation tasks and embodiments, from single-arm and dual-arm grippers to dexterous hands. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate its effectiveness in the physical world. The model, code and dataset are publicly released at https://cshizhe.github.io/projects/hi3r_vla.html.

Introduction sec:intro Language-guided robotic manipulation~ guhur2023hiveformer,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t requires both understanding task-relevant semantics and reasoning about physical geometry to generate precise actions. Recent vision-language-action (VLA)~ intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t models have demonstrated promising capabilities across diverse manipulation tasks, but their predominantly 2D visual representations do not well capture metric 3D structure. This has motivated the development of 3D VLAs~ qu2025spatialvla,chen2026pointact,sun2025geovla that incorporate explicit geometric observations, such as point clouds, to support robot action generation. Existing 3D policies differ in how they represent geometry and combine it with vision and language for action prediction. Some only associate pretrained 2D visual features with 3D coordinates~ gervet2023act3d,ke20243dda,xiong2026geomvla , while others explicitly encode point clouds with dedicated 3D backbones~ qi2017pointnet,wu2024ptv3,zhang2026utonia or fuse the resulting geometric features with visual representations~ fan2026any3dvla,chen2026pointact . The resulting features can be integrated into a shared VLM backbone~ yang2026fp3,fan2026any3dvla or fed into a separate action expert~ sun2025geovla . PointACT~ chen2026pointact compares these architectures and highlights the benefits of an action expert with multi-scale point features. Despite these advances, it remains unclear which design choices are most critical for mapping explicit geometry into effective action learning, and how well they apply across manipulation tasks and embodiments, from single-arm grippers to bimanual dexterous hands. These questions motivate our investigation: What makes explicit 3D geometry effective for action prediction, and how robust are these design choices across different manipulation settings? We introduce , a 3D-based policy that grounds heterogeneous modalities---vision, language, and action---in explicit 3D geometry, as illustrated in~ . Our key idea is to use 3D point representations as a common geometric reference for multimodal perception and action generation. On the perception side, we integrate spatially-aligned image features and language conditioning into point representations, enriching scene geometry with fine-grained, task-relevant semantics. On the action side, a flow-matching action expert attends to these multimodal point representations in a coarse-to-fine manner. However, action representations, such as joint configurations or relative motion commands, may not be directly aligned with the 3D geometry of the observed scene. To bridge this gap, we introduce spatial anchors that augment the original action representations with 3D end-effector positions. These anchors lie in the scene coordinate frame, allowing 3D rotary positional encoding (RoPE)~ su2024rope in action-to-point attention to capture relative spatial relationships between action targets and observed points. Additionally, we investigate the benefits of pretraining on a large-scale real-robot dataset DROID~ khazatsky2024droid . We extensively evaluate on multiple manipulation benchmarks, including RoboCasa24~ nasiriany2024robocasa , RLBench~ james2020rlbench , RoboTwin2~ chen2025robotwin2 , DexJoCo~ wang2026dexjoco , and DexSuite~ houssaini2026dexsuite , which cover diverse tasks and embodiments, from single-arm and dual-arm manipulators to dexterous hands. achieves state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks with over 10 fewer trainable parameters than state-of-the-art methods such as ~ intelligence2025pi05 , even without pretraining on large-scale real-robot data. Extensive ablations show that spatial anchors and 3D positional encoding are critical for precise action prediction by aligning actions with observed geometry, while fusing visual and language features into the point backbone provides gains beyond multimodal conditioning in the action expert. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce , a 3D-based policy that uses explicit geometric representations to connect multimodal perception with spatially grounded action generation. We investigate key design choices in , including multimodal fusion, spatially grounded action prediction, and pretraining, providing empirical insights for building effective 3D policies. achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks with fewer than 250M trainable parameters. Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 , OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , ~ intelligence2025pi05,intelligence2026pi07 and GR00T~ bjorck2025gr00t , have advanced generalist manipulation by fine-tuning pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)~ bai2025qwen3vl,beyer2024paligemma on large-scale robot demonstrations. A growing body of work incorporates geometric knowledge into visual policies to improve spatial understanding and manipulation. SpatialVLA~ qu2025spatialvla and SPEAR-1~ nikolov2026spear1 augment visual representations with pretrained depth estimators, while E0.5~ team2026e05 adopts geometric foundation models like VGGT~ wang2025vggt as policy backbones. To better connect the observation and action space, some works first predict 3D intermediate representations such as 3D object pose~ lin2026posevla , camera-frame SE(3) end-effector trajectory~ lin2026posevla,chen2026oasis or 3D scene flows~ wang2026lamp , then condition an action expert on the resulting latent features. However, this formulation does not align multi-view visual observations, and requires large-scale 3D pretraining~ lin2026posevla,wang2026lamp . Our approach directly encodes metric point clouds aggregated from multiple views and uses spatial anchors to align action tokens with scene points in a common coordinate frame, enabling data- and compute-efficient action prediction. 3D-based robotic manipulation. The prevalence of 3D sensors has encouraged explicit 3D policy learning. Existing 3D-based policies differ in how they represent scene geometry and incorporate it into action prediction. Rendering-based methods~ goyal2023rvt,goyal2024rvt2,li2026bridgevla project point clouds into virtual views, allowing to reuse pretrained image models. Depth- or point-map-based methods~ jia2026pointmappolicy,lee2026seervla represent geometry on RGB-aligned 2D grids, facilitating image-based encoding and fusion. Another family constructs 3D feature clouds by lifting image features to 3D with their corresponding 3D coordinates~ gervet2023act3d,ke20243dda,gkanatsios20253dflowmatchactor,xiong2026geomvla and enhances action prediction via 3D rotary position embeddings~ su2024rope . Due to improvements in 3D point encoders~ qi2017pointnet,wu2024ptv3,zhang2026utonia , more recent methods directly encode point clouds~ chen2023polarnet,ze2024dp3,wang2024rise,garcia2025gembench and inject them into VLAs. Some feed point features into the VLM backbone~ yang2026fp3,fan2026any3dvla , whereas others~ li2026pointvla,sun2025geovla,li2026bridge3d incorporate them into the action expert. PointACT~ chen2026pointact compares these two architectures and shows the benefits of a separate action expert conditioned on multi-scale point features. PointWAM~ park2026pointwam extends point-based modeling to cascaded world action models for dexterous manipulation. title: FabricBench: A Standardized Policy Benchmark for Bimanual Fabric Manipulation with a Contact-Driven Deformable Simulator
summary: Fabric manipulation challenges robot policies with changing geometry, self-occlusion, and contact, yet standardized evaluation remains focused on rigid objects. We introduce FabricBench, a benchmark for bimanual fabric manipulation with six tasks spanning garments, silk, and bags, 10,000 simulation-ready assets, and controlled tests of configuration and appearance generalization. Built on an open-source solver in Newton, our simulator enables stable bimanual grasping, holding, and release through contact forces, without artificial attachment. Redesigned cloth-rigid contact and bidirectional force coupling support interactions among robot arms, fabric, and free rigid objects, allowing a bag to support its contents and transmit their weight to the grippers. In a controlled grasp-hold-release evaluation, our solver succeeds in all 45 trials, compared with none for the tested baseline configurations. Evaluating six representative policies, including vision-language-action models and world action models, reveals substantial remaining challenges: the best policy achieves 77% average success, while no policy exceeds 36% on long-horizon T-shirt folding. Under the most deformed initial T-shirt configurations, success falls to 6-14% across policies, with larger drops than under the evaluated appearance shifts. Zero-shot deployment of $π_{0.5}$ on a real robot largely preserves task difficulty ordering across six tasks (Spearman $ρ=0.94$). These results establish FabricBench as a reproducible testbed for measuring fabric-manipulation capabilities and exposing limitations in configuration generalization. The project website is available at https://fabricbench.github.io/.

Introduction sec:intro Fabric manipulation is central to everyday tasks such as folding laundry and carrying bags, yet folds, self-occlusion, and changing contacts make it difficult to evaluate reliably~ lin2020softgym,lu2024garmentlab . Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) show progress on fabric tasks, including laundry folding with ~ black2024pi0 and towel folding with Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam , while standardized manipulation benchmarks remain focused on rigid objects~ mu2025robotwin,liu2023libero . We introduce , a standardized benchmark for evaluating learned policies on bimanual fabric manipulation. Simulation can make fabric evaluation scalable and reproducible, but reliable cloth contact remains challenging. Existing environments report penetration, jitter, and instability~ wang2025dexgarmentlab,flatlab2026 ; others use attachment rules to bind cloth to the gripper~ lu2024garmentlab,flash2026 . Under learned policies, small fluctuations in continuous gripper commands can repeatedly trigger attachment and release, making outcomes depend on simulator rules rather than policy capability. To address this limitation, we develop an improved open-source cloth solver based on the Style3D cloth solver in the Newton physics engine. Redesigned cloth--rigid contact and bidirectional force coupling among the arm, fabric, and free rigid objects allow grasping, release, and load transfer to arise from contact and remain stable under learned policies. Six tasks cover T-shirt folding and flattening, silk flattening and lifting, bag carrying, and packing, spanning multilayer self-contact, dynamic manipulation, self-occlusion, and load-bearing fabric--object interactions. Beyond task success, separates generalization across initial fabric configurations from generalization across appearance. Folding or crumpling the same garment changes visibility, contacts, and feasible actions. For the two flattening tasks, seeded configuration levels (C0--C2) vary initial deformation while sharing assets and placement distributions. Held-out appearance variants instead change color and texture while keeping geometry and physics fixed. These controlled axes test whether policies cope with changes in fabric state as well as visual appearance. This paper makes the following contributions: [leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=2pt] A fabric manipulation benchmark. : six tasks over garments, silk cloth, and fabric bags; held-out variations in initial deformation and appearance on the flattening tasks; a unified training and evaluation protocol with demonstration generation. An open-source simulator. An improved cloth solver based on the Style3D solver in the Newton physics engine, with redesigned cloth--rigid contact and bidirectional force coupling among the arm, the fabric, and free rigid objects, so that grasping, release, and load transfer arise from contact forces and remain stable under learned policies. A systematic assessment of policy limitations. Our evaluation shows that current policies remain unreliable on fabric manipulation, especially long-horizon folding. Appearance shifts reduce performance, although some policies show partial robustness to these changes. On the flattening tasks, performance degrades systematically with increasing initial deformation, with drops far exceeding those under appearance shift. Related Work Manipulation Policies and Benchmarks sec:rw-bench Manipulation policies have progressed rapidly from classical imitation learning~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusionpolicy to large-scale generalist models. Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , , ~ black2024pi0,pi052025 , and GR00T~ bjorck2025gr00t are pretrained on large multi-robot datasets and improve instruction following and cross-embodiment transfer, and world action models such as LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva and Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam further predict future observations jointly with actions. Standardized simulation benchmarks such as RoboTwin~ mu2025robotwin,chen2025robotwin2 , LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboDojo~ robodojo2026 , and RoboLab~ yang2026robolab have driven this progress on rigid bodies through fixed task suites, public demonstrations, and shared protocols. Studies of policy degradation under object-layout, camera-viewpoint, and initial-pose perturbations~ liberopro2025,liberoplus2025 have further exposed where these policies break and guided their improvement. Deformable objects are absent from these suites or appear as a single task~ robodojo2026 , and the deformation state of the object lies outside their perturbation axes. Early benchmarks for deformable objects, SoftGym~ lin2020softgym , DaXBench~ chen2023daxbench , and Deformable Ravens~ seita2021deformable , introduced simulated task suites for cloth, rope, and bags, but observe through low-resolution renders, heightmaps, or particle states, whereas simulated scores track real-robot performance once the visual gap is controlled~ li2024simplerenv . Recent Isaac Sim suites such as LeHome~ lehome2026 and FlatLab~ flatlab2026 narrow this visual gap for specific categories of deformable objects. further narrows the physics gap, bringing simulated evaluation of deformable manipulation closer to the real world. Cloth Simulation for Robotic Manipulation sec:rw-sim Position-based dynamics (PBD/XPBD)~ muller2007pbd,macklin2016xpbd underlies many cloth-manipulation environments: SoftGym builds on the PBD-based FleX engine~ macklin2014unified , and GarmentLab~ lu2024garmentlab , DexGarmentLab~ wang2025dexgarmentlab , LeHome, and FlatLab use the PBD cloth of Isaac Sim~ isaacsim . PBD is stable and easy to implement, but it approximates continuum mechanics with geometric constraint projections, producing over-stretching and self-penetration, and its gap to real garment dynamics has been measured~ blancomulero2024simtoreal,hu2026rgbench . Finite-element and intersection-free solvers~ faure2012sofa,li2020ipc,li2021cipc , including the cloth solver of Genesis~ genesis2024 , are more accurate but about an order of magnitude slower, too slow for policy-scale rollouts (Appendix~ app:sim-criteria ), whereas recent fast FEM cloth solvers reach continuum-level accuracy at practical rates~ hu2026rgbench,flash2026 . A simplified open-source version of the Style3D solver following this principle is available in the Newton physics engine~ newton2025,nvidia2025newtonblog , and we build on it. Contact between cloth and rigid bodies, such as a gripper or objects in a bag, is typically handled by rules or artificial forces rather than simulated physically: SoftGym grasps with pickers that attach nearby particles, DaXBench with pick-and-place macro actions, and Deformable Ravens with fixed constraints; GarmentLab~ lu2024garmentlab and FLASH~ flash2026 bind cloth vertices within a distance threshold when the gripper closes, and DexGarmentLab~ wang2025dexgarmentlab adds artificial adhesion between the fingers and the fabric; the released Style3D solver~ newton2025 couples cloth and rigid bodies only one way, so objects in a bag follow it only if a rule binds them to it. In all these cases, whether the cloth or the bag's contents follow the gripper is decided by these mechanisms rather than by contact forces, and, as discussed in Section~ sec:intro , end-to-end policies have no access to them. In , grasp, release, and load transfer arise from bidirectional contact forces alone, so task outcomes reflect the policy's actions under real physical contact. Deformable Simulation and Contact Formulation sec:platform We state the cloth dynamics, the contact energy between cloth and rigid bodies, and the force exchange with the rigid-body solver; implementation details are in Appendix~ app:sim . Cloth Dynamics sec:cloth Material model. A garment is a triangle mesh. Its in-plane energy is the anisotropic membrane model of baraff1998large , with warp, weft, and shear stiffness specified per triangle; its out-of-plane energy is the discrete bending model of bergou2006quadratic on mesh edges. These stiffnesses and the areal density correspond directly to standard fabric tests, so they are loaded from measured values and carry no non-physical tuning parameters. Time integration. Positions advance by implicit Euler with a fixed substep . title: Enhancing Sparse-View Gaussian Splatting with Feed-Forward Priors via Spectral Fusion and Distillation
summary: Gaussian splatting from sparse training views renders high-quality images near training views, but reconstruction quality degrades at distant regions, which are undersampled by the training set. Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models use strong learned priors to resample the scene from substantially different viewpoints, but they take more than ten times as long to render and produce high-frequency artifacts on out-of-domain scenes. We propose a plug-and-play method that enhances an existing sparse-view Gaussian model with a pretrained feed-forward NVS model. We observe that the two are complementary in the frequency domain: the prior is more accurate at low frequencies, and the Gaussians at high frequencies. The reliability of the prior relative to the Gaussians is inversely proportional to the image frequency, so the optimal fusion weight is a first-order low-pass filter with one parameter that can be fitted. Our key idea is then to intelligently fuse the reliable part of each of the two methods. To remove the slow feed-forward model at render time, we use these fused images as teachers and distill them back into Gaussians, balanced with supervision from input views. Our method improves the quality of various sparse-view Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed, and our analysis works on different prior models. Project page: https://linwk20.github.io/spectral-fusion-gs/

Project page: linwk20.github.io/spectral-fusion-gs Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d renders photorealistic novel views in real time~ zhu2026seele and is used in XR~ lin2025metasapiens,lin2025powergs,lin2026controlgs,franke2025vrsplatting,tu2025vrsplat , streaming~ sun20243dgstream,yan2025instant,hu20254dgc,wu2025immersive , autonomous driving~ yan2024street,hess2025splatad,chen2025omnire and teleoperation~ wildersmith2024radiance . However, with only a few input views, it overfits to the inputs and performs poorly at novel views. Sparse-view methods regularize the optimization with dropout~ park2025dropgaussian,xu2025dropoutgs , depth~ zhu2024fsgs,li2024dngaussian or stereo priors~ han2024binocular,yuan2026stereogs . They stay sharp near the training views and break at views far from them. Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models~ jin2025lvsm,szymanowicz2026lagernvs carry a prior learned from many scenes. However, they cannot replace Gaussians, because (1) they render more than slower, and (2) their results carry high-frequency artifacts on out-of-domain scenes ( ) . This paper targets Gaussian splatting with sparse inputs. We introduce a plug-and-play method that enhances any sparse-view Gaussian model with a pretrained feed-forward NVS model (NVS prior). Our key idea is to combine the strengths of the two methods. It combines three ingredients. Spectral analysis. We compare the errors of the two models at every spatial frequency ( ). Both methods have high errors at high frequencies. We find that the error of the Gaussians rises on a straight line in log frequency, while the error of the NVS prior starts lower and rises faster. The two curves cross once: before the crossover, the prior has the lower error, and after it, the Gaussians are more reliable. Spectral fusion. We derive the optimal way to combine them in . Given a real image, a render by the Gaussians and a render by the prior, we can compute the optimal weighting across frequency. We find that the relative reliability of the NVS prior falls with frequency. However, the measured optimal weight is noisy. To characterize the optimum in a principled way and to improve generalization, we parameterize the optimal weight with a curve. Our key finding is that the optimal fusion weight is well approximated by a first-order low-pass filter, which has only a single parameter: the crossover frequency where both models are equally reliable. We fit this single-parameter curve on a development set and find that it generalizes well to the held-out test set and provides high-quality fused results. Distillation. Obtaining the fused results requires running the feed-forward model, which is slow. To keep rendering as fast as Gaussians, we use the fused images as teachers ( ), mix them with the real training views, and distill this hybrid supervision into the Gaussians ( ). Result. We evaluate on LLFF and Mip-NeRF 360 with different input views. The distilled models improve in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS ( ) by to \,dB on average and render as fast as their base models, at \,FPS on average for on an RTX 5090. Our contributions are: We show that a feed-forward NVS prior and sparse-view Gaussians are complementary in frequency. We characterize and fit the reliability of the prior relative to the Gaussians with a parameterized first-order low-pass filter, which is used to fuse the results of the two methods. We propose a plug-and-play distillation that distills the fused results back into the Gaussians, enabling both high-quality and high-efficiency rendering. Our method improves different Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed. It also generalizes to different methods that provide an NVS prior. Related Work sec:related Novel View Synthesis (NVS) from Sparse Views NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233d optimize one scene at a time and need dense views. NeRF-based methods regularize the radiance field under sparse inputs~ jain2021dietnerf,niemeyer2022regnerf,yang2023freenerf,wang2023sparsenerf . Sparse-view 3DGS follows two directions. One regularizes the optimization: ~ park2025dropgaussian and ~ xu2025dropoutgs drop Gaussians during training, and ~ zhang2024corgs penalizes disagreement between two models. The other adds geometric priors: ~ zhu2024fsgs and ~ li2024dngaussian use monocular depth, ~ han2024binocular builds stereo pairs from the inputs, ~ yuan2026stereogs uses stereo and multi-view stereo priors, and ~ fan2024instantsplat starts from feed-forward geometry. These methods add no appearance information at views the inputs do not cover. Our method takes their trained model as input and leaves their training unchanged. Novel View Synthesis with Prior Feed-forward models learn to synthesize views across scenes, which removes the need for dense views. ~ charatan2024pixelsplat , ~ chen2024mvsplat , ~ zhang2024gslrm , ~ xu2025depthsplat and ~ jiang2025anysplat predict Gaussians from images. Feed-forward NVS~ jin2025lvsm,wang2025clift,lin2026glodlvsm , such as ~ szymanowicz2026lagernvs , predict target images directly with no explicit 3D representation. They render slowly, so we use one only as a frozen teacher. Diffusion models generate content at novel views, and ~ zhou2025seva synthesizes them directly with a multi-view diffusion model; we test it as a prior in . ~ lin2026controlhair guides a diffusion model with control signals and renders bullet-time novel views of hair. ~ wu2024reconfusion and ~ kong2025generative regularize the reconstruction with a diffusion prior. ~ liu20243dgsenhancer , ~ wu2025difix3d and ~ wu2025genfusion restore artifact-prone renders and feed them back into reconstruction. ~ zhu2026gaps selects pseudo views by informativeness and generative reliability. These methods use the prior at all frequencies. We use a deterministic feed-forward model and weight it by frequency, because it is reliable only at low frequencies. Frequency Analysis in View Synthesis Frequency is a common tool to regularize view synthesis. ~ yang2023freenerf masks the high-frequency positional encoding early in training, and ~ zhang2024fregs and ~ nguyen2025dwtgs supervise Gaussians progressively or separately across frequency bands. These methods treat frequency as a schedule for one model. In contrast, we use frequency to decide which of two models to trust. This is the setting of classical linear estimation: the optimal weight between two noisy estimates at each frequency follows their relative reliability~ wiener1949extrapolation . We measure this weight for a feed-forward prior and sparse-view Gaussians, and find that a one-parameter filter describes it. Motivation sec:motivation Feed-forward priors fail as direct supervision. sec:mot:artifact A straightforward way to help sparse-view Gaussians is to supervise them with the outputs of a model that carries a prior~ wu2024reconfusion,kong2025generative,liu20243dgsenhancer,wu2025difix3d,wu2025genfusion . However, we find that this does not work well with a feed-forward NVS model. title: Ground, Guide, Act: Improving VLA Spatial Generalization with Multimodal Foundation Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models effectively learn action policies from robot demonstrations, but struggle to generalize to changes in object positions and task goals. General multimodal foundation models (MFMs) offer complementary scene understanding and spatial reasoning, but remain slow and unreliable for direct fine-grained control. To understand how MFMs can improve VLA spatial generalization, we conduct a systematic capability analysis across multiple VLA architectures using atomic-stage interventions, revealing that many failures stem from poor target grounding and global spatial routing, while local manipulation skills remain largely usable. Based on these findings, we propose MFM-VLA, a selective collaboration framework in which an MFM provides target grounding and spatial guidance, controllers execute free-space motion, and the VLA retains control over fine-grained manipulation. We fine-tune the VLA with action-chunk-level dense geometric captions and perturbed-state recovery data to improve local guidance following and recovery from unfamiliar handoff states. A development-calibrated capability router selects between direct VLA execution and MFM-assisted execution to avoid unnecessary intervention. Across LIBERO-PRO, ALOHA-Sim-PRO, RoboCasa365, and real-world chemistry tasks, MFM-VLA improves success rates by 14.9, 74.0, 3.6, and 30.9 percentage points, respectively, over the corresponding base VLA. The project page is available at https://tom-zgt.github.io/MFM-VLA

The project page is available at . Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models learn manipulation policies from demonstrations~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,octo , but struggle with changes in object positions and task goals due in part to limited demonstration coverage~ openx,droid . General multimodal foundation models (MFMs) offer complementary capabilities in scene understanding, spatial reasoning, and task planning~ saycan,palme,voxposer . Yet direct action generation with these models is slow and unreliable for fine-grained manipulation, while local trajectory corrections alone may not resolve errors in target selection and spatial routing~ hirobot,gpt_vla_assistance . This raises a central question: how can MFMs improve VLA spatial generalization? To answer this question, we conduct a capability analysis across multiple VLA architectures, combining counterfactual instruction tests with a five-level Phase-Decoupled Intervention Staircase (PDIS). Counterfactual tests provide evidence of visual scene shortcuts: policies often select the original training target despite updated instructions. By decomposing manipulation into atomic stages, PDIS further identifies target grounding and global spatial routing as major bottlenecks, while showing that local manipulation skills remain largely usable under appropriate spatial guidance. For example, guiding the end effector to the correct target increases the target-lifting rate of from 42.3 to 93.1 . These findings suggest that MFMs should provide target grounding and spatial guidance, while VLAs retain fine-grained manipulation control. Based on these findings, we propose MFM-VLA, a selective collaboration framework in which an MFM identifies task-relevant manipulation targets and provides spatial guidance, controllers execute free-space motion, and the VLA handles fine-grained manipulation. To help the VLA use external guidance, we fine-tune it with action-chunk-level dense geometric captions and perturbed-state recovery data, improving local guidance following and recovery from unfamiliar handoff states. We further introduce a development-calibrated capability router that selects between direct VLA execution and MFM-assisted execution, avoiding unnecessary intervention on tasks the VLA already handles well. We evaluate MFM-VLA on the LIBERO-PRO benchmark~ libero_pro , ALOHA-Sim-PRO~ aloha , RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 , and real-world multi-stage chemistry tasks~ tang2026labdex , achieving success-rate gains of 14.9, 74.0, 3.6, and 30.9 percentage points over the corresponding base VLAs, respectively. We also explore an extended system in which the MFM selects between the adapted VLA and task-specific code-based controllers for operations beyond the VLA's skills. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We systematically analyze multiple pretrained VLAs through counterfactual instruction tests and phase-decoupled interventions, revealing the visual scene shortcuts and identifying the roles of target grounding, spatial routing, and local manipulation in VLA failures. We propose MFM-VLA, a selective collaboration framework combining dense geometric policy adaptation, perturbed-state recovery, development-calibrated routing, and MFM-based spatial guidance. We evaluate MFM-VLA on three simulation benchmarks and real-world chemistry tasks, demonstrating its generalization and effectiveness across scenes and tasks. Related Work sec:related_work -Language-Action Models. VLA models have made significant progress in robotic manipulation. RT-2~ rt2 transfers vision-language knowledge to robot control, while OpenVLA~ openvla provides an open-source model trained on large-scale robot demonstrations. ~ pi0 uses flow matching for continuous action generation, and ~ pi05 extends this approach toward open-world generalization. OpenVLA-OFT~ openvlaoft and OpenWAM~ openwam explore efficient policy fine-tuning and unified world-action modeling, respectively. Despite these advances, generalization remains challenging when scenes, object positions, or task goals differ from training data~ libero_pro . We analyze the roles of target grounding, spatial routing, and local control in these failures to identify where external MFMs can effectively assist VLA policies. Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation. Language and multimodal foundation models have been used for robotic task planning, executable program generation, and spatial grounding~ saycan,voxposer,code_as_policies,roborefer . Other approaches integrate vision-language models (VLMs) into robot policies for spatial guidance and action correction~ omniguide,fpc_vla , while coding agents generate and refine manipulation skills through execution feedback~ graph_as_policy,cap_x,aspire,enpire,rats . PLD further improves pretrained VLAs through reinforcement learning and recovery data generation~ pld . Effective collaboration also requires identifying VLA capability gaps, adapting policies to external guidance, and avoiding unnecessary intervention. Concurrent work explores learned intervention for selective GPT assistance~ call_astra , visual-trace guidance for VLA policies~ gt_vla , and hybrid control with pretrained VLAs~ galbot_astra,ebench . Other studies investigate direct VLM action generation~ easg and hierarchical VLM--policy collaboration~ leap_vla . Unlike uniform guidance, MFM-VLA combines capability analysis, geometric policy adaptation, and calibrated routing for selective MFM assistance. Capability Analysis of Pretrained VLAs sec:analysis To understand the limitations of pretrained VLAs and identify where MFM assistance is needed, we investigate their generalization under perturbations, instruction following, and stage-wise manipulation capabilities. Performance Gap Under Perturbations sec:analysis_gap High success on familiar scenes does not necessarily indicate that a VLA can adapt to new spatial configurations or task goals. To examine this, we evaluate the official , trained on LIBERO, on LIBERO-PRO over episodes with four types of perturbations: Semantic (instruction paraphrases), Object (appearance changes), Position (object location swaps), and Task (changes to the instructed target). While Semantic and Object perturbations preserve the required spatial trajectories, Position and Task perturbations require changes in target selection or spatial movement. As shown in (a), maintains high success under Semantic ( ) and Object ( ) perturbations, but drops sharply under Position ( ) and Task ( ) perturbations, reaching only on LIBERO-10 Position. This gap suggests that pretrained VLAs handle surface-level variations better than changes requiring new target selection and spatial trajectories. We next investigate whether these failures arise from an over-reliance on familiar visual scenes rather than insufficient local manipulation skills. Visual Scene Shortcuts sec:analysis_shortcut The performance gap under Task perturbations raises a question: do VLAs fail to manipulate the newly instructed targets, or do they simply ignore updated instructions? To investigate this, we conduct counterfactual instruction tests by keeping the scene fixed while changing the instruction. Specifically, we compare an updated instruction , which specifies a new target instead of the original training target , with an empty instruction . We evaluate , , OpenVLA-OFT, and OpenWAM on LIBERO-Object Task perturbations, with episodes per condition. We measure the lifting rates of both targets and the Same-Lift Rate, which measures whether paired rollouts under the two instructions lift the same object first. As shown in (b), OpenVLA-OFT and OpenWAM lift the original training target in and of empty-instruction episodes, respectively. Updated instructions often fail to redirect this behavior: OpenVLA-OFT never lifts the newly instructed target, lifts the original target in of episodes, and achieves a Same-Lift Rate. Similar patterns are observed for on LIBERO-10 ( agreement) and on bimanual ALOHA-Sim ( agreement). These results suggest a visual scene shortcut: pretrained VLAs may use familiar visual configurations to retrieve manipulation behaviors, often overriding updated language goals. This indicates that improving local action execution alone may be insufficient; explicit target grounding and spatial guidance are also needed. Atomic Stage Analysis sec:analysis_pdis The preceding analysis reveals target-selection failures but does not determine whether VLA policies retain local manipulation skills once the correct target is identified. To investigate this, we decompose pick-and-place tasks into four atomic stages: Reach ( ), moving the open gripper above the target; Grasp, acquiring and lifting the object; Carry ( ), transporting it above the destination; and Lower/Place ( ), lowering and releasing the object. We introduce a five-level Phase-Decoupled Intervention Staircase (PDIS) to isolate the effects of assistance at different stages: Base uses the VLA throughout; +R assists Reach; +C assists Carry after a successful grasp; +RC assists both Reach and Carry; and +RCL additionally assists Lower/Place. We use ground-truth spatial guidance with fixed VLA weights to isolate stage-specific assistance benefits without introducing MFM grounding errors. title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
summary: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Robot manipulation policies have made substantial progress in static scenes diffusionpolicy,pi05 . In these scenes, the world stays still during inference, so the observed scene remains valid when the action executes. In dynamic manipulation, however, the target keeps moving during inference, so the observed pose is already outdated when the action executes. For example, a block sliding down a ramp at about 0.9\,m/s travels 18\,cm during a 200\,ms inference interval, far exceeding the positional tolerance of accurate contact. Successful manipulation therefore requires predicting the target's pose at execution time. Predicting the target’s motion requires accounting for surrounding objects, but the target continues to move while the prediction is being computed. The longer prediction takes, the further ahead the policy must predict. This creates a tension between Existing methods vary in what they predict (Fig.~ fig:paradigms ). Scene-level predictors model future images or video dbctfp,dreamzero,openwam_alpha,dynamicwam or 3D motion physmani . These predictions capture surrounding motion, but a dense forecast can spend computation on parts of the scene with little bearing on contact. In a video forecast, the target may occupy only a small region, and its pose remains implicit in the predicted pixels. AHEAD limits its rollout to task-relevant latent patches ahead . PUMA supervises future features of the target domino , and SPOT predicts target pose trajectories spot . Focusing on the target can omit surrounding objects that block access or alter its motion. For example, a moving obstacle can close the approach path even if the target follows the predicted trajectory. Determining whether that path stays clear and estimating the target's pose at contact impose different demands on a forecast. What should a policy predict about a moving scene, and how precisely, Our key insight is that prediction requirements differ by role (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The target's position and orientation at execution time directly determine contact success and therefore require precise prediction. In contrast, the surroundings affect the contact only indirectly, by obstructing access or altering the target's motion, so their motion requires only coarse prediction. Finally, the rest of the scene is static, so it is already available in the current frame and requires no prediction. A policy can therefore make accurate contact in time by concentrating precise prediction on the target and capturing the surroundings at low cost. This allocation resembles biological vision, where the fovea resolves fine detail and peripheral vision preserves Based on this insight, we propose , a native 4D world--action model that allocates precision by role (Fig.~ fig:paradigms c). observes and predicts scene motion directly in metric 3D space over time, rather than in pixels. In this space, each part of the scene can be represented separately, so each receives the precision that its role requires. The target is predicted precisely, as a metric SE(3) trajectory that gives its future position and orientation explicitly with only a few parameters. In contrast, the surroundings are predicted coarsely, as sparse 3D flow, and the static scene is not predicted. The same allocation applies to the input. A single frame already shows the static scene and the layout of the surroundings, so only the target's motion requires a history. therefore reads one RGB-D frame and a short SE(3) pose history of the target, instead of the image or optical-flow histories used by existing dynamic policies~ dynamicvla,domino,dynamicwam . Since both the input and the predictions are compact, acts in 15.1\,ms on one , about faster than video world--action models, and the scene has little time to move before the action executes. The tension between accurate prediction and timely action can be measured only when the evaluation accounts for inference time. However, the default evaluators of DOMINO domino and PhysMani-Bench physmani pause the simulation during inference, so a slow policy is scored as if it were instant. We therefore introduce , a benchmark of 14 dynamic manipulation tasks in which the world never pauses and every policy is evaluated at its native latency. On the same scenes, pausing the world overestimates slow policies and changes the ranking of methods (Fig.~ fig:latency c). Experiments show that makes accurate contact in time. On , it reaches 82.1 success at native latency, points above the strongest baseline. It also leads by 19.9 points on the single-arm tasks of DOMINO domino , whose evaluator pauses during inference, so its advantage does not come from speed alone. On six real-robot tasks, it achieves the highest success on every task and 48.3 on average, 17.5 points above the strongest baseline. Finally, ablations show that each part of the role-aware design contributes to success, with the largest drop from removing the target's pose history. Our key contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,topsep=2pt,itemsep=1pt] We identify distinct prediction requirements in dynamic manipulation and propose a role-aware prediction paradigm. It forecasts target motion precisely and surrounding motion coarsely, using the current frame for static geometry. This allocation preserves the precision needed for contact while reducing prediction cost. We present , a native 4D world--action model that instantiates this paradigm and achieves precise, low-latency action generation. It acts in 15.1\,ms, about faster than video world--action models, and outperforms the strongest baseline by points on . It also leads on DOMINO's single-arm tasks with paused physics and across six dynamic real-robot tasks. We build , a benchmark of 14 dynamic manipulation tasks in which the world never pauses and every policy is evaluated at its native latency, exposing the cost of latency that paused evaluation hides.

title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming for Robot Foundation Models
summary: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.

title: DAA for an Autonomous Delivery Drone: Maneuver Selection Policies for Near-Collision Risk Avoidance

summary:
Detect-and-avoid (DAA) systems for autonomous drones operating in shared airspace must select avoidance maneuvers under conditions that differ markedly from those assumed by conventional DAA architectures designed for crewed aircraft. Limited on-board sensing capabilities restrict detection of collision risk to near distances (sub-km), the time available for decision-making is severely limited, uncertainty in the predicted closest point of approach (CPA) and the time to reach it is substantial, and the maneuver envelope of a small uncrewed aircraft at low altitude is tightly constrained.
  This paper presents and compares two maneuver-selection strategies that address these challenges: (1) a purely geometric approach, steering in the direction away from the intruder at CPA, and (2) a method that also takes into account the known sources of uncertainty in the intruder's location, and steers away from a plane expected to contain the intruder's location distribution at CPA.
  Performance is evaluated using the risk ratio metric on a large dataset of simulated near-collision encounters with crewed intruders. Results indicate that both strategies are feasible (i.e., computable in closed form from an onboard track estimate), and that the second strategy substantially outperforms the first.

Introduction sec:introduction etect and Avoid (DAA) is a critical enabling capability for the integration of uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) into non-segregated airspace~ rtca_do365 . Generally speaking, UAS operators (especially commercial ones) should follow a multi-layered approach for air traffic deconfliction, including mission planning, advance re-routing, and coordination with other operators. However, safe autonomous operation in uncontrolled and traffic-dense environments often requires an additional independent avoidance layer. This ``last resort'' layer is the context for the present work. While existing DAA standards such as RTCA DO-365 address cooperative and non-cooperative surveillance for large remotely-piloted aircraft, the problem takes a fundamentally different character for slow autonomous drones operating at low altitude in close proximity to other traffic and terrain. At least four factors distinguish the autonomous drone's DAA problem from the conventional setting. First, the flight patterns of small aircraft at low altitude are less predictable (for example, patrol helicopters and hobbyists' paramotors turn more often than aircraft cruising at high altitude), implying greater uncertainty in predicting conflicts in the near future. Second, conflicting traffic, which may not be ADS-B equipped, can be reliably detected and tracked at sub-kilometer ranges only, implying decision times on the order of seconds rather than tens of seconds. Third, limits in detector performance and short tracking histories imply significant uncertainties in the estimated intruder state, which propagate into larger uncertainty in both the predicted CPA geometry and the time remaining before it is reached. Lastly, operational limits on the drone's speed, turn-rate, and free maneuver space may severely restrict the set of attainable avoidance maneuvers. Prior work on UAS DAA has largely focused on well-clear definitions and alerting logic~ cook2015detecting , with maneuver guidance often adapted from TCAS-style resolution advisories~ kochenderfer2012next . The maneuver-selection problem under the specific constraints of small autonomous platforms, particularly when the uncertainty envelope around the predicted CPA is comparable in magnitude to the available maneuver authority, has received attention only more recently (e.g., in ACAS sXu~ lusk2019acas_sxu ). This paper addresses the following question: given a detected collision risk with an uncertain intruder trajectory, how should an autonomous drone select an avoidance maneuver that best mitigates risk within its constrained maneuver space? We formulate and compare two such maneuver selection policies: Away from CPA (ACPA): a simple policy that uses the alert-time estimate of the intruder's location at CPA, and steers the ownship directly away from it within the available maneuver envelope. Away from Plane of Danger (APD): a policy that explicitly attempts to identify at alert time a plane in 3D space where collision risk is maximal, and steers the drone away from it. Performance is evaluated using risk ratio metrics applied to a large dataset of simulated near-collision encounters with crewed intruders. Results indicate that both strategies are feasible (i.e., computable in closed form from an onboard track estimate), and that the APD strategy substantially outperforms ACPA. Problem Formulation Maneuver Space The extent of a drone's collision-avoidance maneuver will generally be restricted by policy constraints, e.g., minimum allowable separation between planned drone routes and known ground obstacles, regulatory limit on ceiling, etc. Further constraints stem from the drone's own operational environment: maneuvering too far from a planned route at low altitude where many other drones are operating concurrently can create a secondary conflict risk. Such constraints can be thought of as defining a maneuver space surrounding the ownship's planned mission path. Without much loss of generality, we shall restrict to be a closed generalized cylinder (a tube) coaxial to the mission path, which the drone is required to never exit from. Practical and regulatory considerations will generally limit the cross-section diameter of the maneuver tube to a few tens of meters, enough to avoid a collision but not so large that it may intersect different hazards, e.g., ground obstacles or other drones' routes. The cross-section shape will generally be dictated by a combination of the same constraints and the maneuver authority of the UAS. Avoidance Maneuvers sec:maneuver_direction The set of feasible avoidance maneuvers is bounded by both and flight control constraints, e.g., maximum bank angle, climb/descent rate, speed envelope. Therefore, a feasible maneuver is a change of trajectory from the planned mission that keeps the ownship within , and predictably mitigates the risk of collision. It does so by increasing separation, that is, by altering the location and time of the predicted CPA toward safer values. Because the cross section of is limited to a few tens of meters, the time required for an avoidance maneuver to attain its maximal allowable deviation in space from the mission path will generally be on the order of several seconds. We shall restrict our analysis to one-shot avoidance maneuvers, i.e., those where the drone commits to a pre-programmed maneuver that returns to the original mission path after a few tens of seconds. Active modification of an already in-progress avoidance maneuver, in response to novel information about the threat, has limited benefits in our regime of short time available before CPA, and is out of the scope of this paper. We shall further restrict the maneuver set to purely transverse deviations from the mission path, i.e., maneuvers that keep unchanged the ownship's velocity along the planned mission path, and only add a purely transverse, time-varying offset. Such maneuvers consist of three phases: Initiate: the drone is steered toward the boundary of the maneuver space ; Stay: the drone remains on the boundary of while flying parallel to the planned mission path, for a predefined duration longer than the maximum time-to-CPA the DAA system is designed for; Return: the drone returns to the mission path. Throughout the maneuver the forward velocity is kept as close as possible to the mission plan. This restriction is desirable, as it keeps the forward progress of the ownship nearly unchanged, thus helping with traffic management on commercial UAV routes. However, it may be sub-optimal in cases where substantially slowing or accelerating the drone may prove beneficial in mitigating the collision risk. For simplicity, we shall also assume that the guidance and control laws used in the Initiate and Return phases are pre-programmed, and parametrized only on the transverse direction followed to reach the maneuver space boundary. All such maneuvers can then be uniquely identified by their transverse direction. Specifically, we will consider maneuvers parametrized by a unit maneuver direction vector . The vector is defined on the plane transverse to the ownship path (i.e., orthogonal to the ownship velocity) at alert time, see Figure~ fig:maneuver_section and Section~ sec:kinematics . The Problem: Maneuver Selection Within the above constraints, the problem thus reduces to selecting a maneuver direction that significantly reduces collision risk at alert time, when the avoidance maneuver is triggered. In particular, we should expect a well-performing maneuver selection policy to be relatively insensitive to the uncertainty in the future path of the intruder, given known properties of the threat detection system. Performance Metric and Evaluation Alternative maneuver selection policies may be systematically compared using the risk ratio on a pre-defined set of encounters. The risk ratio of a maneuver policy is simply: where is the count of encounters resulting in a collision or unsafe separation under policy , and is the null policy where no avoidance maneuver is taken. Unsafe separation is defined as an event where the distance between ownship and the intruder at CPA is below a pre-defined threshold. All else being equal, a policy with a lower risk ratio is preferred. For rather obvious safety and practicality reasons, the set of encounters used in the comparison is created by a realistic simulation of paired trajectories for the UAS and crewed aircraft traffic. Section~ sec:encounter_data presents the simulation harness used in this work. Encounter Kinematics and Notation sec:kinematics We now formalize the encounter geometry, and introduce the notation used throughout. Consider an autonomous UAS (henceforth ownship, drone) flying along a pre-planned mission path, while a crewed intruder aircraft flies on a converging path with risk of collision. This is schematically depicted in Figure~ fig:maneuver_tube , along with some of the entities defined below. We assume that the planned (a.k.a. mission) trajectory of the ownship is precisely known throughout, along with its velocity . At an alert time , when an avoidance decision is to be made, an airborne threat detection system produces an estimate of the intruder state, namely the intruder's location and velocity . These are input to an intruder motion model used to predict the future motion of the intruder. Following common practice, we shall use for this purpose a simple constant velocity assumption, which approximately models an unaware, non-cooperative intruder: Note that this is a time-varying prediction of the intruder's entire future trajectory, recomputed as new sensor data is input to the threat detection system, and is affected by uncertainty depending on the properties of the sensing and tracking technology in use. Ordinarily, it will be regarded as valid only for a certain duration , thus defining a prediction interval : To reduce verbosity, in the following we will systematically drop mentions of the alert time when it is obvious from context, for example writing for . Based on this intruder prediction model, we define the predicted line of sight (a shorthand for ): and the predicted closing distance from its norm: . The predicted time of CPA, , is the time when the predicted closing distance is minimized: The predicted CPA is then simply defined as the pair of ownship and intruder locations at the predicted time of CPA: and the predicted time-to-CPA as the amount of time left before the CPA is attained: The predicted miss vector is the displacement from ownship to intruder at the CPA: and its length is the predicted miss distance. title: Many Senses, One World: Learning Hierarchical Multimodal World Representations for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Bimanual dexterous manipulation relies on multimodal inputs that capture visual context and non-visual physical interaction cues for precise and coordinated control. To address the challenge of effectively integrating these modalities for policy learning, we propose HiMoDex, a two-stage framework centered on hierarchical multimodal world-state representations. In Stage 1, we pretrain a hierarchical representation network on the collected dataset of 1.19 million synchronized multimodal time steps. The network integrates visual context with tactile, force-torque, and audio cues into unified world-state embeddings. In Stage 2, we freeze the pretrained network and use its embeddings to condition a shared world-action transformer. The transformer jointly learns action generation and action-conditioned future-state prediction. Experiments across five real-world tasks show that HiMoDex achieves an average success rate of 78.7\%, representing an absolute improvement of 32.0\% over the strongest evaluated baseline. Extensive ablations validate the benefits of hierarchical representation learning and two-stage training. Failure analysis helps explain performance differences across variants. Code, data, and demos will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/research-website-BAB4/.
