Introduction sec:intro Bimanual dexterous manipulation is essential for robots to perform real-world tasks, enabling coordinated actions, tool use, and fine manipulation~ shaw2025bidex . Building on advances in vision-language models and world models, vision-language-action (VLA) models~ black2025pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05,kim2025openvla and world-action models (WAM)~ yuan2026fastwam,lin2026jepawam have made progress in robotic manipulation. Early methods primarily focused on parallel-jaw grippers, while recent methods have extended these models to bimanual systems with multi-fingered hands~ luo2026beingh05 . However, these methods face challenges in contact-rich tasks requiring precise control, due to limited physical interaction information from vision alone~ yu2025forcevla . Tactile, force-torque, and audio feedback provide complementary cues about physical interaction. Tactile sensing captures hand-object contact, while force sensing measures interaction forces and torques. Audio can reveal impacts, friction, and events such as switch activation~ liu2025maniwav . Previous methods have incorporated subsets of these modalities into vision-based policies to improve manipulation reliability~ li2023seehearfeel,lin2025hato,yu2025forcevla . However, jointly exploiting tactile, force-torque, and audio feedback for bimanual dexterous manipulation remains underexplored. A key challenge is to integrate heterogeneous interaction cues with visual context into a unified world-state representation for policy learning. To this end, we build a bimanual dexterous system with multi-view vision, fingertip tactile sensing, wrist force-torque sensing, and audio. We introduce HiMoDex, a two-stage multimodal world-action learning framework for bimanual Dexterous manipulation, with Hierarchical Multimodal world-state representation learning as its core, as shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction . In Stage 1, we learn world-state representations from aligned multimodal observation histories through hierarchical encoding and fusion. Multi-view visual histories are encoded into visual context embeddings, while tactile, force-torque, and audio histories are encoded and fused into physical interaction embeddings. A world-state encoder then integrates these intermediate embeddings into unified world-state embeddings. We train this representation network using three complementary objectives: cross-representation consistency, signal reconstruction and change prediction, and task-state contrastive learning. In Stage 2, we freeze this representation network and use its world-state embeddings for policy learning. The policy combines these embeddings with proprioceptive histories and uses task instructions to guide action generation. A shared world-action transformer jointly learns action generation and action-conditioned future world-state prediction. The future prediction objective provides auxiliary supervision for policy learning. At deployment, only the action generation pathway is retained, avoiding the overhead of future world-state prediction~ yuan2026fastwam,lin2026jepawam . We evaluate HiMoDex on five real-world tasks covering bimanual coordination, precise manipulation, coordinated tool use, and sustained contact. HiMoDex achieves an average success rate of 78.7 , an absolute improvement of 32.0 over the strongest evaluated baseline. We further conduct extensive ablations to assess the contributions of key components. Task-specific failure statistics further characterize the performance differences across variants. Our main contributions are as follows: [1.] We propose a hierarchical multimodal world-state representation learning method that integrates visual context with tactile, force-torque, and audio interaction cues into unified world-state embeddings. [2.] We introduce HiMoDex, a two-stage framework using frozen pretrained encoders to learn world-action policies for bimanual dexterous manipulation. [3.] HiMoDex outperforms the strongest baseline by 32.0 percentage points in average success rate. Ablations and failure analysis clarify component contributions and performance differences. Related Work sec:relatedwork Multimodal Representation Learning for Robotic Manipulation. Multimodal representation learning integrates heterogeneous observations to support robot decision-making and control. Some studies use language supervision to learn representations that support manipulation policies~ kang2025cliprt,feng2026anytouch2,ma2026fgcltp,yang2026sota . Specifically, FuSe~ jones2025fuse and OmniVTLA~ cheng2025omnivtla align visual and tactile observations with language descriptions to establish semantic correspondences across modalities. Beyond language supervision, paired multimodal observations provide self-supervised learning signals. Visuo-tactile pretraining learns cross-modal correspondences from spatially paired observations~ kerr2023ssvtp . Masked reconstruction~ krohn2026msdp and self-distillation~ higuera2025sparshx learn robust multimodal representations, while predicting contact events or future observations~ liu2025vitamin,heng2026vitacformer . HiMoDex introduces a hierarchical representation learning approach that integrates visual context and non-visual interaction cues into a unified world-state representation. This representation is shared by action learning and future-state prediction. Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation. Compared with bimanual systems using parallel-jaw grippers, those equipped with multifingered hands enable more versatile grasping. Their higher-dimensional action spaces make coordinated control more challenging~ shaw2025bidex . To address this challenge, existing methods learn visuomotor policies from expert demonstrations~ cheng2025opentelevision,wang2024dexcap,jiang2025dexmimicgen,luo2026beingh05 . However, visual observations provide limited information about physical interactions. Recent studies therefore incorporate tactile sensing to complement visual observations~ ding2025bunnyvisionpro,wang2026robotacdex,li2026deco,liu2026star . For example, HATO~ lin2025hato incorporates fingertip tactile feedback into diffusion policies to improve robustness in bimanual block stacking. VTAO-BiManip~ sun2025vtaobimanip uses visual-tactile-action pretraining for bimanual bottle-cap unscrewing. In addition to tactile feedback, MoDE-VLA~ tang2026modevla incorporates force observations into a VLA model for contact-rich bimanual dexterous manipulation. In this work, HiMoDex fuses visual, tactile, force, and audio feedback for coordinated control across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks. World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation. World-action models extend world models by coupling future-state prediction with action generation. Based on their prediction targets, existing methods can be broadly categorized into generative approaches and latent-space approaches. Generative approaches couple future observation prediction with action learning~ wu2024gr1,guo2024pad,yuan2026dextacwam . For example, DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero jointly generates future videos and actions using a pretrained video diffusion backbone. Latent-space approaches instead predict or align future representations to avoid costly reconstruction of action-irrelevant observation details~ luo2026beingh07,fang2026lewam,clemente2026lajepa . JEPA-WAM~ lin2026jepawam couples action learning with prediction of a joint representation of current and future observations. Beyond the prediction target, the deployment efficiency of WAMs also depends on whether future prediction is performed at inference. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam demonstrates that training-time future prediction improves policy performance under action-only inference~ lin2026jepawam,clemente2026lajepa . In this work, HiMoDex adopts a latent-space approach, jointly learning action generation and future world-state prediction through a shared world-action transformer. We learn a bimanual dexterous manipulation policy from expert demonstrations, conditioned on a natural-language task instruction , multimodal observation history , and proprioceptive history . Each action chunk contains consecutive actions. comprises multi-view vision, fingertip tactile, tool force-torque, and audio signals. All data are synchronized using timestamps. In Stage 1 (S1), we pretrain a hierarchical multimodal representation network to encode temporally aligned observation histories into unified world-state embeddings. We maintain an online network and a target network , whose parameters are updated via an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online parameters. The online network is optimized using three pretraining objectives: cross-representation consistency, signal reconstruction and prediction, and task-state contrastive learning. In Stage 2 (S2), we freeze the EMA target network from S1 and use it to encode observation histories from downstream tasks into world-state embeddings. title: RESET: One Demonstration, One Verified World, Self-Improved Skills Across Embodiments
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents can iteratively self-improve robot manipulation skills in simulation benchmarks, yet real-world tasks provide neither ground-truth success scorers nor resettable practice environments. Our key observation is that a single real demonstration simultaneously specifies scene geometry, defines the terminal success criterion, and serves as a physical reference trajectory for verifying world fidelity---all decoupled from the source robot's kinematics. We present {RESET}: we reconstruct a contact-rich world and derive a frozen read-only criterion from one demonstration ({R}ebuild); check that world against the demonstration by open-loop replay and silhouette consistency ({E}xamine); evolve modular white-box task graphs and skill code from per-node failure evidence ({S}elf-improve); deploy frozen code on real robots with zero runtime LLM calls ({E}xecute); and share the verified world and criterion with unseen robots without new demonstrations ({T}ransfer). On 8 manipulation tasks, each rebuilt from one real demonstration, RESET achieves 97% average success on unseen layouts in simulation, whereas zero-shot code reaches 27%, per-task fine-tuned pi0.5 policies 31%, and Diffusion Policy 50%; injecting reconstruction defects shows that practice tolerates many reconstruction errors, that geometric errors can still stall or mislead it, and that the check flags most of them while physical randomization covers the rest. Without any target demonstrations, 3 heterogeneous robots acquire the same task skills in the shared world: a robot with similar arms copies 95% of its skill functions unchanged from the source robot, while robots with different arms and hands write their own. In real-robot experiments, the resulting programs run on 4 robots and succeed in 80% of 280 trials.

Introduction sec:intro LLM-driven coding agents are emerging as a compelling paradigm for acquiring robot manipulation skills. Whereas hand-crafted or one-shot synthesized control programs~ liang2023code struggle to scale across contact-rich tasks and diverse robots, closed-loop recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets an agent inspect failure evidence, revise control code, and retain verified improvements, steadily advancing performance on simulation benchmarks such as RoboDojo~ zhang2026playful,wang2026reconstruct,li2026embodiedevo,tian2026physevo,hu2026embodied,chen2026robodojo . Yet this paradigm relies on a strong hidden premise: human engineers have already built the simulation scene, reset mechanism, and ground-truth success scorer. Physical tasks supply none of these. Recent attempts to run self-improvement directly on real robots~ xiao2026enpire rely on manual or heuristic self-checks and custom reset fixtures, requiring hours to tens of hours of physical trial-and-error per task without generalizing across embodiments. Scaling code self-improvement to the real world thus hinges on a foundational question: without a hand-engineered benchmark, where do a reliable success criterion and a trustworthy practice world come from? Reconstructing real scenes into simulation, practicing inside them, and transferring back to the real world (Real-to-Sim-to-Real) offers a natural route~ torne2024reconciling,han2026re,dan2025x , but existing pipelines . First, reconstructed worlds lack pre-training verification: prior methods proceed straight from scene reconstruction to policy learning, leaving world fidelity to be discovered only post hoc via real-world failure~ nishizawa2026yubi . Second, success criteria rely on manual reward design and invite reward hacking: under multi-round code search, agents readily exploit loose criteria with unintended behaviors~ torne2024reconciling . Third, demonstrations remain entangled with source kinematics: imitating recorded trajectories binds task knowledge to one robot morphology, invalidating the demonstration whenever degrees of freedom (DoF) or end-effectors change~ torne2024reconciling,dan2025x . Our core insight is that a single successful real-world demonstration simultaneously provides . The initial RGB-D frame captures scene geometry, while the terminal state specifies exact geometric completion relations. Crucially, because the demonstration is a known-successful physical trajectory, an accurate world should reproduce object grasps and motion under open-loop contact replay of the recorded joint commands and align rendered object silhouettes with observed masks. Moreover, by distilling the demonstration into an embodiment-agnostic specification (world + frozen criterion + local contact priors) rather than imitating its trajectory, an agent can . This both resolves the scalability bottleneck of manual code-skill authoring and exploits the white-box nature of code skills---explicit geometric guards, stage-level verification, and deterministic execution---for long-horizon stability. Guided by this insight, we propose RESET (Rebuild, Examine, Self-improve, Execute, Transfer; ). Rebuild reconstructs an interactive MuJoCo scene from one RGB-D demonstration and extracts a read-only terminal scorer. Self-improve evolves an object-centric task graph and white-box skill library from per-node failure evidence under diagnostic/hold-out gating. Execute runs frozen code online with zero LLM calls, low cost, and node-level debuggability. Transfer hands the verified world and criterion unchanged to target robots that adapt only a thin hardware layer. We evaluate RESET across 4 diverse embodiments and 8 real manipulation tasks. From one demonstration on the source robot, RESET achieves 97 success on unseen layouts in simulation, where zero-shot code and per-task fine-tuned policies stay near 30 . Without any target demonstration, Dual-arm Franka, ARX LIFT2, and Unitree G1 acquire their own skills in the shared world. The final programs succeed in 80 of 280 real-robot trials on 4 physical platforms. Our main contributions are threefold: Evidence on eight real tasks and four embodiments. RESET reaches 97 success on unseen layouts in simulation where zero-shot code reaches 27 ; three target robots learn the tasks with no new demonstration and frozen skills run on 4 physical platforms (80 success over 280 real-robot trials). Code as Policies~ liang2023code and Voyager~ wang2023voyager pioneered synthesizing control programs and skill libraries with LLMs. Recent closed-loop RSI frameworks---including RATs~ zhang2026playful , RPG~ wang2026reconstruct , EmbodiedEvo~ li2026embodiedevo , PhysEvo~ tian2026physevo , Embodied Turing Machines~ hu2026embodied , PyRUA-Lean~ si2026fewer , ---iteratively refine task graphs and skill code from execution feedback on benchmarks such as RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo . However, all assume human-engineered simulation scenes, resets, and ground-truth scorers. RESET removes this benchmark dependency by running self-improvement inside a world reconstructed from and verified against a single real demonstration, while . Self-improvement on physical robots. To bypass simulation benchmarks, ENPIRE~ xiao2026enpire explores and revises policies directly on real robots. While demonstrating real-world RSI feasibility, physical exploration demands hours of robot wear, custom reset mechanisms, and robot-specific verification logic. RESET confines trial-and-error to a verified simulation world, reserving the real robot for executing the final code and reusing the world across embodiments. Real-to-Sim-to-Real and scene verification. RialTo~ torne2024reconciling , Re3Sim~ han2026re , and RoboSplat~ yang2025novel reconstruct scenes to train neural policies or synthesize data; X-Sim~ dan2025x derives cross-embodiment dense rewards from simulated object motion; EmbodiRSI~ lang2026embodirsi and D-World~ wen2026d update digital twins from single images or online rollouts. Yet prior pipelines treat reconstruction as an open-loop preprocessing step ~ nishizawa2026yubi . RESET uses the demonstration itself as a dynamic and visual verification standard, characterizes how reconstruction errors affect code policies, and outputs inspectable white-box programs. Learning from a single demonstration. Demo2Code~ wang2023demo2code summarizes demonstrations into code specifications, RoboSplat~ yang2025novel augments single demonstrations via novel-view synthesis, and Human2Sim2Robot~ lum2025crossing bridges human-robot morphology gaps via RL from one video. Unlike methods that imitate demonstrated trajectories, RESET uses the demonstration solely to build and verify the environment and terminal criterion; runtime controllers never replay the demonstration, unlocking zero-demonstration transfer. Method sec:method Motivation sec:motivation Three questions shape the design of RESET. Each starts from an observation about what happens without the corresponding component ( ). Why does code need practice, and where can it practice? Code written once is not enough. Given the same interfaces and contact hints that RESET uses, an agent's first program succeeds on 27 of unseen simulated layouts on average, varies widely between samples (70 , 0 , and 36 on one task), and never succeeds on the four hardest tasks ( ). Such a program improves only by being run, failing, and being revised, which takes an environment that resets at will and a score that needs no human. A real task offers neither, and practicing on a real robot costs hours of supervised trials per task~ xiao2026enpire . One successful demonstration, however, already contains both: its first frame shows the scene and its final state defines success, which motivates Rebuild. Why check the rebuilt world against the demonstration? No reconstruction is perfect, and a success rate measured in a wrong world says little about the real one. When object scale is off by 10 or the table is too low, a skill that is perfect in the correct world falls to 0 on several tasks ( ); and under a loosely worded criterion, a program that knocks the carton flat is scored 100 . The demonstration gives a check for both. It is a physical execution known to succeed, so a usable world must reproduce it; and its final state, not a text description, defines success. What one demonstration cannot determine, mass and friction, we do not claim to verify and instead randomize during practice. This motivates Examine. Why code, and why share the task rather than the motion? The demonstrated motion itself transfers poorly: replayed open-loop it succeeds on 8 of new layouts, and a vision-language-action policy fine-tuned on 100 trajectories per task reaches 31 . A program differs in three ways. It exposes which step failed, which gives an agent something specific to revise ( ). It runs on the real robot with no model in the loop. And it keeps what the task requires, the world and the criterion, apart from how one robot meets that requirement, so a robot with different arms or hands can practice in the same world ( ). This motivates Self-improve, Execute, and Transfer. title: RePT: 3D Geometry Emerges from 2D Relational Pretraining
summary: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.

Introduction Spatial intelligence requires representations that make the structure of the physical world accessible for reasoning and interaction. Existing approaches often obtain explicit geometry by predicting quantities such as depth, camera pose, point maps, or reconstructed scenes for downstream applications~ ranftl2022midas,smith2025flowmap,wang2024dust3r,wang2025vggt,zhang2026d4rt . At the same time, latent representations learned from purely visual objectives, including reconstruction, correspondence, and cross-view prediction, can also encode substantial geometric information~ weinzaepfel2022croco,weinzaepfel2023crocov2,sajjadi2023rust,mitchel2026xfactor . Together, these results suggest that geometric structure can arise under a range of different training objectives. In these formulations, geometry is typically anchored to a single observation, as in depth or surface orientation, or to the transformation between views, as in camera motion and cross-view correspondence~ ranftl2022midas,smith2025flowmap,jabri2020space,sarlin2020superglue . However, how geometric information is organized in these representations remains less understood. Recent work has probed learned visual features with readouts of varying capacity, showing that coarse geometric quantities, such as relative depth and viewpoint, can often be recovered with linear or lightweight probes~ ma2024imagenet3d,simeoni2025dinov3 , whereas richer metric structure, such as dense 3D geometry, is typically recovered with stronger nonlinear task-specific decoders~ elbanani2024probing,chen2025feat2gs , and camera-motion structure becomes accessible through a learned adapter~ chen2026seese3 . This suggests an important distinction between a representation that contains recoverable geometric information and one whose latent space is itself geometrically organized. We ask whether metric 3D relations can emerge in a geometrically organized latent space and admit a linear readout without explicit 3D prediction targets. To study this question, we use point-to-point relations as a minimal relational primitive. Unlike depth or camera motion, a relation between two physical points is defined directly between scene points rather than with respect to a particular viewpoint. Its physical meaning is tied to their underlying 3D displacement, and it can be supervised entirely through their 2D observations across views. This makes point relations a natural testbed for this question. We instantiate this idea with 2D Relational Pretraining (RePT), which explicitly represents the directed relation between two distinct physical points while training it only through 2D image-space prediction. Given a set of context images of the same physical scene and observations of two physical points and in different views, RePT constructs a scene representation and a compact 16-dimensional directed relation token representing their relationship. Given an observation of in one context image, the model uses this relation to recover the 2D location of in another view where it is visible, with all predictions conditioned on . The relational objective predicts only 2D coordinates, without depth, camera-pose, or 3D-coordinate targets. As a result, the learned relation space develops a coherent metric 3D organization. Consider three physical points , , and . The angle between and closely tracks the angle between their corresponding physical 3D displacements, and the norm correlates with the physical distance as well. Moreover, a simple linear readout maps relation tokens to metric 3D displacements, yielding coherent relative point clouds. A shared readout preserves this structure in both readout-fitting scenes and scenes excluded from fitting, and the ARKitScenes-trained model retains it on another dataset. Controlled experiments further clarify what gives rise to this geometric organization. A matched same-point correspondence baseline also develops 3D structure, but RePT remains stronger and degrades less under shared and held-out readouts, suggesting that distinct-point relational prediction promotes stronger displacement-aligned organization than same-point correspondence. Notably, replacing the additive relation parameterization with an MLP improves point-transfer accuracy but substantially weakens geometric organization, showing that better task performance does not necessarily yield a more geometrically organized representation. This organization also depends strongly on adapting the shared context representation during relational training. Auxiliary reconstruction is not necessary for geometric emergence, but improves optimization and point-transfer performance. These results reveal a complementary route to geometric representation learning. RePT shows that purely 2D relational supervision can induce a representation whose latent organization aligns with physical 3D space through a simple linear readout. This is attractive for scaling spatial representation learning because image-space relational supervision does not require metric 3D annotations: training on RGB-only CoTracker3 tracks yields comparable geometry. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce 2D relational pretraining to learn directed relations between distinct scene points through cross-view 2D prediction, without predicting 3D geometry. We show that the learned relation space develops a scene-centric 3D organization: its native structure reflects physical displacement, and a simple linear readout recovers coherent metric 3D geometry. We show that this organization is shared across scenes and transfers to unseen environments, and that distinct-point relational prediction strengthens cross-scene consistency over matched same-point correspondence learning. Related Work We review explicit geometric prediction, spatial representations learned from 2D prediction, and geometric structure in learned visual representations. Geometry from Explicit 3D Prediction Recent geometric vision models learn spatial representations by directly predicting explicit 3D quantities. DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r formulates multi-view reconstruction through dense pointmap prediction, while MASt3R~ leroy2024grounding extends this formulation with feature matching for improved correspondence and reconstruction. VGGT~ wang2025vggt further unifies several geometric outputs, jointly predicting camera parameters, depth, point maps, and tracks from multiple images. More recently, D4RT~ zhang2026d4rt extends this paradigm to dynamic scenes through a unified query-based formulation for recovering 3D point trajectories across space and time. Together, these approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit geometric prediction for learning spatial representations. RePT instead asks what geometric structure can arise when depth, pose, point maps, trajectories, and other 3D quantities are never used as prediction targets. Spatial Representations from 2D Prediction A complementary line of work learns spatial structure from relationships between 2D observations. Early context-prediction methods learn visual representations by predicting the relative positions of patches within an image~ doersch2015context . FlowMap~ smith2025flowmap recovers depth and camera parameters through optimization against 2D correspondences. CroCo~ weinzaepfel2022croco and subsequent cross-view masked modeling approaches~ weinzaepfel2023crocov2 reconstruct missing image content with information from another view, encouraging representations to capture geometric dependencies across viewpoints. Correspondence and consistency objectives~ wang2019learning, jabri2020space encourage observations of the same physical point to remain identifiable across viewpoints, thereby learning geometric consistency through point identity. RePT instead learns relations between distinct physical points that transfer across views. Novel-view prediction has also been used to learn scene representations, as in GQN~ eslami2018gqn , and view-synthesis mappings with minimal 3D inductive bias, as in LVSM~ jin2025lvsm . Prior work has learned latent scene, pose, or transformation representations through novel-view synthesis and related predictive objectives~ sajjadi2023rust,jiang2025rayzer,wang2026less,mitchel2026xfactor , with some showing that these latent variables align with physically meaningful camera geometry and transfer across scenes~ mitchel2026xfactor . RePT instead studies whether 2D prediction induces point-to-point relations whose 3D organization is shared across scenes and accessible through a linear readout. Geometry in Learned Representations A growing body of work investigates how geometric structure is encoded in learned visual representations. Linear or lightweight probes have shown that pretrained image and video features expose information about 3D viewpoint, depth, surface geometry, and related attributes~ ma2024imagenet3d,elbanani2024probing,huang2026much,zhou2026understanding . Other studies identify geometric regularities directly in feature space, including emergent cross-view correspondence in representations trained for non-geometric objectives~ tang2023emergent and extreme-view geometry that 3D foundation models acquire without being trained on such views~ zhang2026extremeview . Together, these results suggest that geometric information can arise without being the explicit prediction target. More complex readouts reveal richer geometric structure. Feat2GS~ chen2025feat2gs decodes frozen visual features into 3D Gaussian scenes, while related work studies the recovery of dense scene geometry from pretrained representations~ huang2026much . SeeSE3~ chen2026seese3 examines relative camera-motion geometry and asks how structure becomes accessible under different feature-space readouts. RePT is complementary to these studies. Rather than asking whether geometric quantities can be recovered by a task-specific deep decoder, we ask whether relational representations themselves become organized in the latent space, and whether the information can be decoded with simple readouts. 2D Relational Pretraining We introduce 2D relational pretraining, in which a model learns to transfer relations between distinct scene points through cros

title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
summary: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.
full_text: 2532900@tongji.edu.cn World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts. Introduction sec:intro Robot demonstrations specify what action to take, while the accompanying observations reveal how the scene changes as that action unfolds. World-action modeling uses both signals, combining action learning with prediction of future observations. Latent prediction makes this combination particularly attractive: a visual encoder supplies dense supervision from videos, and a policy can learn to anticipate transitions without reconstructing every pixel vlajepa,jepawam . Making future supervision useful for control involves two design dimensions: the representation of future observations and the formulation of their prediction. Future frames mix persistent content, manipulation-induced changes, and appearance variations, whose relative emphasis depends on the prediction space. Image self-supervision, video reconstruction, and predictive video learning impart different biases toward spatial correspondence, appearance detail, and temporal structure. We investigate how these representational biases affect the information a policy learns from future supervision and its ability to act beyond the training distribution. Our controlled study reveals that prediction spaces with similar standard-task performance differ in their robustness to visual changes. Spatial semantic supervision provides the strongest overall generalization, while reconstruction supervision retains advantages in some categories. Displacement readout provides complementary evidence: motion information remains more accessible under perturbations in policies trained with spatial semantic targets. The second dimension concerns how prediction targets are organized over time. Supervising only the future state leaves the change from the source implicit, while a fixed prediction interval restricts supervision to a single temporal scale. We introduce Residual World Prediction (RWP) and Temporal-Scale Prediction (TSP) to make both relationships explicit. RWP predicts changes relative to a source state and jointly supervises these changes and the future states they reconstruct. TSP conditions world queries on temporal distance, providing supervision over several horizons within the same clip. We instantiate this design in , where world prediction and action learning jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone. Pretraining combines robot demonstrations, which provide both objectives, with human videos that supply additional predictive supervision. Downstream posttraining continues joint prediction and action learning on the target manipulation data. At deployment, only the policy backbone and action expert are required. We evaluate PreWAM on standard manipulation tasks and a range of distribution shifts. It achieves 98.1 success on LIBERO, 79.1 on LIBERO-Plus, and 58.7 on LIBERO-Pro. LIBERO-Pro2.0 further tests robustness to static and runtime disturbances. SimplerEnv and RoboTwin 2.0 further extend the evaluation to real-to-sim transfer and multitask bimanual manipulation. Three tasks on a physical Piper platform further evaluate single-arm and bimanual manipulation. Our contributions are: Controlled comparisons reveal that prediction spaces supporting similar in-distribution performance can yield substantially different policy generalization, with spatial semantic supervision providing stronger overall robustness to visual perturbations. We introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes across temporal horizons, allowing predictive learning to shape the shared representations used for action generation. Experiments demonstrate strong generalization across the LIBERO benchmark family and effective manipulation in SimplerEnv and RoboTwin 2.0, complemented by real-world evaluation of single-arm and bimanual tasks on a Piper platform. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-language-action models transfer the perceptual and linguistic knowledge of pretrained multimodal backbones to robot control. Action-token prediction provides a direct extension of vision-language modeling to robot demonstrations openvla , while dedicated continuous-action experts generate action sequences from multimodal representations pi05,gr00t . These methods learn to map observations and language instructions to actions from robot demonstrations, making the quality of multimodal representations an important foundation for policy learning. Representations for Prediction and Control. Visual pretraining objectives emphasize different aspects of an observation. Reconstruction preserves appearance information, image self-supervision learns dense semantic features, and predictive video learning captures temporal regularities in representation space wan,dinov3,vjepa2 . When these representations become prediction targets, their properties also influence the information emphasized during policy training. Feature-space world models use pretrained visual representations for future-state prediction and action-conditioned planning without reconstructing pixels dinoworld . World Modeling for Policy Learning. World-action models couple visual prediction with robot control, but differ in how predictive information reaches the policy. Video-based architectures can connect world and action experts through shared latent interfaces, allowing joint supervision to shape the visual features used for action generation bridgewam . Prediction can also operate directly in a pretrained feature space without reconstructing future images. Such methods predict future features or jointly model current and future representations to provide auxiliary supervision for action learning vlajepa,jepawam , and can also learn from videos without action annotations vlajepa . PreWAM explicitly models changes relative to source states and organizes predictive supervision across multiple temporal horizons. World Representations for Policy Generalization sec:representations World representations define the visual content that future prediction brings into policy learning. How does the content emphasized by these representations affect a policy when observations depart from familiar scenes? We approach this question through policy evaluation under perturbations and motion readout from the learned predictive representations. We compare spatial semantic features from DINOv3 dinov3 , reconstruction latents from the Wan 2.1 video VAE wan , and predictive video features from V-JEPA 2 vjepa2 . The comparison uses direct future-state prediction within a common Qwen-based policy framework and training data, with each frozen encoder supplying its own visual prediction targets. Downstream training uses the same optimization settings across prediction spaces, with a global batch size of 256 and 36,000 updates. Generalization across Prediction Spaces Similar task success in familiar scenes masks differences in the effects of predictive supervision. The three policies fall within a 0.20-point range on LIBERO, yet separate more clearly under the seven perturbation categories of LIBERO-Plus (Figure~ fig:representations ). Spatial semantic supervision provides the strongest aggregate performance, while the relative strengths of the other spaces depend on the perturbation. The category results help characterize these distinctions. Spatial semantic supervision has its clearest advantages over reconstruction supervision under camera, background, and lighting changes. Such changes can substantially alter an image while preserving the intended interaction, making correspondence across appearances useful for control. This pattern is consistent with the benefit of targets that preserve spatial scene content without emphasizing every appearance detail. Reconstruction supervision remains competitive: it leads on the Robot and Language categories and closely matches spatial semantic supervision under noise. Its Robot performance suggests that retaining fine visual configurations can also be useful when the robot's appearance changes. Overall, DINOv3 provides the most effective predictive supervision for generalization in this comparison. Motion Information in Policy Representations Displacement readout from world queries. We first examine whether the world queries supplied to the world predictor contain motion information. We mean-pool their final-layer VLM features and fit a linear ridge probe to three-dimensional end-effector displacement. The probe is fitted on clean observations and held fixed across perturbations. We evaluate on held-out episodes using five-fold cross-validation grouped by episode. Across the three prediction spaces, mean readout errors range from 16.80 to 18.45 mm, well below the 55.10 mm baseline that always predicts the training-fold mean displacement, indicating that world queries encode recoverable motion information. Readout errors are close on clean observations but diverge under camera shifts and noise. Spatial semantic and reconstruction supervision both outperform predictive video supervision in these conditions, with spatial semantic supervision yielding the lowest error, also under background changes. These results show that world queries learned with spatial semantic supervision retain more readily accessible motion information under these visual perturbations. Action-query attention. Figure~ fig:representations visualizes attention from the action queries that condition the action expert in a task that places cheese on a plate. With spatial semantic supervision, these queries focus on manipulation-relevant regions in both external and wrist views. Reconstruction and predictive video supervision show less consistent focus across views, with more diffuse responses or attention away from the manipulation region in one view. This example illustrates the task-relevant visual focus of action queries learned with spatial semantic supervision. The study above shows that the prediction space affects policy generalization, the accessibility of motion information in world queries, and the visual attention of action queries. We next investigate how to organize prediction targets within this space, explicitly modeling source-relative changes and temporal distance through Residual World Prediction and Temporal-Scale Prediction. PreWAM sec:method Overview Shared policy architecture. PreWAM couples action generation and visual transition prediction through a shared vision-language backbone (Figure~ fig:framework ). Given current multi-view observations , a language instruction , and available proprioception , it predicts an action chunk . Learned world queries and embodied action queries are processed together

title: RoboHarness-RL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for VLM-Based Robot Manipulation
summary: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/RoboHarness-RL/

Introduction sec:intro Agentic harnesses let vision-language models (VLMs) manipulate robots through tool calls for perception, planning, and control~ li2026robo,ora2026code,chen2026show . Robot systems have traditionally separated a slow model that reasons about the task (System~2) from a fast learned policy that produces motor actions (System~1). In a harness, this boundary blurs: the VLM not only decides what to do next, but also specifies end-effector poses and gripper commands, so its decisions directly shape how the robot moves. Yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. On randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, the ORA harness reaches 69.2 success with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash but only 6.8 with the open-weight Qwen3.5-9B (Sec.~ sec:comparison ). Approaches to improving compact VLM agents include refining the harness~ wang2026harnesspai,gong2026tinyastral or distilling frontier models through supervised learning~ li2026robo,chen2026show . Building on these advances, we investigate whether reinforcement learning from the model's own interactions can further improve manipulation performance beyond supervised imitation. Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ chen2025conrft,wagenmaker2025steering,li2025gr and world action models (WAMs)~ qian2026wam,ye2026halo beyond imitation. In parallel, agentic RL trains language models through multi-turn tool use in digital environments such as web search~ jin2025search and graphical interfaces~ wang2025ui . Harness-based manipulation lies between the two (Fig.~ fig:positioning ): the VLM uses high-level tool calls as in agentic RL, while controlling physical robot actions. Concurrent approaches include RL with a learned VLA executor~ liu2026agenticroborl and single-turn RL for control-program generation~ fu2026cap . We instead train the VLM to specify robot actions itself through multi-turn tool calls. Two challenges make RL costly in this setting. First, every model call carries a growing interaction history, including camera images, across episodes of up to 200 calls, increasing the cost of both rollout collection and policy updates. Second, tasks that the current policy consistently solves or fails may provide little group-relative learning signal, yet still consume rollout budget. We address both with RoboHarness-RL, an agentic RL framework that trains VLMs to manipulate through tool calls, with no VLA or WAM generating actions. After fine-tuning on teacher demonstrations, the VLM learns through multi-turn GRPO with task-outcome rewards. Interaction runs through LiteHarness, whose hierarchical memory keeps recent interactions in detail, summarizes older actions, and records failures separately. Compared with compressed full history, it roughly halves the prompt tokens per call while achieving higher success. Adaptive scheduling postpones solved tasks, removes persistently failed ones, and allocates more rollouts to tasks with a learning signal. With Qwen3.5-9B~ qwen2026qwen35 , RL raises success from 31.2 after SFT to 44.0 on RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin and from 57.8 to 73.3 on LIBERO-Pro. Although trained only in clean scenes, the policy also improves from 26.4 to 38.0 in randomized RoboTwin scenes. RL also succeeds on tasks that SFT fails to solve in evaluation. Behavioral analysis shows how RL changes the way the model uses the harness: on RoboTwin, repetitive-call rates drop from about 10 to under 3 , jointly successful episodes require about a third fewer model calls, and the policy more often recovers to complete the task after execution failures (Fig.~ fig:teaser c). Our main contributions are as follows: We propose RoboHarness-RL, an agentic RL framework that trains VLMs to manipulate robots through multi-turn tool calls without relying on VLAs or WAMs. We design LiteHarness and adaptive task scheduling for efficient multi-turn RL. Hierarchical memory roughly halves prompt tokens per call and improves success. We show that RL improves over supervised imitation by 12.8 and 15.5 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO-Pro, respectively. These gains extend to randomized scenes unseen during training. RL also reduces repetitive tool calls, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery after negative feedback. Related Work sec:related Agentic harnesses for robot manipulation sec:rw-harness Early language-guided systems compose predefined skills~ ahn2022can,huang2022inner,singh2022progprompt , generate policy code~ liang2023code , or guide motion planning with spatial representations~ huang2023voxposer ; hierarchical VLM planning also supports long-horizon mobile manipulation~ wang2026odyssey . Recent harnesses enable closed-loop control through code and tools. Code-based systems compose perception and control primitives and revise programs from execution feedback~ fu2026cap,naouali2026vlcp,jia2026agent,gao2026hexashelluniversalharnessrobot . Tool-based systems expose perception, planning, and control functions for direct invocation~ li2026robo,ora2026code,chen2026show,zhang2026world,yuan2026democratizing,zhang2026unexpected . Other harnesses connect VLM motion commands to deterministic control with asynchronous monitoring~ li2026motormind . Across episodes, agents refine code through repeated trials~ xiao2026enpire,wen2026roborsi , evolve harnesses around frozen models~ wang2026harnesspai,gong2026tinyastral , or retain experience as persistent memory~ wang2026regenharness,liu2026phyagentos , transferable spatial lessons~ zhang2026spatialmemory , and reusable skills~ huang2026scaling . RoboHarness-RL instead improves model decisions through multi-turn RL. Agentic reinforcement learning for language models sec:rw-agentic-rl Agentic RL trains language models through multi-turn interaction, including search~ jin2025search,zheng2025deepresearcher , tool-assisted reasoning~ feng2026retool,li2025torl , and graphical or web interfaces~ wang2025ui,wei2025webagent . Broader studies examine training stability, exploration, and rollout design~ wang2025ragen,xi2025agentgym , while fine-grained credit assignment combines trajectory-level advantages with step-level estimates~ feng2026group . Training frameworks decouple agent execution from policy optimization through standardized interfaces or rollout services~ luo2025agent,zhang2026prorl . They record model interactions for training while leaving tool use, context management, and execution to the harness~ xu2026polar,he2026agent . We adopt this approach for robot manipulation. Training embodied agents sec:rw-training Robot policies use sparse plans with action experts~ liu2025gae , sparse trajectory interfaces~ huang2026notvla , or joint-aligned actions and adversarial learning for cross-embodiment demonstration transfer~ zhao2026advdex . Yet demonstration learning can leave modality shortcuts~ liu2026perturbot and insufficient recovery-state coverage~ liu2026perfect . RL improves VLAs and diffusion policies beyond imitation~ chen2025conrft,wagenmaker2025steering,li2025gr,lu2025vla,li2026simplevla,wang2026learning,intelligence2025pi , and extends to world action models~ qian2026wam,ye2026halo . SFT and multi-turn RL are also studied for embodied agents acting on visual feedback~ li2026look . For robot harnesses, teacher distillation transfers frontier-model capabilities to compact agents~ li2026robo,chen2026show,gong2026tinyastral . CaP-RL studies single-turn RL for control programs, while Guava explores RL refinement on two selected manipulation tasks~ fu2026cap,liu2026guava . AgenticRoboRL~ liu2026agenticroborl invokes VLAs through RPent and generates code with privileged state through CaP-X; PyRUA-Lean Coder~ si2026fewer generates Python programs over primitives including frozen VLAs. CaPtain combines SFT and multi-turn RL for code-as-policy agents with a privileged-state critic~ fan2026captain , while ZAP uses manually designed progress rewards~ pikus2026pretrainingknowssimulationteaches . We use direct tool calls, task-success rewards, and general tool-use penalties, without VLAs, privileged-state critics, or task-specific reward shaping. We train and evaluate on RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO-Pro with hierarchical memory and adaptive task scheduling. Method sec:method Overview sec:method-overview RoboHarness-RL trains a VLM policy through multi-turn interaction with a robot environment. Interaction is supported by LiteHarness, a lightweight harness built on the tools of ORA~ ora2026code and designed for efficient agentic RL. For a manipulation task with instruction , a VLM policy , parameterized by , interacts with the environment through LiteHarness. At model call , the policy generates a response , where denotes the interaction context provided by LiteHarness for that call. Tool calls within these responses provide access to perception, planning, and control, with execution feedback guiding subsequent decisions. The resulting interaction is represented by a trajectory , where is the number of model calls until the episode ends. Training proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on teacher demonstrations establishes basic manipulation procedures, followed by multi-turn agentic RL to improve decision-making through interaction. title: KeyMemVLA: Subtask-Guided Key Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
summary: Memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation requires vision-language-action (VLA) policies to infer task progress and recall evidence absent from current observations. Under a limited memory budget, the challenge is to retain history that resolves stage ambiguity and supports subsequent decisions. We present KeyMemVLA, a subtask-guided key memory framework based on progress indication and decision-evidence retention. A two-level annotation process selects subtasks satisfying either criterion and labels their final frames as keyframes to supervise online memory writes. A shared vision-language backbone jointly learns subtask, action, and keyframe prediction. At inference, the policy first predicts the current subtask from the instruction, visual context, and memory, then uses this semantic condition to predict actions and future memory-write positions. Actual observations are retained at the selected times during execution. We introduce KMBench to evaluate active memory retention for decisions across subtasks. Evaluations on RMBench-$M(n)$, RoboTwin-MeM, KMBench, and real-world manipulation tasks show higher average success rates than the compared baselines. Ablation studies and representation analysis support the roles of key memory and explicit task-progress semantics. These results highlight the value of coupling sparse key memory with online progress inference for history-dependent control.
full_text: Method sec:method Overview sec:method_overview We define key memory as task-relevant information selectively retained from execution history. Selection follows two criteria. Progress indication retains cues that distinguish task stages with similar current observations. Decision-evidence retention preserves information needed for current or later decisions, even when the stage is known. Let denote the complete observation--action history and the task instruction. Following EventVLA's visual anchoring strategy~ yang2026eventvla , we group the initial observation, sampled recent observations, and the current observation into visual anchors , where . The initial frame provides a stable reference and recent frames capture local temporal context, paralleling the functions of Mem-0's anchor and sliding memories~ chen2026rmbench . In our implementation, current observations include all camera views, whereas historical anchors and keyframes use only the main view. We aim to approximate the full-history optimal policy with a policy conditioned on these anchors and key memory: where and denote the key-memory cost and budget. The framework combines current-subtask prediction, subtask-conditioned action generation, and online memory updates to support decisions across task stages. Subtask-Guided Key Memory Construction sec:key_memory_construction We construct key memory at two levels: key-subtask selection and keyframe extraction. A subtask is selected if it satisfies at least one of the key memory selection criteria in Sec.~ sec:method_overview : it provides an important cue to overall task progress, or it exposes evidence needed for current or later decisions. In Find Heaviest, weighing a box marks measurement progress and yields evidence for the final comparison. Returning it can be omitted from key-subtask selection because it adds neither necessary progress information nor comparison evidence. For each key subtask, only its last frame is labeled as a keyframe. Where needed, subtask boundaries are refined so that the final frame captures observable outcomes or transient evidence. This frame marks a stage boundary and often preserves object attributes, spatial relations, or measurements needed later. We use a semi-automatic annotation process. An annotator first defines subtask segmentation and key subtask selection rules from representative demonstrations and encodes these rules in task-specific scripts. These scripts are then applied to annotate the remaining demonstrations, with the last frame of each key subtask labeled as a keyframe. Dataset-specific adaptations are detailed in Appendix~ sec:annotation_pipeline . We consider three key memory modes. First, SPH generates the current subtask from autoregressively. The predicted text is then fed back as the subtask response to obtain , from which the action head and KPH predict and , respectively. title: ActiveBridge: Scaling Active Prior for Robots through Egocentric Perception-Interaction Modeling
summary: Robotics foundation models are now widely used for manipulation, and egocentric videos offer rich data for scaling. However, existing methods overlook the human active priors captured in egocentric videos, which limits performance in unstructured scenes. They act on given observations instead of actively seeking information as humans do. We propose ActiveBridge, a training framework that learns these human active priors and transfers them to robots through world-action modeling. We design a robot that actively controls its viewpoint through head actions to acquire the visual information needed for manipulation using a single head camera, without wrist cameras. During human training, an instruction-conditioned model jointly predicts future egocentric videos and synchronized head-wrist action trajectories, with head actions providing explicit supervision for active perception. Experiments show that ActiveBridge outperforms baselines on active manipulation tasks, while ablations demonstrate the benefit of joint head-wrist action supervision.
full_text: ActiveBridge learns human active priors from egocentric videos and transfers them to robots. Top: Head-wrist action trajectories from egocentric videos form a 21D human action representation. Jointly predicting future video and human actions helps the model learn active perception and physical interaction. Bottom: Human training and robot deployment examples span real-world (a) pick-and-place and (b) assembly tasks, and simulation (c) placement and (d) storage tasks. fig:transfer Robotics foundation models are now widely used for manipulation, and egocentric videos offer rich data for scaling. They act on given observations instead of actively seeking information as humans do. We propose ActiveBridge, a training framework that learns these human active priors and transfers them to robots through world-action modeling. We design a robot that actively controls its viewpoint through head actions to acquire the visual information needed for manipulation using a single head camera, without wrist cameras. During human training, an instruction-conditioned model jointly predicts future egocentric videos and synchronized head-wrist action trajectories, with head actions providing explicit supervision for active perception. Experiments show that ActiveBridge outperforms baselines on active manipulation tasks, while ablations demonstrate the benefit of joint head-wrist action supervision. Introduction sec:intro Robotics foundation models have expanded from multitask vision policies such as RT-1~ brohan2022rt to vision-language-action (VLA) models that adapt pretrained vision-language models for robot control~ brohan2023rt . Recent world-action models (WAMs) couple future prediction with action generation, drawing on pretrained video models to learn visual dynamics~ lu2026world,li2026causal,ye2026world . Under partial observability, manipulation also requires active perception: acquiring missing information through actions such as changing the viewpoint to locate an occluded object ( ). Data collection has also expanded beyond robot-specific demonstrations, with Open X-Embodiment pooling robot experience across embodiments~ o2024open . The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables robot-free collection with handheld grippers and a policy interface designed for transfer across robot platforms~ chi2024universal . Human egocentric video further extends the available experience to everyday interactions across diverse objects and environments~ grauman2022ego4d,punamiya2026egoverse,lu2026world . Recent methods incorporate human action supervision into WAMs~ li2026egowam,sun2026ego4wam and train policies that coordinate viewpoint changes with manipulation~ li2026act . Egocentric video captures how people actively gather visual information, use it to guide physical interaction, and respond to the resulting visual changes. This raises our first question: how can egocentric video unlock active perception and interaction capabilities in existing world-action models? More specifically, the wrist-only action supervision used in previous work leaves active perception implicit~ li2026egowam,sun2026ego4wam . Transferring human active priors to robots also calls for closer alignment between human perception and robot sensing. Humans rely on head-centered vision for active perception, whereas many manipulation systems combine wrist cameras with a head or external camera~ black2024pi_0,xiong2025vision . Wrist-camera views are constrained by arm motion, and the additional hardware increases costs and collision risks. This raises our second question: how can active perception be explicitly supervised, and how can robot sensing be better aligned with human perception? We introduce ActiveBridge, a training framework that uses egocentric videos to train existing WAMs for coordinated active perception and physical interaction. Conditioned on instructions and observations, the model jointly predicts future egocentric videos and synchronized human action trajectories. By jointly modeling active perception and physical interaction, the model learns human priors that can be adapted to each robot embodiment. To provide explicit supervision for active perception, we include head actions as prediction targets alongside wrist trajectories and future video. The synchronized targets link head movements to the accompanying physical interactions and visual observations. To better align robot sensing with human perception, we design a platform with a single movable head camera and no wrist cameras. On this platform, the policy coordinates active perception and physical interaction by jointly controlling the head and arms. This design supports active manipulation while reducing sensor costs and collision risks associated with wrist-mounted hardware. Our experiments validate the advantages of ActiveBridge. On the TAVIS-Head benchmark, which focuses on active manipulation, ActiveBridge outperforms baselines and the wrist-only variant across all six evaluation conditions. The in-distribution success rate reaches 77.1 on Reachy-2 and 63.8 on GR1T2. Under spatial distribution shifts, gains over direct adaptation reach 5.7 and 3.4 on Reachy-2 and GR1T2, respectively. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate the effectiveness of ActiveBridge across diverse manipulation tasks and the feasibility of our robot platform with a single movable head camera and no wrist cameras. The ablation study supports the benefit of the joint human video-action objective and explicit head-action supervision. Our contributions are as follows: Human Active Prior Scaling from Egocentric Videos. We explore how embodied models can learn from egocentric videos to actively acquire task-relevant perception and use it to guide physical interaction in unstructured environments, including those with occlusions. A Novel ActiveBridge Framework and Active Robot Platform. We propose ActiveBridge, which explicitly supervises active perception by predicting head actions. To align robot sensing with human perception, we design a platform with a single head camera. State-of-the-Art Performance and Active Manipulation Improvement. Experiments in simulation and the real world show that ActiveBridge outperforms baselines on active manipulation tasks. Ablations further demonstrate the performance improvements from ActiveBridge. Related Work sec:related World-action models. World-action models link control to future visual prediction. Early approaches use generated videos or visual subgoals to guide separate controllers~ du2023learning,black2024zero , or learn action-conditioned simulators~ yang2023learning . Subsequent methods integrate future prediction with action learning~ wu2024unleashing,tian2025predictive , jointly predict videos and actions using pretrained generators~ shen2026videovla,ye2026world , and develop causal video-action modeling for closed-loop control~ li2026causal . Further work examines value-guided planning~ kim2026cosmos as well as architectures, information flow, and training mixtures~ wang2026openwam . Egocentric WAMs study prediction targets, data alignment, action supervision, and human--robot integration~ li2026egowam,sun2026ego4wam,wu2026atomego . AnyWorld factorizes action, camera, and embodiment controls to generate robot-domain experience~ chen2026anyworld . ActiveBridge extends wrist-supervised human WAM training with explicit head-action targets to jointly learn active perception, physical interaction, and their future visual consequences. Egocentric training. Egocentric videos support representation and reward learning~ nair2022r3m,ma2022vip , affordance extraction~ bahl2023affordances , and latent planning for control~ wang2023mimicplay . EgoVerse expands this resource with diverse demonstrations and shared transfer protocols~ punamiya2026egoverse . EgoMimic and HAT learn from human motion through joint human--robot training and shared state-action representations~ kareer2025egomimic,qiu2025humanoid , while EgoVLA predicts wrist and hand actions before retargeting and robot fine-tuning~ yang2025egovla . Observation behavior also supplies supervision. CoMe-VLA incorporates visual and proprioceptive memory with subtask-transition supervision, while ActiveScale combines history, camera-pose targets, and mixed human--robot training~ li2026act,zhou2026activescale . ActiveBridge learns human active priors from egocentric demonstrations by jointly predicting future video and synchronized head-wrist trajectories. Head motion provides explicit supervision for viewpoint acquisition. Active perception. Active perception acquires information through sensing actions~ bajcsy1988active , while interactive perception also uses physical interaction~ bohg2017interactive . Learning to Look Around learns view-selection policies from uncertainty-reduction rewards~ jayaraman2018learning . For manipulation, AV-ALOHA uses an independently controlled camera arm, SaPaVe adopts separate camera and manipulation action representations~ chuang2025active,liu2026sapave , and ActiveVLA selects informative views and refines task-relevant 3D regions~ liu2026activevla . ActiveWAM focuses on retaining and acquiring evidence during robot control~ wu2026activewam . TAVIS evaluates information acquisition and viewpoint control under distribution shifts~ spigler2026tavis . ActiveBridge learns observation–interaction priors from human egocentric demonstrations. To align robot sensing with these human priors, our robot platform uses a single movable head camera that provides shared visual feedback for joint head-and-arm control, without wrist cameras. We adapt these priors to coordinated head and arm control on our robot platform, which uses a single movable head camera and no wrist cameras. Overview. title: Ego2Real: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations
summary: Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition. Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator's force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions. Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer. We present Ego2Real, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands. Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages: (1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry; and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards. By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation. Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability.
