From egocentric demonstrations recorded with an RGB-D camera and tactile gloves, Ego2Real reconstructs bimanual hand--object interactions with tactile-guided refinement, yielding both a motion reference and a finger-wise contact reference. These references supervise contact-informed residual RL for robotic hands in simulation, and the resulting policies are deployed on real bimanual robots. fig:teaser ] Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition. Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator's force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions. Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer. We present Ego2Real, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands. Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages: (1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry; and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards. By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation. Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability. Introduction sec:intro Dexterous manipulation requires precise finger coordination and controlled hand--object interactions. Learning from human demonstrations offers a natural way for robots to acquire such skills. Egocentric recordings are particularly appealing~ egomatrix,unidex,egoscale because they allow everyday manipulation to be captured with lightweight setups and allow demonstrators to perform tasks naturally with their hands. Such activities usually involve two hands working cooperatively, making bimanual coordination an essential capability to learn from these demonstrations. Contact plays a central role in this coordination: when two hands interact through a shared object, successful manipulation depends not only on how the hands move, but also on where, when, and how strongly each hand makes and breaks contact. Yet egocentric visual demonstrations lack direct measurements of these physical interactions. Prior skill transfer methods often infer contact states and locations from reference hand--object geometry~ maniptrans,chord,dexmachina . However, obtaining sufficiently accurate references typically requires high-precision motion capture that restricts collection to instrumented settings, and kinematic geometry alone still cannot reveal actual interaction forces. Reconstructing hand--object motion directly from videos~ doasido,galatea,chord removes the need for motion capture, but occlusion and depth ambiguity frequently lead to contact gaps, interpenetration, and unreliable contact estimates. While tactile gloves~ osmo have recently enabled direct measurement of human touch for robot learning, most existing approaches~ tactidex,touchbridge,touch2robot still pair gloves with external motion-capture tracking, leaving their role in egocentric bimanual transfer from noisy visual observations underexplored. This raises our central question: how can we combine visual information with directly measured human tactile signals to improve dexterous human-to-robot skill transfer when learning from egocentric data? To address this question, we introduce Ego2Real (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), a tactile-guided framework that learns bimanual dexterous manipulation from egocentric demonstrations recorded with tactile gloves and an RGB-D camera. Given a raw demonstration, Ego2Real extracts a reference encoding a contact-plausible kinematic motion prior, contact states, and force intent, which is used to train residual reinforcement learning policies in simulation for real-world deployment. Within this pipeline, measured human touch plays a central role at two complementary stages. First, tactile-guided hand--object interaction (HOI) reconstruction maps spatially distributed glove readings onto the hand surface to resolve visual ambiguities, constraining contact geometry and preserving sustained contacts over time. The refined human trajectories are then retargeted to the robot by preserving hand--object topological interaction relationships, providing a physically plausible motion reference. Second, contact-informed reinforcement learning translates the recorded glove signals into region-wise contact-state, force, and contact-timing rewards that complement motion tracking. Rather than enforcing rigid trajectory imitation, these rewards guide a residual policy to adapt the retargeted motion to the robot's own morphology and actuation constraints while emulating the demonstrated interaction patterns. At deployment, the learned policies enable closed-loop execution using tracked object poses and robot proprioception, without requiring robot-side tactile sensing. Experiments and ablations across simulation and real-world bimanual tasks demonstrate that tactile-guided reconstruction effectively improves downstream skill transfer, while contact-informed policy learning provides additional gains in contact-demanding interactions. In summary, our contributions are threefold: Bimanual Skill Transfer from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations. We present Ego2Real, a framework that learns dexterous manipulation from synchronized RGB-D and tactile-glove recordings, and show through systematic ablations that incorporating human tactile signals into both reconstruction and policy learning yields complementary gains on real robots. Tactile-Guided HOI Reconstruction. We leverage spatially distributed tactile measurements to constrain hand--object contact geometry and preserve sustained contacts over time, reducing contact ambiguities in visual reconstruction and providing physically plausible references for downstream robot learning. Contact-Informed Reinforcement Learning. We translate human tactile signals into region-wise contact rewards to supervise residual policy learning beyond motion tracking, enabling more human-like contact behaviors and more reliable real-world execution in bimanual tasks. Related Work Human Demonstrations for Dexterous Manipulation Learning dexterous manipulation requires demonstrations that are both scalable to collect and faithful to the underlying physical interaction. Existing demonstration sources trade off these two properties in different ways. Real-robot teleoperation~ dexpilot,shaw2024bimanual yields directly executable demonstrations but requires robot hardware and substantial operator effort, especially for contact-rich behaviors where operators lack high-fidelity tactile feedback. Simulation-based generation~ dexmimicgen expands a few source demonstrations but relies on accurate physical models. Wearable interfaces such as DexUMI~ dexumi and RealDexUMI~ realdexumi narrow the human--robot embodiment gap but tie demonstrations to specialized hardware configurations. Motion-capture datasets~ grab,arctic,oakink2 provide accurate hand--object trajectories and serve as common references for physics-based transfer methods~ maniptrans,dexmachina , yet their capture systems confine collection to instrumented laboratory environments. Human videos remove the need for specialized hardware by reconstructing trajectories from everyday, egocentric, or generated videos for simulation-based policy learning~ human2sim2robot,doasido,egomatrix,galatea , or by retargeting large-scale egocentric data for policy pretraining~ egoscale,unidex . However, vision-only demonstrations do not directly capture physical contact. Tactile sensing offers direct evidence of where and when contact occurs. OSMO~ osmo introduces an open-source tactile glove compatible with vision-based hand tracking, and transfers human contact signals to a robot equipped with the same glove. TactiDex~ tactidex and DexTaG~ dextag pair tactile gloves with instrumented kinematic capture, using an optical motion-capture system and an electromagnetic motion-capture glove, respectively, to obtain accurate hand--object trajectories, which confines collection to instrumented settings. In contrast, Ego2Real collects synchronized egocentric RGB-D observations and spatially distributed tactile measurements without external motion capture and recovers hand--object motion from vision. Hand--Object Interaction Reconstruction sec:rw_hoi Recent methods, including EasyHOI~ liu2025easyhoi , MagicHOI~ wang2025magichoi , and AGILE~ shi2026agile , combine visual observations with foundation-model priors and contact constraints inferred from visual and geometric cues for hand--object reconstruction. Other approaches explicitly predict contact representations for reconstruction refinement: CPF~ yang2021cpf uses predicted contact relationships within a contact potential field, while TactoHand~ xi2026tactohand uses video-predicted contact and proximity fields. Reconstruction is also a core component of video-based robot learning pipelines: Do as I Do~ doasido , EgoMatrix~ egomatrix , and GALATEA~ galatea reconstruct hand--object interactions from everyday, egocentric, and generated videos, respectively, to obtain references for robot execution. Across these approaches, contact is inferred from visual or geometric evidence and can remain ambiguous under hand--object occlusion, motivating the use of direct contact measurements. ContactOpt~ grady2021contactopt refines hand poses toward predicted contact maps and further shows that thermally measured contact on static grasps can guide the same refinement, while VTacOH~ xu2023vtaco combines visual point clouds with tactile observations for joint hand--object reconstruction. ViTaM-D~ yu2025vitamd uses distributed tactile measurements for hand--object reconstruction with a supervised network and object-category-specific fine-tuning. Ego2Real uses human tactile signals to guide both bimanual reconstruction and robot policy learning, without task-specific reconstruction training. Human-to-Robot Dexterous Hand Transfer Transferring human manipulation skills to dexterous robotic hands is challenging due to differences in hand morphology, kinematics, and contact dynamics. Existing approaches primarily rely on kinematic retargeting, physics-based optimization, and reinforcement learning. Kinematic methods~ dexpilot,toporetarget align human and robot hand configurations through fingertip correspondence or geometric interaction constraints, while physics-based methods such as SPIDER~ spider incorporate physical feasibility through sampling-based optimization. Reinforcement-learning-based approaches~ maniptrans,regrind,dexmachina,adadex further adapt human demonstrations to robot-specific dynamics, enabling physically executable manipulation behaviors. Contact information is increasingly used to guide cross-embodiment transfer. CHORD~ chord guides RL with object-centric contact wrench spaces, while DemoMimic~ demomimic rewards precise contact around the local geometry of demonstrated contact points. These contact targets are derived from the reference hand--object geometry and therefore heavily rely on its accuracy. Human tactile demonstrations provide contact targets independent of this geometry. title: Wind-Aware Trajectory Planning for Deformable Aerial Formations
summary: Coordinated aerial transport in dense urban environments requires drone formations to navigate confined spaces and adapt to spatially varying winds around buildings. Formation deformation enables passage through narrow spaces but changes individual drone velocities and the local winds they encounter, coupling formation motion with aerodynamic effects. We propose Family-Air, a wind-aware trajectory-family planner that constructs a virtual tube as shared collision-free flight space and jointly optimizes formation-center motion, deformation, and timing. A shared affine transformation represents a continuous trajectory family, incorporating spatially varying wind and deformation-induced velocities into a unified air-relative motion objective. The optimization enforces virtual-tube containment, inter-drone separation, and kinematic feasibility. Simulations across four urban wind-field scenarios demonstrate the importance of local wind-deformation coupling. Flight simulations further show improvements in trajectory tracking accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of wind-aware trajectory-family planning for coordinated aerial transport in complex urban environments.
full_text: Coordinated aerial transport in dense urban environments requires drone formations to navigate confined spaces and adapt to spatially varying winds around buildings. Formation deformation enables passage through narrow spaces but changes individual drone velocities and the local winds they encounter, coupling formation motion with aerodynamic effects. We propose Family-Air, a wind-aware trajectory-family planner that constructs a virtual tube as shared collision-free flight space and jointly optimizes formation-center motion, deformation, and timing. A shared affine transformation represents a continuous trajectory family, incorporating spatially varying wind and deformation-induced velocities into a unified air-relative motion objective. The optimization enforces virtual-tube containment, inter-drone separation, and kinematic feasibility. Simulations across four urban wind-field scenarios demonstrate the importance of local wind–deformation coupling. Flight simulations further show improvements in trajectory tracking accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of wind-aware trajectory-family planning for coordinated aerial transport in complex urban environments. Constrained motion planning, optimization and optimal control, swarm robotics, virtual tubes, wind-aware planning. Introduction sec:intro Urban aerial transport is attracting growing attention, with the safety of low-altitude operations becoming a key challenge for wider deployment~ huang2025small,pang2022risk . Coordinated aerial delivery can involve multiple drones flying in formation along shared routes~ alkouz2020formation . Such missions require obstacle avoidance, coordinated motion, and safe separation among drones~ quan2023formation . However, a path that is collision-free for a single drone may not accommodate an entire formation. Navigating narrow gaps or turns between buildings may require the formation to contract or rotate. Meanwhile, urban buildings create spatially varying wind fields, exposing drones within the same formation to different local wind conditions. These winds alter the air-relative velocities of individual drones, affecting aerodynamic loading and potentially influencing propulsion power~ zeng2019energy,bauersfeld2022range . Such wind conditions can also complicate trajectory tracking and coordinated flight~ folk2025planning . Consequently, urban formation trajectory planning must address both the geometric constraints of confined flight space and the effects of spatially varying winds. To address the geometric constraints of flight in cluttered environments, safe-corridor methods incorporate obstacle avoidance into continuous trajectory optimization and provide an effective approach to motion planning~ liu2017corridor . For multi-drone systems, virtual-tube methods further provide shared flight space for coordinated formation motion and support the construction of trajectory families~ mao2024tube . These methods establish a geometric basis for coordinated passage, but identifying feasible flight space does not determine how the formation should move within it. In particular, under spatially varying winds, the formation must still adapt its trajectory, shape, and flight speed to local conditions. Existing studies have addressed coordinated formation motion and deformation in cluttered environments~ quan2023formation,sha2024affine , but do not explicitly account for spatially varying winds during trajectory optimization. Wind-aware planning studies have incorporated spatial wind information into path selection~ pensado2024turbulence,veiga2025hybrid , local motion planning~ folk2025planning , and trajectory and speed optimization~ qin2026geowind2plan . However, these wind-aware methods primarily focus on individual drones, with limited consideration of deformable formations. In spatially varying wind, formation deformation affects each drone's air-relative velocity by changing both its ground-relative velocity and the position at which it samples the wind field, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:method . Evaluating wind only at the formation center neglects spatial wind variations across the formation and may therefore misestimate the air-relative motion cost. We propose Family-Air (FA), a wind-aware trajectory-family planner to address this problem. The planner first automatically constructs a virtual tube from the start, goal, and surrounding obstacles, then jointly optimizes formation-center motion, deformation, and flight time within the tube. A time-varying formation center and a shared affine deformation map represent a continuous family of trajectories. The air-relative motion cost is evaluated over the entire family, accounting for deformation-induced drone velocities and position-dependent local wind. The optimization balances air-relative motion cost, trajectory smoothness, flight time, and deformation regularization, subject to virtual-tube containment, inter-drone separation, ground-relative kinematic bounds, and sampled air-relative speed limits. The main contributions of this work are as follows: 2pt 0pt Wind--deformation coupling formulation. We formulate an air-relative motion cost over a continuous trajectory family that jointly accounts for deformation-induced changes in drone velocities and position-dependent local wind. Tube-constrained joint trajectory optimization. We jointly optimize formation-center motion, deformation, and timing within an automatically constructed virtual tube, enforcing continuous geometric and kinematic constraints and sampled air-relative speed limits. Urban wind-field simulation and validation. We evaluate the method through benchmark and ablation studies in three urban wind-field scenes and a Chicago-derived heightfield scene, examining the performance of wind-aware planning. Related Work sec:related Safe Corridors and Virtual Tubes Safe-corridor methods constrain trajectories to convex collision-free regions, simplifying obstacle avoidance in trajectory optimization. For example, Liu et al. combine safe-flight corridors with piecewise-polynomial optimization to generate dynamically feasible trajectories in 3D environments~ liu2017corridor . Ren et al. use overlapping spherical corridors with receding updates for high-speed flight in unknown environments~ ren2022bubble . Park et al. extend linear safe corridors to distributed multi-drone trajectory optimization with inter-drone collision avoidance and dynamic feasibility~ park2022lsc . By contrast, virtual-tube methods offer another planning and control framework for organizing group motion within shared flight space. Mao and Quan develop regular virtual tubes by constraining tube surfaces, cross sections, and geometric continuity~ mao2022regular . Quan et al. study distributed control for robots passing through straight and curved tubes, addressing tube containment and collision avoidance~ quan2023curve,quan2022vtol . For trajectory planning, Mao et al. show that a continuous trajectory family can be constructed from convex combinations of finitely many optimal trajectories under specified conditions~ mao2024tube . Tube RRT* considers passage volume and path length in homotopic path search to select group routes with greater spatial clearance~ mao2025tuberrt . In this work, we further combine virtual-tube containment with wind-aware optimization of a shared affine trajectory family. Formation and Deformation Planning Low-dimensional representations describe coordinated formation motion through shared variables. Zhao develops an affine formation maneuver control framework that enables formation translation, rotation, scaling, and deformation~ zhao2018affine . In cluttered environments, Alonso-Mora et al. optimize formation parameters under collision constraints~ alonsomora2017formation , and Quan et al. combine formation similarity, adaptive reorganization, obstacle avoidance, and dynamic feasibility in distributed trajectory optimization~ quan2023formation . Sha et al. further perform global trajectory search and optimization directly in the space of affine formation parameters~ sha2024affine . Our method represents formation motion and deformation through shared affine variables, allowing the trajectories of all drones to be optimized within a compact parameterization. Wind-Aware Path and Trajectory Planning Wind-field estimation provides spatial wind information for low-altitude planning. Folk et al. estimate local urban airflow using building geometry and sparse observations~ folk2024learning . At the path-planning level, several studies account for turbulence and wind risk in route selection~ pensado2024turbulence,veiga2025hybrid . Gu et al. combine computational fluid dynamics (CFD) wind fields with wind-aware path search and flight-speed adjustment for urban logistics drones~ gu2026windfield . Beyond route selection, wind information has also been incorporated into formation configuration selection and continuous trajectory optimization. Alkouz and Bouguettaya investigate fixed and adaptive formation configurations under varying wind conditions along delivery routes~ alkouz2020formation . For single-drone trajectory planning, Habib et al. integrate rapid CFD wind-field generation with wind-aware path search and B\'ezier trajectory optimization~ habib2026wespr . Recently, GeoWind2Plan jointly optimizes spatial trajectories and speed profiles using predicted 3D wind and a rotor-power model~ qin2026geowind2plan . Existing studies have considered wind in formation configuration selection and continuous single-drone trajectory optimization. Extending wind-aware planning to continuously deformable formations introduces coupling among drone trajectories through shared deformation variables. These variables affect both individual drone velocities and the positions where local wind is sampled, jointly influencing air-relative motion cost. Our method incorporates this coupling into a cost evaluated over the entire continuous trajectory family and jointly optimizes formation-center motion, shared affine deformation, and flight time within a virtual tube. title: Roboclock: A Unified Benchmark for Time-Aware Robotic Intelligence
summary: Time is a fundamental dimension of robotic intelligence: a robot may fail despite physically correct actions if it acts outside a valid time window, responds too slowly to an event, or fails to meet required throughput. Yet existing robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize spatial correctness and logical task completion, largely overlooking the temporal constraints of real-world applications. We present RoboClock, a unified benchmark for time-aware robotic manipulation featuring 60 tasks across five application domains. Mirroring these failure modes, RoboClock structures tasks around three types of temporal constraints: Temporal Window, Event-Reactive, and Throughput. Furthermore, RoboClock incorporates a Latency-Aligned evaluation protocol that continuously advances environment time during model inference and control-interface delays, paired with time-sensitive metrics. Evaluating over 30 methods, we find that the best-performing approach is the trained VLA, yet it achieves only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy-level tasks, with persistent challenges in generalization and transfer. These findings reveal fundamental limitations in current robotic systems and highlight the need to jointly optimize physical competence, temporal reasoning, and execution latency.
full_text: Experimental Setup sec:experiments Additional experimental details, a temporal-difficulty study (App.~ app:emh ), and a real-robot pilot (App.~ app:real-robot ) are provided in the appendix. sec:baselines The main evaluation protocol uses the easy level of all 60 tasks, with 10 seeds per task for every model. We evaluate two groups of methods and report them separately (Tabs.~ tab:main-results -- tab:agent-results ): end-to-end policies (VLAs and WAMs) and foundation-model agents (VLMs and agent frameworks). End-to-end policies. An end-to-end policy maps the current observation and instruction to actions in a single model call. We cover two classes, VLAs and WAMs, taken from the RoboDojo leaderboard~ chen2026robodojo , since shares its embodiment: WALL-OSS-1.0-lite~ zhai2025walloss , Galaxea G0.5~ liu2026g05 , ~ black2025pi05 , and X-VLA~ zheng2026xvla as VLAs, and VPP2~ guo2026vpp2 , Awomo-0.5~ awomo2026awomo05 , InternW0- ~ miao2026internw0delta , and OpenWAM- ~ wang2026openwam as WAMs. Fine-tuning. sec:finetune We fine-tune two VLAs ( and X-VLA) and two WAMs (OpenWAM- and InternW0- ) from their released RoboDojo checkpoints on oracle demonstrations from 45 tasks, holding out 15 tasks for generalization evaluation. Every model is trained for three epochs on the same demonstration set. Tab.~ tab:main-results compares released and fine-tuned checkpoints on all 60 tasks, and Tab.~ tab:seen-unseen separates seen and held-out tasks; settings are in App.~ app:finetune . VLM agents. We compare agent configurations using Qwen3.8-27B~ qwen2026qwen38 with a shared budget of 100 model calls per episode (Tab.~ tab:interface-results ). These include six open frameworks---PyRUA-Lean~ si2026pyrualean , RPent~ zhang2026harnessvla , HexaShell~ gao2026hexashell , PhysicalRSI~ mmlab2026physicalrsi , uni-robot-agent~ yuan2026unirobotagent , and SenseNova-RoboRSI~ sensenova2026roborsi ---as well as Agent-as-Policy~ roboprobe2026 , RoboDojo EEF control~ chen2026robodojo , and Tool-augmented EEF. We use the best-performing Tool-augmented EEF for all VLM backbones. Its tools operate on visual observations and measured robot state, without access to privileged simulator ground truth (App.~ app:tool-eef ). VLM backbones. VLMs are queried in closed loop without robot-specific training, using Tool-augmented EEF. We evaluate four proprietary models, Gemini~4 Argon~ google2026gemini4argon , Claude Opus~5.5~ anthropic2026opus55 , GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026gpt6astra , and GPT-6.1 Sol~ openai2026gpt61sol , and seven open-weight models: Qwen3.5-4B/9B~ qwen2026qwen35 , Gemma~4 26B-A4B~ google2026gemma4 , Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next~ qwen2026qwen38 , Muse Glimmer 30B~ meta2026museglimmer , and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash~ deepseek2026v41 . As a text-only reference we also run the official GLM-5.3~ zai2026glm53 , a language model without image input: it receives the same requests, but the camera images are dropped, so it acts only from the instruction, the measured robot state, and tool feedback. All run with provider-recommended settings and low thinking mode. For LTSR, open-weight models run on eight A100 GPUs with their fastest speculative-decoding configuration; proprietary models are charged their API latency. Results and Ablation Study sec:results Main Results All policies and agents share the same low-level 16-D joint-position action interface (Tabs.~ tab:main-results -- tab:agent-results ). VLAs and WAMs: training improves success, but generalization remains limited. The eight released checkpoints achieve at most 2.3 overall PSR and 0.5 TSR, indicating little zero-shot transfer to (Tab.~ tab:main-results ). Three epochs of task-specific training improve all four models: OpenWAM- reaches the highest PSR, 14.8 at 10.0 TSR, and the highest TSR, 10.3 at 12.8 PSR, followed by InternW0- (12.3 , 8.0 ) and X-VLA (10.2 , 6.7 ). Most gains come from Event-Reactive tasks, where three of the four exceed 17 TSR, while Throughput TSR stays at or below 1.8 . The gains remain on seen tasks: seen-task TSR rises to 8.2--13.8 , but on the 15 held-out tasks only X-VLA reaches nonzero TSR (2.0 ; Tab.~ tab:seen-unseen ). Demonstrations thus improve execution but barely transfer to unseen tasks. Inference speed decides how much of these gains survives Latency-Aligned evaluation. The VLAs keep most of their TSR: retains 8.3 LTSR against 10.3 TSR, and X-VLA 4.8 against 6.7 . The slower WAMs lose most of it: OpenWAM- falls from 10.0 to 3.8 and InternW0- from 8.0 to 2.2 , so also has the highest LTSR. VLM agents: zero-shot transfer is constrained by inference latency. Without robot-specific training, Gemini~4 Argon achieves 24.5 PSR and 18.2 TSR through Tool-augmented EEF, while GPT-6 Astra reaches 22.8 and 19.0 (Tab.~ tab:agent-results ). For context, GPT-6 Astra's physical completion rate is close to its 22.48 simulation SR on RoboDojo~ robodojo2026leaderboard ; the different interfaces preclude a controlled comparison of task difficulty. With inference latency included, Gemini and GPT-6 Astra fall to 8.2 and 3.0 LTSR, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus~5.5 to 2.3 and 1.0 , and no open-weight VLM exceeds 1.2 . Gemini keeps more of its TSR because it needs fewer turns (a median of 3 against 6 for GPT-6 Astra per successful episode), which brings it close to the fine-tuned (8.3 LTSR); these rates depend on the API serving speed (App.~ app:api-speed ). sec:interface-comparison Fine-tuning relies on the training clock. We fine-tune on 224 Lab demonstrations with elapsed time in the prompt, then perturb its training episodes (Tab.~ tab:pi05-perturb ). Lighting and physics barely change TSR; object pose reduces it nonsignificantly by 25 points. Later events reduce TSR from 50.0 to 10.5 , with 66 premature responses; earlier events preserve success. Changing A5's duration yields zero success: a 15\,s instruction still produces a lift at 16.1\,s, about 3\,s early (Tab.~ tab:pi05-example ). Delayed immersion also causes premature lifting, suggesting reliance on demonstration timing rather than the required waiting interval. Ablation: VLM Decode Speed sec:ablation-tps To isolate decoding latency, we assume speeds of 35--3K tokens/s and compute each query's delay as its output token count divided by the assumed speed. We add this delay to environment time in closed-loop reruns of GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Fig.~ fig:ablation-tps ). For GPT-6 Astra, success rises monotonically with speed: overall LTSR grows from 5.7 to 18.0 (Event-Reactive 6.2 to 26.3 , Temporal Window 10.0 to 23.8 ) and completed Throughput jobs from 55 to 92. Event-Reactive tasks benefit most, as each call consumes part of their response deadline, and gains diminish beyond 1K tokens/s as LTSR approaches the inference-paused reference. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Fig.~ fig:ablation-tps-qwen ) stays near zero at every speed; its zero-latency reference is already low, so its loss is capability-limited. These results show how our benchmark can guide targeted inference acceleration for VLM agents by identifying where faster decoding improves task success. Analysis: Latency Cost Across Policy Families sec:ablation-latency Per action step, a 25\,Hz policy step for VLAs and WAMs and a 50\,Hz control step for VLM tool calls (Fig.~ fig:ablation-latency ), only the two VLAs stay within their 40\,ms step period, at 4.2 and 9.3\,ms, and keep 81 and 72 of their TSR. The other plotted models need 48--147\,ms and keep at most 38 (OpenWAM- at 51\,ms); the proprietary VLMs keep at most 16 despite the highest TSRs. Failure Case Study sec:failure-analysis Fig.~ fig:failure-casestudy shows one titration task failed in three ways: Claude Opus~5.5 knocks the lever shut after 0.7 of the required 18\,mL; GPT-6 Astra closes it at 60.4\,s, after the flask has turned strongly pink; and in another Opus episode, the trigger fires on time but the grasp misses the lever. Our evaluation distinguishes these outcomes by relating physical completion to the cue and valid time window: the first two close the lever outside the window, whereas the third fails to execute a timely response. These traces suggest different interventions---better cue-conditioned action selection, shorter response delays, and more reliable manipulation---showing how can guide improvements beyond a single success score.

title: LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) couple robot action learning with future prediction~ dreamzero,motus,lingbotva,fastwam . Built on pretrained video generators, they bring two benefits to control: joint video-action learning provides dense supervision for anticipating scene dynamics~ uwm,dreamzero , and video pretraining supplies spatiotemporal priors that robot demonstrations alone may not capture~ cosmospolicy . This framework also supports learning from videos without action labels~ du2023learning,wu2024unleashing . However, these benefits come at a substantial cost. Many WAMs rely on billion-parameter video backbones over dense visual latents~ motus,lingbotva,fastwam . Their representations preserve background, texture, and appearance alongside the robot and object motion needed for control. Modeling all these details increases computation without necessarily improving actions. Compact latent actions~ lapa,univla and compressed perceptual features~ rewam offer alternatives, but do not use a pretrained video generator to shape their representations. They therefore do not directly benefit from the motion and interaction priors encoded in these generators, which could complement the supervision available in robot demonstrations. In this paper, we ask: what information about the future does a policy need, and how compactly can it be represented? Recent studies suggest that useful signals lie both in future observations and in the intermediate features of video models~ vpp,liang2025video,wen2024vidman,invisiblehand . Our probing study (Sec.~ sec:probe ) shows that joint video--action training makes robot actions substantially easier to decode from video features. Combining these adapted features with VAE latents and semantic features improves decoding further. In contrast, adding features from the original pretrained video model provides no gain. These combined features can also be compressed into a few tokens: a single aggregated token retains most of the action-decoding performance achieved with 32 tokens. Intermediate frames further improve decoding within the same action horizon and token budget. Together, these findings motivate a compact, action-supervised representation that combines complementary cues across a short clip. We present LeanWAM, a latent world action model that transfers the priors of a frozen pretrained video generator into a lightweight policy. Figure~ fig:overview illustrates how LeanWAM learns compact predictive representations and distills them into the deployed policy. In Stage~1, a Future Extractor compresses a short clip into a predictive code that conditions the frozen video model. The current frame supplies scene context, while the code describes the transition. Semantic, geometric, and RGB supervision at increasing depths guides this description without additional generation branches. An action DiT reads both the predictive code and a compact readout of the model's hidden states, called world tokens. Action gradients shape this predictive interface through the frozen model. In Stage~2, a lightweight Mixture-of-Transformers policy learns to predict both representations from current observations while generating actions. Only this policy is deployed, and the video generator is used exclusively during training. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt] We introduce a two-stage framework that transfers a frozen video generator's priors through compact predictive codes and world tokens into a lean deployed policy, without updating or deploying the video generator. Our probes show that a few tokens retain most of the action information in complementary future representations (Sec.~ sec:probe ), and that the learned code supports better action decoding than dense future representations. Behavior analysis further reveals greater cross-task consistency with action supervision (Sec.~ sec:analysis ). Without large-scale embodied pretraining, our 1.4B-parameter policy surpasses strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO~ libero , LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus , and RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin2 . It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, with 12.3--41.5 lower latency than representative WAMs (Figure~ fig:efficiency ). Related Work sec:related Vision-language-action models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer the knowledge of pretrained vision-language models to robot control. RT-2~ rt2 and OpenVLA~ openvla represent actions as discrete tokens, while ~ pi0 and GR00T N1~ gr00tn1 pair a vision-language backbone with a continuous action generator. Other work scales training across tasks and data sources~ pi05 , robot embodiments~ lingbotvla , memory augmentation~ robomme , or aligned heterogeneous manipulation data~ qwenrobotmanip . LeanWAM retains a language-conditioned continuous-action policy and uses future observations as additional training supervision. World action models. WAMs couple action learning with the prediction of how the visual world evolves. DreamZero~ dreamzero adapts a 14B video generation model to jointly predict videos and actions. Motus~ motus combines understanding, video, and action experts in a Mixture-of-Transformers~ mot , and the LingBot-VA series~ lingbotva,lingbotva2 studies causal modeling and native video--action pretraining. Flex- ~ flexpi and DreamWAM~ dreamwam extend future prediction to geometry, motion, or semantics. Fast-WAM~ fastwam retains video co-training while skipping future generation at inference. These approaches retain a video backbone at deployment. InternVLA-A1.5~ internvlaa15 and PDRVLA~ pdrvla instead use frozen video models only during training. Recent analyses further show that, beyond the predicted future, intermediate video features also provide useful action representations~ vpp,liang2025video,wen2024vidman,invisiblehand . LeanWAM learns a compact code and an action-supervised readout of these features, then distills both into a separate policy. Latent world action models. WoG~ wog and Being-H0.7~ beingh07 use future observations to supervise compact latents for action generation. LaWAM~ lawam predicts visual subgoals in a frozen feature space. VLA-JEPA~ vlajepa and JEPA-WAM~ jepawam learn policies with future-state prediction in pretrained video representation spaces. ReWAM~ rewam compresses DINOv3 features through a bottleneck trained only by action gradients, and GE-Act~2.0~ geact2 aligns its visual latents with multiple perception teachers. LeanWAM complements these approaches by shaping its predictive code through a pretrained video generator, jointly using action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision. What Does a Policy Need from the Future? sec:probe LeanWAM rests on the premise that a policy needs only a small, action-relevant part of the future. To test this premise, we train a probe to recover actions from representations of observed transitions. We evaluate action , which measures the relative reduction in squared prediction error compared with predicting the mean action. title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
summary: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.

These results suggest that the key to robust agent--policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the Introduction sec:intro Robot manipulation needs both task-level decisions and precise physical interaction with objects. Agents built on general-purpose multimodal models now handle the task level through tool calls: they capture images, segment objects, plan multi-step tasks and recover when a step fails~ codeaspolicies2023,voxposer2023,maestro2025,alrm2026,roboclaw2026 . Such an agent generalizes across layouts and instructions but executes contact poorly, whereas a learned visuomotor policy executes contact well. Recent systems therefore combine their strengths: the agent orchestrates the task and hands over physical interaction with objects to such a policy~ harnessvla2026,huang2026roboharness,xu2026baton,semantichandoff2026,robocop2026,hu2026orchestrating , a paradigm we refer to as agent-orchestrated robot manipulation. =1 However, a policy completes its command reliably only from a limited range of states, and the agent may hand over outside this range. We refer to this range as the handoff boundary of the policy. These systems call an off-the-shelf policy that is trained to complete whole tasks from initial states, which leaves this boundary narrow and hard to describe in the middle of a task ( a). As a result, the agent tends to hand over the whole task from the initial pose. When the policy fails, the agent corrects the arm and hands over once more, but often from a state outside the boundary, so the policy fails again, as we observe in . Existing systems mostly mitigate such failures on the agent side, through exploration, memory and verification~ harnessvla2026,huang2026roboharness,semantichandoff2026,xu2026baton , but these measures cannot change the boundary, which is mainly set by the data on which the policy is trained. This raises a natural question: Can a policy be trained to have a handoff boundary that is wide and explicit to the agent, for more In this paper, we propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning. The key idea is to define and expand the handoff boundary through training, instead of constraining the agent through prompts or letting the agent discover the boundary through exploration. In its first stage, Boundary-Explicit Training, the policy is fine-tuned only on contact segments, in which the robot physically interacts with objects. We collect these segments with diverse start poses around the target object to make the boundary wide ( b), and the well-defined rules for collecting them make the boundary explicit. With a short handoff protocol that describes this boundary, the agent calls the policy reliably. However, these reliable calls come at a cost: the policy covers only the contact segment, and the agent completes the rest of each task through many slow and costly language-model calls. To reduce these calls, the second stage, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement, first collects the successful rollouts of entire tasks that the system produces and removes their suboptimal segments with a data curation pipeline, as illustrated in c. We then retrain the policy on these curated rollouts together with the contact segments from the first stage, so that the handoff boundary extends to earlier stages of each task while preserving the boundary learned in the first stage. After re-exploring each task with the retrained policy, the agent hands over earlier and needs fewer language-model calls. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which defines and expands the handoff boundary through training, for more reliable agent--policy coordination. To this end, we introduce Boundary-Explicit Training ( ), which makes the handoff boundary wide and explicit, and Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement ( ), which extends it to earlier stages of each task. With boundary-explicit training alone, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by more than 26 percentage points in randomized scenes of RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin2_2025 and on RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo . On RoboTwin~2.0, self-improvement further reduces its API cost and time per episode by 41.3 and 37.5 on average, without loss in success rate ( d). Related Work sec:related Agentic robot manipulation Language models were first used as robot planners that compose a fixed set of primitives~ saycan2022,codeaspolicies2023,innermonologue2022,voxposer2023 . More recently, frontier models have made it possible for an agent to control a robot arm directly, with no robot-specific training~ astranomy2026,sensenova2026astra,astra2026robodojo,ora2026 . However, such an agent still falls short on physical interaction with objects, so a growing line of work on agent-orchestrated robot manipulation integrates a learned visuomotor policy, typically a vision-language-action (VLA) model, into the agent framework~ harnessvla2026,chen2026volo,huang2026roboharness,galanti2026gap,zhao2026retriever,xu2026baton,claro2026,maestro2025 . In these systems, the agent decides when to call the policy and how to instruct the policy, and the interface between the agent and the policy becomes the main bottleneck~ hu2026orchestrating . Most existing attempts address this bottleneck from the agent side by adding verification and memory around a frozen policy~ semantichandoff2026,huang2026roboharness,xu2026baton . In this paper, we address this bottleneck from the policy side: we train the policy so that its handoff boundary is wide and explicit to the agent, and then expand this boundary as the system runs. Robot skill learning Rather than learning one policy for the whole task, a long line of work decomposes tasks into reusable skills and composes them at run time~ robomatrix2024,atomiclib2025,voyager2023,aspire2026,li2026recover . With generalist VLA policies~ rt2_2023,openvla2024,octo2024,pi0_2024,pi05_2025 , these skills are now fine-tuned from, or prompted out of, one shared model~ primskills2026,atomicvla2026,mastvla2026,skillvla2026,skillretrieval2026 . Each such skill can start only from certain states, which are classically modeled as the initiation set of an option~ sutton1999options and are learned so that skills can be chained~ konidaris2009skillchaining . In this paper, the contact segments on which we fine-tune the policy in boundary-explicit training can also be viewed as such skills, but we do so to give the policy an explicit handoff boundary, so that the agent knows when and where to hand over. Self-improving robot systems Beyond a fixed memory, a robot system can keep improving after deployment. Early work rewrites the agent's memory from failures~ reflexion2023,voyager2023 . More recently, robot agents discover new skills~ aspire2026,li2026recover , curate their own executions into training data~ chen2025curating,roboclaw2026,enpire2026 , and fine-tune the policy from model-guided exploration~ eximo2026,insight2026,agenticvla2026 . Closest to our work, Robo-COP fine-tunes a VLA policy on its own executions to fix recurring failures and revises the agent's memory after each update~ robocop2026 . In this paper, we retrain the policy on the system's successful rollouts and let the agent re-explore each task with the retrained policy, so that the agent hands over earlier and needs Method sec:method In this paper, we study agent-orchestrated robot manipulation, which combines a general-purpose agent, equipped with a system prompt, a memory and tools, with a learned visuomotor policy to solve robot manipulation tasks, as shown in . We consider this paradigm a better choice than letting the agent control the robot directly, which we examine in an early exploratory study ( ). Boundary-Aware Policy Learning improves this system through the handoff between the agent and the policy: boundary-explicit training ( ) makes the handoff reliable, and boundary-expanding self-improvement ( ) lets the agent hand over earlier. Preliminaries sec:prelim Task setup In a robot manipulation task, a robot acts in an environment to follow a language instruction . At each control step , the robot provides an observation with RGB images, depth maps and the proprioceptive state, and a policy outputs an action . The robot executes , which changes the environment, and this loop repeats until the task is completed. Agent-orchestrated robot manipulation Here, we use a general-purpose agent that orchestrates a learned visuomotor policy to solve the manipulation task. The agent calls tools in a loop, where the -th call is conditioned on the instruction, a memory and the history of earlier calls. Each call either perceives the scene, reads or writes the memory, or controls the robot through motion tools, such as a planner that reaches an end-effector target , or through the policy , which runs with a short command for chunks of actions. After each call, the agent receives the new observation, and this loop continues until the agent finishes the task or a budget of calls is spent. Following Harness VLA~ harnessvla2026 , the agent first explores each task and writes what it learns into the memory , which stays fixed at evaluation. Handoff boundary When the agent calls the policy, it hands over control of the robot to the policy, and we refer to this transfer as a handoff. A handoff is reliable only if the agent hands over in a state from which the policy can complete its command. Formally, we define the handoff boundary as the set of observations from which the policy completes command with probability at least : where is the probability that completes command when it starts from observation . Since this probability cannot be measured for every observation, we estimate the boundary in from the success rate of the policy at increasing distances from its training trajectories. Boundary-explicit training sec:aligned_learning sec:aligned The handoff boundary in is mainly set by the data on which the policy is trained. A whole-task policy, which is trained on complete demonstrations of entire tasks, often has a handoff boundary that is narrow and hard to describe in the middle of a task. Data collection and policy training To address this problem, we first define the roles of the agent and the policy: the policy handles only the contact segments of each task, in which the robot physically interacts with objects, and the agent does the rest. The handoff boundary therefore lies near the graspable points of the target object. We then collect demonstrations of contact segments from diverse start poses

title: Motion Chain of Thought: Disentangling Motion Semantics from Visual Appearance for Robotic Manipulation
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) aim to construct a unified architecture capable of understanding world state evolution and guiding action generation. However, existing visual branches focus on predicting static visual observation, rather than reflecting potential transition information that captures the evolution of world states under motion interactions. This leads to representational entanglement between high-level physical condition evolution and low-level action trajectory generation within the Action Model, creating a structural bottleneck while weakening the predictive capability of world evolution modeling for action generation. We propose PILOT (Physical Inference for Latent Optimized Trajectories), whose core Representational Deduction (RD) bridges this gap by integrating motion chain-of-thought (CoT) guidance as a native model capability. Specifically, RD aims to encourage the action branch to explicitly model potential state transition tokens, which are retained as CoT in the reasoning space to guide fine-grained motion trajectory. Experiments demonstrate that RD not only improves the success rate and generalization ability of WAMs in complex robotic manipulation tasks but also enhances the model's physical interpretability by decoupling high-level motion semantics from low-level trajectory details. Furthermore, the abundant state transition supervision signals introduced by RD effectively alleviate the sparse supervision in action generation, supporting data-efficient real-robot adaptation with reduced demonstration sets.

Introduction section:introduction World Models~ hafner2023dreamerv3,bruce2024genie and Embodied Intelligence~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,kim2024openvla,xu2026reaction are dedicated to ``understanding how the physical world evolves during human interaction'' and ``planning the action trajectory based on current observations,'' respectively. figures/motiv The unification of these paradigms represents a significant step toward General Spatial Intelligence~ yang2025thinking . Recent World Action Models (WAMs)~ bi2026motus,lyu2026lda,team2026motubrain,li2026wallwm,li2026lingbotva approach this goal by leveraging world models to predict future states and introducing the Inverse Dynamics Module (IDM)~ chen2025moto,liu2026lara,zhang2026defi to convert these predictions into trajectory. However, future states are confined to the visual latent space constructed by frozen VAEs~ pai2025mimic,cen2025rynnvla2,zhang2026dreamvla . This structural bottleneck causes the joint optimization objective of WAMs to primarily target visual reconstruction over trajectory generation. Guiding WAMs to focus on motion semantic representations to eliminate the visual bottleneck via an end-to-end framework remains a long-term goal. Recent experiments~ yuan2026fastwam,yang2026mantisvla,sun2026vlajepa indicate that while explicit future prediction aids training, it provides limited foresight for trajectory generation during inference. The effectiveness of WAMs stems from the future supervision to World Model, promoting the learning of physically meaningful visual priors. We attribute this to the fact that static visual representations at a single moment fail to reflect the evolution process of physical states under action interactions. Without explicit modeling of state transitions, directly generating actions through the diffusion process leads to representational entanglement, which is visualized in Fig.~ fig:motiv . To address this, we propose that action model should simultaneously learn high-level motion intention structures and low-level manipulation details from the same inputs. How to supervise the model to learn the motion semantic representations that contain state transition information? The existing WAM~ ye2026dreamzero,gao2026dreamdojo,cen2025worldvla,feng2025vidar can precisely predict what will happen in the future, but still doesn't know how to do it. Most relevant works are Latent Action Models (LAMs), which typically capture pixel-level differences and reconstruct future frames from the current frame via IDM~ ye2025lapa,bu2025univla,routray2025vipra . However, this kind of visual-aware-only supervision, fails to prompt the model to understand what action conditions led to the variation in the visual state. Instead of deriving latent motions directly from consecutive frames, we employ them exclusively as supervision, guiding the model to summarize physical state transitions and motion semantics within learnable tokens. We propose not to pursue to capture motion-related state transition semantics from pixel variations between two frames, but rather to use variations in physical spatial states as supervisions. In this paper, we propose Physical Inference for Latent Optimized Trajectories (PILOT), an end-to-end framework grounded in the Representational Deduction (RD) mechanism that bridges the gap between static visual prediction and dynamic action manipulation by establishing motion semantic CoT reasoning as an innate capability of WAMs. Architecturally, PILOT decouples the World Model into understanding and generation pipelines to substitute explicit future image prediction with the Motion-CoT during inference, thereby accelerating deployment speed while improving both simulation and real-world. Specifically, the Action Model derives high-level Motion-CoT tokens from the current observation, instruction, and proprioceptive state; future observations are used only as training supervision for learning predictive state-transition representations. Subsequently, we freeze the pre-trained VJEPA-as-Encoder~ assran2025vjepa2,mur2026vjepa21,maes2026leworldmodel to capture deterministic features tightly coupled with action conditions, and train a Causal Dynamics Engine (CDE) to predict future spatial positions, trajectories, shapes, and interaction relationships conditioned on motion semantic CoT, rather than probabilistic underlying visual rendering details. Meanwhile, these motion semantics are retained as context tokens in the reasoning space, allowing the subsequent diffusion process to concentrate on refining fine-grained end-effector trajectories and achieve representational decoupling. This brings an additional benefit: Motion-CoT serves as an extra supervision signal, alleviating the sparse supervision problem faced by the action model due to the low information density of action signals. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. We propose PILOT, a novel WAM framework that decouples motion intention from trajectory generation via a Representational Deduction mechanism, and internalizes latent state transition information as Motion CoT to alleviate representational entanglement. We introduce a Causal Dynamics Engine for future-representation supervision and asymmetric attention in Action-Perceiver that prevents noised actions from influencing motion-semantic queries, enabling action inference without future pixel reconstruction. PILOT achieves 97.9 , 80.3 , and 59.75 success on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa-GR1, respectively, and 82.5 average success on the eight standard real-world tasks. A separate pipeline-timing comparison reports 91.6 lower latency for action-only inference than predict-then-act inference. Related Work section:relatedwork World Models for Robotic Manipulations Recently, WAMs~ cen2025worldvla,li2026wallwm,li2026lingbotva,cen2025rynnvla2,zhang2026dreamvla,zhang2026imagewam have emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages world model to predict future, thereby guiding motion manipulation. Existing video-model-based WAMs~ kim2026cosmospolicy generally follow two paradigms. The serial-paradigm first predicts future observation and then reconstructs actions via an inverse dynamic~ pai2025mimic,chen2025moto,zhou2024robodreamer , while the parallel-paradigm jointly models the visual-action space through shared attention mechanism (MoT)~ bi2026motus,lyu2026lda,yuan2026fastwam or joint denoising~ ye2026dreamzero,gao2026dreamdojo . Unlike generative pixel reconstruction strategies, joint embedding predictive frameworks (JEPA)~ maes2026leworldmodel,assran2025vjepa2,mur2026vjepa21 focus on predicting dynamic features such as object spatial positions and trajectories. Some studies~ jha2026reconstruction,su2026wog incorporated JEPA-as-encoder to obtain abundant representations. Most relevant to our work is VLA-JEPA~ sun2026vlajepa , which introduces JEPA to extract latent states, addressing the challenges of pixel reconstruction bias and future information leakage. Latent Action Learning for Robotics LAMs~ routray2025vipra,liu2026lara,bruce2024genie aim to pre-train backbones on large-scale human videos lacking action labels, thereby establishing prior knowledge of latent motion. Existing approaches~ ye2025lapa,bu2025univla,chen2025moto,zhang2026defi,yang2026como typically align vision and manipulation representations using Q-former~ li2023blip2 and unified codebook~ zhang2026clap,ma2026unifying,chen2025moto,chen2026lawam to integrate robotic manipulation into the Next-Token-Prediction framework. Despite the promise of LAMs, their performance is hindered by noise from camera-induced background variations and future frame leakage, which encourages trivial encoding of future frames rather than learning state transitions~ sun2026vlajepa . These issues cause structural bottlenecks in learning control-oriented latent actions. Recent works mitigate this via latent constraints~ luo2026beingh07 or multi-encoder-query~ su2026wog . However, the LAMs inherently aligns latent actions with visual space rather than actionable control signals. PILOT fundamentally avoids these defects by ensuring that future visual information is used exclusively as a supervision target, not as a source for capturing latent motion representations, thereby guaranteeing that model focuses on dynamic representations independent of camera motion and background changes. title: VLAs Execute, Code Recovers: 3D Skill Envelopes Bridge the Compositional Gap in Agentic Manipulation
summary: Composing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) skills under an agentic planner promises scalable long-horizon manipulation without long-horizon demonstrations, yet strong atomic skills routinely fail at seams even under a correct plan. Standard remedies reset the robot's pose or draft entry conditions in language, missing the physical cause we uncover via causal interventions: even after re-homing, a frozen VLA rigidly retraces its habitual trajectory and collides with displaced scene residue, whether or not it can see it. We propose the Skill Envelope, a policy-measured 3D geometric precondition capturing the volume a frozen skill sweeps during successful executions. Exploiting the insight that the rigidity making a frozen skill fragile at seams also makes its trajectory predictable in advance, we expose each envelope as two classical 3D tools (CHECK to detect blocking residue and FREE to locate safe placement regions), establishing a division of labor where VLAs execute in-distribution manipulation and code repairs out-of-distribution states. On LIBERO-Goal with frozen $π_{0.5}$, our zero-failure envelope predicts collisions at 0.946 AUROC (0.944 from one RGB-D view) and beats frontier VLMs on seam readiness (0.902 vs. 0.793); using it for skill ordering and code repair lifts success from 82.8% to 92.3% on two-step seams and from 29.7% to 93.8% on drawer-bearing 3-4 step chains, matching privileged world reset. Together, these results show that reliable VLA composition hinges on measuring a policy's physical workspace rather than guessing preconditions in language. Ongoing work closes the loop with autonomous LLM orchestration, synthesized free-object recovery, and cross-policy evaluation on cluttered benchmarks and real hardware.

Introduction sec:intro Everyday long-horizon manipulation cannot be solved by enumerating end-to-end demonstrations: even ten atomic skills yield 5 , 040 four-step permutations, each creating distinct intermediate world states. A natural alternative is agentic composition: pairing a high-level planner or LLM agent with a library of frozen manipulation or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) skills~ saycan,cap,baton,harnessvla . Yet strong atomic skills routinely collapse at the transitions (or seams) between them. Consider a two-step kitchen routine in LIBERO-Goal~ libero : open the middle drawer, then push the plate to the front of the stove. A frozen policy~ pi05 executes both skills reliably in isolation. Chained directly, however, the second skill drops to ; even after returning the robot arm to its home pose (re-homing), the standard fix, it remains at because the arm runs into the open drawer (Fig.~ fig:seam ). Across ordered skill pairs ( handoff states), mean success drops from in isolation to under direct chaining, and recovers only to after re-homing. The predecessor is done, yet the successor is not ready. Recent work has recognized this compositional gap, but addresses it through proxies rather than querying the policy itself. Skill-chaining frameworks address only the robot's configuration while leaving scene objects untouched~ robocombine,causeway,atombridge . Agentic orchestrators prompt a language model to draft natural-language entry conditions at seams and invoke programmatic primitives when those conditions fail~ baton , or ask a vision-language model whether to advance or retry~ rui2026handoff . Others diagnose scene-residue failures only after the policy gets stuck, relying on learned recovery policies or fine-tuning~ wagh2026seams . What remains missing is a physical question: what exact precondition does a frozen policy require to succeed, and how can an agent check it beforehand? We answer this question in two steps. First, by intervening on the exact same re-homed handoff states, we causally separate visual observation shift from physical world shift. Contrary to the common assumption that seam failures stem primarily from visual distractors, rendering residual objects invisible in the camera feed barely helps, while physically removing them recovers most of what re-homing leaves and slashes collisions (Fig.~ fig:diagnosis a). Seam failure is therefore governed by physical, policy-specific hidden preconditions: a frozen VLA follows its habitual trajectory and collides with any residue standing in its way. Second, we turn this weakness into a measurement tool: the rigidity that makes a frozen skill fragile at seams is the very property that makes its trajectory measurable in advance. By running each skill in isolation, without human demonstrations or failure rollouts, we record the 3D volume swept by the arm, gripper, and carried object, yielding a Skill Envelope. Exposed to an agent as two classical 3D tools ( and ), the envelope establishes a clean division of labor: VLA policies execute in-distribution manipulation, classical code repairs out-of-distribution world states, and the boundary between them is drawn by policy measurement rather than language. In this Stage-1 submission, we establish the empirical foundation and core mechanism of this framework: Causal seam diagnosis (Sec.~ sec:diagnosis ): We decompose the compositional gap across body, view, and world states on the same handoffs, showing that failures remaining after robot re-homing are dominated by policy-specific physical collisions rather than visual shift. Skill Envelopes as agent tools (Sec.~ sec:method ): We introduce an , zero-failure 3D envelope profiling method and formalize two geometric tools ( and ) linking frozen VLAs with classical recovery code, supporting both pre-built primitives and future agent-synthesized skills. Validation across sensing, language, and multi-step seams (Sec.~ sec:results ): We show that zero-failure envelopes detect collisions even from one RGB-D view, generalize across unseen predecessors and categories, and beat frontier VLMs. Grounding why cleanup belongs to code over the VLA, envelope-guided planning and repair match privileged reset on two-skill seams and compound on 3--4 step chains. A frozen VLA encodes its hidden preconditions in its weights: never having seen an open drawer along its approach path, it neither recognizes the obstacle nor replans around it, rigidly replaying its habitual sweep straight into contact. Yet that very rigidity points directly to the cure: because the arm traces a repeatable corridor, we can measure its swept volume in advance and flag obstructions before the skill is ever called. title: RoboDemo: Reconciling Demonstration Intent and Execution Progress for Long-Horizon Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks. Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.

The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions.
