title: MXI-MemICL: Towards In-Context Robot Manipulation through Self-Retrieved Interaction Memory
summary: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.
full_text: Method sec:method sec:memory In this section, we first formulate the problem in Section~ sec:formulation , then describe stage and memory generation in Section~ sec:generation , experience retrieval in Section~ sec:retrieval , and experience injection in Section~ sec:injection . Section~ sec:training presents our training strategy. Figure~ fig:method provides an overview of our method. Problem Formulation sec:formulation Given a language instruction and observation , a VLA policy predicts successive controls at decision ~ pi05 . The observation contains one or more camera images and proprioceptive state , and each control has action dimensions. further conditions action generation on memory from completed interactions and an optional successful demonstration . With , the current stage embedding and prior intent form the gated query . Query formation and experience retrieval condition action generation: which grounds robot behavior in relevant experience. The memory bank stores key--memory pairs. Query formation combines and into , while experience retrieval retrieves and fuses experience from into experience tokens . Stage and Memory Generation sec:generation encodes the current stage to form queries and completed interactions to build indexed memories (Figure~ fig:method ). The backbone feature extractor produces hidden representations . Mean pooling yields , which the intention decoder maps to a normalized stage embedding . In parallel, the interaction memory comes from a visual--action causal encoder based on the causal three-stream architecture~ behaviorvla,zeva . Its visual, action, and interaction-state streams process executed controls together with observations before and after execution, using recurrent updates and attention across streams. Fusing the interaction states, visual changes, and an action summary produces a memory of what was executed during the stage and its observed effects. We index this memory with a retrieval key , generated by an MLP from the pooled feature and pre-execution interaction state . Key-memory pairs from completed interactions enter the shared memory bank , which holds up to 64 pairs. The current attempt's latest records provide short-term execution context , while the remaining records form long-term memory . These disjoint views update as new interactions enter the bank. Intention-Guided Experience Retrieval sec:retrieval At each decision, the stage embedding summarizes the current observation and instruction, while carries the intent predicted for this step at the preceding decision. The gated query mapping combines these cues through a learned gate and normalization, with : Experience retrieval. The query selects experience from long-term memory through soft retrieval slots. Each slot adds a learned query offset, computes cosine similarities between projected queries and keys, and aggregates memory values with normalized weights : Records assigned high weights become less available to later slots, promoting complementary retrieval. The retrieved experience is fused with recent execution context into experience tokens for backbone injection. Memory-based in-context adaptation. sec:stage3 To support robotic ICL, turns a single successful demonstration into retrievable experience that guides action generation without parameter updates at deployment. The demonstration and target execution come from distinct source trajectories of the same task and are encoded separately by the causal encoder. All completed demonstration records form the read-only bank , while execution memory contains interactions completed before decision . The latest execution records form the short-term context, while the long-term candidates combine the full demonstration with the remaining execution records: Execution initializes its own intent and encoder states from its initial observation and instruction. title: HiGS: A Hierarchical Architecture for Fast Differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes one screen tile the cell of partitioning, the cell of rasterization, and the unit of parallel work. Partitioning favors large tiles and rasterization small ones, and with one unit per tile the densest tiles set the frame time. We present Hierarchically Tiled Gaussian Splatting (HiGS), a unified architecture for rendering and reconstruction that gives each role its own granularity: Gaussians are partitioned over coarse macro-tiles, rasterized over the fine render tiles within them, and processed in bounded depth-sorted batches. A dense region issues more batches instead of one longer unit, so frame time follows the work in a view rather than its densest tile. The same batches carry reconstruction: compositing supplies the transmittance and color needed to differentiate each one independently, leaving optimizer memory traffic as the dominant training cost. We fuse the optimizer into the backward pass, halve the parameters and moments it stores and updates directly, and defer appearance updates outside the view. HiGS renders scenes faster than every published method we evaluate, by the widest margin on views with uneven load, and reconstructs them faster and in less memory, at equal image quality and with exact front-to-back alpha compositing.

Partitioning favors large tiles and rasterization small ones, and with one unit per tile the densest tiles set the frame time. We present Hierarchically Tiled Gaussian Splatting (HiGS), a unified architecture for rendering and reconstruction that gives each role its own granularity: Gaussians are partitioned over coarse macro-tiles, rasterized over the fine render tiles within them, and processed in bounded depth-sorted batches. A dense region issues more batches instead of one longer unit, so frame time follows the work in a view rather than its densest tile. The same batches carry reconstruction: compositing supplies the transmittance and color needed to differentiate each one independently, leaving optimizer memory traffic as the dominant training cost. We fuse the optimizer into the backward pass, halve the parameters and moments it stores and updates directly, and defer appearance updates outside the view. HiGS renders scenes faster than every published method we evaluate, by the widest margin on views with uneven load, and reconstructs them faster and in less memory, at equal image quality and with exact front-to-back alpha compositing. Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussian has become the leading approach to real-time photorealistic rendering of captured scenes, combining the fidelity of neural radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf with an explicit, differentiable representation that commodity GPUs rasterize at high throughput. Reconstruction runs its rasterizer forward and backward tens of thousands of times, so rasterization cost governs both reconstruction and display. Most variants of 3DGS share one pipeline: Gaussians are projected to the screen, assigned to the tiles they overlap, sorted globally by tile and depth into one Gaussian list per tile, and rasterized with one thread block per tile. The tile serves three conflicting roles: partition cell, rasterization cell, and unit of parallel work. Partitioning favors large tiles, which reduce the number of (tile, Gaussian) pairs to bin and sort. Rasterization favors small tiles, which reduce pixel--Gaussian evaluations outside the Gaussian's effective support. At any size, a few dense tiles hold far more Gaussians than the rest and, with one thread block each, produce a tail effect that dominates frame time ( ). A single tile size cannot serve all three, and 3DGS pays with a global radix sort over tens of millions of pairs per frame at 4K and with a frame time set by the densest tile rather than by the work in the view. Prior work lowers these costs without separating all three roles. Pairs are reduced, models compressed, and single stages accelerated~ hanson2024speedysplat,feng2024flashgs,wang2024adrgaussian,radl2024stopthepop,hahlbohm2026fastergs,fan2024lightgaussian,liao2025tcgs,schutz2025splatshop,mallick2024taming,durvasula2024distwar , and methods that leave the pipeline pay with approximate compositing~ hou2025sortfree,rueckert2025stochastic or custom hardware~ li2025gaurast,yang2025gsacc . Sorting at a coarser granularity than rasterization~ lee2024gscore,jo2025gstg,ding2026sharpgs shrinks the sort but leaves each tile one unbounded Gaussian list, as does rescheduling tiles~ gui2024balanced , and dividing the lists of the densest ones among thread blocks~ zhang2026catgs shortens the tail but keeps the global sort. Each of these remedies changes one or two roles of the tile, and none carries the change into the backward pass of training. We present HiGS, a unified architecture for commodity GPUs that gives each role its own granularity, with one unit of work for rendering and reconstruction. Gaussians are binned and depth-sorted over coarse macro-tiles, each a group of the fine render tiles over which they are rasterized, and the unit of work is a (macro-tile, Gaussian-batch) pair: a depth-sorted batch of bounded size, rasterized independently and then composited with the others in depth order. Three consequences follow from this single decomposition. Sorting splits into independent macro-tile segments. Every batch, of a dense tile or not, fits in fast local storage, where it is loaded once and shared across its render tiles. Dense macro-tiles issue proportionally more units, so no unit processes a dense tile's entire Gaussian list, which removes the cause of the tail effect. The same units carry reconstruction, so both passes of a training step inherit this schedule. Compositing leaves every batch with the transmittance in front of it and the color from it onward, and batches are differentiated as independently as they are rendered. The optimizer then dominates training, and we reduce its memory traffic until it, too, scales with what a view sees: fused into the backward pass, it updates low-precision parameters and moments directly and defers the appearance updates of the Gaussians a view culls. HiGS renders 1.5 to 5.6 faster than recent optimized rasterizers on standard benchmark scenes, and 6.8 to 20.0 faster on driving views with a strongly uneven load. It reconstructs scenes 2.3 to 3.0 faster than the fastest published method we evaluate, with 1.9 less memory than the most memory-efficient one, at equal image quality. Our contributions are the architecture and its three parts: a unified architecture for rendering and reconstruction that separates partitioning, rasterization, and parallel work around one unit, a bounded depth batch of a macro-tile; a renderer on these units, with a segmented depth sort, load-balanced batch rasterization with inline visibility, and a stable half-precision (FP16) data path; a backward pass over the same batches, which differentiates each independently from boundary state left by compositing; a bandwidth-lean optimizer fused with backward projection, which updates stochastically rounded 16-bit state directly and defers appearance updates a view does not need. Related Work sec:related Kerbl~ ~ kerbl2023gaussian established the tile-based pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting, and gsplat~ ye2024gsplat popularized it in a widely adopted open-source library. Most of the work that followed keeps the rendering model and lowers the cost of this pipeline. reduction. Many pairs are false positives: a Gaussian's bounding box overlaps a tile the Gaussian does not visibly reach. StopThePop~ radl2024stopthepop introduced opacity-aware bounds and an exact test of which tiles an ellipse reaches. FlashGS~ feng2024flashgs , AdR-Gaussian~ wang2024adrgaussian , and Speedy-Splat~ hanson2024speedysplat derive similar bounds, the first and the last with exact tests of their own, and Faster-GS~ hahlbohm2026fastergs adopts them. HiGS tests ellipse overlap during binning and rasterization, but most of its pair reduction comes from binning over macro-tiles. -side reduction. Fewer Gaussians also mean fewer pairs, and work complementary to ours shrinks the model: by pruning in Speedy-Splat and RadSplat~ niemeyer2024radsplat , by budgeted densification in Taming~3DGS~ mallick2024taming , by importance-weighted sampling in Mini-Splatting~ fang2024minisplatting , by multi-view consistent densification and pruning in FastGS~ ren2026fastgs , and by the quantization and codebook schemes of LightGaussian~ fan2024lightgaussian , EAGLES~ girish2024eagles , Compact-3DGS~ lee2024compact3dgs , and Compressed 3DGS~ niedermayr2024compressed . Kerbl~ ~ kerbl2024hierarchical build a level-of-detail hierarchy over the scene, rather than over the work of rendering it, for very large captures. acceleration. Several of these methods act during training, whose time is dominated by the backward pass and the optimizer. The backward pass of 3DGS accumulates gradients per pixel and contends on atomic updates, which Taming~3DGS avoids by parallelizing over splats and DISTWAR~ durvasula2024distwar reduces by aggregating a warp's updates to the same Gaussian in registers before issuing one atomic per parameter. LiteGS~ liao2025litegs reduces gradients within the one warp that owns a tile, and culls and updates Morton-ordered Gaussians in clusters. On the optimizer side, Faster-GS pairs the per-splat backward pass with its own Adam implementation, which it can fuse into that pass, and reports up to faster training end to end. GS-Scale~ lee2026gsscale keeps only geometry on the GPU and defers the Adam updates of the other parameters, held in host memory, while a Gaussian is outside the view frustum. Other methods lower the work of a run rather than the cost of a step: DashGaussian~ chen2025dashgaussian schedules the rendering resolution and the Gaussian count, SAD-GS~ lyu2026sadgs shortens convergence by guiding densification with multiscale image structure, and Grendel~ zhao2025grendel distributes training over many GPUs. These complement HiGS, which redesigns the training step itself. acceleration. In the forward pass, GPU implementations have tuned the pipeline stage by stage, most keeping its global sort and the screen tile as the unit of work. FlashGS fuses the preprocessing kernels and pipelines the dependent Gaussian fetches in software, and TC-GS~ liao2025tcgs reformulates the alpha-blending exponent as a Tensor-Core matrix multiplication, reporting up to speedup when integrated into 3DGS. Splatshop~ schutz2025splatshop narrows the sort keys by ordering visible splats by 32-bit depth before tile-fragment creation. TileGS~ tan2026tilegs replaces the global sort by depth bins inside each tile and sorts only selected bins exactly. Against uneven load, StopThePop balances the per-Gaussian stages, and AdR-Gaussian trains with a loss that evens the number of Gaussians per pixel. In the rasterizer, Balanced 3DGS~ gui2024balanced counters load imbalance by letting thread blocks claim tiles at run time, shrinking the tile to four pixels, and spreading the Gaussians of a pixel across the threads of a warp. CaT-GS~ zhang2026catgs divides the depth-ordered list of a tile above twice the mean load into slices that separate thread blocks rasterize and that are then composited in order, within the per-tile pipeline and its global sort. For ultra-high resolutions, SHARP-GS~ ding2026sharpgs bins at a tile size that grows with resolution, culls against the finer tiles it rasterizes through a bitmask per batch of 32 Gaussians, and stores Gaussians in Morton order. GS-TG~ jo2025gstg , an accelerator design that is also evaluated on a GPU, sorts over groups of tiles and rasterizes the original tiles through per-Gaussian bitmasks, and other hardware proposals~ lee2024gscore,li2025gaurast,yang2025gsacc leave the commodity GPU. In HiGS one bounded batch is the unit of work for every list, in rendering and in both passes of reconstruction. formulations. The remaining work changes the rendering model itself, which HiGS keeps. title: RoboRecast: Intent-Preserving Demonstration Augmentation via Diagnosis-Driven Optimization
comment: 18 pages, including supplementary material. Corresponding author: Ruizhen Hu
summary: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior that is semantically implausible or physically infeasible in the new setting. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. This flexibility allows RoboRecast to generate synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations and to adapt them to new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments. When target demonstrations are available, adding RoboRecast data improves policy success on both real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments.
full_text: RoboRecast augments real demonstrations by preserving their interaction requirements while adapting scenes and trajectories for physically plausible execution. The bimanual example schematically illustrates how simulation feedback guides corrections to collision geometry, friction, and waypoints. The framework supports augmentation across demonstration types—including single-arm robot, bimanual robot, and human demonstrations—through initial-pose variation, object replacement, and robot replacement. fig:teaser -1 Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments. Project Page: zju3dv.github.io/RoboRecast/ Introduction sec:intro Robot policies require diverse demonstrations to generalize across objects, layouts, and robot embodiments, yet collecting such coverage in the real world is costly, motivating the augmentation of existing demonstrations. For the resulting synthetic data to support policy learning, the generated interactions must preserve the source manipulation intent and remain physically executable with the specified objects, layout, and robot. Image and video augmentation typically enriches observations around given robot motions~ chen2023genaug,yu2023scaling,wang2026robovip,liu2026robotransfer,ye2026robodream , limiting its ability to accommodate changes in initial object poses, object assets, or robot embodiments. Recreating interactions in simulation allows scenes and motions to be varied together, with explicit control and execution feedback for checking and improving physical plausibility. Such control and execution-based refinement make simulation a promising route to augmenting real-world manipulation demonstrations. The goal of simulation-based augmentation is to generate synthetic data in which the robot completes the demonstrated task under the physical constraints of the target setting. Existing work provides two building blocks for this goal: real-to-sim methods reconstruct the environment~ zhang2026robosnap,han2026re,chen2026agentic , while demonstration transfer adapts robot motions to new configurations. Errors in reconstructed geometry or physical properties can prevent the intended interaction, and adjusting the motion alone leaves those errors unresolved. On the motion side, demonstration transfer adapts source motion segments~ mandlekar2023mimicgen,garrett2024skillmimicgen,jiang2025dexmimicgen or keypoint-trajectory constraints~ lin2025constraint to the target configuration. When a new object or layout calls for a different grasp or approach, these inherited constraints can rule out feasible motions or produce unnatural movements. These limitations raise two questions: what must be preserved from the source demonstration, and how should the scene and robot motion be adapted to the target configuration? Our key insight is that the same task intent can be realized in different ways, so augmentation should preserve the intended effects of the interaction while allowing the scene and motion to adapt. We therefore propose expressing the intended effects as interaction requirements for each phase and jointly optimizing the scene and robot motion to satisfy them under observation, target, and physical constraints. Inferring these requirements from a real-world demonstration requires understanding what the demonstrator is doing and what each phase is intended to achieve. Even with these requirements identified, the search spans a large space of object geometries, physical properties, and robot motions, while evaluating a candidate requires simulation rollouts that provide no direct gradient for improving it. We introduce RoboRecast (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), an agentic optimization framework that uses an agent to infer interaction requirements from demonstrations and uses simulation feedback to guide joint optimization of scenes and robot motions. An agent is well suited to this problem because its semantic understanding and reasoning enable it to infer the intent behind observed actions, diagnose likely causes of execution failures, and revise the scene or motion accordingly. By interpreting object roles, contacts, and resulting state changes in the source demonstration, the agent identifies the essential interactions and their ordering, then maps these requirements to the target configuration. When a phase fails to meet one of these fixed requirements or violates a physical constraint, the agent examines visual and numerical evidence from that phase to identify a likely cause in the reconstructed scene or robot motion. This diagnosis narrows each update to the relevant object parameters or motion waypoints, allowing the agent to test focused revisions in simulation and reduce trial and error. With target demonstrations available, RoboRecast reconstructions yield 38.3 policy success across three real-to-sim tasks, compared with 18.3 for RoboSnap~ zhang2026robosnap and 23.3 for AR2S~ chen2026agentic . Across four layout augmentation tasks, RoboRecast data yields 53.8 policy success, compared with 33.8 for MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen and 40.0 for CP-Gen~ lin2025constraint . On the same four tasks, adding robot trajectories converted from human demonstrations yields 46.3 policy success with RoboRecast and 32.5 with Ego2Robot~ wang2026ego2robot . Our synthetic data also improves policy success in bimanual simulation. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robots. Our contributions are threefold: 2pt 0pt We formulate demonstration augmentation as joint scene and motion optimization, preserving task-defining interaction requirements while allowing their realization to adapt to target configurations. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that extracts interaction requirements from demonstrations and jointly optimizes scenes and motions through execution-guided diagnosis and targeted updates. We demonstrate that RoboRecast generates effective policy training data both with and without demonstrations available for the target configuration. Related Work sec:related_work and Video Augmentation. Image editing and video synthesis expand the range of visual conditions covered by robot demonstrations. GenAug~ chen2023genaug and ROSIE~ yu2023scaling edit demonstration images to vary objects, backgrounds, and distractors. RoboVIP~ wang2026robovip and RoboTransfer~ liu2026robotransfer emphasize temporally consistent multi-view video generation, while RoboDream~ ye2026robodream conditions synthesis on robot motion, object priors, and scene priors. Because these methods primarily vary observations around a given motion, they offer limited flexibility when changes in initial layout, object, or robot embodiment require a new grasp or path. Moreover, their appearance and geometry controls do not establish physical executability. -to-Sim for Manipulation Data Generation. Real-to-sim methods turn real-world observations into interactive environments for demonstration generation and policy learning heppert2026scaling . RE Sim~ han2026re combines multi-view reconstruction with neural rendering, while RoboSnap~ zhang2026robosnap builds interactive foreground assets and a Gaussian-splatting background from a single image. RE Sim generates motions using scripts that access object poses, while ReBot~ fang2025rebot replays recorded robot trajectories. AR2S~ chen2026agentic uses vision-language models to support scene reconstruction and refines replayed interactions through simulator feedback, including object-placement adjustments for grasping. Even after such adjustments, errors in reconstructed geometry can prevent the intended contact. RoboRecast therefore uses execution feedback to choose between scene and motion updates. Transfer and Augmentation. Demonstration transfer adapts source motions to new configurations, reducing the need for additional demonstrations~ xue2025demogen,ameperosa2025rocoda . MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen transforms object-relative segments, SkillGen~ garrett2024skillmimicgen connects manipulation skills through planning, and DexMimicGen~ jiang2025dexmimicgen extends transfer to bimanual and dexterous manipulation. CP-Gen~ lin2025constraint adapts keypoint-trajectory constraints to object variations, accounts for smoothness during trajectory optimization, and uses motion planning to connect segments. When a target configuration calls for a different grasp or approach direction, transferred motion segments or adapted keypoint constraints may exclude feasible motions or produce unnatural movements. We instead fix interaction requirements---object roles, essential contacts, and state changes---while allowing paths, timing, and unconstrained contact choices to adapt. 3D Modeling and Manipulation. Agentic methods coordinate specialized tools and feedback for 3D modeling and robot manipulation. For 3D asset modeling, AgentSTAR~ mazur2026agentstar reconstructs and tracks objects from video, while Articraft~ zhou2026articraft generates articulated assets. At the scene level, Lucida~ qin2026lucida reconstructs observed scenes, while SceneSmith~ pfaff2026scenesmith and SAGE~ xia2026sage generate environments from language or task descriptions. In concurrent work, ARSTAG~ li2026arstag coordinates reconstruction and data generation through cross-stage feedback, while Real2Gym~ ren2026real2gym builds interactive environments from demonstrations for skill acquisition and transfer. Our agent extracts interaction requirements from the source demonstration and uses them to diagnose which scene parameters or semantic waypoints need revision. Method sec:method . Given a real demonstration and a target configuration (objects, layout, and robot), RoboRecast seeks a successful rollout that preserves the demonstrated task intent (Fig.~ fig:overview ). The agent infers the required interactions from , maps their roles to target entities, and initializes the scene and trajectory. If a validity check fails or the rollout misses a required interaction, the agent uses the evidence to diagnose the failure and update the scene or motion. To infer what each interaction must accomplish, the agent examines keyframes and their surrounding segments in the source demonstration to identify the participating roles, essential contacts, and intended state changes. The agent then maps each participating role to the corresponding entity in the target configuration . title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. Project page: Introduction sec:intro In long-horizon manipulation, the success of a subtask depends on both its execution and the state inherited from preceding stages. Completing one subtask therefore does not guarantee successful continuation. Imitation learning gives vision-language-action (VLA) policies a strong initialization by supervising actions along expert trajectories~ black2025pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t . At deployment, however, successive subtasks begin from states produced by the policy itself, and demonstrations provide limited supervision for handling the deviations that accumulate along the way, resulting in failure. Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables VLA policies to learn beyond demonstrations with further environmental interactions by themselves. However, most online RL methods, which learn from full-task rollouts using only binary terminal feedback, still struggle with long-horizon tasks. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:repractice_motivation (a), two episodes with different failures—one from bowl transport and the other from shelf placement—receive the same zero reward despite different amounts of completed work. Our diagnostic further reveals concentrations of failures at specific stages, as shown in Figs.~ fig:robocasa_failure_stages and~ fig:robocasa_task_bottlenecks of Appendix~ sec:supp_failure_stages . Although some work recovers intermediate supervision by estimating progress between observations or rewarding verifiable subtask completions~ tan2026general,yin2026structrl , two challenges remain: 1) Reward Imbalance. To characterize intermediate progress, we group verifiable subtasks with shared prerequisites into stages, within which subtasks can be completed in any order. Even with prerequisite gating and one-time credit, the total reward assigned to a stage can depend on its decomposition granularity. Uniform per-subtask rewards, for example, give a stage more weight simply because it contains more completion events. 2) Limited Bottleneck Practice. Under a fixed interaction budget, the stage limiting full-task success can receive few opportunities for practice and less comprehensive analysis. For example, in Fig.~ fig:repractice_motivation (a), each new attempt at shelf placement requires another grasp and transport, and an earlier failure prevents that attempt altogether. Moreover, there is no deeper analysis of the reason for the failure of shelf placement. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided RL framework for long-horizon manipulation. ReFocus alternates Global RL with Local RL to improve a shared VLA policy. During Global RL, we represent each task as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks and their dependencies. To address Reward Imbalance, DAG-based Progress Reward allocates a fixed task-level reward budget equally across stages. Each stage's share is then divided equally among its subtasks. The total budget allocated to a stage is therefore independent of its number of subtasks, preventing finer decompositions from receiving disproportionate weight. Subtask-completion records also provide structured evidence of task progress to support bottleneck diagnosis. Based on progress feedback, an LLM-based Scheduler identifies stages where the policy repeatedly stalls and selects Adaptive Practice Windows for Local RL. Normal window rollouts concentrate practice on the selected bottleneck, while prefix window and suffix window rollouts connect it with execution from the normal task start and continuation toward full-task completion, respectively. Milestone rewards provide finer feedback within the selected task segment. Together, these rollout modes connect targeted practice with the states inherited from earlier stages and the requirements of later stages. After each round, evaluations assess task progress and full-task success. The Scheduler uses these results, previous windows, and interaction costs to retain, revise, or skip subsequent practice windows. By keeping practice allocation aligned with the remaining difficulties, multi-round training helps translate local gains into progressively more reliable full-task execution. We evaluate ReFocus on LIBERO-Long~ liu2023libero and RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 . Based on a supervised finetuning (SFT) baseline ~ black2025pi05 , ReFocus improves its performance from 90.6 and 39.3 to 97.8 and 51.3 respectively. On three long-horizon real-world tasks, we compare a RECAP-based adaptation of ReFocus with SFT and RECAP~ physicalintelligence2025recap . On BreadBaker, RECAP improves the success rate from 30 to 70 . ReFocus further increases it to 95 . ReFocus also achieves 100 on both StackBowl and PickFruit, compared with 90 and 85 for RECAP, respectively. We introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided RL framework that alternates Global RL with Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate targeted practice in long-horizon manipulation. ReFocus uses DAG-based progress rewards during Global RL to provide dense feedback and identify bottleneck subtasks. Adaptive Practice Windows then focus Local RL on these bottlenecks. Extensive experiments show that ReFocus improves the long-horizon manipulation performance of SFT baselines on the LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 benchmarks and on real-world manipulation tasks. Related Work sec:related_work Foundation Models. Large-scale robot demonstrations enable VLA models to learn generalist manipulation across diverse tasks and embodiments~ black2025pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2025openvla . Recent efforts further scale heterogeneous robot data to improve policy capabilities~ wu2026lingbotvla2,xiaomi2026robotics1,meituan2026robotics0,yuan2026qwenrobotmanip,zhang2026hyvla . Embodied reasoning and steerable conditioning support multi-step execution~ gemini2025robotics15,physicalintelligence2026pi07 , while world-action models integrate visual prediction with robot control~ ye2026dreamzero,nvidia2026gr00t2,huang2026long . However, policies trained on demonstrations may struggle with unfamiliar states and accumulated errors during long-horizon manipulation, motivating further improvement through RL. Learning for VLAs. Reinforcement learning improves pretrained VLA policies using offline data or online interaction. Offline methods use preferences, action values, or recovery data~ zhang2024grape,huang2025corft,gao2026ogpo , while online methods optimize policies with actor--critic or group-relative objectives~ lu2025vlarl,liu2025rlvlageneralization,li2026simplevla,chen2025tgrpo . Further work studies efficient training and real-world adaptation~ zang2026rlinfvla,wang2026policytrim,chen2025conrft,physicalintelligence2025recap,wagenmaker2025dsrl,dong2026expoft . For long-horizon tasks, terminal outcomes provide limited feedback on partially completed trajectories. To provide feedback beyond task outcomes, reward and critic models incorporate intermediate progress~ zhang2026vlac,tan2026general,liang2026robometer,fei2025srpo,kim2026progvla , stage structure~ chen2026sarm2,feng2026procvlm , or execution history~ xu2026robodopamine2,chen2026robolongr . Building on these approaches, ReFocus uses DAG-based progress feedback to allocate equal reward budgets across stages and credit subtask completions according to prerequisites. -Horizon Manipulation. Long-horizon tasks require policies to complete multiple subtasks while handling errors accumulated during execution. Prior work addresses long-horizon tasks by incorporating subtask prerequisites or downstream success into rewards~ yin2026structrl,liu2026foresight . Other approaches focus learning on difficult subtasks through specialist policies~ su2026parts,jiang2026repair,liu2026mobiagent , or allocate practice using budget-aware scheduling, reset curricula, and task selection~ vats2026deliberate,florensa2017reverse,aphale2026percontext,fang2026find . Execution feedback has also been used to improve skills and policies across iterations~ wang2026adarsi,chen2026recursia,xu2026baton . In contrast, ReFocus adaptively selects task-specific practice windows across rounds using subtask progress, full-task evaluations, and practice history. Method sec:method In this section, we first introduce Global RL with Progress Reward for full-task policy learning ( sec:global_rl ). We then present Local RL, which directs interaction toward stages requiring further improvement ( sec:window_selection ). Finally, we describe the optimization paradigm that alternates between phases to improve a shared policy across training rounds ( sec:global_local ). title: EffectWAM: Learning Action-Grounded Effects for Robot Manipulation
summary: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.
full_text: Introduction sect:intro Language-conditioned robot manipulation requires a policy to translate a task instruction into a sequence of actions that brings about the intended change in the environment. In closed-loop execution, the policy repeatedly observes the scene and adjusts its actions as the task progresses. Anticipating how the scene may evolve over an action horizon can help the policy connect its immediate commands to the intended outcome. The choice of what to predict about the future is therefore central to learning visual dynamics for robot control. Vision--language--action (VLA) models learn to map observations and instructions to robot actions kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . Their action supervision leaves the visual consequences of those commands implicit. World--action models (WAMs) add an explicit objective for predicting visual dynamics ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,miao2026internw0delta . Future video provides a rich training signal, but synthesizing it at every decision adds latency to closed-loop control. Fast-WAM avoids this cost by using future video only during training~ yuan2026fastwam . In matched experiments, LAWA found that this approach generalized less well than joint video and action prediction, especially with limited robot demonstrations, and showed that predicting a compact latent alongside actions could achieve comparable success to joint video and action prediction on RoboCasa at lower latency~ li2026lawa . This motivates a policy that retains a compact prediction of action consequences at test time to support manipulation performance while keeping video synthesis off the control path. The choice of target determines which changes the policy learns to anticipate. La-JEPA, for example, uses a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to supervise future prediction alongside robot actions~ murlabadia2026vjepa21,clemente2026lajepa . Frozen video features inherit the distinctions learned during pretraining. A generic video prediction objective provides no direct supervision for retaining small changes in gripper opening or end-effector pose, even when those changes matter for control. Robot demonstrations provide that signal through synchronized images and measured state changes. We use these measurements to shape the representation that supplies the policy's future prediction targets. To this end, we introduce Effect, a compact representation of visual change over the action horizon that learns from paired observations and robot measurements in the same demonstration. A shared encoder processes the current and selected future observations independently. We subtract the current feature from each future feature so that changes at different horizons are expressed relative to the state from which the robot acts. An auxiliary head reads out measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state from the feature difference, encouraging the encoder to preserve information about the executed motion. An exponential moving average (EMA) of the encoder supplies the resulting Effect targets during policy training. Across robot embodiments and camera setups, similar manipulation motions can yield different image changes because cameras are mounted and move differently. For example, as a wrist camera approaches a drawer, the handle can shift in the image before the drawer moves. Qwen-RobotManip uses explicit camera geometry to align visual observations and end-effector motion across heterogeneous robot data~ yuan2026qwenrobotmanip . To support transfer across embodiments and camera setups, we condition Effect's attention pooling on the camera pose relative to the current observation when reliable extrinsics are available. This gives the encoder geometric context for distinguishing changes due to camera motion from changes in the scene. When extrinsics are unavailable, the same encoder uses pose-free pooling with shared weights, allowing both types of trajectory to contribute to training. EffectWAM integrates Effect, CaPE, and Action Grounding through two complementary flow-matching objectives. The first jointly models Effect and the demonstrated action chunk given the current observation and instruction. The second models future video latents given the same context, the clean Effect target, and the demonstrated action. At inference, the policy jointly samples Effect and the action chunk, retaining a prediction of visual change in each control decision. The controller can execute the sampled chunk as soon as joint sampling finishes. When a visual forecast is requested, the video mode uses the same Effect--action pair. We train with more than 20,000 hours of embodied data spanning heterogeneous action representations. We evaluate the Small (8B) configuration on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus , RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2026robotwin , RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 , and RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo , and additionally evaluate the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. The experimental comparisons distinguish these configurations and compare Small (8B) with existing policies. We also examine Action Grounding across multiple baseline models, where it consistently improves performance, supporting its value beyond a single architecture. Our contributions are as follows. Effect: a compact prediction of visual change. We represent future observations relative to a shared current-observation anchor and jointly predict the resulting Effect sequence with executable action chunks. The same Effect--action pair conditions optional video generation, connecting control to visual forecasting without requiring video synthesis at each decision. CaPE: geometry-aware visual transition encoding. We condition endpoint pooling on relative camera pose to account for viewpoint changes across robot and camera configurations. Calibrated and uncalibrated trajectories share the same learned pooling parameters, supporting joint learning from heterogeneous demonstrations. Action Grounding: supervision from measured motion. We make end-effector and gripper changes recoverable from Effect, shaping the visual representation around motion relevant to robot control. Evaluations across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from this objective, indicating that its benefit extends beyond our complete model. Related Work Predictive targets for world--action models. Future video provides a learning signal for control, but different models use that signal at different points in the policy. Video-first policies infer controls from predicted frames du2023learninguniversalpoliciestextguided , while DreamZero jointly generates video and actions ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot . Fast-WAM retains video prediction during training and skips it during action inference yuan2026fastwam . Predicting in a compact feature space offers another way to use future observations. V-JEPA 2.1 learns dense spatiotemporal features through self-supervised video pretraining murlabadia2026vjepa21 . La-JEPA uses a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to define the future features that its policy predicts alongside actions during training clemente2026lajepa . InternW0- uses changes in video features more explicitly. Its Causal Imprint regresses differences between adjacent video latents and aligns intermediate features with future-video features before conditioning a separate action expert miao2026internw0delta . In each case, the feature space used to construct the prediction targets shapes which visual changes the policy is trained to anticipate. Learning representations of visual transitions. Latent-action models learn a representation of the transition itself. LAPA compresses changes between frame pairs into discrete codes that support future-frame reconstruction and uses those codes for policy pretraining ye2025lapa . Subsequent work uses additional signals to emphasize manipulation. WALA learns latent actions by predicting current-anchored changes in pretrained semantic features and estimated depth, then uses its pretrained latent-action encoder to supervise the policy liu2026wala . LAWA uses a tokenizer trained with next-frame reconstruction and manipulation-region masks, then jointly denoises a continuous latent and executable actions li2026lawa . Robot measurements can also shape the representation. WLA encodes synchronized views together with available embodiment-state changes and learns through multimodal reconstruction and consistency across overlapping windows liu2026wla3 . In our method, end-effector and gripper measurements supervise an auxiliary readout from visual feature differences. The observation encoder learns during policy training, and its EMA copy supplies the Effect targets. The resulting Effect is jointly predicted with actions and can also condition a video forecast together with the sampled action chunk. We treat Action Grounding as a distinct supervision mechanism and evaluate its contribution across multiple baseline policies, in addition to evaluating the complete model. Camera geometry in visual transition encoding. A visual transition can reflect both physical interaction and a change in viewpoint. EscherNet introduces camera positional encoding (CaPE) to express relative camera pose in attention, and PRoPE extends relative camera encoding to include camera intrinsics and extrinsics kong2024eschernet,li2025camerasrelative . We use CaPE to provide the Effect encoder with explicit viewpoint information when it pools each endpoint. We express available camera poses relative to the current observation and use the same pooling weights for trajectories with and without reliable extrinsics. Model Design sect:model Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulation At each decision time , the policy observes the available RGB camera views and receives a language instruction . We denote the conditioning information by , where specifies the robot's action representation and specifies the prediction horizons relative to . The model predicts an executable action chunk and an Effect sequence . Each represents the change from the current observation to a requested future time. Actions and Effects are indexed by their respective temporal supports. We denote the latent of the future video by . We model the three variables through the conditional factorization The first factor gives the policy an action chunk and a prediction of the accompanying visual change. The second uses that pair to produce a visual forecast on request. During training, future observations provide the targets for and . The policy conditions its joint Effect--action prediction on the current information in . Architecture Overview sect:overview sec:architecture_overview EffectWAM builds a common observation--language context for both factors in Eq.~ , linking joint Effect--action prediction with conditional video generation (Fig.~ fig:framework ). The task instruction is embedded as text tokens, and a trainable vision transformer (ViT) maps the available current camera views to merged image tokens. SEM receives both sets of tokens, with intermediate visual features injected into early SEM blocks. In parallel, the frozen video VAE encodes the current observation alone. A learned projection maps its latent to visual tokens for GEN. The mixture-of-transformers (MoT) uses masked self-attention to couple SEM and GEN. GEN shares its transformer backbone across Effect, action, and video, with modality-specific input and output projections. It first samples the Effect and action streams jointly. The optional video pass reuses the sampled pair and the original observation context, as detailed in Sec.~ sec:closed_loop_inference . During training, the ViT also supplies pre-merger patch features to the observation endpoint encoder in Sec.~ sec:effect_learning .
