title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $π_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
full_text: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world--action models (WAMs) extend vision--language--action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce , a unified world--actor--critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of- selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75 average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45 for . Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy. Introduction Large-scale learning from demonstrations has enabled robot policies to operate across tasks and embodiments, offering a scalable path toward general-purpose physical intelligence~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_, nvidia2026cosmos3 . Yet imitating actions alone leaves much of the supervision in these demonstrations unused. A demonstration reveals not only which action an expert chose, but also how it changes the world~ wu2024unleashing and how those changes contribute to task success~ zhang2023interpretable . Data collection and policy execution also yield suboptimal trajectories, failed attempts, and unstructured play, which are often underused by imitation-based policies. Exploiting this supervision can help a policy understand both what its actions can change and which factors matter for the task~ liu2023learning . Recent world--action models (WAMs) jointly predict actions and future observations~ bi2025motus,guo2026video , but use this prediction mainly as an auxiliary objective for policy learning. Meanwhile, methods to improve pretrained policies often introduce separately trained world models~ guo2026ctrlworld, zhang2026vlambpo and reward or value models~ lee2026roboreward, wang2026world . For a generalist policy, these models must themselves generalize across the same broad range of tasks and embodiments as the policy~ liang2026robometer . Pretraining them separately at this scale can duplicate computation and relearn overlapping representations. It also keeps the predictive and value objectives from jointly shaping the features the actor uses~ cobbe2021ppg . These observations motivate two questions: Can a single pretraining stage jointly acquire an actor, a world model, and a critic? And can their complementary objectives constrain a shared representation that improves policy learning? We therefore introduce (Fig.~ fig:workflow ), a unified orld-- ctor-- ritic model for dexterous manipulation that learns all three components in a single pretraining stage. To share one representation across these components, we adopt a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture~ liang2025mot that couples a generative world model backbone with a compact actor--critic expert. The backbone encodes the language instruction, current visual observations, and proprioception as a shared prefix of attention keys and values (K/V). During joint training, action-conditioned forward prediction encourages this prefix to capture how an action chunk changes the scene and robot state, while value supervision uses bootstrapped temporal-difference targets to shape the same prefix around progress toward task success. Through action imitation, the actor learns to use these complementary control- and task-relevant features to generate expert action chunks (Fig.~ fig:attention ). To make imagination efficient, we build the world model on an image-editing backbone and align its predictions with the actor's action chunks: it predicts only the visual latent and proprioception at each chunk endpoint rather than intermediate video frames, and these predictions serve as context for the next imagined chunk. After pretraining, we adapt the world model and critic on successful and failed rollouts of the pretrained actor. We then freeze the world backbone and use it to generate imagined experience, on which the critic is further trained for model-based policy optimization~ janner2019mbpo . We instantiate this stage with two methods: PPO~ schulman2017ppo regularized by behavior cloning on expert actions, and critic-guided best-of- (BoN) selection inspired by MAC~ park2026mac , where an action-value critic trained on imagined transitions ranks candidate chunks from the frozen actor. We evaluate DexWAC on two simulation benchmarks, DexJoCo~ wang2026dexjoco and RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 , and on two contact-rich manipulation tasks using a physical dexterous robot. Joint pretraining alone yields a policy that reaches 65.5 success on DexJoCo, compared with 57.9 for ~ intelligence2025pi_ , and the best average success on RoboTwin~2.0 (88.1 ). Its world model achieves the best prediction quality on all six image-quality metrics, reducing wrist-view LPIPS by 38 while running faster than the strongest baseline. Using only 50 executions per task for adaptation, PPO in imagination raises DexJoCo success to 67.8 , surpassing the large-scale pretrained WAMs, and improves bimanual success from 47.8 to 52.9 . On a physical robot, DexWAC outperforms on two contact-rich tasks (50 vs.\ 20 and 100 vs.\ 70 ). Ablations further show that removing either world prediction or value supervision reduces policy success. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose , which jointly trains an actor, a world model, and a critic with shared representations in a single pretraining stage. We evaluate the pretrained policy in two simulations and on two contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks with a physical robot, and demonstrate the benefits of joint supervision through ablations. We adapt the world model and critic to execution data, evaluate world-model accuracy and efficiency, and demonstrate their utility for multi-task policy improvement through imagined PPO and critic-guided BoN. Related Work Unified Foundation Models Unified foundation models learn shared representations across multiple objectives, enabling mutually beneficial transfer. Transfusion~ zhou2025transfusion , Show-o~ xie2025showo , and BAGEL~ deng2025bagel demonstrate the benefits of jointly learning multimodal understanding and generation. Embodied models extend this paradigm to action generation, often leveraging visual generative priors~ guo2026video,zhang2026imagewam . UWM~ zhu2025uwm , Cosmos~3~ nvidia2026cosmos3 , and Motus~ bi2025motus unify understanding, future prediction, and action generation, but primarily use dynamics prediction as auxiliary supervision. LeWAM~ fu2026lewam uses the learned dynamics at test time to evaluate sampled actions, but learns neither rewards nor values. FACT~ peng2026fact and Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos further incorporate value prediction into world--action modeling. However, they supervise value prediction with trajectory-derived normalized progress labels, rather than learning a temporal-difference critic for policy improvement. Shared policy–value representations have also been explored in reinforcement learning (PPG~ cobbe2021ppg ) and language agents liang2026sapo . DexWAC extends this unification to joint learning of action generation, action-conditioned world modeling, reward prediction, and temporal-difference value estimation through shared representations. Policy Improvement for Pretrained Policies Pretrained policies can fail on states poorly covered by their demonstrations, motivating further learning from suboptimal and failed executions. Online RL addresses this gap through environment interaction~ chen2025pirl,wagenmaker2025dsrl , but real-world exploration is slow and costly, especially across multiple tasks and embodiments. Offline RL learns from existing data, but unreliable value estimates can destabilize policy optimization and lead to policy collapse~ kumar2020cql,kostrikov2022iql . V-GPS~ BoN and SeeQ~ singh2026seeq instead learn critics from diverse robot data and use them to rank candidate actions at test time, steering behavior without directly updating the policy. World models offer an alternative by learning environment dynamics and generating imagined experience for policy optimization and value learning~ zhang2026vlambpo,park2026mac,guo2026vlaw, hafner2025dreamerv3 . However, achieving broad dynamics coverage often requires separate world-model pretraining and adaptation, introducing additional training costs~ guo2026ctrlworld . DexWAC instead adapts the dynamics, reward model, and critic learned during joint pretraining and reuses them for policy optimization, reducing the need for a separately trained world model. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Language-conditioned robot control. We formulate robotic manipulation as a language-conditioned MDP , where , , and are the state, action, and instruction spaces, respectively; denotes the transition dynamics, the reward function, the initial-state distribution, and the discount factor. Given state and instruction , the policy samples an action chunk . The objective is to maximize the expected discounted return: where is the instruction distribution, is the episode length, and is the reward at step . Method sec:method DexWAC proceeds in three stages (Fig.~ fig:workflow ). Joint pretraining learns, from the same demonstrations, an actor for action generation, a world model for predicting the visual and proprioceptive consequences of actions, and a critic for state-value estimation (Sec.~ sec:pretrain ). Next, we adapt the world model and critic on real rollouts of the pretrained actor, so that they remain accurate on the states the policy actually visits (Sec.~ sec:adapt ). Finally, the adapted components improve control, either by updating the actor in imagination or by ranking its proposals (Sec.~ sec:imagine ). Hyperparameters and implementation details are given in Appendix~ app:hyperparameters . Learning to Act, Predict, and Evaluate sec:pretrain We design the pretraining stage so that one representation serves acting, predicting, and evaluating. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture~ liang2025mot couples a generative world backbone with a compact actor--critic expert (Fig.~ fig:architecture ). The backbone encodes the context of instruction, visual latents ~ rombach2022high , and proprioceptive state, and the expert reads its keys and values (K/V). The two thus share features through attention but keep separate weights, which limits interference with the backbone's pretrained visual priors~ deng2025bagel . Two choices make the backbone a complete simulator for imagination. First, given and an action chunk, it predicts only the visual latent and proprioceptive state at the chunk endpoint ~ park2026mac , so each imagined step needs a single prediction. Second, it predicts reward and continuation from the reached state, so each imagined transition, including its feedback, comes entirely from the world model

title: DiffGR00T: Execution-Aware Differentiable Training for Humanoid Whole-Body Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Conference preprint. Corresponding author: Hesheng Wang
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.
full_text: DiffGR00T teaser. The VLA action head is updated while SONIC and the world model are frozen; the world model replaces the simulator during training. Simulation-only average task success rises from 59.2 to 71.7 . fig:teaser Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2 71.7 ), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made remarkable progress in arm-centric manipulation, where predicted end-effector poses or joint-space targets can be executed through low-level servo controllers black2024pi0,chen2026dial . Extending these capabilities to humanoid robots, however, introduces fundamentally different control challenges. Unlike fixed-base manipulators, humanoids exhibit underactuated floating-base dynamics in which locomotion, manipulation, and posture regulation must be coordinated under changing contact and balance constraints. Directly predicting joint targets does not guarantee stable whole-body execution, while learning high-frequency stabilization directly inside a large VLA remains difficult. Consequently, many humanoid systems adopt a hierarchical architecture in which a VLA generates high-level motion intentions and a pretrained behavior foundation model (BFM) or whole-body controller realizes them through proprioceptive feedback. This hierarchical paradigm has driven substantial progress in humanoid loco-manipulation. SONIC establishes a generalizable whole-body motion foundation through a shared latent interface, while systems such as WholeBodyVLA and OpenHLM pair task-conditioned action generation with pretrained motion controllers luo2025sonic,jiang2025wholebodyvla,hu2026openhlm . Because these architectures train the VLA to emit motion references and the controller to track them independently, the controller provides reactive whole-body stabilization at deployment, yet an action--execution training gap remains: tracking and balance errors have no direct gradient path back into the VLA's motion-generation objective. Closing this gap via end-to-end differentiable training requires establishing a differentiable gradient pathway across the policy--controller interface. Bridging this gap is non-trivial because robust whole-body control and differentiable optimization have traditionally followed separate training paradigms. Humanoid motion trackers are commonly trained with model-free reinforcement learning, where physical execution feedback arrives as scalar rewards rather than differentiable state transitions. Moreover, contact-rich humanoid dynamics involve non-smooth support switches, making direct differentiation through conventional rigid-body simulators numerically brittle and computationally expensive. Although differentiable physics methods such as DiffMimic have explored analytical motion-imitation gradients ren2023diffmimic , scaling such optimization to high-dimensional whole-body control and large VLA generators remains computationally prohibitive. An alternative to differentiating through the simulator is to differentiate through a learned world model. Fitted to state transitions collected from the simulator or the robot, an action-conditioned neural world model is differentiable everywhere---including across contact transitions---allowing execution objectives to be backpropagated through predicted states without invoking a contact solver, while short rollout windows bound compounding prediction error. SuperMimic~ liao2026supermimic demonstrates this paradigm for humanoid tracking by training a tracking policy with short-horizon backpropagation through time (BPTT) on a learned world model, and in a velocity-tracking experiment further routes gradients through a shared decoder into a lightweight goal encoder. Extending this execution-gradient pathway across a frozen token-conditioned controller and a multi-step flow-matching sampler into a humanoid VLA, however, remains largely unexplored. We present DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T~N1.7 with the pretrained SONIC behavior foundation model. We first fine-tune the GR00T~N1.7 action head on HumanoidArena demonstrations carrying recorded SONIC motion tokens~ nvidia2026groot,wang2026humanoidarena to align the VLA with SONIC's latent motion interface. During execution-aware differentiable training, a learned action-conditioned world model supplies multi-step state transitions to evaluate a body-execution loss, allowing execution gradients to propagate through the world model, the frozen SONIC decoder, and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. Our mechanism exploits the temporal structure of the VLA's action chunks. The flow-matching VLA generates a 40-step motion-token sequence, of which the first 20 tokens are executed in closed loop. At each 50\,Hz control step, the frozen SONIC decoder maps the current token and proprioceptive history to 29 joint targets, and the world model predicts the resulting robot state, which is fed back as proprioception for the next step. Multi-step body-execution losses are then backpropagated through a ten-step rollout window, the frozen decoder, and the four-step flow-matching sampler to update only the VLA action head (via LoRA adapters and the output projection), while the world model and the training-only critic remain fixed throughout. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T raises average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2 71.7 ). Our main contributions are as follows: A differentiable world model for whole-body execution. We learn an action-conditioned dynamics model for a 29-DoF humanoid from controller-excitation replay and a small amount of closed-loop policy data, holding its parameters fixed during execution-aware differentiable training to serve as a differentiable surrogate for the simulator over short rollouts. Execution gradients into a flow-matching VLA. We backpropagate multi-step body-execution losses through the learned world model, the frozen SONIC decoder, and the four-step flow-matching sampler to update the VLA action head, while keeping the vision-language backbone, controller, world model, and training-only critic fixed. Execution-aligned supervision. We identify the key supervision terms required for effective humanoid execution feedback---root position and drift to curb per-window drift, transition-frame weighting for task-phase changes, and speed-coverage window sampling to retain locomotion in the gradient budget---calibrated to maintain scale consistency across objectives. Related Work sec:related Flow-Matching Policies and Policy Improvement sec:related_fm combines a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert to generate continuous action chunks black2024pi0 . Building on this paradigm, recent work explores alternative gradient pathways for supervised policy learning: DIAL links the VLM and a reactive action expert through predicted visual intent, backpropagating the supervised flow-matching loss through this latent intent into trainable VLM components during joint fine-tuning chen2026dial ; VITA, a visuomotor policy mapping image encodings to latent actions, differentiates a supervised action-reconstruction loss directly through the Euler steps of the flow-matching ODE solver gao2025vita . A complementary line of research incorporates robot execution experience into flow-matching policy updates. RECAP fits a value function to execution rollouts and conditions supervised VLA updates on value-derived advantage indicators pi2025recap , whereas Q-VGM learns an action-chunk critic from rollout rewards and converts critic gradients with respect to denoised action chunks into local velocity targets, avoiding backpropagation through the full denoising trajectory wang2026qvgm . While these methods leverage ODE differentiation, advantage conditioning, or value guidance, none propagates a multi-step body-execution objective through a whole-body controller and learned action-conditioned dynamics into the flow-matching generator. Humanoid Whole-Body Action Generation and Control sec:related_humanoid Humanoid loco-manipulation systems span diverse interfaces between high-level action generation and low-level control. SONIC learns a generalizable whole-body motion tracker from motion-capture data and demonstrates VLA-driven loco-manipulation with GR00T N1.5 through a shared motion-token interface luo2025sonic . HumanoidArena benchmarks hierarchical policy--tracker pairings and documents a direct prediction mode in which a VLA outputs 64-dimensional SONIC body latents wang2026humanoidarena , providing the interface and benchmark setting adopted in this work. Other hierarchical frameworks rely on different intermediate representations: WholeBodyVLA learns locomotion and manipulation latents from action-free egocentric video and decodes them into upper-body joint targets alongside locomotion commands executed by a reinforcement-learning controller jiang2025wholebodyvla , while OpenHLM combines joint-space teleoperation with heterogeneous data co-training to generate whole-body joint references tracked by an independent low-level policy hu2026openhlm . Beyond single-stage reference generation, HAF-VLA produces cumulative whole-body commands via stage-wise flow matching and cross-stage conditioning, with existing reinforcement-learning controllers executing locomotion and waist commands gu2026hafvla . Departing from explicit reference tracking, SENTINEL clones a simulator-trained whole-body controller into a language-and-proprioception policy that predicts low-level action targets directly, then freezes that policy and trains a residual action head with PPO wang2025sentinel . Across these interfaces---shared motion tokens, joint-space references, staged commands, and direct low-level targets---execution discrepancies are absorbed by downstream trackers or a separate residual head rather than backpropagated through the controller to update the high-level VLA generator. Differentiable Whole-Body Control and Execution-Aware Learning sec:related_diff Propagating physical execution gradients directly into policy learning has progressed from differentiable physics to learned dynamics surrogates. DiffMimic trains a humanoid motion-tracking policy by differentiating imitation losses through a differentiable rigid-body simulator ren2023diffmimic . To avoid differentiating through contact solvers, ControlVAE optimizes task policies for simulated characters by backpropagating task losses through a frozen latent skill controller and a learned world model yao2022controlvae . MoConVQ similarly uses a learned world model to train discrete motion representations and their decoder, while training its text-conditioned generator separately via token prediction yao2024moconvq . Closest to our humanoid setting are SuperMimic and HWAM. SuperMimic fits a differentiable world

title: AG-WAM: Attention-Guided World Action Model for Accurate and Efficient Robot Manipulation
summary: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module. Without any external plugin module adopted, our end-to-end framework with the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance boosts the accuracy and efficiency of WAMs. Without using any private embodied training data, our AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple public robotic manipulation benchmarks including LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency.
full_text: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module. Without any external plugin module adopted, our end-to-end framework with the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance boosts the accuracy and efficiency of WAMs. Without using any private embodied training data, our AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple public robotic manipulation benchmarks including LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency. Introduction sec:intro World models for robotics aim to predict how the physical world evolves in response to an agent’s actions. Building on this foundation, World Action Models~ wang2026wam,zhu2025uwm,ye2026dreamzero jointly model future visual observations and robot actions to support precise and robust robotic control. Compared with policies that directly map observations and task instructions to actions, WAMs incorporate an additional visual prediction objective to capture dynamics and temporal dependencies relevant to control, providing predictive context for action generation. However, achieving accurate control meanwhile maintaining inference efficiency remains challenging. Attention plays a central role in WAMs by determining how action stream accesses visual observations and task instructions. In existing WAMs~ ye2026dreamzero,bi2026motus,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam , however, attention allocation is typically learned implicitly, and action stream may attend to visual regions or text tokens with limited relevance to the current execution stage. This observation motivates us to introduce explicit attention guidance toward action-relevant visual and language context. To this end, we propose Attention-Guided WAM, an end-to-end framework that incorporates explicit attention guidance for action generation. AG-WAM provides unified attention guidance centered on action-relevant information by selectively allocating attention to informative video tokens, directing visual attention toward interaction-relevant regions, and guiding instruction attention according to the evolving execution state. Accordingly, we propose three plug-and-play explicit attention guidance modules. The Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention (CAPA) module uses spatiotemporal information from the observed video history to predict video token retention indices for the next chunk. By restricting subsequent video token processing to the retained subset, CAPA allocates attention to task-relevant information meanwhile reducing computational burden. The Guidance-Point Visual Attention (GPVA) module infers guidance points from visual observation, task context, and robot proprioception. GPVA incorporates complementary 2D appearance and 3D geometric priors into visual attention, guiding action tokens to attend to interaction-relevant visual regions. The State-Conditioned Text Attention (SCTA) module explicitly guides instruction attention toward relevant text segments based on the evolving execution state, in which a state-dependent semantic condition is first produced, then used to integrate relevant instruction information into action features through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM)~ perez2018film . Overall, built on the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance, our proposed AG-WAM integrates the CAPA, GPVA, and SCTA modules, providing complementary attention guidance that explicitly directs attention toward action-relevant information, unleashing strong capabilities of WAMs, and ultimately achieving accurate and efficient action generation. We evaluate AG-WAM on three public robotic manipulation benchmarks: LIBERO-X~ wang2026liberox , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus , and RoboTwin-2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 . Without using any private embodied training data, AG-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three benchmarks with success rates of , , and respectively, outperforming other methods by a notable margin, meanwhile delivering a inference speedup. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance. Our contributions are as follows: We address the problem of implicit attention allocation in WAMs. To this end, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle to unleash strong capabilities of WAMs. Formally, we propose AG-WAM, an end-to-end framework for accurate and efficient action generation, without any external plugin module adopted. We propose three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: CAPA predicts token retention guiding attention to select video tokens most informative for action generation; GPVA directs visual attention toward interaction-relevant regions using 2D appearance and 3D geometric priors; SCTA guides instruction attention based on the evolving execution state. AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on three public benchmarks, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency. Related Work sec:related_work World Action Models sec:related_wam Different from Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) policies that map observations to actions~ brohan2023rt2, kim2025openvlaoft, team2024octo, black2024pi0 , WAMs jointly model forward visual dynamics and action generation to capture physical foresight~ wang2026wam . Existing architectures generally follow two paradigms: Cascade WAMs first synthesize future frames~ du2023unipi, bharadhwaj2024gen2act , intermediate diffusion features~ hu2024vpp , or visual goals~ pi2026pi07 before decoding actions; Joint WAMs co-optimize video prediction and action generation within a shared network via autoregression~ wu2024gr1, cheang2024gr2, cen2025worldvla , predictive inverse dynamics~ tian2025seer , unified diffusion or flow-matching~ guo2024pad, li2025uva, zhu2025uwm, bi2026motus, xiang2026motubrain, li2026lingbotva, zhang2026lingbotva2 , and representation alignment~ qiu2026agra . Recent works augment robot manipulation pretraining with web-scale egocentric videos to model physical dynamics and latent actions~ wang2023mimicplay, gao2026dreamdojo, ye2025lapa . However, corresponding representations may entangle with complex generalizations of multi-modal context. To improve the capability or efficiency of WAMs, recent works mainly pursue through external avenues: attaching external multi-modal reasoners~ zhao2025cotvla, tang2026adawam, lin2026worldpilot , which correspondingly introduces the high latency and distributional mismatch with low-level control; or bypassing the test-time video generation~ li2025uva, yuan2026fastwam, ma2026fasterwam, ye2026gigaworld . Attention Guidance sec:related_attention Selection. To reduce redundancy, a few WAMs rely on fixed-stride temporal downsampling~ bi2026motus, ye2026gigaworld that ignores spatial foreground-background differences. Meanwhile, token pruning and merging in VLA~ chen2024fastv, xu2026vlacache, yang2026efficientvla and video diffusion~ bolya2023tomesd, xi2025sparsevideogen, xia2025adaspa are agnostic to future action generation, limiting access to task-relevant information. Guidance. Prior manipulation policies inject spatial cues by querying external VLMs for 2D keypoints or constraints~ yuan2024robopoint, fang2024moka, huang2024rekep , overlaying visual markers onto RGB inputs~ nasiriany2025rtaffordance, zheng2025tracevla , or adding static 3D encodings~ qu2025spatialvla . However, these methods rely on slow external two-stage VLMs or extra input augmentations. Conditioning. Action stream accesses multi-modal context either indiscriminately~ pi2026pi07, hu2024vpp or through predefined attention masks~ liang2024mot, zhu2025uwm, bi2026motus, li2026lingbotva, yuan2026fastwam . However, these methods lack explicit guidance to adapt instruction attention to the evolving execution state. title: PoseVLN: Learning Geometric State Evolution for Vision-Language Navigation
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures, including appendix. Project page: https://houpengyu123.github.io/PoseVLN/
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to relate past experience, current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions. Recent approaches improve these capabilities through long-horizon memory, state-aware reasoning, and future prediction, yet these components are often modeled separately, leaving navigation state evolution insufficiently connected across time. We argue that camera pose provides a natural geometric representation for bridging past, present, and future states. Based on this insight, we propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that jointly learns navigation decisions and geometric state evolution. PoseVLN organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame, and jointly predicts the next K navigation actions together with a local $Δ$Pose over the same horizon. The predicted $Δ$Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is recursively propagated throughout navigation, forming a continuous geometric state evolution from past memory to future motion. Experiments on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric state evolution, with PoseVLN outperforming the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate, respectively, using only single RGB observations.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and navigate to a target by interpreting visual observations and taking appropriate actions. Recent advances have extended VLN beyond direct instruction and observation matching, with increasing attention to memory, spatial reasoning, and predictive modeling. Memory-based approaches preserve information from previous observations and decisions~ wei2025streamvln,song2025towards,zhang2025mapnav,xue2026profocus,liu2026memvln , while state-aware and geometric methods support navigation through progress reasoning, structured scene representations, or explicit spatial features~ wang2026progress,wang2026dynam3d,li2026bridging,zhang2025mapnav,xue2026profocus . Predictive approaches further anticipate future actions, observations, landmarks, or latent dynamics before execution~ yao2025navmorph,dai2026history,huang2026wnm,xu2025navq,wang2026monodream,wang2026think,zhang2026futurenav . Together, these directions highlight the importance of relating past experience, the current navigation context, and future motion. Despite these advances, two aspects of spatial modeling remain insufficiently addressed. First, past and current observations are not necessarily anchored in an explicit common spatial reference. Retrieving a relevant memory therefore does not by itself establish its viewpoint's position and orientation relative to the agent, leaving this relationship to be inferred for spatial decision-making. Second, future prediction does not necessarily specify an explicit geometric transition of the navigation state. Anticipated actions or visual content can guide action selection without providing an updated position and orientation for subsequent decisions. These gaps motivate a common geometric representation that explicitly relates past observations to the current state and describes how that state changes over the upcoming action horizon. Camera pose provides a compact representation for addressing both needs. A trajectory-level pose specifies the position and orientation of the camera in a shared coordinate frame, associating each past and current observation with the spatial state from which it was acquired. Relative poses between these observations then make their spatial relationships explicit. For future motion, a local pose change describes the translation and rotation over the upcoming action horizon. Composing this change with the current pose yields a future pose in the same coordinate frame, allowing the resulting state to be carried forward and associated with subsequent observations. Together, trajectory-level poses and local pose changes provide a common geometric description of past observations, the current viewpoint, and future motion. We refer to this continual maintenance and update of the agent's spatial state as geometric state evolution . Based on this insight, we introduce PoseVLN , a pose-aware VLN framework that explicitly models navigation as geometric state evolution in a trajectory-level coordinate space. We define the first observation as the origin of an episode-relative coordinate system and associate each subsequent visual observation in memory with a trajectory-level pose state, allowing past observations and the current state to be organized within a common spatial reference. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:intro , given the instruction, current observation, visual memory, and their associated pose states, PoseVLN jointly predicts the next navigation actions and a local Pose that describes the geometric state transition over the same action horizon. The predicted Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is stored back into memory and reused in subsequent navigation. During training, ground-truth trajectory poses provide supervision for geometric state transitions. At inference, PoseVLN operates solely on a monocular RGB stream, without depth or external odometry. The first observation is assigned the identity pose to define the episode-relative frame. No ground-truth pose is used, and all subsequent pose states are recursively predicted by the model. Our main contributions are three-fold: We propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that models geometric state evolution through joint action and local Pose prediction, recursively propagating poses without step-wise ground-truth pose or odometry at inference. We demonstrate strong performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, showing that geometric state evolution improves long-horizon navigation using only monocular RGB observations. We conduct comprehensive ablations and pose evaluations to analyze the relationship between pose estimation and navigation, providing new insights into their interplay. Related Work sec:related_work Memory and State-Aware Navigation Video-based approaches such as NaVid~ zhang2024navid and Uni-NaVid~ zhang2024uni demonstrate the effectiveness of VLM/VLA models for continuous navigation. To support longer horizons, StreamVLN~ wei2025streamvln combines fast short-term context with slow-updating compressed memory, while Towards Long-Horizon VLN~ song2025towards introduces multi-granularity dynamic memory. MapNav~ zhang2025mapnav , ProFocus~ xue2026profocus , MemVLN~ liu2026memvln , and JanusVLN~ zeng2026janusvln further improve memory utilization through semantic maps, selective reasoning, episodic/procedural memory, or decoupled semantic--spatial memory. Complementarily, Dynam3D~ wang2026dynam3d constructs hierarchical 3D representations from posed RGB-D observations, GA-VLN~ yang2026ga uses depth and camera poses to build geometry-aware bird's-eye-view representations, and Progress-Think~ wang2026progress models semantic instruction progress from observation memory. Beyond VLN, Cambrian-P~ yang2026cambrian highlights camera pose as a geometric signal for relating observations across viewpoints. Predictive and World-Model-Based Navigation Predictive approaches anticipate future outcomes to support navigation decisions. NavMorph~ yao2025navmorph models latent environmental dynamics for foresighted planning, while NavQ~ xu2025navq estimates the future prospects of candidate actions. MonoDream~ wang2026monodream predicts current and future panoramic cues from monocular observations, while SpaAct~ li2026spaact learns action-conditioned visual transitions through future-frame selection. WNM-3D~ huang2026wnm further couples future-view prediction with navigation actions under geometry-aware scene representations. LatentPilot~ hao2026latentpilot incorporates latent visual reasoning to anticipate future scene information for navigation. These methods support navigation through future prediction and structured scene representations. PoseVLN focuses on explicitly propagating a camera-pose state: trajectory-level poses associate past and current observations within a shared coordinate frame, while local Pose specifies the state transition over the predicted action horizon. Method sec:method Framework Overview. We propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework built upon StreamVLN under the single-RGB streaming setting. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:framework , pose-aware memory associates observations with camera poses in a shared episode-relative coordinate frame, where poses are encoded into embeddings and inserted alongside the corresponding visual tokens. Conditioned on these inputs and the instruction, the VLM produces a shared representation for jointly predicting the next navigation actions and a local Pose over the same horizon. title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
comment: 27 pages. Project page: https://sim-pwm.pages.dev Code: https://github.com/TingtingLiao/SimPWM
summary: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro [t] 0.485 0.485 Action-conditioned video world models take an observation and a sequence of robot actions and render the future~ yang2024unisim,agarwal2025cosmos,zhu2024irasim . They must follow the actions strictly: the arm must move exactly as commanded, an object may move only when the gripper grasps it, and it must stay where it is released. To this end they are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, such as the commanded robot rendered from its model~ kim2026rofacto , a 4D occupancy sequence~ yang2026orv , structural controls such as depth~ nvidia2025cosmostransfer or a physics simulation~ liu2024physgen,li2025wonderplay , on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. does so: with the simulated cup frozen while the arm moves as recorded, one video model leaves the cup in place, as the proxy does, and another still lifts it. Such a proxy also combines the strengths of the two current kinds of models, which fail in opposite ways ( ). End-to-end video world models~ zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld,agarwal2025cosmos focus mostly on visual quality: their frames look realistic, but they often do not follow the actions. The arm drifts from the commanded trajectory, and grasped objects split, stay behind or dissolve. Because the consequence is never represented, these errors are hard to detect or correct. Simulators compute the consequences from kinematics and contact, but they need a scene. A scene rebuilt from a real image, by hand, automatically~ ranawaka2026simfoundry or by agents~ chen2026agentic , does not match it exactly, and a few centimetres decide whether a grasp succeeds; rigid-body physics also mishandles ropes and cloth, and the rendered video does not look real. We combine the two into a model that returns two outputs: a realistic video from a video model, and an explicit state of what the actions cause, from a simulator, that the video can be tested against. What moves where (the arm, the grasped object and where it goes) depends mainly on coarse geometry and the commanded motion, which a simple simulator computes explicitly. How it looks, from appearance and shadows to how a rope or a cloth hangs ( ), depends on fine physics and appearance, which video models learn well from data. Accordingly, we credit arm following to the robot rendering, which prior work also uses~ kim2026rofacto , and evaluate the simulator only on what it adds: which object moves, and whether the video follows it. Our model, SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model), is built on this split ( ). From the first frame it separates the scene into three parts, the robot as its 3D model, the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points, and the background (real-to-sim); a simple simulator moves the robot and the objects under the actions with explicit rules for grasp, carry, release and gravity ( ); and the simulated scene is rendered per frame as a proxy: the first frame, with the robot and every moved object redrawn where the simulator puts them. A video model that takes a reference video, fine-tuned to render such proxies, turns them into a realistic video (sim-to-real); we instantiate it with three base models, MiniMax-H3, LTX-2.3 and Cosmos-Transfer~2.5. The proxy pins down the arm whatever the base model, more closely than end-to-end models, but the rendered robot alone does this; the simulated objects add the pick-ups that the robot alone misses. [t] 0.6 Unlike the arm, the object state is followed only by some base models ( ): with the simulated objects frozen, MiniMax-H3 mostly leaves the object in place, even without fine-tuning, whereas LTX-2.3 lifts it as if inferring the grasp from the arm motion. With any base model, the simulated state is returned as an explicit record of what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state. What the simulator adds is that whether the video follows the objects can be tested by perturbing the simulation, a test that end-to-end models, having no simulated state, do not admit. Three choices make this work without training the simulator: (i) objects are point sets lifted from the first frame, without categories or CAD models, so the scene matches the image by construction; (ii) the actions correct perception, since an object the gripper closes on must lie at the gripper's depth; and (iii) robot-specific knowledge enters only through a configuration file, so the same pipeline runs on single-arm and bimanual robots. Contributions. (i) A real-to-sim-to-real world model that returns a realistic video together with an explicit state of what the actions cause, simulated at test time from the first frame; under perturbed actions the state reveals videos that ignore it. (ii) A class-agnostic, image-aligned point-set scene whose depth is corrected by the commanded gripper closure, so that carried objects are placed more accurately. (iii) Perturbation and frozen-object tests showing that every base model follows the rendered arm, whereas the simulated object state is followed only by a base model whose prior favours the reference video (MiniMax-H3); against a robot-only proxy, the simulated objects reduce missed pick-ups by points ( ) and account for points ( ) of the drop under frozen objects. (iv) An evaluation on DROID episodes from unseen setups against end-to-end video world models and a learned 3D world model. SimPWM also runs on WorldArena and is compared with an agentic real-to-sim pipeline in the appendix. Related Work sec:related Robot world models. Action-conditioned video generators serve as learned simulators for games and robots~ finn2016unsupervised,ebert2018visualforesight,ha2018worldmodels,hafner2023dreamerv3,wu2022daydreamer,bruce2024genie,valevski2025gamengen,yang2024unisim,du2023unipi,ko2024avdc,wu2024ivideogpt,zhu2024irasim,agarwal2025cosmos,liao2026memorizon . For manipulation, Ctrl-World and WorldGym roll out and rank policies~ guo2025ctrlworld,quevedo2026worldgym , RoboScape adds depth and keypoint objectives~ shang2025roboscape , EnerVerse-AC projects end-effector actions into the image~ jiang2025enerverseac , and DreamDojo pretrains on human video with latent actions~ gao2026dreamdojo . These models are trained end to end, so the effect of an action is implicit in the weights. Other models learn how the 3D scene moves, as particles, scene flow, point flows or voxel latents~ whitney2024hdvpd,guo2025flowdreamer,huang2026pointworld,wang2026worldsim3d ; SimPWM computes it with rules that need no training (we compare with PointWorld in and~ sec:exp_render ). Physics and proxies for video generation. Closest to our approach ( ) are methods that drive a video generator with a physics simulation of a single image~ liu2024physgen,li2025wonderplay ; SimPWM shares this split but simulates a robot: its inputs are joint and gripper commands, it decides grasps rather than applying forces, and it needs no material estimation. Video can also be rendered from structural conditions such as label maps, depth, edges or masks~ wang2018vid2vid,mallya2020worldconsistent,zhang2023controlnet,esser2023gen1,wang2023videocomposer,guo2024sparsectrl,nvidia2025cosmostransfer,li2025manipdreamer or 3D tracking videos~ gu2025das , for robots from 4D occupancy~ yang2026orv or a render of the commanded robot~ kim2026rofacto . These conditions are given, extracted from a reference video, or cover only the robot; in SimPWM they are simulated at test time from the first frame and the actions, so they encode what the actions do to objects. Our robot-only proxy is the closest analogue of RoFacto ( and~ sec:evaluator ). Real-to-sim. Evaluating policies in simulation requires matching the simulated scene to the real one~ li2024simpler . Agentic Real2Sim turns a DROID recording into a MuJoCo twin with vision-language agents~ chen2026agentic ; others build scenes or objects from videos or scans~ torne2024rialto,ranawaka2026simfoundry,jiang2025phystwin,yu2025r2r2r . These need recorded videos or scans, and their scenes need not match the image; SimPWM lifts an image-aligned point set from the first frame, poses the robot with MuJoCo~ todorov2012mujoco , and leaves appearance to the video model. title: Sparse Poison, Strong Hijack: Efficient Trajectory-Level Backdoors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Only 1\% Poisoning
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, including supplementary material. Simin Huang and Jiawei Chen contributed equally. Code: https://github.com/vla-attack/Sparse_Poison_Strong_Hijack
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than behavior-disrupting attacks: rather than merely causing task failures or local action deviations, they must sustain closed-loop redirection to complete an attacker-specified multi-step task. To reliably induce such behaviors, existing methods typically rely on high poisoning rates to obtain sufficient target-trajectory supervision. However, high poisoning rates may compromise clean-task performance, whereas low rates leave target-trajectory supervision scarce and backdoor learning vulnerable to interference from dominant clean-task updates. To resolve this trade-off at low poisoning rates, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action. Stage I freezes the policy and uses differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision to optimize a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale, strengthening trigger-target associations from limited poisoned demonstrations. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II applies source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to decouple clean and backdoor updates and mitigate their interference, followed by learned column-wise calibration and analytic fusion into a unified policy. Experiments on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, $π_0$, and $π_{0.5}$ across four LIBERO suites show consistent gains over all evaluated attack baselines. With only 1% poisoned data, our method achieves 86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial. Real-robot trials also demonstrate trajectory-level hijacking.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than behavior-disrupting attacks: rather than merely causing task failures or local action deviations, they must sustain closed-loop redirection to complete an attacker-specified multi-step task. To reliably induce such behaviors, existing methods typically rely on high poisoning rates to obtain sufficient target-trajectory supervision. However, high poisoning rates may compromise clean-task performance, whereas low rates leave target-trajectory supervision scarce and backdoor learning vulnerable to interference from dominant clean-task updates. To resolve this trade-off at low poisoning rates, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action. Stage I freezes the policy and uses differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision to optimize a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale, strengthening trigger--target associations from limited poisoned demonstrations. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II applies source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to decouple clean and backdoor updates and mitigate their interference, followed by learned column-wise calibration and analytic fusion into a unified policy. Experiments on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, , and across four LIBERO suites show consistent gains over all evaluated attack baselines. With only 1 poisoned data, our method achieves 86.4 target success and 95.2 clean-task success on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial. Real-robot trials also demonstrate trajectory-level hijacking.Our code is available at . Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable physical-world robotic manipulation by mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Representative models, including OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla , OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft , ~ black2025pi0 , and ~ black2025pi05 , demonstrate strong manipulation capabilities and generalization potential across manipulation tasks. However, their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to data poisoning and backdoor attacks during training and fine-tuning. Of particular concern, backdoors that hijack entire manipulation trajectories may induce unintended multi-step behaviors, potentially causing equipment damage, economic losses, or threats to human safety. Existing VLA backdoor attacks can be broadly categorized by their objectives into behavior-disrupting and trajectory-level targeted attacks. The former have received considerable attention, with BadVLA~ zhou2025badvla , FlowHijack~ an2026flowhijack , and DropVLA~ xu2026dropvla exploring task disruption and malicious action manipulation. In contrast, GoBA~ zhou2025goba and BackdoorVLA-VT~ li2025attackvla pursue goal-directed trajectory hijacking, where a trigger redirects the robot toward an attacker-specified task, such as picking up and placing a cup instead of the instructed bowl. Unlike isolated failures or local action deviations, completing such a task requires sustained behavioral redirection across multiple closed-loop stages, making reliable attacks substantially harder. This need for sustained control across successive action steps intensifies the trade-off among poisoning rate, attack reliability, and clean-task performance in trajectory-level hijacking. As Fig.~ fig:overview (a,b) shows, increasing the poisoning rate improves existing attacks' target success rate (TSR), but often at the expense of clean success rate (CSR). At low poisoning rates, attacks face two fundamental bottlenecks. First, scarce target-trajectory supervision weakens trigger--target associations, making it difficult to learn reliable multi-step redirection. Second, interference from dominant clean-task updates hinders backdoor learning: in conventional mixed training, clean demonstrations dominate shared parameter updates, and conflicting clean and backdoor gradients can further suppress learning from rare poisoned samples, as confirmed by our preliminary gradient analysis in Fig.~ fig:gradient_conflict (a). To address these complementary bottlenecks, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action, targeting reliable trajectory-level hijacking under sparse poisoning while preserving clean-task performance. Figure~ fig:overview (c,d) contrasts our approach with fixed-trigger, shared-update training, while Fig.~ fig:framework details the two-stage optimization pipeline. Stage I performs trigger efficacy optimization: with the VLA policy frozen, it optimizes a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale through differentiable rendering under joint visual-attention, language, and action guidance. This strengthens trigger--target trajectory associations without increasing the poisoning budget. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II performs conflict-aware dual-LoRA adaptation to mitigate interference during backdoor learning. Clean and poisoned demonstrations selectively update separate serial LoRA adapters, while both remain active in the forward pass. Together with clean-reference gradient projection correcting conflicting Trigger-LoRA updates, this decoupling protects learning from scarce poisoned demonstrations against dominant clean-task updates. Learned column-wise coefficients calibrate the Trigger-LoRA transformation before both adapters are analytically fused into a unified dense VLA policy. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose multimodal 3D trigger optimization to jointly refine the trigger's texture, translation, and scale under visual, language, and action guidance, strengthening trigger efficacy at low poisoning rates. We introduce source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation with clean-reference gradient projection and column-wise calibrated fusion, decoupling clean and backdoor parameter updates to mitigate optimization interference between objectives and improve attack effectiveness under sparse poisoning while preserving clean-task performance. With only 1 poisoned data, our method achieves 78.2 average TSR across four VLA models and four LIBERO suites, surpassing the strongest baseline by 62.7 percentage points (pp) with the smallest clean-task degradation. Real-robot trials further demonstrate sustained trajectory-level hijacking, highlighting the risks of sparse malicious demonstrations to VLA behavioral integrity. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models sec:related_vla Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models learn instruction-conditioned robot control from demonstrations, enabling policies to map multimodal observations and language instructions into executable actions. Early work explored vision--language knowledge transfer through action tokenization (RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt2 ) and large-scale cross-embodiment training (Open X-Embodiment~ openx2024 ), establishing foundations for general-purpose robotic manipulation. Recent VLA models differ substantially in their action representations and prediction mechanisms. OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla predicts discretized actions autoregressively, whereas OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft adopts continuous action chunks and parallel decoding to improve manipulation efficiency. ~ black2025pi0 generates continuous actions through flow matching, while ~ black2025pi05 further enhances generalization through heterogeneous training data. These architectural differences influence how policies represent and execute multi-step manipulation behaviors. Nevertheless, all four models rely on demonstration-based learning, exposing their training and adaptation processes to potentially poisoned data. This shared dependency motivates our cross-architecture evaluation of trajectory-level backdoor risks, spanning both discrete and continuous action generation. Attacks on VLA Models sec:related_attacks Attacks on VLA models fall into inference-time perturbations and training-time backdoors. Related work examines decision-level attacks on LLM-based embodied agents~ liu2024exploring , LLM jailbreaking~ chen2025autobreach , and reasoning-model red teaming~ chen2026red . Inference-time attacks manipulate observations or instructions during deployment without modifying parameters. Methods exploit adversarial visual patches~ wang2025vlaattacks,xu2025edpa,lu2026uparfas , text~ jones2025robogcg , or 3D object textures~ chen2026tex3d,dai2026unitexture . These approaches expose vulnerabilities to manipulated inputs, but differ from backdoors embedded during policy adaptation. Training-time backdoors associate specific triggers with malicious behaviors through poisoned demonstrations, allowing policies to behave normally on clean inputs while deviating when triggered. Existing attacks induce task failures, action manipulation, or stealthy trajectory deviations~ zhou2025badvla,an2026flowhijack,guo2026statebackdoor,xu2026dropvla,xu2026silentdrift . Unlike such disruptions, trajectory-level targeted backdoors require sustained redirection to complete an attacker-specified manipulation task. Such completion entails coherent approach, grasp, transport, and placement across multiple closed-loop control stages. GoBA~ zhou2025goba and BackdoorVLA-VT~ li2025attackvla pursue goal-directed trajectory hijacking, yet reliable completion remains difficult under sparse poisoning: scarce supervision weakens trigger--target associations, while dominant clean-task updates interfere with backdoor learning. Their use of fixed triggers and shared parameter updates motivates optimizing both the trigger and adaptation process. Related to our second stage, ATAAT~ chen2026ataat addresses gradient conflicts through feature orthogonalization or parameter isolation. In contrast, our framework combines differentiable multimodal 3D trigger optimization with source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation, conflict-aware updates, and calibrated fusion, targeting reliable trajectory hijacking under limited poisoning budgets while preserving clean-task performance. Method sec:method Our two-stage multimodal framework induces trajectory-level targeted backdoors under sparse poisoning (Fig.~ fig:framework ). Stage I optimizes a 3D trigger; Stage II mitigates update interference and fuses the learned adaptations into one policy. Problem Formulation sec:method_setup setting and objective. We consider white-box offline adaptation of a VLA policy that predicts actions from visual observations , language instructions , and optional proprioception . The attacker controls limited poisoned demonstrations with a physical 3D trigger but retains the original instructions. The goal is to induce a complete attacker-specified manipulation trajectory with the trigger while preserving normal task execution otherwise. Let and denote clean and poisoned demonstrations, where parameterizes the trigger and denotes policy adaptation parameters. We formulate the overall objective as where and measure target-trajectory and clean-task errors, denotes adaptation, and the attacker seeks to keep the poisoning rate as low as possible. In our experiments, a poisoning rate of already enables reliable hijacking. Two bottlenecks arise: scarce target-trajectory supervision and interference from dominant clean-task updates. We first optimize the trigger with a frozen policy (Sec.~ sec:method_trigger_optimization ), then adapt the policy with the optimized trigger fixed (Sec.~ sec:method_serial_lora ). We strengthen trigger--target associations without increasing the poisoning rate by optimizing a 3D trigger through differentiable rendering and joint visual, language, and action supervision. 3D trigger optimization.
