title: Supply Geometry, Learn Execution: Screw Attention for Zero-Shot Policy Transfer in Robot Manipulation
summary: We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied.
full_text: \@oldmaketitle\@maketitle \@oldmaketitle ! The Screw Attention Policy learns manipulation from geometry rather than appearance. Frozen perception and language models convert images and instructions into object poses, task goals, and geometric relations. The policy observes only the relations between the hand and scene objects to produce an end-effector twist. A 30K-parameter policy trained in simulation on a single robot transfers zero-shot to a real robot and to five unseen robot arms. fig:architecture Supply Geometry, Learn Execution:\\ Screw Attention for Zero-Shot Policy Transfer\\ in Robot Manipulation 1 We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96 success on LIBERO, 85.8 under layout changes, 80.2 across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied. Introduction sec:intro Manipulation policies learned from demonstrations have mainly adopted a scaling paradigm, in which performance is improved through larger datasets and models. This strategy has driven significant progress, but at a substantial cost in data, computational resources, and real-world fine-tuning. Most manipulation policies are grounded in image observations. Although this design provides rich sensory information, it also means that the geometric and physical structure required for manipulation is not directly available to the policy. The model must therefore learn to infer scene geometry, object relations, robot kinematics, and contact dynamics from pixels, in addition to learning the task-specific behaviour. A direct consequence is a brittleness to changes in observations and embodiments. Variations in viewpoint, lighting, background, robot appearance, or kinematic structure often cause substantial degradation in performance. Sim-to-real and cross-embodiment transfer are visible manifestations of this challenge. Cross-embodiment policies are typically trained on data from many robot platforms so that embodiment-invariant behaviour can be discovered from experience ghosh2024octo,doshi2024crossformer . Similarly, sim-to-real approaches rely on extensive domain randomisation, exposing the policy to a wide range of appearances until the real world falls within the training distribution deshpande2026molmobot . Differently, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have been shifting towards explicit geometric representations, including 3D foundation models lin2025evo0,li2025spatialforcing,wang2025vggt , dedicated 3D reasoning modules xia20263dvla , and pose-centric pretraining objectives lin2026posevla . Taken together, these developments share a common premise: the policy spends substantial capacity learning the geometric structure of the scene and the robot. We challenge the prevailing end-to-end paradigm in which manipulation policies are expected to infer geometry, kinematics, and dynamics from visual observations. While learning such representations is necessary when they are unavailable, much of this information can already be provided explicitly: object poses from modern perception systems~ wen2024foundationpose and kinematic structure from robot models. We therefore argue that the challenge is not how to learn geometric structure more efficiently, but whether it should be learned in the first place when it is already explicitly available. Modular systems have explored a similar decomposition~ ichter2023saycan,liang2023codeaspolicies , yet they typically learn task planning while executing hand-engineered or pre-generated skills. We instead supply geometry and learn the execution policy itself. Given object poses and the robot model, the policy does not need to reason about appearance, viewpoint, or image statistics, and can instead operate on the geometric relations that define the task. We instantiate this idea through the Screw Attention Policy, built on Screw Attention magassouba2026screw , a Transformer architecture designed to reason over rigid-body geometric relations. In this framework, object and end-effector tokens carry screw representations and exchange geometric messages through relative transforms. The policy operates on end-effector-centric geometric relations, encoding the scene objects relative to the end-effector rather than a specific embodiment. This design decouples task geometry from embodiment-specific kinematics. Using this representation, a 30K-parameter policy trained solely on a single simulated arm transfers zero-shot across embodiments and to the real world, without target demonstrations or fine-tuning. Unlike existing approaches xmop2024, wu2026dexgraspzero, niu2026skelwam , transfer is not an explicit training objective, but a consequence of our representation. Our contributions are as follows. We introduce the Screw Attention Policy, which operates on object poses and relative transforms supplied by off-the-shelf perception and robot models. With 30K trainable parameters, it achieves 96 on LIBERO and 85.8 on LIBERO-Plus under layout changes. Trained on a single simulated arm, the policy transfers zero-shot to five other arms (80.2 , against 33.0 for the previous best~ niu2026skelwam ) and to a real robot (21 of 24 trials). We show that supplied poses alone are not sufficient: baselines given the same object poses remain below 30 success on rearranged layouts, whereas our policy reaches 74.7 . The same policy further exhibits compositional behaviour on unseen object pairings and recovers from failed grasps without explicit recovery training. Method sec:method Preliminaries on Screw Attention sec:prelim Motivation Consider the task of grasping a bowl. To decide the next motion, a robot needs to know where the bowl is relative to the hand: its distance, direction, and orientation. If the entire scene is translated or rotated, these relations remain unchanged, and so does the desired motion. Manipulation can therefore be viewed as reasoning over geometric relations between bodies, rather than directly over pixels. Screws provide a natural representation for such relations~ featherstone2008 . A screw is a six-dimensional vector that combines angular and linear components in the coordinate frame of a body. Poses, relative displacements, end-effector motions, and articulation constraints can all be represented in this form. For example, the displacement from the hand to the bowl is represented as the screw . The commanded hand motion is another type of screw, a twist , which combines angular and linear velocity. This shared representation enables the policy to reason about objects, robot states, and their interactions with the same underlying operations. Core principle Manipulation requires combining geometric quantities attached to different bodies. Let and denote the poses of bodies and , and let be their relative pose with the rotation matrix . The associated spatial transform \[ _ ij = & \\ [ ]_ & \] re-expresses any screw from the frame of into the frame of . Screws expressed in different frames can then be compared and combined within a common coordinate system. Consequently, the representation is independent of how coordinate frames are attached to robots, grippers, or objects. Changing a frame modifies both the screws and transforms consistently while preserving the underlying geometry. Screw Attention~ magassouba2026screw exploits this property by exchanging screw messages through relative transforms, forming the basis of our manipulation policy. Screw Attention In Screw Attention, each body is represented by a Transformer token associated with a pose . Each ordered pair of tokens carries the relative transform . Additionally, articulated bodies carry a joint screw encoding the type and axis of the joint (Section~ sec:tokens ). Neither nor is learned. Both are supplied by the robot model and object pose estimates. Each token encodes two feature streams. The scalar features are frame-independent quantities, such as distances. The geometric features contain screw-valued channels expressed in the local frame of token , encoding quantities such as object directions, gravity, or joint axes. title: MRBench: Benchmarking Physical Necessity Reasoning in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Manipulation
summary: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.

Website:~ https://showlab.github.io/MRBench Introduction sec:intro ``Plurality is never to be posited without necessity." --- William of Ockham Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled robots to coordinate manipulation tasks through task decomposition, collaborative planning, and shared execution~ mandi2024roco,kannan2024smartllm,chen2024hmas,chen2025emos,kang2026coenv . Yet successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. In practical workcells, robots may become unavailable, be replaced by different models, or have their roles taken over by simple fixtures. This raises a question beyond coordination: Which physical capabilities does a task truly require, and which robots or objects are necessary to provide them? The answer depends on the task's physical constraints rather than robot count alone. Some tasks require several independent actions at once, while others span locations beyond a single arm's reach ( A). Crucially, required physical roles do not always require additional robots. As shown in B, the same tomato-flume task needs three arms under its reference configuration, becomes infeasible when a key arm is removed, but can be completed with two when a different arm reaches farther or a suitable chute replaces the missing support. The task goal remains unchanged, yet its minimal feasible team changes. This motivates physical necessity reasoning: determining what a task demands, what the available resources can provide, and which combination is minimally sufficient. Classical multi-robot task allocation studies capability-based team formation~ gerkey2004taxonomy,korsah2013taxonomy , while recent embodied agents extend robot selection and coordination to heterogeneous teams~ kannan2024smartllm,chen2025emos,kang2025vikir,zhang2025toolroco . However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate coordination ability with fixed teams or selection from available robots~ mandi2024roco,qin2025robofactory . They do not systematically test whether agents can infer task requirements, assess physical capabilities, and recognize when passive objects can replace robotic roles. A successful execution proves that a team is sufficient, not that it is necessary. To investigate this gap, we introduce , a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. comprises eight tasks spanning two sources of multi-arm necessity: and constraints ( ). Each task is evaluated under five configurations--- , , , , and ---that preserve the goal while changing the available physical resources. Ground-truth minimal teams are computed from geometric constraints and exact search, with feasible solutions validated in Isaac Sim~ mittal2025isaaclab . This design tests whether agents can distinguish necessary, redundant, missing, and replaceable robotic support. Our evaluation reveals a striking gap: agents that coordinate reference teams successfully often struggle when physical resources change. Existing coordination methods achieve high accuracy under reference configurations, yet degrade substantially when robot embodiments are swapped or passive objects can replace robotic roles. To address this gap, we propose , which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities. A team-independent task representation identifies the required jobs, physical tools determine which robots or objects can perform them, and constrained search produces a minimal feasible team with a verifiable assignment. Nevertheless, passive substitution remains challenging, revealing a persistent gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity. Our contributions are threefold: Empirical Insight. We reveal a gap between multi-robot coordination and physical necessity reasoning as robot capabilities and environmental support change. . We introduce a benchmark evaluating feasibility, minimality, and functional substitution across heterogeneous configurations under unchanged task goals. . title: Distractors are the Real Enemy: Visual Distraction Adversarial Perturbations on SAM2-Based Video Tracking and Segmentation
summary: Promptable video trackers such as SAM2 achieve accurate and robust performance through strong temporal consistency, making them important foundations for downstream video understanding and tracking applications. As their use continues to expand, understanding their robustness to adversarial perturbations becomes increasingly important. Existing attacks on SAM2 largely focus on local mask degradation and short-term temporal feature disruption, leaving its longer-term dynamics and competing object interferences (Distractors) insufficiently explored. We observe that SAM2 itself exposes useful distractor cues when tracking becomes uncertain. Based on these observations, we propose DistractAttack, a white-box attack that uses background distractors to disrupt target tracking persistently. Its core procedure, Counterfactual Distractor Search (CDS), propagates clean and attacked trajectories in parallel to discover plausible competing regions and identify those that become increasingly effective under perturbation. The discovered evidence is accumulated over time to weaken target support and promote recurrent alternatives or disappearance predictions. Extensive experiments under video-level and one-shot perturbations across Visual Object Tracking and Video Object Segmentation demonstrate strong attack effectiveness, raising DRE to $4.4\times$ and NRE to $7.3\times$ their nearest baselines under video perturbation, while transferring effectively across model scales and tracker variants in black-box settings. Project page: https://adonaydem.github.io/sam2-da-page/

Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in promptable video segmentation have demonstrated strong and generalizable performance across downstream tasks such as Visual Object Tracking (VOT) and Video Object Segmentation (VOS). SAM2 sam2 , in particular, extends promptable segmentation to video through a recurrent memory mechanism that propagates object information across frames. Building on this foundational model, recent methods have further improved long-term tracking through stronger motion modeling, memory management, and distractor handling samurai,sam2long,dam4sam,samite,him2sam . While promptable trackers have become increasingly robust, it remains unclear whether their specialized designs resist adversarial perturbations or share transferable vulnerabilities. Attacks against single-object tracking and VOS manipulate classification, bounding-box regression, temporal consistency, trajectories, and motion cues~ csa,fan,iouattack,spark,aba,chen2020one , or exploit initialization errors and hard regions to induce persistent segmentation failure~ jiang2023exploring,li2023adversarial . Although these studies show that temporal recurrence and stored representations can amplify brief perturbations, their objectives were developed largely for earlier architectures such as Siamese networks~ fan and do not readily transfer to foundation models such as SAM2. In parallel, attacks on the Segment Anything Model (SAM)~ sam consider mask manipulation, universal and prompt-agnostic perturbations, and feature-specific objectives ~ attacksam,samuap,pata,huang2023robustness,jiang2024cross,liu2024cross,9614158,uad,sra,darksam,xiao2026diffusion,umigrat,qin2025sam , but remain image-based and overlook the memory-driven dynamics of promptable video trackers. For SAM2, Robust-SAM showed that adversarial perturbations can disrupt temporal consistency~ long2025robust , while UAP-SAM2 jointly perturbs semantic features and consecutive-frame consistency~ uapsam2 . BadVSFM further considers training-time backdoors~ zhang2025backdoor . Yet existing SAM2 attacks still largely target segmentation degradation or mask disappearance, while their temporal objectives remain centered on relatively local feature interactions rather than the long-term object trajectory. This leaves open how an attack can exploit the longer-term mechanisms that modern promptable trackers use to preserve and recover target identity under adverse challenges. We introduce DistractAttack, a distractor-centric white-box attack for recurrent promptable segmentation that uses model-supported distractors to destabilize target tracking rather than merely erase the current mask. Its core, Counterfactual Distractor Search (CDS), propagates clean and attacked trajectories in parallel: the clean trajectory identifies plausible non-target competitors, while the attacked trajectory reveals which become increasingly influential under a bounded perturbation. Accumulating this evidence over time, CDS turns local ambiguity into persistent tracking failures, including wrong-object capture, spatial displacement, unstable localization, and disappearance. We evaluate video-level and one-shot perturbations across VOT and VOS, with transfer studies across model scales and state-of-the-art tracker variants. SAM2's memory mechanism is particularly vulnerable to one-shot initialization perturbations, whose effects persist throughout the video. Under video-perturbation and matched protocol, DistractAttack achieves the highest Drift-Rate Error (DRE) and Not-Reported Error (NRE)~ kristan2023first by a substantial margin (see Fig.~ fig:hook ). Our core contributions are summarized as follows: We propose the first distractor-centric adversarial attack against SAM2, exposing its vulnerability to distractors in the surrounding scene. Counterfactual Distractor Search couples clean and attacked trajectories to exploit evolving distractor evidence and induce persistent tracking failure. We extensively study DistractAttack under two complementary perturbation settings: Video Perturbation (VP) and One-shot Perturbation (OP) across both VOT and VOS tasks. We provide a broad evaluation against existing attacks and assess real-world practicality of our method via black-box transferability across model sizes and SAM2 tracker variants. Related Work sec:related Promptable Video Segmentation and Tracking SAM introduced promptable class-agnostic image segmentation sam , and SAM2 extended this paradigm to video through a streaming memory that propagates an initialized object across frames sam2 . SAM2 further broadened the family toward concept-prompted detection, segmentation, and tracking sam3 . Recent SAM2 extensions strengthen long-term tracking through motion-aware memory selection in SAMURAI samurai , multiple temporal hypotheses in SAM2Long sam2long , distractor-aware memory in DAM4SAM dam4sam , position prompting in SAMITE samite , and combined long- and short-term modeling in HiM2SAM him2sam . Their shared focus on distractors and memory reliability identifies identity confusion as a central challenge in promptable tracking. We study the complementary adversarial question of whether a bounded perturbation can exploit such distractors to progressively confuse the tracker’s target representation and disrupt its temporal consistency. Adversarial Video Tracking and Segmentation Adversarial video tracking has shown that recurrence, association, and stored representations can turn brief perturbations into persistent errors. In visual object tracking, FAN, IoU Attack, SPARK, CSA, and ABA attack temporal box consistency, sparse online updates, classification responses, and motion blur fan,iouattack,spark,csa,aba , while adversarial VOS exploits initialization errors that aim to induce mask degradation jiang2023exploring,li2023adversarial . However, these frameworks remain closely tied to their victim architectures and have limited compatibility with recent SAM-based trackers. Attacks on SAM have covered mask removal, targeted generation, prompt-agnostic feature manipulation, region suppression and spatial--frequency attacks attacksam,samuap,pata,huang2023robustness,jiang2024cross,liu2024cross, uad,sra,darksam,xiao2026diffusion,umigrat,qin2025sam . Direct studies of SAM2 include Robust~SAM (CPA), UAP-SAM2, BadVSFM, and DarkLLM long2025robust,uapsam2,zhang2025backdoor,sun2026darkllm . Among these methods, UAP-SAM2 alone introduces an explicit temporal objective, yet it merely relates consecutive encoder features rather than the history accumulated in recurrent memory. We aim to exploit accumulated target history and recurring distractor evidence to induce persistent confusion between the target and plausible competing regions. title: Atomic Policy: Composing Atomic Manipulation Skills with Agentic Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy/

Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. Project page: aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy Introduction Long-horizon manipulation requires a robot to pursue its task goal while reasoning about a scene that changes with every interaction. Instructions may leave intermediate steps implicit, and an unsuccessful action can alter what is feasible next. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a basis for this reasoning, enabling robotic agents to interpret instructions and coordinate perception, planning, and control~ fu2026capx,chen2026volo,guo2026planar . Perceptual and geometric tools help these agents resolve spatial relationships and ground ambiguous or underspecified instructions in the scene~ chen2026spacetools . Visual feedback then allows them to monitor progress and revise decisions as execution unfolds~ chen2026volo,gemini2025robotics . Translating these decisions into reliable manipulation remains difficult. The physical interactions available to an agent are constrained by its execution interface~ fu2026capx,zhang2026playful : identifying the correct object and operation does not specify the motion needed to complete the interaction. Analytic primitives can struggle with complex grasps, constrained placement, and articulated-object interaction~ zhang2026harness . Imitation learning provides fine-grained motor behaviors learned from demonstrations~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion . Vision-language-action models (VLAs) extend this capability to language-conditioned control, demonstrating semantic generalization and extended task execution in unfamiliar settings~ black2025pi05,gemini2025robotics . Reliable execution nevertheless remains challenging when a familiar behavior must be redirected toward a different target or composed with other skills in a new sequence~ chen2026volo,zhang2026harness . Recent efforts address skill reuse and coordination through procedural knowledge and code-based skills~ lu2026aspire,he2026skill2real , orchestration of learned motor policies~ li2026roboclaw,zhang2026robocop,chen2026volo,zhang2026harness , and skill transitions guided by world models~ zhang2026wap . We focus on how task reasoning can steer these motor behaviors while remaining responsive to their outcomes. The agent must specify the intended interaction and its target, then determine whether the resulting state supports the next step. Grounded steering and verification therefore become part of skill composition. We introduce Atomic Policy (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), a framework that separates local manipulation skills from task-level reasoning and composition. Each atomic skill is a reusable behavior with a phase-level completion condition, implemented by either a dedicated visuomotor policy or a shared language-conditioned model. A VLM-based agentic harness estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver composes the skills according to their preconditions and effects. The harness steers each phase through language, visual pointing, or both: language specifies the interaction and its referents, while points make spatial targets explicit. A VLM checker verifies the outcome and determines whether to continue, advance, or replan from the current scene. This common interface allows task reasoning to redirect and compose skills while learned policies generate local motion, supporting recovery as execution unfolds. Our contributions are threefold. (1) We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework for complex, long-horizon manipulation that connects task-level reasoning to learned skill execution through grounded steering and verification. (2) We formulate point and language steering as complementary interfaces for skill composition. A common phase-level abstraction supports specialized visuomotor policies and generalist action models within the same planning and execution loop. (3) We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks requiring dependent skill sequences and interpretation of ambiguous or underspecified goals. Comparisons, ablations, and failure analysis examine how steering and replanning contribute to task following and recovery. Related Work sec:related Agentic Robotics. Frontier multimodal models provide reasoning and tool-use capabilities~ comanici2025gemini25 . Robot agents use these capabilities to call learned policies as tools~ chen2026volo,li2026roboclaw,zhang2026robocop or generate executable robot programs~ fu2026capx,shi2026maestro,xie2026pusht . Harness VLA~ zhang2026harness combines a frozen VLA contact primitive with analytic actions. Other systems co-design physical tools and action plans~ gao2026vlmgineer or learn to use tools for spatial reasoning~ chen2026spacetools . Agents also acquire reusable skills or refine programs through practice~ lu2026aspire,zhang2026playful,he2026skill2real,chen2026gap , and improve policies or execution through real-world trials~ xiao2026enpire . Agent-generated demonstrations and program annotations also support policy learning~ shen2026embodiedswe,liu2026aw0 . Benchmarks test automation~ xie2026vabar , manipulation for evidence gathering~ bhat2026mgvqa , and memory~ wang2026memoreval . Plans can also be evaluated using world and video models~ zhang2026wap,fu2026novaplan . Neuro-symbolic representations further structure task reasoning~ mao2025neurosymbolic . title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
comment: 27 pages, 7 figures, 18 tables. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq
summary: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
full_text: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2~points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12~points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: . Introduction sec:intro A policy that predicts action chunks can be given a finite vocabulary of motions in one of two places. The vocabulary can sit inside the policy, as a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder lee2024vqbet, mete2024quest, zheng2024prise . It can also sit after the policy and be applied to the predictions of a continuous policy, which then trains as usual while every chunk it executes belongs to a finite set. Either placement allows a pretrained vision-language model to emit actions as tokens pertsch2025fast , but the two differ in what the vocabulary costs. This paper measures that cost. Placing the vocabulary inside the policy has two consequences. First, a codebook trained jointly with its selector and decoder entangles the costs of the vocabulary, the selection and the execution, so closed-loop success reports only their sum. Second, a code becomes a trajectory only through the learned decoder, so the library is judged by offline reconstruction rather than by closed-loop success. We separate these costs by placing the vocabulary after the policy. If a continuous reference policy keeps its success when executed through an explicit library, the library covers the motions the task requires. The reference executed through the library, the library reference, is then a baseline for any selector over that library. A trained selector's shortfall against it can be split into the cost of its choice and the cost of its placement and correction ( sec:instrument ). This requires two things. Every library element must execute without a learned decoder, and the layer that applies the library must cost the reference nothing. Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ) provides such a layer. Its elements, , are demonstration segments stored as B-spline control points zhou2025beast . A fixed linear map decodes them, so every element is an executable trajectory. At execution time, MPQ replaces each predicted chunk with its nearest and corrects it toward the prediction, within a bound set by the demonstrations' own spread (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Nothing on the execution path is trained. The layer costs the policies it wraps almost nothing ( sec:exp ). Pooled over 13 combinations of policy and benchmark on LIBERO liu2023libero and RoboCasa nasiriany2024robocasa , covering six architectures including a 7B vision-language-action model, MPQ changes success by ~points (95 CI ). Its cost does not grow under observation shift, and on a real robot it runs with the bound selected in simulation. Relative to the library reference, selectors on three backbones lose almost all of their gap in placing and correcting the chosen element ( sec:placement ). On LIBERO-90 with 256 , quantization costs nothing. A selector's choice often differs from the nearest , yet with the reference's placement and correction it costs at most 2~points. The selectors' own placement and correction cost between 0 and 12~points. Offline reconstruction, the standard criterion for validating a library, predicts none of these differences ( sec:libraries ). It keeps improving after closed-loop success has saturated, it ranks library designs differently than closed-loop success does, and it misses a transfer loss of 4 to 8~points. As with policy checkpoints mandlekar2021matters , offline criteria therefore cannot select a library. Contributions. [leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt,parsep=0pt] A closed-loop decomposition that splits a discrete skill policy's shortfall into quantization, selection and execution, measured against the library reference ( sec:instrument ). MPQ, an execution layer that keeps every executed chunk within a bounded distance of a demonstrated segment and is statistically equivalent to the unwrapped policy, within the noise of repeated evaluation ( sec:method , sec:exp ). The finding that on three backbones, a selector's gap to the library reference arises in executing the chosen element rather than in the vocabulary or the choice ( sec:placement ). Evidence that offline reconstruction misjudges library size, design and transfer ( sec:libraries ). Related work sec:related Discrete skill policies and how they are measured. VQ-BeT lee2024vqbet , QueST mete2024quest and PRISE zheng2024prise discretize action chunks into latent codebooks learned as vector-quantized autoencoders oord2017vqvae . FAST pertsch2025fast and its successors liu2026oat,kang2026xtokenizer instead tokenize chunks so that autoregressive vision-language-action models can predict them. In the codebook methods, a learned head selects the element, and a code becomes a trajectory only through a learned decoder. The codebook is therefore validated offline, by reconstruction. In imitation learning, mandlekar2021matters showed that selecting checkpoints by validation loss yields policies far below the best, and evaluated them in closed loop instead. The library reference applies the same principle to the vocabulary ( sec:libraries ). Selectors with learned offsets. BeT shafiullah2022bet bins single-step actions and adds a learned offset to the selected bin. This combination of bin and offset makes it the closest structural relative of a selector over MPQ's library. It differs from MPQ in three respects, however. Its bins are means of raw single-step actions, its selector is a trained classifier, and its offsets are unbounded. Concurrent work pairs a learned selector with a residual that is free to overwrite the selected code lei2026pfdag,wang2026arp . For such a design, Eq.~ eq:decomp measures the cost of the choice and the cost of the heads separately. In MPQ the residual is bounded, so the executed segment keeps the identity of the selected element. Motion primitives and prototypes. Our construction, which clusters demonstration segments and projects the centroids onto real ones, has classical relatives in libraries of motion primitives ijspeert2013dynamical,paraschos2013probabilistic,li2023prodmp,loedige2025force and in skills segmented from demonstrations niekum2012learning,konidaris2012robot,lioutikov2017learning,blank2024nils,blank2026sparc . These libraries are sequenced by planners or grammars lioutikov2018pcfg,lioutikov2020attribute rather than placed after a chunk-predicting policy. The tolerance of a plays the role that the variance plays in a probabilistic movement primitive paraschos2013probabilistic , except that MPQ uses it as a bound on execution rather than as a distribution to sample from. We represent segments as B-spline control points following BEAST zhou2025beast , which tokenizes chunks without a learned encoder. Other work places primitives scheikl2024mpd or splines tian2026splinepolicy,han2026bsplinepolicy inside the policy head. The projection of cluster centroids onto real examples follows ProtoPNet chen2019protopnet . We introduce no new primitive. Our contribution lies in where the library sits and in the measurement this placement enables. Execution-time constraints. Retrieval-based policies match observations to demonstrations and leave the executed action unconstrained pari2021vinn,du2023behaviorretrieval,odonchimed2025ragdp . MPQ instead matches actions at execution time, so that each executed chunk has an identity and a deviation bound. Two further lines of work act on the chunk at execution time. Bidirectional decoding selects among chunks sampled from a policy liu2025bid , and residual policies learn corrections to a fixed controller or a reference trajectory silver2018residual,johannink2019residual,huang2025moreerl . Like a residual policy, MPQ corrects a fixed base, but the base is a demonstrated segment and the correction is bounded rather than learned. Safety shields alshiekh2018shielding and control barrier functions ames2019cbf likewise project actions, but onto an implicit safe set rather than an explicit library. sec:method Measuring a vocabulary against a library reference sec:instrument A vocabulary can be measured in closed loop only against a policy that already succeeds without it. Let denote closed-loop success rate, and let be a continuous reference policy that succeeds on the benchmark. A library is a finite set of executable chunks, and an execution layer ( sec:method:policy ) wraps through this library. For each chunk that predicts, the layer selects a library element, places it in the frame of the prediction and applies a bounded correction. The library reference is the success rate of executed through this layer. Since succeeds without the layer, any drop in success can be attributed to the library. is a baseline rather than an upper bound, since a selector that chooses or corrects better could exceed it. A discrete skill policy~ over the same library replaces the layer's decisions with learned heads. A choice head selects the element, and further heads place and correct it. To isolate what its choice costs, we define a hybrid that executes 's choice with the reference's placement and correction ( sec:method:policy ). The shortfall of then decomposes as The quantization term is what the library cannot represent. The selection term is what 's choice costs when the reference supplies the placement and correction, and the execution term is what 's learned placement and correction lose relative to the reference's. Eq.~ eq:decomp substitutes 's choice before its placement and correction, and we call it the choice-first order. In the correction-first order, a hybrid executes the reference's choice with 's placement and correction. sec:placement:results reports both. The decomposition holds only if library elements execute without a learned decoder, since otherwise part of any drop could come from the decoder. A latent codebook does not meet this requirement (Appendix~ app:extra:codec ). The layer must also cost the reference nothing, which we verify in sec:exp . Representing action chunks sec:method:spline We represent an action chunk of horizon over geometric degrees of freedom as a B-spline curve zhou2025beast with control points . Evaluating the basis functions at the timesteps gives the collocation matrix . Decoding control points to a trajectory is then the linear map , and fitting control points to a trajectory is its closed-form least-squares inverse. Since neither operation is learned, every point of decodes to a valid trajectory. The gripper is fit on the same basis as a separate channel, with control points . title: View Management with Gaussian Placement and Opacity Regularization for Online 3DGS
summary: The realistic rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has drawn interest from real-time applications that require maps to be built online. This led to coupling 3DGS with SLAM, providing camera poses and initial Gaussians for the map. However, the map is still optimized with designs inherited from conventional SLAM, which train only on keyframes selected for localization and regularize geometry with uncertain frontend depth. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map: with millions of parameters but few views of each region, the map overfits to sparse inputs. Resolving this is challenging, as every view and Gaussian added to the map competes for the same real-time budget. We close this gap from both sides. To add views while keyframes preserve the structure of the map, we progressively admit non-keyframe images as mapping updates complete and allocate the limited updates across different groups of frames according to the supervision each group provides. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR) uses accumulated rendering evidence, at no extra rendering cost, to suppress the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a map-derived surface reference. Together, these designs improve both the appearance and the geometry of online maps within the real-time budget.
full_text: The realistic rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has drawn interest from real-time applications that require maps to be built online. This led to coupling 3DGS with SLAM, providing camera poses and initial Gaussians for the map. However, the map is still optimized with designs inherited from conventional SLAM, which train only on keyframes selected for localization and regularize geometry with uncertain frontend depth. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map: with millions of parameters but few views of each region, the map overfits to sparse inputs. Resolving this is challenging, as every view and Gaussian added to the map competes for the same real-time budget. We close this gap from both sides. To add views while keyframes preserve the structure of the map, we progressively admit non-keyframe images as mapping updates complete and allocate the limited updates across different groups of frames according to the supervision each group provides. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Ref\-er\-enced Opac\-ity Reg\-u\-lar\-iza\-tion (SOR) uses accumulated rendering evidence, at no extra rendering cost, to suppress the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a map-derived surface reference. Together, these designs improve both the appearance and the geometry of online maps within the real-time budget. Introduction sec:intro Building geometrically accurate and photorealistic 3D maps online remains an important challenge in 3D vision and autonomous robotics. Among the variety of 3D representations (including point clouds, meshes~ lin2023immesh , and surfels~ chen2019suma ), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs has gained attention for enabling dense, photorealistic maps with real-time rendering from novel viewpoints~ matsuki2024monogs,huang2024photoslam , offering opportunities for vision-based perception and decision-making~ chen2025splat, intro_Shorinwa2025splatmover,intro_zitkovich2023rt2 . To achieve this level of quality, the representation requires careful optimization of numerous parameters—including position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity—for millions of primitives. Since this optimization process is computationally intensive and relies on dense multi-view constraints, 3DGS frameworks are predominantly trained offline using pre-collected datasets. Autonomous systems, however, need to construct and update maps as they navigate and explore their environments, providing the spatial context beyond the current field of view to support timely planning and action. Coupling 3DGS with SLAM has enabled online pose estimation and Gaussian initialization~ matsuki2024monogs,huang2024photoslam,zhang2025hislam2,splatslam2024,vigsslam : a frontend tracks the camera, selects keyframes, and estimates their depth, from which the mapper inserts Gaussians as keyframes arrive. The Gaussian map itself, however, is still optimized with mapping designs inherited from conventional SLAM. First, the map is optimized only on keyframes, which SLAM selects with little overlap to build a geometric map for localization. Second, geometric regularization relies on frontend depth, which is uncertain where viewpoints are few. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map, which renders novel views and thus needs dense views with large overlap to constrain its parameters. The map therefore overfits to sparse inputs, degrading at unseen viewpoints and retaining floaters, Gaussians that render in front of the true surface. Offline, more views and longer training would resolve this; online, the mapper must keep pace with the stream, and each optimization step renders a single image, so every added view and every added Gaussian takes updates away from the rest of the map. The problem is most pronounced in egocentric sequences, where head motion makes the observations of each region brief and intermittent, so a region often leaves the view before its Gaussians have converged. Our method closes the gap between the model complexity of a 3DGS map and the views available to constrain it from both sides. The dense views that a 3DGS map needs are already in the input stream: the images between consecutive keyframes largely overlap the keyframes. We therefore progressively admit these non-keyframe images (blue in ) into the training set as mapping updates complete, so that admitted images receive enough updates within the real-time budget. Because the images provide different supervision but compete for the same steps, we allocate updates across three groups with fixed shares: recent keyframes refine newly initialized Gaussians, all keyframes revisit previously mapped regions as the frontend refines their poses and depth, and non-keyframe images constrain each region from additional viewpoints. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them (green in ), since every Gaussian adds parameters for the available views to constrain and limited updates to refine. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR) accumulates evidence of where each surface lies from the views that training already renders, and suppresses the opacity of floaters, Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of this map-derived surface (red in ). In summary, we reduce overfitting in online 3DGS mapping within a real-time budget through the following contributions: View management, which progressively admits the non-keyframe images between keyframes as mapping updates complete and allocates the limited updates across recent keyframes, all keyframes, and non-keyframe images according to the supervision each group provides. Edge-guided initialization, which uses image gradients to decide both how many Gaussians each keyframe adds relative to earlier keyframes and where they are placed within the image, so that the model complexity of the map follows the detail of the scene. Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR), which suppresses the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a surface reference accumulated from training renders, complementing uncertain frontend depth at no extra rendering cost. Experiments on egocentric and public sequences at their original frame rate, showing that our method improves both the appearance and the geometry of online maps over existing 3DGS-SLAM systems. Related Work sec:related_work Training Views and Gaussian Initialization Online 3DGS mapping optimizes the map from a growing stream of frames under a limited number of updates, so each system decides which frames to train on and how often. Most systems inherit this decision from the localization frontend: they optimize the map on a window of recent or covisible frames that the frontend keeps for localization and replay frames from earlier in the sequence~ matsuki2024monogs,splatam2024,huang2024photoslam,splatslam2024,vigsslam . Replaying past frames keeps mapped regions from being forgotten, as studied in continual learning for neural implicit maps~ sucar2021imap,yan2021continual . However, the frames kept for localization overlap little, leaving each region with too few views to constrain the many parameters of a 3DGS map, which therefore overfits to sparse inputs. We progressively admit the frames between them, which observe the same surfaces from additional viewpoints, into the training set. Other methods allocate updates by scoring frames. Error-driven scheduling revisits past frames where the map fits poorly, measured by the last training loss of each frame~ cartgs or by rendering error accumulated over spatial regions~ ellensohn2026eligsir . These errors are recorded when frames are trained and do not reflect later updates of the map, and filtering out incoming frames that overlap the map~ ellensohn2026eligsir removes the overlapping views that a 3DGS map needs to constrain its parameters. Information-driven selection chooses views by the uncertainty of the map in each view, estimated from the scales and positional gradients of the Gaussians~ lee2025novelview or from the Fisher information of the map~ jiang2024fisherrf . Both evaluate every candidate view against the map, leaving fewer updates for optimization within the same real-time budget. Rather than spending the available time on scoring frames, we group frames by the supervision they provide and allocate updates to each group accordingly. Each keyframe also inserts new Gaussians, and their number sets the model complexity that the few views of each region constrain. Most systems back-project keyframe depth and downsample it uniformly~ matsuki2024monogs,splatslam2024,zhang2025hislam2 , or insert Gaussians where the rendered opacity is low or the rendering error is large~ splatam2024,rtgslam2024 , placing as many Gaussians in smooth regions as in detailed ones. Image-guided sampling concentrates new Gaussians on image structure, measured by color gradients~ yugay2023gaussianslam , image contrast~ wei2024gsfusion , or edge responses~ thomas2026gausslite,meuleman2025onthefly , but still inserts a fixed number per frame or lets the number follow the absolute magnitude of the image response, which varies with the contrast of each scene. Neither adapts the number to how much detail a keyframe holds. We use image gradients to set both how many Gaussians each keyframe inserts relative to earlier keyframes and where they are placed within the image, so that the model complexity of the map follows the detail of the scene rather than a fixed budget or its contrast. Geometric Convergence and Floater Suppression Photometric reconstruction is geometrically under-constrained, since many opacity and depth configurations explain similar colors. Depth supervision constrains the rendering weights along each ray toward a given depth~ deng2022dsnerf , but in online mapping this depth comes from the frontend and is uncertain where viewpoints are few. Geometric regularization instead constrains the map itself: a distortion loss concentrates the rendering weights along each ray~ mipnerf360 , and surface-oriented Gaussians are aligned with their normals and with planar depth that is consistent across neighboring views~ huang20242dgs,chen2024pgsr . These regularizers assume long offline optimization over all posed images, and their multi-view terms require additional renders. We complement frontend depth with a surface reference derived from the map itself, which accumulates over the views that training already renders. Floaters can be handled by removing Gaussians or by lowering their opacity. Contribution-based pruning removes Gaussians whose blending weights across training views are small relative to their scale~ fan2024trimgs . Frequency-aware optimization emphasizes low-frequency structure to avoid floaters from poor initialization~ wang2025efags , and decoupled opacity separates the opacity used for geometry from that used for appearance~ stablegs . These offline methods judge each Gaussian over all posed images; online, a Gaussian is judged after only a few views, so removing it can discard surface that later views would support. Online mapping systems instead constrain opacity, forcing each Gaussian to be either opaque or nearly transparent~ rtgslam2024 or penalizing the opacity of all Gaussians~ cartgs , but they constrain Gaussians on the surface as well as those in front of it. We lower only the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of the map-derived surface, rather than removing them on the evidence of few views. Method sec:method Given an image stream with the camera poses, keyframes, and keyframe depth estimated online by the frontend~ vigsslam , our goal is to optimize a 3DGS map that renders unseen viewpoints accurately and keeps its geometry

title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
summary: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
full_text: Implicit World-Action Models ( ). Left (inference): provides future-specific conditioning within a single video-model evaluation, without explicitly generating a future. It draws a noise endpoint from the flow prior and conditions the action expert on activations from a single noise-to-clean evaluation. Right: DROID simulation success and inference latency. approaches IDM's success rate with approximately lower latency under a common two-step action-denoising budget. Success rates use each policy's evaluation budget (Section~ sec:experiments ). fig:primer fig:perf_latency fig:overview_inference Introduction sec:intro Video generation models have become an attractive source of pretrained priors for robotic manipulation~ wamsurvey,vid2world . Trained on video data, which is far more abundant than robot data, they learn generalizable priors about objects, spatial relations, and physical dynamics that could help robotic policies generalize beyond limited robot demonstrations. World-action models (WAMs) adapt these models to predict actions by finetuning on robot data. Some jointly predict future video and actions~ dreamzero,unifiedWM,motus , while others generate future video to condition a separate action network, as in inverse dynamics models (IDMs)~ unipi,causalWM . During training, IDMs condition the action policy on activations from ground-truth futures; at deployment, these futures must instead be generated. Both approaches benefit from pretrained video priors but incur substantial inference cost from generating full, high-resolution videos, a major obstacle for real-time robotic control. Lighter-weight alternatives such as FastWAM~ yuan2026fastwam still train the video model to predict future observations alongside the action policy, but remove future observations from action conditioning entirely. Instead, the policy uses only intermediate features computed from the current observation, substantially reducing inference cost by avoiding future generation. In principle, explicitly generating a future may be unnecessary if the video model's features already contain enough information about that future for action prediction. Is this possible? What information must these features retain, and how can we obtain it without generating the future itself? Typically, video generation spends test-time compute to progressively transform a sample from the noise prior into a future frame. Our goal is to amortize this computation through training, so that a single forward pass produces features that support accurate action prediction. The challenge is therefore to preserve the useful information obtained through future generation while avoiding the full generation process. Simply omitting that test-time computation does not guarantee that the remaining features contain the information needed to act. Our analysis shows that directly reading out actions from frozen video-backbone features using a FastWAM-style conditioning scheme generalizes poorly out of distribution. For example, when training on LIBERO this prior approach attains a strong in-distribution performance, but fails on perturbations in LIBERO-PRO (Sections~ sec:liberopro and~ sec:experiments ). These results suggest that access to pretrained features alone is insufficient in this setting: the computation used to construct a possible future may also contribute to generalization. Our aim is to retain the benefits of this computation by learning a shortcut that provides informative future-conditioning features in a single forward pass. To construct this shortcut, we exploit the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models. For a fixed conditioning vector, the underlying continuous flow defines a one-to-one correspondence between a noise vector and the future latent it generates. We can therefore invert any given future, the information an IDM would ordinarily condition on, to recover its corresponding noise. This raises a concrete question: can intermediate features from a single evaluation at this noise endpoint provide useful future conditioning without reconstructing the future itself? Reversibility alone does not guarantee this. A standard flow model predicts instantaneous velocities, and the corresponding future is obtained by integrating these velocities along the generative trajectory. Features from a single velocity evaluation need not capture the information that becomes accessible through this iterative generation process. To make this correspondence useful, we propose , which learns a bidirectional flow map on robot data. Motivated by prior work on amortizing flow-matching processes~ flowmaps,meanflow,shortcut , this model approximates the average velocity of standard flow-matching over finite time intervals in both directions. This quantity summarizes the transformation along a trajectory segment, allowing the model to learn a shortcut to the computation required for future generation. We condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single evaluation of this bidirectional model. During training, we integrate each demonstrated future in the clean-to-noise direction to recover its noise endpoint, then extract features from one evaluation at that endpoint. This aligns the policy's conditioning features with the future corresponding to its supervising actions, and allows us to effectively fit the action expert. At inference, we sample an endpoint from the noise prior and extract features in the same way. The action policy combines these activations with features from past observations, requiring only one video-backbone evaluation for future conditioning. Observing this result, we ask: At first glance, this may appear to require a ``free lunch'': if the benefits of imagination arise from spending compute iteratively to generate a future at test time, eliminating this computation might inevitably sacrifice the generalization it provides. However, we note that action prediction does not require reconstructing the full high-resolution future; it only requires a sufficiently informative proxy for it. This suggests that if the computation performed by iterative generation can be even reasonably approximately amortized into substantially fewer model evaluations, we may retain its benefits for action prediction at much lower cost. Crucially, prior work~ flowmaps,meanflow,shortcut suggests that such amortizations of flow-matching processes can often be represented by networks of comparable capacity, in part due to the underlying flow being deterministic. Our method exploits this structure of flow models by learning a bidirectional flow map that approximately associates each noise vector with its corresponding future in either direction. This bidirectional map allows us to extract future-specific information with just a single model evaluation, rather than explicitly integrating the full generative trajectory. Building on this insight, we propose , an implicit world-action model that conditions the action policy directly on intermediate activations from a single evaluation of a bidirectional video flow model that we train on robot data. During training, we integrate each demonstrated future in the clean-to-noise direction to recover its corresponding noise endpoint; evaluating the model once at this endpoint yields activations associated with the same future as the actions supervising the policy. At inference, we instead sample a noise endpoint from the flow prior and perform a single model evaluation, conditioning the action policy on its intermediate activations together with features from past observations. Thus, replaces iterative video generation with a single evaluation while retaining the future-specific conditioning that enables generalization. In pursuit of video-based robotic policies that enjoy both high performance and efficient inference, we ask: What is the minimal amount of information that a video prediction must provide to a robot policy to enable the latter to generalize? Based on (A), how can we design a more inference-efficient WAM that leverages these mechanisms without excess inference overhead? Answering (B) requires escaping a trade-off taken for granted by existing methods. Current approaches operate at two extremes. At one end, an explicitly generated high-resolution future provides the most complete specification available, but at the greatest inference cost. At the other, intermediate-layer activations offer a compressed representation of future dynamics at far lower cost, but one that has not resolved to any particular future. Existing methods thus resolve which future to act toward only by fully rendering it, at significant inference cost, leaving the space between these two poles largely unexplored. Contributions In this paper, we propose the implicit WAM (iWAM) that conditions the action policy on intermediate activations from a single forward pass of the video model, without explicitly generating the future. iWAM is based on the key insight that an action policy does not require a high-resolution realization of the future; it only needs enough information to specify a particular mode of the future distribution, and to instruct that mode to the action policy. In a traditional flow-based video model, the noise endpoint determines which future mode will be generated, while successive video-model evaluations transform that endpoint into the corresponding high-resolution future. However, standard flow models offer no cheap way to access the earlier ``high-level information;'' determining the future associated with a noise endpoint requires integrating the flow trajectory through multiple video-model evaluations. In iWAM, we propose to extract only the high-level mode instruction via a bidirectional flow map, which predicts the average velocity between arbitrary time pairs in either direction. Because a single noise-to-clean evaluation must transport the endpoint all the way to its corresponding future, the activations computed in producing it already identify that future, even if a single flow-map evaluation would not on its own afford high-resolution image prediction. Subsequently, iWAM conditions the action policy directly on these activations, rather than explicitly generating the observations they would produce. Across simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks~ liberopro,droid,simevals , recovers the generalization benefits of explicitly future-conditioned policies at the inference cost nearing that of approaches that discard future generation entirely. This clarifies what an action policy requires from a video model to generalize: neither a highly precise future nor observation-conditioned activations that leave the future unresolved, but sufficient information to identify the relevant mode of the future-video distribution. Explicit future generation is sufficient to specify such a mode; the success of iWAM shows that it is not necessary. Related Work sec:related Video generation models for robot control. Video models pretrained on large video datasets capture how objects and scenes evolve, providing a useful prior for robot control~ wamsurvey,vid2world . World-action models (WAMs) adapt this prior by finetuning on robot data and predicting actions from imagined futures~ unipi,dreamitate,unifiedWM,motus,causalWM,dreamzero,cosmospolicy . WAMs show promising generalization to unseen objects, scenes, and tasks, but repeatedly evaluating a large video backbone to generate futures makes inference slow. Our goal is to retain the benefits of conditioning on imagined futures without iterative generation. Efficient action prediction from video models. Several methods avoid generating the future at inference. FastWAM~ yuan2026fastwam and UVA~ uva train the video model to predict the future alongside actions, but at test time predict actions from representations of the current observation alone.
