title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction. Counting mugs across a home, for example, requires searching multiple rooms, opening closed storage, and tracking objects across views to avoid double-counting (Fig.~ fig:overview ). The agent must also choose views that reveal occluded targets and decide when the search is complete. Yet an agent may report the correct count without observing every mug or checking every room. It may also make incorrect spatial judgments after collecting the required observations. Outcome correctness must therefore be evaluated alongside the task's required observations and interactions. Existing benchmarks address different parts of this process. VSI-Bench~ yang2024thinking and MMSI-Bench~ yang2025mmsi evaluate spatial question answering from preselected videos or images. EmbodiedQA~ das2018embodied and OpenEQA~ majumdar2024openeqa shift information gathering to the agent through question-driven navigation. EXPRESS-Bench~ jiang2025express assesses answer grounding in the final observed image, while ESI-Bench~ hong2026esibench evaluates perception, locomotion, and manipulation for spatial QA. EmbodiedBench~ yang2025embodiedbench and BEHAVIOR-Spatial~ behavior2026spatial evaluate embodied tasks and spatial skills. Across these settings, final scores do not consistently distinguish correct outcomes from completed observation and interaction requirements. To address this gap, we introduce , which evaluates task outcomes together with the observations and interactions required to reach them. The benchmark comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups: grounding, aggregation, geometry, reference-frame integration, and goal-directed spatial action. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and separately verify required observations, search coverage, ordered interactions, geometry, and object placement. This verification helps distinguish missing observations from mistakes made after collecting them for deeper failure analysis. Task success requires these conditions together with a correct outcome, measuring how exploration, spatial judgment, and action work together. Our platform, built on Isaac Sim~ nvidiaIsaacSim51 , provides 27 furnished indoor environments generated with SceneSmith~ pfaff2026scenesmith and manually corrected for benchmark use. A vision-language model (VLM) chooses predefined navigation and interaction skills, including moving, observing, opening, picking, and placing. The simulator executes these atomic skills under declared motion and interaction constraints. After each skill, the agent receives a new view and action feedback before choosing its next step. The feedback reports collisions and object-handling outcomes, which the agent can use to adjust its plan. Our contributions are (1) A comprehensive benchmark and evaluation protocol for embodied spatial intelligence, connecting exploration, spatial judgment, and goal-directed action. (2) An executable exploration platform with atomic actions, leveraging simulation oracles to verify task outcomes and task-required evidence. (3) Human and frontier VLM evaluations with supporting diagnostics covering information acquisition, precision, relocation failures, input sensitivity, and costs that include failures. Related Work sec:related Spatial intelligence and embodied task evaluation. Work in this area studies spatial understanding from images and video. VSI-Bench~ yang2024thinking evaluates video-based inference, and MindCube~ wang2025mindcube tests limited-view spatial modeling. MMSI-Bench~ yang2025mmsi evaluates multi-image reasoning with reference-assisted diagnosis. SpatialBench~ xu2025spatialbench and SITE~ wang2025site examine capability and modality coverage. BLINK~ fu2024blink tests depth and correspondence. Beyond interpreting visual observations, embodied evaluations test goal completion through navigation and interaction. EmbodiedBench~ yang2025embodiedbench evaluates vision-driven tasks, while Embodied Agent Arena~ huang2026arena checks outcomes and execution conditions. ALFRED~ shridhar2019alfred and BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2024behavior evaluate household activities. Room-to-Room~ anderson2017vln tests instruction-following navigation. Beyond Spatial Benchmarks~ huang2026spatialnav examines spatial-reasoning transfer. Habitat~ savva2019habitat and AI2-THOR~ kolve2017ai2thor provide simulation. EgoPlan-Bench2~ qiu2024egoplan2 evaluates planning. BEHAVIOR-Spatial~ behavior2026spatial connects QA, grounding, and robot action. Robot policies and high-level decisions. This line of work links visual and language understanding to robot behavior. SayCan~ ahn2022saycan grounds plans in skill affordances. PaLM-E~ driess2023palme integrates observations and language. RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 transfers vision-language knowledge to control. OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and Octo~ octo2024policy develop generalist policies. RoboVQA~ sermanet2023robovqa evaluates long-horizon reasoning. Active embodied question answering. These tasks require agents to seek observations before answering. EmbodiedQA~ das2018embodied and Multi-Target EQA~ yu2019multitarget evaluate question-conditioned navigation. IQA~ gordon2018iqa tests information-revealing interactions. OpenEQA~ majumdar2024openeqa evaluates memory and exploration. Explore until Confident~ ren2024explore studies stopping, while EfficientEQA~ cheng2024efficienteqa combines exploration with retrieval. E3VS-Bench~ sakamoto2026e3vs evaluates viewpoint-dependent search. EXPRESS-Bench~ jiang2025express uses a VLM to score answer correctness and grounding in the final first-person image. ESI-Bench~ hong2026esibench tests perception, locomotion, and manipulation across 10 categories and compares active, passive, and oracle inputs. From outcome scores to task completion assessment. These directions address complementary parts of embodied tasks: understanding space, choosing actions, and gathering observations. To evaluate how these capabilities work together under robot motion and collision constraints, independently checks outcomes and task-required observations and interactions across complete episodes. Additional checks examine geometry and post-placement support. This connects final performance to the exploration and interaction process and supports detailed analysis of failures in observation acquisition, spatial judgment, and action (Table~ tab:benchmark_settings ). Benchmark Design sec:benchmark Task Taxonomy and Interaction To evaluate embodied active spatial intelligence, we design tasks that combine exploration, spatial reasoning, and interaction in different ways. For example, counting may require searching several rooms, gap measurement requires observing both edges, and relocation requires finding and moving the correct object. On our platform based on Isaac Sim~ nvidiaIsaacSim51 , the agent gathers observations and interacts with objects until it completes the task. We then check the final result and whether the task is carried out as required. We group the 11 task types by their main answer or action (Fig.~ fig:task_atlas ). G1, semantic-spatial grounding, identifies objects and rooms. G2, spatial aggregation, counts objects or rooms across views. G3, metric and comparative geometry, estimates distances, areas, and gaps or compares proximity. G4, reference-frame integration, judges directions from reference objects or the agent's final position and heading. G5, goal-directed spatial action, finds and transfers the specified object to its destination. Tasks describe targets through reference images of objects or surfaces, category names, and room names. To find a named room, the agent must infer its function from the layout and furnishings. The instructions also guide exploration and spatial judgment: counting questions specify where to search, while direction questions specify the position and orientation from which directions are judged. The agent therefore needs to interpret the task before deciding where to look and what to observe. Atomic actions. All groups allow navigation---move, strafe, turn, look---and object interaction---open, close, pick, place. G1, G2, and G5 also permit navigation to an object or ground point selected in the latest image, emphasizing search and object handling. G3 and G4 require movement distances and directions to be specified, testing metric and reference-frame reasoning. To specify target objects and navigation locations without ambiguity, we use pixel selection in the latest camera image for object interaction and image-point navigation. Task Setup and Environments Each task specifies where the agent starts, what it must do, its action budget, and how its result and task execution are checked: The scene and initial state specify the objects, their geometry and poses, and interaction states such as whether containers are open. The starting pose gives the agent's position and heading. The remaining fields specify the instruction , answer or goal rule , evidence requirements , action budget , and environment and evaluation settings . The required observation and interaction checks are derived from the instruction, including where the agent must search. They define N in Eq.~ and are fixed together with the reference answers before evaluation. Simulation environments. We use SceneSmith~ pfaff2026scenesmith to generate 27 furnished environments in five setting categories and manually correct them. Environments contain 1--13 rooms and 45--604 objects. Action budgets scale with room count to accommodate multi-room search and object transport. Category details and median scene sizes appear in Appendix~ sec:appendix_tasks . Task Generation and Validation We generate questions, reference answers, and goal conditions from the objects, room assignments, and geometry recorded in each scene. We check task feasibility through an oracle trajectory generated using simulator state and the available skills. We then manually inspect the scene to verify the instructions, answers or goals, and observation and interaction checks described below. This includes checking which objects and rooms must be counted, how directions are defined, and which object must be picked and subsequently placed at which destination. Outcome and Evidence Verification sec:evidence Agent Interaction At each round, the agent receives the task, reference images, latest camera image, available sensor readings, and feedback from its actions. Earlier observations and a visualization of the traveled path help it relate the current view to previous locations. Before executing a skill or submitting an answer or completion report, it can retrieve relevant earlier images using their text summaries. Retrieved images are added to the current round. Executing a skill produces the next observation and action feedback. Actions that select image points refer to the latest camera image. Once the agent finishes, the evaluator checks the final result and whether the task is carried out as required (Fig.~ fig:protocol ). Outcome and Evidence Criteria sec:evidence_criteria A correct answer alone does not show that the agent completes the task's required exploration and interactions. Conversely, an agent can complete the required observations yet answer incorrectly. We therefore check the result and task execution separately. For task , records its observations and actions, is the final response, and is the final scene state. Outcome correctness ( ) checks whether the answer or final scene state meets the task's answer or goal rule. Numeric answers are converted to common units before scoring. Tolerances for distance and floor area are and . Gap-width tolerance is . Human evaluators' RGB-only estimates pass the default tolerances in 110/120 judgments (91.7 ). Task-required evidence ( ) checks whether the agent observes the required targe

title: Interactive Neural Computers
summary: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.
full_text: [] #1 From today's paradigm, where a human uses a computer (a), the current trend trains an AI agent to use a computer on the user's behalf (b). We take a different path (c) where a human uses an AI that is a computer. fig:teaser ] Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction ( ), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2 of trials (chance is 33.3 ), compared with at most 56.0 for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3 to 50.1 . Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders. Introduction sec:intro Much recent work on computer use aims to build agents that operate a computer in the way a person does, reading the screen, moving a cursor, and selecting from menus, to complete tasks on users' behalf xie2024osworld,rawles2024androidworld,anthropic2024computeruse . This setting has three fundamental issues. First, the user is removed from the loop, which serves to replace human capabilities rather than augment them. Second, removing the user makes execution hard to supervise, which is risky, given documented deceptive and alignment-faking behavior in frontier models hubinger2024sleeper,greenblatt2024alignmentfaking,meinke2024scheming . Third, this setting treats computer interfaces as fixed environments to be `completed'. In reality, an interface is an arbitrary construct, so we should care less about whether an agent can `solve' it \`a la MiniGrid~ chevalierboisvert2023minigrid , and more about whether an AI can generate a useful interface that augments human capabilities. Ultimately, if the AI is the computer, human-AI collaboration can move toward open-ended interfaces. Following hughes2024oeasi , we call a system open-ended with respect to an observer when it keeps producing artifacts that the observer finds both novel and learnable. Here the observer is the user, and the artifacts are interfaces that adapt to their evolving workflow while remaining easy to learn, without anyone having to rewrite, recompile, and reload static source code. We therefore set out to build a generative interactive neural computer ( ) that learns, directly from pixel and action trajectories, to remember abstract concepts, execute symbolic operations, and render crisp updates, all without a hand-crafted symbolic memory state. Each of these three requirements is an open problem for world models at large, and each takes a specific form on a computer. The first is long-horizon object permanence. World models of 3D scenes can use camera pose and scene geometry to decide where to store an observation and when to retrieve it~ xiao2025worldmem,li2025vmem , but a desktop offers no such index. A file opened in a pane overwrites exactly the pixels of the file that was there before, so the model must learn for itself what to store, when, and where. The second is symbolic reasoning inside a generated world. Approximate dynamics look convincing in natural video, but a terminal that receives 3+3 must print 6 every time. The third is rendering. Most of the screen is static from one frame to the next, which tempts a model to simply copy the previous frame, yet the regions that do change include 10--12\,px text that must stay legible at interactive frame rates. To address these three problems, we introduce the Interactive Neural Computer ( ), an end-to-end architecture analogous to a Neural Turing Machine~ graves2014ntm,graves2016dnc organized into three core modules: [leftmargin=1.3em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] Memory (surprise-gated concept slots): To sustain object permanence without camera pose or hand-crafted state, we introduce a coordinate-free concept-slot memory grounded in predictive coding~ rao1999predictive,friston2010free and surprise-driven memory selection ( ~ yang2025cambrians ), whose differentiable writes are gated by latent prediction surprise and self-supervised in representation space ( ). Compute (exploratory single-pass VLM query bridge): As a preliminary step toward symbolic reasoning inside a generated world, we extend learnable query bridges~ pan2025metaqueries,chen2025blip3o,panteam2025pan beyond diffusion-only supervision by placing causal queries strictly before training-only outcome text, extracting symbolic execution states into latent tokens ( ) in a single forward pass without test-time text decoding. Interface (residual latent-diffusion rendering): To render crisp updates at interactive speeds without collapsing into frame copying, we pair both modules with residual latent diffusion~ yang2023diffusion,salehi2026rfdm that predicts frame-to-frame latent deltas rather than re-synthesizing the full screen at every step, lifting persistent terminal-text OCR from with full-frame diffusion to at a matched training budget. Our full model reaches at , close to the 4-channel codec's ceiling, and with a 16-channel FLUX.1-schnell autoencoder at . Standard perceptual metrics cannot tell whether a world model remembers what is off screen, because a frame can look plausible while its content is wrong. We therefore evaluate memory directly ( ). In our hidden-shape recall task, a file containing a shape is closed, the user works elsewhere, and the file is later reopened, so the correct shape can only come from memory. A harder variant first overwrites the same pane with a competing file. Because our memory is an explicit bank rather than part of an entangled hidden state, we can also transplant or erase it at test time and check that what the model renders changes accordingly ( ). Public GUI corpora rarely revisit occluded content or test symbolic execution after the screen is cleared, so we built two controlled datasets, Desktop and Maths, that do ( ). We will release the full five-source aligned corpus, including both controlled datasets and our conversion and alignment pipelines, together with all training code and model weights. Related Work sec:related World models of computers. Modeling the machine rather than the agent has begun to be explored in recent work. Neural Computers~ zhuge2026neural models the desktop as an open-loop generated video of a user interacting with a computer, which generates compelling open-loop videos, but does not support closed-loop user interaction. StateCraft~ venturoli2026statecraftaugmentingvideoworld similarly uses video diffusion as its substrate, but augments its model with an explicit symbolic memory. This helps recall (object permanence), but its design requires access to hand-crafted symbolic accessibility-tree state graphs. Other concurrent GUI world models rely on external scaffolds or omit persistent memory: Solaris~ alaluf2026solaris stores state in text prompts, while CUWM~ guan2026cuwm and yu2026latentgui pair VLM or latent predictors with separate decoders without a persistent learned memory bank. NeuralOS~ rivard2025neuralos , the precursor to these approaches, is the only open-weight, interactive, pixel-to-pixel desktop world model, available for direct closed-loop rollouts, without privileged symbolic state requirements. NeuralOS requires only pixel supervision, but compressing observation history into a single recurrent LSTM state degrades performance over long rollouts. Our model differs from all of the above in that we learn an addressable external memory end-to-end from pixels and actions without hand-crafted state schemas. Generative interactive world models and memory. More broadly, action-conditioned world models have progressed from single-vector recurrent state spaces~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2023dreamerv3 to large-scale video generation for driving~ hu2023gaia1 , 2D and 3D worlds~ bruce2024genie,parkerholder2024genie2,parkerholder2025genie3 , and games~ valevski2025diffusion,alonso2024diamond . Across all of these domains, world models face a trade-off between storing raw history frames, which scales poorly with rollout length, and compressing history into a fixed-size state, which risks overwriting older information~ graves2014ntm,graves2016dnc,zhang2025framepack,po2025longcontext . Fixed-size memory is much easier to manage when the environment provides an external index for reads and writes. In 3D physical environments, geometry provides that index `for free' via camera pose, field-of-view overlap~ xiao2025worldmem,yu2025context , 3D surfels~ li2025vmem , or raymaps~ cetin2026smart,wu2026worldt3 . A 2D interface offers no such index ( ), so the model must learn what, where, and when to write. Existing 2D world models avoid this indexing problem by keeping a short sliding window of frames~ alonso2024diamond,valevski2025diffusion,zhang2025framepack or compressing history into a single recurrent vector~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2023dreamerv3,rivard2025neuralos , both of which lose occluded state over long rollouts. To build an indexed, fixed-capacity memory without 3D geometry, we instead draw on three complementary ideas from the representation-learning and sequence-modeling literature. First, to decide where and when to write without spatial coordinates, sequence models such as Differentiable Neural Computers~ graves2014ntm,graves2016dnc , slot attention~ locatello2020object,zhang2024gated , and gated delta networks~ schlag2021linear,katharopoulos2020transformers,yang2024gated,gu2024mamba,yang2025gated address discrete slots by content similarity and free capacity (where). Predictive-coding models~ rao1999predictive,friston2010free,sun2025learning,behrouz2025titans and ~ yang2025cambrians gate memory writes by whether a new observation is surprising (when). However, content addressing and surprise gating only work if the underlying representations capture high-level semantics rather than static background pixels. For what to store, we therefore draw on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures~ assran2023ijepa,bardes2024vjepa,zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2,zhang2026rlawm , self-supervising our concept slots via latent next-state prediction ( ) rather than pixel reconstruction alone. Symbolic reasoning in generated worlds. Learning symbolic rules and multi-digit arithmetic purely through pixel diffusion~ bruce2024genie,parkerholder2024genie2,parkerholder2025genie3 is sample-inefficient. Pretrained vision--language models (VLMs)~ bai2025qwen25vl,bai2025qwen3vl already possess strong symbolic reasoning, though in computer use research they are typically trained as external agents operating existing interfaces~ lee2023pix2struct,shaw2023pix2act,toyama2021androidenv,rawles2023aitw,deng2023mind2web,zhou2024webarena,xie2024osworld,rawles2024androidworld,anthropic2024computeruse . title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
summary: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment relates to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. Introduction sec:intro A single policy capable of controlling robots with diverse embodiments must solve two related problems: transferring task knowledge across robots and adapting behavior to each robot's physical capabilities. Existing approaches have made substantial progress on the former by identifying representations and interfaces that can be shared across embodiments. Generalist vision-language-action models use shared end-effector commands, unified action tokenizers, or learned action latents~ embodimentcollaboration2025openxembodimentroboticlearning,octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,liu2025rdt1bdiffusionfoundationmodel,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . Object-centric methods represent desired object motions or interactions that can be transferred between robots~ bharadhwaj2024track2actpredictingpointtracks,yuan2024generalflowfoundationaffordance,huang2024rekepspatiotemporalreasoningrelational,liu2024mokaopenworldroboticmanipulation . These approaches facilitate transfer by exploiting commonalities across embodiments. However, transferring task knowledge does not necessarily lead to effective control of each robot. Two robots pursuing the same goal may require different grasps, trajectories, or contact strategies because of differences in their kinematics, workspace, and dexterity. Learning embodiment-specific behaviors presents several challenges. First, a policy must reason about the robot's geometry in relation to the observed scene. The usefulness of a joint configuration depends on where its joints and motion axes lie relative to the objects and obstacles it must interact with. Existing policies incorporate descriptions such as URDFs or kinematic graphs, but often encode the robot independently of the scene~ chen2019hardwareconditionedpoliciesmultirobot,patel2024getzerographembodimenttransformer,suzuki2026embeddingmorphologytransformerscrossrobot . Second, the policy must accommodate different kinematic structures, including variations in joint types, degrees of freedom, and link topology, while still supporting a common control interface. Existing approaches have demonstrated transfer across relatively small collections of manipulators~ zhao2026geopropgroundingrobotstate,vosylius2024renderdiffusealigningimage,lv2025kinematicsawarediffusionpolicyconsistent . Third, the policy must learn how changes in morphology affect behavior so that it can control embodiments not encountered during training. This requires experience across a sufficiently diverse set of physical structures. Prior efforts to scale learning across hundreds of morphologies have primarily focused on locomotion~ ai2025embodimentscalinglawsrobot,gupta2022metamorphlearninguniversalcontrollers and not manipulation. We introduce , a policy trained across one million embodiments, capable of adapting behavior to each embodiment and what it can achieve in a given scene. Our approach represents each robot through a scene-grounded kinematic graph, expressing its joint geometry in the 3D coordinate frame of each observing camera. Each joint and fingertip is represented as a node containing its camera-frame position, motion axis, joint type, proprioceptive state, and kinematic connectivity. This allows the policy to relate the robot's physical structure to the corresponding visual observations. We pair this representation with a variable-DoF action representation that jointly predicts relative joint motions and end-effector pose updates using a flow-matching policy. By unifying the indexing scheme across all embodiments, our model learn to support different numbers and configurations of joints within the same network. These two components allow the policy to generate motions directly from each robot's kinematic structure and its relationship to the scene. Training a policy to exploit these differences requires substantial diversity in robot morphology. A policy trained on a handful of embodiments may learn effective manipulation strategies for those robots without learning how to adapt them to new ones. We develop a procedure to instantiate one million unique robot embodiments and create algorithms to automatically generate trajectories for each of them in simulation. Our data generation pipeline varies joint configurations, link geometry, and kinematic topology to generate embodiments; we use inverse-kinematics screening and physics-based acceptance to ensure feasibility of each trajectory. The resulting training distribution exposes the policy to a broad range of robot configurations and allow us to test on unseen embodiments. We evaluate on embodiments and scenes held out from training. On , it succeeds in 63.0 of episodes within 500 steps, against 57.9 for the strongest baseline and 17.8 for ; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it reaches 64.7 against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1 at the same step budget and 54.8 with twice the budget ( ). On a real OpenYAM arm with a fine-tip gripper, neither seen in training, completes 13 of 20 pick-and-place trials. The only baseline to succeed at all is MolmoAct2-BimanualYAM, for which this arm is in distribution, at 7 of 20; every other baseline completes none ( ). We observe that on this arm the policy sometimes makes use of the long final link specific to this unseen embodiment, extending it horizontally and then rotating the gripper to reach far targets ( ), a behavior not seen from MolmoAct2 trained exclusively on YAM. These results suggest that policies grounded in a robot's kinematics are a path towards better cross-embodiment generalization. Method sec:method We introduce , a single policy that learns cross-embodiment manipulation across robots with different kinematic structures. Our approach has three components. First, we represent each robot through a scene-grounded kinematic graph that expresses its geometry in the coordinate frame of its visual observations. Second, we develop a variable-DoF action representation that jointly predicts joint motions and end-effector poses across different robot configurations. Third, we generate diverse embodiments and collect successful manipulation trajectories in simulation to train the policy across one million robots. Policy formulation. We consider manipulation tasks across robots with different numbers of joints, link geometries, and kinematic structures. At each time step , the policy receives a language instruction , multi-view RGB observations , and the robot's current configuration and proprioceptive state. The robot's embodiment specifies its kinematic topology, joint types, limits, and geometric parameters. The policy predicts an action chunk containing relative joint motions and end-effector (EE) pose updates. Both predictions are supervised during training and used for control during execution. A prefix of the predicted chunk is executed before obtaining updated observations and replanning. The same policy parameters are shared across all embodiments. We encode RGB observations using SigLIP v2~ tschannen2025siglip2multilingualvisionlanguage and language instructions using Qwen 2.5~ bai2025qwen25vltechnicalreport . Kinematic structure. We decompose each robot into nodes representing arm joints, gripper drivers, gripper tips, and annotated points such as the tool center point (TCP). Each node has a type and an actuation indicator that distinguishes driven joints, terminal joints, and annotated points. The kinematic topology is encoded through shortest-path distances between nodes, which enter the Transformer as attention biases~ ying2021transformersreallyperformbad . Nodes are ordered according to their kinematic structure and left-padded to a maximum supported node count, keeping end-effector nodes at the final positions of the sequence. This provides a consistent indexing scheme across different embodiments while preserving their variable numbers of joints. Joint proprioception. Revolute joints are expressed in radians and prismatic joints in decimeters. The centered scalar is expanded into Fourier features and encoded through an MLP. Camera-frame geometric grounding. For each node and camera , we compute its current geometry using forward kinematics and known camera extrinsics. The geometry is represented in metric 3D camera coordinates through three fields: , where denotes the node center, is a point one unit along its motion axis, and represents translation and orientation using a continuous 6D rotation representation~ zhou2020continuityrotationrepresentationsneural . title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
summary: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

Introduction sec:intro Hospitals are 3D environments where small spatial errors carry clinical consequences~ wrongsite,wrongside . A nurse walking through a ward knows which bed a lit bed-head light belongs to, what lies on the patient's left, and whether a transport bed can pass a bedside cart. MLLMs supporting hospital assistants need to make these judgments from egocentric video. This is challenging because similar equipment repeats across beds, the patient's left and right may differ from the viewer's, and passage depends on both obstacle geometry and equipment width. Existing benchmarks evaluate spatial reasoning in general scenes~ simsv,viewspatial,ostbench,sat,vsibench,mmsibench , but provide limited coverage of patient-relative directions, equipment ownership, and width-constrained passage. This requires videos with clear visual evidence and accurate spatial annotations. Collecting such data in hospitals is difficult because of patient privacy and the cost of measuring scene geometry. We therefore use simulation to construct hospital scenes with controlled layouts and scene-derived answers. We introduce ( ), with 3,368 questions across eight question types and 373 layouts spanning 16 hospital room types ( ). Layouts follow constraints derived from hospital design guidelines, and answers are computed from the underlying 3D scenes, including routes and passage widths. Paired states of the same layout differ in one scene condition, such as which bed-head light is on, allowing us to test whether models change their answers when the relevant evidence changes. Rendered walkthroughs are converted to photorealistic videos and checked for camera-path consistency. Ten physicians screened the layouts, reviewing one video per layout. We also provide , a training set with 44,750 questions from layouts disjoint from the benchmark. We evaluate 32 open MLLMs and three proprietary models, and fine-tune two models on . The best open and proprietary models reach 45.7 and 53.6 macro accuracy. For reference, a test-fitted answer prior scores 40.8 , and physicians score 79.0 on a 400-question subset. Patient-relative directions are particularly challenging: 27 of the 32 open zero-shot models score below 40 , against 50 chance. Fine-tuning VideoJev-4B~ videojev raises its macro accuracy from 45.5 to 73.9 and its patient-frame accuracy from 17.0 to 93.7 . On paired states with different correct answers, evaluated zero-shot models retain the same answer more often than their answer preferences predict; fine-tuning reduces this excess repetition. However, route planning and passability remain the fine-tuned model's weakest tasks, at 58.3 and 66.0 , respectively. These results motivate testing whether explicit 3D input vlm3r,gpt4scene,spatialmllm can improve spatial reasoning. However, adding bird's-eye-view (BEV) tokens~ liftsplat , local map reads, or a geometry head during MLLM fine-tuning yields no clear gain in overall accuracy. For BEV tokens and local map reads, replacing the correct map with another clip's barely changes accuracy; the ground-truth map setting shows the same pattern. These findings motivate computing evidence from 3D representations and using it directly to score answer options. To this end, we introduce ( , ), which reconstructs a scene memory from each video and uses three 3D primitives for object-track queries, free-space analysis, and learned BEV map reads. Linear heads on the fine-tuned VideoJev-4B's question state select a primitive and its arguments, and the resulting evidence is added to the model's option scores. This requires no second language model. improves macro accuracy from 73.9 to 75.7 , with gains mainly in counting, re-identification, passability, and direction; route accuracy improves only from 58.3 to 59.5 . Replacing its scene memory with another layout's lowers accuracy to 70.4 , showing that its predictions depend on scene-specific evidence. Our contributions are threefold: (1) , a hospital spatial reasoning benchmark with scene-derived answers and paired scene states, accompanied by . (2) An evaluation of 35 MLLMs and fine-tuning experiments that reveal persistent difficulties in route planning and passability, alongside limited gains from the tested 3D input strategies. (3) , a framework that selects 3D computations from an MLLM's question state and combines their evidence with option scores, improving accuracy over the fine-tuned baseline. Related work sec:related Spatial benchmarks for MLLMs. Existing benchmarks test spatial reasoning from videos~ vsibench , multiple images~ mmsibench , online observations~ ostbench , and different viewpoints~ viewspatial . VSI-Bench includes human-annotated routes. SAT and SIMS-V generate spatial questions through simulation~ sat,simsv , while Open3D-VQA uses real and simulated aerial scenes~ open3dvqa . Clinical3D-Bench evaluates patient-relative directions, equipment relations, and routes and passage widths computed from hospital scene occupancy. Paired scene states with different correct answers test whether models respond to changes in the scene ( ). Clinical spatial reasoning. Medical VQA benchmarks focus on medical images~ vqarad,pathvqa,omnimedvqa , including 3D spatial reasoning in SpatialMed~ spatialmed . MM-OR and EgoExOR study surgical scenes and activities~ mmor,egoexor , while OR-Expert addresses operating-room spatial reasoning orexpert . Clinical3D-Bench complements these tasks with patient-relative directions, equipment ownership, and clearance-constrained navigation across diverse hospital rooms. 3D-aware MLLMs and tools. MLLMs incorporate geometry through reconstruction features~ vlm3r,spatialmllm , position encodings~ video3dllm,llava3d , BEV prompts~ gpt4scene , or spatial supervision~ ross3d,spatialladder . Other approaches use 3D priors spatialpin , program synthesis~ vadar , or tool-equipped agents~ spatialscore . GeoJeV selects 3D primitives and their arguments using linear heads on the MLLM's question state, then adds their evidence to its option scores, without generating programs or calling a second language model. sec:bench Overview sec:overview We introduce to measure the 3D spatial intelligence of MLLMs in hospital rooms from egocentric video. It has 3,368 multiple-choice questions on 569 ten-second clips of 373 layouts in 16 room families. Scenes are generated in simulation from hospital design standards and every answer is computed from the scene record; the clips are transferred to photorealistic appearance, verified against the scene and screened by physicians. A disjoint training set, , has 44,750 questions. Tasks. The eight question types form four task groups ( ; shares in a). Spatial memory: Count asks how many instances of a category seen so far are out of view at a given time, and Re-ID asks which instance at a later time is the one named earlier. Ownership and relations: Light owner asks which bed the lit bed-head light belongs to, and Device reference asks what a device is mounted on or which label it carries, where the device is named by its relation to a bed or landmark and a look-alike is in view. Frames of reference: Patient frame asks whether an object is on the left or right of a patient on a named bed; no people are present, so the model imagines a supine patient, and left and right are the patient's. Metric navigation: Direction asks for the first change of direction on the shortest walkable route from the camera's start pose to a goal, or for the goal's quadrant; Route asks to fill in the turn sequence of that route or for the goal nearest by walking; Passability asks whether a passage wide enough for a crash cart (0.9\,m) or transport bed (1.2\,m) reaches the goal. The types comprise 15 subtasks ( ). Construction. is built in five steps ( ): scenes are generated from hospital design standards ( ), questions are generated and checked ( ), clips are transferred to photorealistic appearance ( ), and physicians screen the layouts ( ). Standards-grounded scene generation sec:generation From standards to rules. Hospital planning standards state how large a room must be and how much free space its beds need. We take these requirements for each room type from three public standards (UK Health Building Notes, Australasian Health Facility Guidelines, US VA Space Planning Criteria), recording the source section of each, and use them in three ways. Size requirements, such as room area and the spacing between beds, set the ranges from which a layout's dimensions are sampled. Clearance requirements become geometric checks: a clear strip of 0.9\,m beside each ward bed (1.5\,m in ICU), a clear zone at the foot of the bed and a free zone at the door. Functional requirements become checks on content and access: every bed position has a service panel and the required pumps, the room has a handwash station, drawn curtains do not block the entry, and every bed foot can be reached from the door. Each of the 16 room families has a generator program~ procthor,infinigenindoors,holodeck , and a layout is kept only if it passes every check ( ); random seeds are fixed, so every layout can be regenerated. Assets, rendering and clips. Free-standing equipment (beds, IV poles, patient monitors, ventilators, imaging and surgical units, chairs, carts; 22 of 47 object categories) uses NVIDIA SimReady assets~ simready (CC BY 4.0). Everything else is built procedurally: the parts that questions depend on (infusion pumps with bed labels, bed-head panels, surgical lights and ceiling pendants, curtains, doors, bed labels), equipment with no suitable SimReady model (CT, stretcher, sharps containers, sanitiser dispensers) and other furniture ( ); small wall items are placed by clinical rules. title: RoboProbe: Benchmarking Physical Plausibility of Robot World Models
summary: Evaluating the physical plausibility of generated videos is critical for reliable robotic planning with world models. These videos inform action proposal and assessment before real-world execution, so undetected physical violations can lead to erroneous assessments of action feasibility and safety. Yet current video generators often produce physically implausible interactions. Detecting such violations directly with vision-language models (VLMs) remains challenging as physical verification requires evidence-grounded spatiotemporal reasoning beyond high-level semantic understanding. We develop five law-specific metrics for evaluating physical plausibility by combining spatiotemporal evidence from segmentation, tracking, 3D geometry, or appearance comparisons with targeted VLM reasoning: Contact fidelity, Object persistence, Solidity, Robot deformation, and Object deformation. Building on this metric suite, we introduce RoboProbe, an agentic evaluation framework that coordinates metric execution and selectively refines evaluations through constrained actions. To evaluate the physical plausibility of robot world models, we further introduce RP-Bench, with 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations of 239 manipulation tasks from 12 robot datasets. On RP-Bench, all five metrics achieve AUROCs above 0.85 and outperform the evaluated learned judges, prior evaluators, and a frames-only Gemini baseline. Applying these metrics to five video generators reveals distinct patterns of physical violations across models, in both violation types and frequencies.

Introduction sec:intro Embodied World Models (EWMs) generate future visual rollouts of robot-environment interactions to support planning, synthetic data generation, and policy evaluation~ cosmos,cosmos25,cosmos3,abotphysworld,lvp,unipi . Because these rollouts inform physical decisions, mere perceptual realism is insufficient: a visually convincing rollout can still violate physics, undermining the relationship between robot actions and environmental responses and misleading downstream planning and policy evaluation. In order for the EWMs to be reliable tools for robot agents, evaluating EWMs therefore requires answering a critical question: are the generated robot actions and environmental responses physically plausible? Early evaluations of generated videos measure pixel-level fidelity and temporal consistency~ vbench,fvd,ewmbench , which say little about whether an interaction obeys physics. Most recent physical-plausibility benchmarks instead ask a large vision-language model (VLM) to judge the generated video directly~ videophy2,rbench,pai . VLMs are strong at high-level semantic understanding, but detecting these violations requires precise spatiotemporal reasoning about 3D geometry, which remains a weakness of current VLMs. Simulator-based benchmarks~ robowmbench,kinebench provide more explicit physical measurements, but they are limited to supported environments and vulnerable to action-extraction noise. Existing 3D geometric evaluators either score a single object in isolation~ pdi or need simulator ground truth and leave robot--object contact and interpenetration to a VLM~ robophys3d . To close this gap, we introduce , which grounds physical-plausibility judgments in spatiotemporal evidence measured with segmentation, tracking, and 3D geometry. We design five law-specific metrics covering , , , , and . Beyond the fixed metrics, we adapt our measurement to diverse scenes, tasks, and atypical cases with an agentic framework that reasons over each video's scene, robot type, and entities. It reviews and selectively refines the evidence through constrained actions. To systematically probe whether current evaluators can catch these violations, we curate RP-Bench, with 761 labeled generated videos and 130 real ones from 12 robot datasets. The six task types are pick-and-place, pushing and pressing, multi-step, bimanual, tool-use, and pouring tasks. On RP-Bench, state-of-the-art proprietary VLMs provide meaningful signals but remain limited in precise detection and spatiotemporal evidence grounding. Judging from sampled frames, they fall furthest behind on brief, geometric violations such as surface penetration. By measuring this evidence directly, outperforms the strongest VLM, Gemini 4 Argon~ gemini , on all five violation types (average AUROC 0.894 vs.\ 0.828). Its reported frame lies a median of 0.5 to 7 frames from the human annotation. Our main contributions are as follows: Geometry-Grounded Physical Plausibility Metrics: We develop five geometry-grounded metrics that translate physical laws into concrete checks of object states and interactions over time. Self-Reviewing Agentic Evaluation: We propose , an agentic framework that coordinates the proposed metrics to assess physical plausibility in complex and diverse generated videos. By combining tool-derived evidence with targeted VLM reasoning and self-review, grounds its assessments in specific physical evidence rather than on holistic semantic judgments. RP-Bench for Robotic Physical Plausibility: We introduce RP-Bench, a human-annotated benchmark comprising 761 generated videos and 130 real demonstrations spanning 239 tasks from 12 robot datasets. On RP-Bench, outperforms a frames-only VLM baseline on all five violation types. Related Work sec:related Embodied World Models sec:related_ewm Video generation models trained on internet-scale data learn to predict how a scene evolves~ sora,wan,cogvideox . Conditioned on robot actions, language, or the current observation, they become embodied world models (EWMs) that let a robot agent imagine the outcome of an action before executing it~ cosmos,cosmos25,cosmos3,abotphysworld,lvp,ctrlworld . EWMs now support model-based planning~ unipi , policy evaluation~ worldeval1,worldeval2,worldgym , and VLA training. In each use, the agent acts on what the generated video shows, so an EWM is a reliable verifier of actions only if its rollouts are physically plausible. Open-Loop Visual Benchmarks sec:related_openloop The recent advancement of VLMs makes them a natural choice as an intelligent evaluation tool, and a majority of recent benchmarks directly ask VLMs or learned judges whether a video is physically plausible~ videophy2,worldmodelbench,pai,phyworldbench,rbench,h2rbench . VideoPhy-2~ videophy2 and WorldModelBench~ worldmodelbench train dedicated judges to rate physical commonsense and law adherence, while RBench~ rbench and PAI-Bench~ pai score embodied videos along physical and task dimensions. VLMs and learned judges are strong at high-level semantic understanding but remain limited in spatiotemporal reasoning and in evaluating precise geometric details. Neither shows where or when a violation occurs. instead grounds each judgment in spatiotemporal evidence from segmentation, tracking, and 3D geometry, combined with targeted VLM reasoning, and reports the frames where a violation occurs. Closed-Loop Execution Benchmarks sec:related_sim_geo Closed-loop benchmarks evaluate an EWM by extracting robot actions from the generated video and executing them in a simulator, so task success measures whether the rollout is executable~ robowmbench,kinebench . World-in-World~ worldinworld instead places world models in a closed planning loop that scores candidate actions without extracting them. KineBench~ kinebench replaces learned inverse dynamics models with explicit 6D end-effector pose recovery. However, these protocols are confined to environments that a simulator supports with a compatible action interface, and their verdicts inherit the noise of action extraction. A failed execution may come from an inverse dynamics model or pose tracker that fails on unseen trajectories or deformed robots, which limits their utility on arbitrary generated videos. closes this gap by measuring physical plausibility directly on the video, using VLM reasoning to adapt to each dynamic scene, robot type, and set of entities, without a simulator or a learned action extractor. 3D Geometric Evaluation sec:related_geo Another line of work lifts generated videos to 3D and measures geometry directly. PDI-Bench~ pdi scores the scale, motion, and rigidity of a single tracked object, while RoboPhys-3D~ robophys3d compares rollouts with a matched simulator ground truth. However, both measure entities one at a time: PDI-Bench never evaluates interaction physics between objects, and RoboPhys-3D hands contact and interpenetration back to a VLM. Yet many violations in manipulation arise between entities. closes this gap with law-specific metrics that each test one law of the robot--object interaction with geometric evidence. Method sec:method To evaluate whether EWM rollouts are physically plausible, we introduce , an evidence-grounded evaluation framework with three components. (1) Five law-specific metrics, , , , and , where a higher score means more violation ( ). (2) An agentic framework that understands and adapts to diverse manipulation scenes, and reviews the evidence behind every score, repairing faulty evidence and rerunning the step ( ). (3) RP-Bench, with 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations over 239 tasks of six types ( ). shows the pipeline. Evidence-grounded physical metrics sec:metrics . sec:contact An object should start to move only after the robot touches it. flags object motion that no plausible contact precedes, as a shows. title: Seeing Is Not Reaching: Instruction Shortcuts Override Visual Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 31 pages, including supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/QZhang2111/psg
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are expected to inherit visual grounding from vision-language models, yet often reach for an object's training location after it has been moved. Across six VLAs, we identify two shortcuts: a scene shortcut, where the arm follows the scene's original task despite a new instruction, and an instruction shortcut, where the instruction retrieves the requested object's training location. In $π_{0.5}$, the instruction shortcut persists even though object-name attention follows the moved target. We call this Seeing Is Not Reaching. To determine whether this grounding is unused or overridden, we separately mask an image-mediated grounding pathway and a direct instruction-to-action pathway. Masking the grounding pathway eliminates reaches to moved targets, whereas masking the direct pathway increases them. Thus, grounding already guides action but is often overridden by the instruction shortcut, which acts through the direct pathway. We introduce Pathway-Separated Guidance (PSG), which amplifies grounding and suppresses the shortcut without training or external target locations. On LIBERO-PRO Object under Position perturbations, PSG raises the target-reaching rate from 22.0% to 52.6% and task success from 16.6% to 40.8%, while largely preserving performance on the original tasks.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs) build on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t,black2025pi05,zheng2025xvla . VLMs can locate named objects in images, known as visual grounding~ karamcheti2024prismatic,beyer2024paligemma,kang2025fewheads . VLAs are expected to inherit this ability and use it to reach objects at new locations. Yet benchmarks such as LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-Plus show sharp drops in success after target relocation, with the arm often returning to the target's training location~ zhou2026liberopro,fei2026liberoplus,li2025vlasconfined . Prior studies offer different explanations for these failures. On the original LIBERO scenes, policies often retain much of their success without instructions~ fei2026liberoplus,fang2026cag , suggesting reliance on task-correlated visual cues~ hou2026langgap,guo2026robofollow,xing2025shortcut,gerigk2026scrubbing . Other studies find that instructions select familiar behaviors, while visual feedback adapts their execution~ li2025vlasconfined,liu2026perturbot,chen2026instructions . What drives the arm does not reveal what visual information the model retains. Robot training can weaken visual and semantic abilities inherited from VLMs~ kachaev2025dontblind,hancock2026vlm2vla,driess2025knowledge,zhang2025howinherit . Meanwhile, the target's identity can remain decodable even when the arm reaches for another object~ jiang2026encoded . Yet decodable identity does not establish whether the model can locate the target from its name in the image, much less whether that information guides action. We therefore ask: When the target moves, is visual grounding lost, retained but unused, or overridden by another effect of the instruction? We examine six VLAs under two changes: relocating the target or requesting a different object in the same scene. Two shortcuts emerge (Fig.~ fig:teaser ): a scene shortcut, where the arm goes to the same location despite a changed instruction, and an instruction shortcut, where it goes to the requested object's training location despite relocation~ geirhos2020shortcut . These failures might reflect weakened visual grounding: in several models, name attention fails to follow the relocated target (Fig.~ fig:retention ). In , however, name attention follows the moved object, yet the arm still predominantly takes the instruction shortcut. We call this Seeing Is Not Reaching. To determine whether this apparent grounding is unused or overridden, we separately mask two instruction-to-action pathways (Fig.~ fig:cut ). The grounding pathway passes through image tokens that attend to object names before being read by action tokens~ swann2026causal . The direct pathway allows action tokens to attend directly to the instruction. Across 200 relocated-target episodes in a diagnostic test, masking the grounding pathway reduces target reaches from 29 to 0, while masking the direct pathway increases them from 29 to 64. These opposing effects show that grounding already guides action but is overridden by an instruction shortcut on the direct pathway. Yet in the original scenes, masking the direct pathway still leaves reaches in 199 of 200 episodes, consistent with prior ablations~ shi2026vlatrace . When the target occupies its training location, grounding and the shortcut point to the same place; relocation exposes their conflict. This conflict suggests a correction: amplify grounding while suppressing the instruction shortcut. We introduce Pathway-Separated Guidance (PSG), which estimates each pathway's contribution by masking it and measuring the resulting change in predicted flow velocity. PSG then amplifies the grounding contribution and suppresses the direct-pathway contribution during sampling. Unlike instruction-free guidance, which mixes both effects~ fang2026cag,zhan2026rss , PSG adjusts them separately during sampling. PSG requires neither training nor externally supplied target locations. On LIBERO-PRO Object under Position perturbations, PSG raises 's target-reaching rate (Reach) from 22.0 to 52.6 and task success from 16.6 to 40.8 , while largely preserving original-task performance. Robot demonstrations often couple scenes, instructions, and actions, allowing VLAs to exploit task-correlated shortcuts~ dehaan2019causal,geirhos2020shortcut,xing2025shortcut . Counterfactual benchmarks expose these dependencies by relocating objects, changing instructions, or perturbing scene cues~ zhou2026liberopro,fei2026liberoplus,zhou2026liberopro2,gerigk2026scrubbing . One pattern is scene dependence: policies can execute familiar tasks even when instructions are absent or changed~ fei2026liberoplus,fang2026cag,guo2026robofollow,jiang2026encoded,jiang2026benchmarking . For VLAs, CAG and RSS strengthen language conditioning relative to vision-only or instruction-free predictions~ fang2026cag,zhan2026rss , while IGAR reallocates attention toward instruction tokens~ zhang2026igar . Seeing Is Not Reaching sec:mechanism When a VLA reaches for an object's training place rather than its current position, the behavior alone does not reveal what determines the arm's destination. We first distinguish the roles of the scene and instruction, then examine whether visual grounding is retained and influences action. Scene Shortcut or Instruction Shortcut? sec:behavior We compare six VLAs on five LIBERO-Object tasks~ liu2023libero . Instead of task success, we record where the gripper first closes, and call a close on the requested object a reach. VLAs return to the training place. The Position perturbation of LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2026liberopro swaps the requested object with another object while keeping the instruction unchanged. Five models then close almost exclusively at the requested object's training place, now occupied by another object ( ; see supplementary). \ also usually returns there, but reaches the moved object in 42 of 200 episodes. This result alone cannot tell whether the return follows the scene or the instruction: under Position, the object's training place coincides with the scene's original task location. We therefore use the Task perturbation of LIBERO-PRO, which keeps the scene unchanged but requests another object in it. title: GOLD-SLAM: Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM
summary: Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. Compared with existing panoramic baselines, GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 5.56-9.10 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9-83.9%. To assess deployment feasibility on resource-constrained platforms such as UAVs, we evaluate an embedded configuration of GOLD-SLAM on a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), demonstrating online operation at the cost of reconstruction quality.

Introduction sec:intro Ground and aerial robots require reliable localization, dense geometry, and photorealistic rendering for interaction, often under a limited sensor budget~ kinectfusion,imap . LiDAR provides sparse geometric measurements with metric scale, IMUs supply high-frequency inertial constraints, and cameras capture dense color and texture. Their complementary roles underpin multisensor odometry and mapping systems~ licfusion,lvisam,r2live,fastlivo,fastlivo2 . 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3dgs represents scenes using explicit anisotropic Gaussians. Its efficient rasterization enables faster rendering than NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf , promoting the development of Gaussian-based SLAM~ monogs,photoslam,gaussianlic,gaussianlic2,odgsslam . However, the narrow field of view (FoV) of perspective cameras limits scene coverage and inter-frame correspondences, making pose estimation more vulnerable to repetitive or sparse textures and rapid motion~ panodirectvo . Panoramic cameras expand coverage to a spherical FoV, but their projections introduce stronger nonlinear distortion~ 360vo . ODGS-SLAM~ odgsslam extends incremental Gaussian SLAM to equirectangular projection (ERP) images. However, it suffers from scale drift outdoors, motivating the use of LiDAR geometric constraints for large-scale mapping. Panoramic LiDAR--inertial--visual Gaussian SLAM faces several technical challenges: Nonuniform ERP sampling and polar distortion. ERP projection introduces nonuniform sampling on the sphere and substantial stretching near the poles~ odgsslam,panogs_slam . Greater impact of the LiDAR blind zone. LiDAR--camera FoV mismatch leaves regions without depth support~ gaussianlic2,hdpvslam . Panoramic coverage exposes more such regions, complicating Gaussian initialization (Fig.~ fig:erp-valid-domain ). Interference with new surface reconstruction. In incremental Gaussian SLAM, high accumulated opacity from existing Gaussians can block opacity-only insertion on newly observed nearby surfaces~ splatam,gsslam . Beyond these technical challenges, commonly used LiDAR--visual benchmarks focus on ground-robot or handheld/backpack acquisition~ m2dgr,m3dgr,hiltioxford,oxfordspires , leaving UAV motion underrepresented. In this context, our contributions are: We present GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian splatting SLAM framework fusing LiDAR, IMU, and panoramic cameras with a shared spherical model for tracking and mapping. We combine blind-zone visual constraints with Patch Brightness Uncertainty (PBU) to improve pose estimation under limited LiDAR coverage and illumination changes. We combine measured LiDAR depth with panoramic depth predictions for Gaussian initialization and design Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP) to improve incremental surface reconstruction. We collect WHOLE, a dataset of LiDAR and IMU measurements and panoramic images acquired with a customized UAV platform in indoor, outdoor, and degraded environments. Results on WHOLE and public benchmarks demonstrate competitive localization and improved geometric reconstruction with broad scene coverage. Related Work sec:related Gaussian Splatting SLAM. 3DGS~ kerbl3dgs enables efficient photorealistic rendering through differentiable Gaussian rasterization. MonoGS~ monogs uses differentiable splatting for monocular SLAM, with analytic pose Jacobians and optional depth supervision. Photo-SLAM~ photoslam combines geometric and photometric features with progressive Gaussian pyramid learning and geometric densification for monocular, stereo, and RGB-D SLAM. SplaTAM~ splatam and GS-SLAM~ gsslam use depth-guided Gaussian insertion, with GS-SLAM also suppressing floating artifacts. Unlike these perspective systems, GOLD-SLAM performs panoramic reconstruction with LiDAR geometric supervision and predicted depth for blind-zone Gaussian initialization. SLAM. Omnidirectional SLAM expands visual coverage through multi-camera systems or fisheye cameras. Gaussian projection and rendering must handle polar stretching and horizontal periodicity in ERP images. 360ORB-SLAM~ orb360slam combines panoramic features, triangulation, and depth completion for localization and point-cloud mapping. Panoramic LiDAR DSO~ panodirectvo associates panoramic images with LiDAR observations for robust tracking. ODGS~ odgs reconstructs Gaussian scenes from ERP images, and ODGS-SLAM~ odgsslam extends incremental Gaussian SLAM to ERP input. Fusion. In large-scale scenes, multimodal fusion supports localization and reconstruction under visual degradation or LiDAR degeneracy. LIV-GaussMap~ livgaussmap uses LiDAR--IMU poses and initial geometry, then refines Gaussians photometrically. Gaussian-LIC~ gaussianlic combines tightly coupled LiDAR--IMU--camera localization with Gaussian initialization from LiDAR points and blind-zone visual triangulation. GS-LIVM~ gslivm completes LiDAR surfaces via Gaussian process regression, using predicted covariance for Gaussian initialization. Gaussian-LIC2~ gaussianlic2 combines lightweight depth completion for blind-zone Gaussian initialization with LiDAR depth supervision. Building on this, GOLD-SLAM supports panoramic reconstruction and uses blind-zone visual constraints and PBU for pose estimation. title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
summary: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $π_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
