Introduction sec:intro Can an ordinary mirror reveal limitations in how robots connect visual observations to physical actions? The classical mirror self-recognition test examines whether animals can use reflections to guide actions toward their own bodies~ gallup1970selfrecognition . Inspired by this behavioral probe, we ask whether robot policies can reliably locate and manipulate physical objects when their observations also contain reflections of those objects. Mirrors create a structured discrepancy between visual appearance and actionable space. Reflections preserve recognizable features and change with physical objects, yet their apparent locations contain no additional manipulable targets. They can also adjoin real objects in images, forming composite contours, or reveal otherwise occluded targets. These properties enable tests of two complementary capabilities: maintaining reliable manipulation in the presence of reflections, and using reflected observations to act on occluded targets. Recent advances in generalist robot policies have expanded the range of manipulation tasks that can be performed from visual and language inputs, yet whether these policies possess the two capabilities above remains unclear. Vision-Language-Action models directly generate actions from multimodal observations, while World Action Models jointly model actions and future observations~ BlackK-RSS-25,ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot . Agentic policies provide another approach by selecting and invoking robot tools through repeated observation and reasoning~ jia2026agentpolicyroboticmanipulation . However, strong performance under standard evaluation conditions does not establish robustness to changes in visual evidence. Controlled perturbation benchmarks have demonstrated substantial performance degradation under variations in viewpoints, lighting, backgrounds, and other conditions~ fei2026liberoplus . Reflections are not covered by these perturbations: rather than altering appearance, they duplicate task-relevant content at locations with a known geometric relationship to the physical scene. Existing mirror-based evaluations have begun to examine embodied agents’ self-centric perception and interaction, including tasks inspired by mirror self-recognition~ guo2026mirrorbench . We investigate a different operational setting: generalist policies performing external-object manipulation under controlled mirror configurations. The question posed above breaks down into three parts: how reflections affect task completion, whether observed degradation extends beyond the effects of an inserted physical panel, and what execution behaviors accompany these changes. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, an evaluation benchmark built on RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:currfilebase , it preserves the original manipulation objectives and success criteria while evaluating policies under four conditions: no mirror, a single mirror, dual mirrors, and a mirrored tabletop. On a shared set of eight tasks, we pair layouts and policy seeds across conditions to measure changes relative to each policy’s own mirror-free baseline. For selected policies, geometrically matched non-reflective panels provide additional controls for the effects of inserting physical structures. We further design three diagnostic scenarios, namely grasping on a mirrored tabletop, pushing an object connected to its reflection, and acting with reflections as the main visual cue, combining task outcomes with trajectory and contact observations. This protocol enables researchers to assess reflection robustness using existing policies and task evaluators, and to characterize failures beyond aggregate success rates. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, all three mirror conditions reduce aggregate success rates, with average drops of 10.8--56.7 percentage points across policies. Matched panel comparisons show that 50--88 of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. The accompanying behaviors are consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. The three diagnostics further show more frequent empty grasps, pushing progress that varies with policy and contour, and limited physical-target contact even with mirror-related hints. Real-robot experiments with and FastWAM show a similar overall degradation trend. Together, these results reveal a shared vulnerability to reflections across diverse robot policies. Related Work sec:related_work Robotic Manipulation Benchmarks and Visual Robustness Robotic manipulation benchmarks provide complementary tools for evaluating policy capabilities. LIBERO studies knowledge transfer in lifelong robot learning~ liu2023libero . RoboTwin 2.0 combines scalable data generation with structured domain randomization for bimanual manipulation~ chen2026robotwin2 , while RoboDojo provides a unified simulation and real-world evaluation framework for generalist manipulation policies~ chen2026robodojo . Recent benchmarks place greater emphasis on robustness beyond nominal task success. LIBERO-Plus introduces controlled perturbations to object layouts, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language, lighting, backgrounds, and sensor observations~ fei2026liberoplus . LIBERO-VPro evaluates closed-loop visual robustness by perturbing the evidence available during execution, including observation degradation, camera staleness, and cross-view consistency~ li2026liberovpro . LIBERO-Pro2.0 further covers static and runtime shifts across environmental, observational, execution, robot-state, and language dimensions~ zhou2026liberopro2 . RoboPRO complements success-based evaluation with collision metrics under clutter and controlled perturbations~ li2026robopro . Building on these evaluation principles, our work focuses on mirror-augmented manipulation, where reflections introduce structured visual ambiguity alongside physical scene changes. We evaluate task outcomes and contact behavior, and use geometrically matched non-reflective panels to examine performance differences beyond the presence of the panel itself. Mirror Perception and Spatial Reasoning Mirrors challenge visual understanding because reflected objects can resemble directly observed objects while occupying different physical locations. Early mirror-detection methods identify reflective regions through contextual contrasts~ yang2019mirror , while video-based approaches exploit spatial and temporal correspondences~ lin2023videomirror . These methods address the localization of mirror regions rather than the action consequences of reflected observations. Mirror3D further estimates mirror geometry to refine unreliable depth measurements on reflective surfaces~ Tan_2021_CVPR . More recently, MIRA-Bench evaluates reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and scene-level decisions in real RGB-D mirror scenes, exposing difficulties in reconciling reflected appearance with depth measurements~ yin2026mira . MirrorQA examines subject-centered left--right reasoning in mirror contexts~ liu2026mirrorqa . Related diagnostic benchmarks, including HallusionBench~ guan2024hallusionbench and IllusionVQA~ shahgir2024illusionvqa , investigate visual illusions and failures of image-grounded reasoning. Unlike these perception-focused studies, we evaluate task outcomes and contact behavior during closed-loop manipulation under reflections. Mirror-Mediated Robotic Interaction Robotic mirror research spans geometry and sensorimotor learning. Hart and Scassellati infer mirror viewpoints from learned sensorimotor relationships~ hart2012mirror . Marchand and Chaumette develop visual servoing for robot-mounted mirrors~ marchand2017mirror , while Lanillos et al. combine active inference and sensorimotor prediction for mirror self-recognition and self/other distinction~ lanillos2020mirror . Yoshioka et al. exploit mirror reflections to observe occluded regions, while UMI incorporates side mirrors for manipulation and shows that corrected mirror views can outperform uncorrected ones~ yoshioka2021lookingglassdiminishingocclusions,chi2024universalmanipulationinterfaceinthewild . Recent embodied evaluations extend mirror-based tests to multimodal agents. MirrorBench studies self-centric intelligence through simulated mirror interaction~ guo2026mirrorbench , while Ziliotto et al.\ evaluate whether agents can infer hidden self-attributes from reflections and use this evidence to guide actions~ ziliotto2026mirror . Beyond self-centric tasks, Being-M0.7 evaluates mirror-assisted grasping of a directly occluded toy in a real-world humanoid task~ yue2026beingm07 . Our work studies reflection robustness across multiple generalist policies and manipulation tasks under controlled mirror configurations. title: NativeDrive: Native Multimodal Foundations for Autonomous Driving
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Autonomous driving requires semantic understanding and fine-grained scene perception for precise action prediction. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic priors, but low-dimensional action labels provide limited structural supervision. Some studies extend VLAs with visual generation tasks or adopt video-based world-action models (WAMs), but both approaches introduce appearance-reconstruction overhead, which is less relevant to planning. Native multimodal models offer an alternative to unify understanding and generation within one backbone. On this basis, we propose NativeDrive, a native encoder-free multimodal driving framework adapting the unified backbone for policy learning and introduce a dense supervision task tailored to driving. The Native Action Interface reuses the understanding expert's token-prediction interface for the discrete policy and adapts the generation expert for continuous policy. Driving Semantic Editing reuses the generation expert's editing capability for dense scene-structure supervision during training, while inference runs only the selected planning policy. NativeDrive achieves competitive planning performance among unified understanding-and-generation models on NAVSIM v1 and v2, with ablations validating its components' effectiveness. Code will be released.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Autonomous driving requires models to integrate high-level semantic understanding with fine-grained scene perception for reliable driving actions~ drivevlm,vladbench,drivelm . Large pretrained models offer transferable priors for these tasks: vision-language models (VLMs) supply world knowledge and semantic understanding~ autovla,recogdrive , while video generation models provide motion and temporal dynamics priors for modeling environmental change~ drivewam . Transferring these capabilities to driving policies requires a suitable action interface. Low-dimensional trajectory labels alone only weakly supervise learning scene structure~ w0 . The key question is how to design action interfaces that match the pretrained backbone's modeling mechanisms and dense visual objectives that reflect driving requirements. Existing approaches primarily build driving policies on vision-language or video generation backbones. The VLM-based route, shown in the leftmost column of Fig.~ fig:overview (a), transfers semantic knowledge and instruction understanding into planning through an action interface~ autovla,recogdrive,fsdrive,w0 . Some methods introduce dense visual supervision by adding an external generation module~ w0 or extending the vocabulary with visual tokens~ w0,fsdrive . The video-based route, shown in the second column of Fig.~ fig:overview (a), exploits pretrained motion and temporal dynamics priors by learning from future-scene generation and action prediction~ drivelaw,drivewam,driveva,universe . Prior work uses attention masking to decouple action prediction from future visual tokens, enabling trajectory-only inference~ universe . Both routes achieve competitive planning performance. However, understanding-oriented VLMs typically rely on an extended generation module and lack jointly pretrained understanding and generation foundations~ w0,fsdrive . Video generation backbones model appearance and dynamics~ drivewam , but future-frame reconstruction also captures visual details less relevant to planning~ imagewam . Unified understanding-and-generation backbones provide another route to transfer both types of priors~ doe1,w0,explorevla,vega . In the 3rd column of Fig.~ fig:overview (a), some approaches use unified backbones that natively model discrete visual and text tokens to predict future visual tokens~ doe1,w0,explorevla , either reusing token prediction for discrete actions~ doe1,w0 or extending a continuous trajectory prediction head~ explorevla . Recently, native encoder-free architectures enable multimodal understanding and generation via direct image-patch embeddings and pixel prediction~ u1 , reducing reliance on separate visual encoders and intermediate representation alignment. This design supports jointly developing action interfaces and visual supervision for driving. Building on this, we propose NativeDrive, jointly designing a policy interface and an auxiliary visual task around the backbone’s native modeling mechanisms. In the rightmost column of Fig.~ fig:overview (a), we build discrete and continuous driving policies using the native mechanisms of the understanding and generation experts, respectively. We also use backbone generation for a driving-specific auxiliary visual task. NativeDrive combines these key attributes: a unified backbone, flexible action interfaces, and training-only visual task as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview (b). Our contributions are: We propose NativeDrive, which adapts a native unified multimodal backbone to driving policy learning by pairing discrete action prediction with either continuous trajectory generation or training-only semantic editing. We design a Native Action Interface aligning two policy branches with the backbone's native modeling mechanisms. The discrete branch uses the understanding expert to predict quantized action tokens, while the continuous branch adapts the generation expert into a lightweight action head. We introduce Driving Semantic Editing, adapting the generation expert's pretrained editing capability to produce semantic maps. This training-only task provides dense supervision on road layout and traffic participants without additional inference cost. We investigate key design choices for adapting a unified multimodal model to autonomous driving, including action interface, visual task, and joint training. Comparisons and ablations demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed components. NativeDrive achieves 88.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1~ navsim and 88.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. Under best-of-6 oracle evaluation, it achieves 93.8 PDMS and 93.3 EPDMS. Related Work sec:related Unified multimodal models support understanding and content generation within one framework, enabling capabilities to transfer across modalities~ chameleon,emu3,showo,bagel . Unified multimodal models can be grouped by whether they use discrete or continuous representations for visual generation. Chameleon~ chameleon and Emu3~ emu3 autoregressively model both text and discrete image tokens, whereas Show-o~ showo combines autoregressive language modeling with discrete diffusion for image generation. Continuous approaches generate images or videos in latent or pixel space. BAGEL~ bagel combines autoregressive language modeling with continuous image generation through modality-specific experts that share self-attention. Show-o2~ showo2 uses flow matching for both image and video generation. SenseNova-U1~ u1 unifies visual understanding and generation in an encoder-free architecture with convolutional patch embeddings for input and direct pixel prediction for output. Driving action interfaces typically use discrete token prediction or continuous trajectory generation. Discrete interfaces tokenize trajectories through per-dimension scalar quantization~ drivinggpt , motion-primitive clustering~ autovla , or frequency-domain coding~ w0 . Doe-1~ doe1 builds on Lumina-mGPT~ lumina_mgpt and discretizes displacement and yaw, while DrivingGPT~ drivinggpt uses component-wise binning with a Llama-style autoregressive backbone. AutoVLA~ autovla constructs physical action tokens through K-disk clustering. DriveVLA-W0~ w0 uses FAST~ fast to tokenize trajectories in its Emu3~ emu3 and Qwen2.5-VL~ qwen25vl variants. FAST applies a discrete cosine transform followed by quantization and byte-pair encoding. Continuous action interfaces use regression, diffusion, or flow matching. DriveVLA-W0~ w0 also connects a lightweight action expert to the backbone through joint attention for query-based regression or flow matching. Vega~ vega uses a compact action transformer to generate trajectories through diffusion. DriveWAM~ drivewam and UNIVERSE~ universe jointly model continuous trajectories and video latents within a generative backbone. Beyond driving, action representations in embodied policies~ fast,actioncodec can inform the design of action interfaces for driving policies. Dense visual supervision for driving policies varies in task design, how visual generation is integrated, and whether action inference requires it. For task design, DriveVLA-W0~ w0 and Vega~ vega predict future images, FSDrive~ fsdrive generates future frames annotated with lane dividers and 3D object boxes, and ExploreVLA~ explorevla jointly predicts future images and depth maps. To incorporate visual generation, DriveWAM~ drivewam builds on a pretrained video generation backbone, while ImageWAM~ imagewam reuses pretrained image editing for robot policy learning. DriveVLA-W0~ w0 and FSDrive~ fsdrive extend understanding-oriented backbones with a generation module and an expanded visual vocabulary, respectively. At inference, FSDrive~ fsdrive , DriveWAM~ drivewam , and ImageWAM~ imagewam rely on visual generation for action prediction. DriveVLA-W0~ w0 , Vega~ vega , ExploreVLA~ explorevla , UNIVERSE~ universe , and Fast-WAM~ fastwam can predict actions without visual generation. Method sec:method In this section, we explore native action adaptation and semantic supervision for driving with a unified multimodal backbone (Fig.~ fig:framework ). The Native Action Interface reuses the understanding expert for discrete action token prediction and adapts the generation expert into a lightweight continuous action head. The two training configurations depend on how the generation expert is reused. One jointly trains the discrete and continuous branches to study how discrete supervision supports continuous planning, while the other pairs the discrete branch with training-only Driving Semantic Editing for dense scene-structure supervision. Its encoder-free architecture uses lightweight convolutional patch embeddings for image input and direct pixel prediction for visual output. With multimodal understanding competitive with leading understanding-only models and strong visual generation capabilities, it provides a foundation for transferring both capabilities to driving. title: ST-SfM: Spatio-Temporal Structure-from-Motion for Initialising 4D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Dynamic Gaussian splatting is usually initialised either with random points or with a structure-from-motion (SfM) cloud of the first frame. Neither says anything about what moves, where and when. We introduce ST-SfM, a sparse spatio-temporal SfM for synchronised, calibrated multi-camera video that splits the scene into two branches. Static structure is detected once per camera on a temporal-median image, gated for temporal stability and matched along epi-polar lines. Motion is detected as space-time interest points (STIPs) in the video volume, described with HOG3D and matched only between candidates that agree both epipolarly and in time. Union-find tracks that refuse inconsistent merges are triangulated with RANSAC over all view pairs, giving static 3D points and dynamic 4D points (x, y, z, t) with sub-frame times. We use ST-SfM derived sparse 4D cloud to initialise 4D Gaussian splatting. In comparison with random initialisation on N3DV scenes we get improvements in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS.
full_text: We propose ST-SfM, a novel pipeline for efficient and accurate initialization of 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) using sparse, geometry-consistent spatio-temporal features derived from multi-view video. Unlike current 4DGS methods that rely on structure-from-motion (SfM) cloud or random initialization, our approach leverages structured visual information to guide the initial distribution of Gaussians in space-time. We treat each input video stream as a (x, y, t) volume and detect salient static and dynamic interest points. Static structure is detected once per camera on a temporal-median image, filtered for temporal stability, and matched along epipolar lines; under 2 of the kept static keypoints fall on moving objects. Motion is detected as space-time interest points (STIPs) in the video volume, described with HOG3D, and matched only between candidates that agree both epipolarly and temporally ( frame). A conflict-aware union-find assembles tracks while rejecting inconsistent matches, and RANSAC triangulation over all view pairs yields static 3D points and dynamic 4D points with sub-frame timestamps. On N3DV scenes, reconstructs 39k-113k dynamic points per scene at 0.65-0.83\,px mean reprojection error; detection takes about 6\,s per camera for a 300-frame video volume, and matching and triangulation take 2-20\,s per scene. Our method provides an efficient alternative to heuristic initialization strategies, opening a new direction for structured, spatio-temporal feature-guided dynamic scene reconstruction. Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians and its dynamic extensions~ yang2024real,wu20244d,luiten2024dynamic,li2024spacetime have made photorealistic, real-time novel-view synthesis of dynamic scenes practical. All of them refine a set of primitives by gradient descent and grow the set by heuristic densification, so the primitives they start from matter. For static scenes the answer is settled: initialise from the sparse SfM cloud that already came with the camera poses~ schoenberger2016sfm . For dynamic scenes there is no such standard. Implementations use either points sampled at random in the camera frusta, or an SfM (sometimes multi-view stereo) cloud of the first frame, with a broad, uniform distribution over time~ yang2024real,wu20244d . A first-frame cloud describes one instant. It places static and moving structure at their frame-0 positions and has nothing to say about anything that happens later in the sequence. The information that is missing, where and when something moves, has been studied for twenty years in action recognition. Space-time interest points (STIPs)~ laptev2005space,dollar2005behavior,willems2008efficient are extrema of a spatio-temporal scale space in the video volume, and are well localised in both space and time. Spatio-temporal descriptors~ scovanner20073,klaser2008spatio make them matchable. For a synchronised, calibrated multi-camera rig, a STIP seen in two cameras at the same instant is a correspondence like any other, and triangulating it gives a 3D point with a time stamp. STIPs fire only where the image changes, however, so they say almost nothing about the static scene. We therefore split the problem into two branches ( ). The static branch detects 2D SIFT~ lowe2004distinctive keypoints once per camera on a temporal-median image and rejects any whose patch changes over time. The dynamic branch detects STIPs with a difference-of-Gaussians detector on the video volume and keeps only those whose gradient energy is mainly temporal. Both branches use the known calibration more strongly than generic SfM matching does. A match is searched only among candidates within 1--3\,px of the epipolar line in both images and, for STIPs, within one frame in time. Matches are chained into multi-view tracks by a union-find that refuses inconsistent merges, and each track is triangulated by RANSAC over all of its view pairs. The result is a static cloud and a dynamic cloud of points, which we convert directly into 4D Gaussians with time centres, temporal extents and a static flag. Our contributions are: , a sparse spatio-temporal SfM for synchronised multi-camera video that reconstructs a sparse 4D structure cloud, with sub-pixel accuracy. Epipolar- and time-guided STIP matching with consistent n-view tracks, which replaces pairwise triangulation and removes redundant points. A 4D Gaussian initialisation from , evaluated on three N3DV scenes. Related Work sec:related Dynamic radiance fields and Gaussians. Dynamic NeRFs model time with deformation fields or factorised space-time grids~ li2022neural,fridovich2023k,cao2023hexplane . Gaussian methods either deform a canonical set of 3D Gaussians~ wu20244d , track persistent Gaussians frame by frame~ luiten2024dynamic , attach temporal opacity and polynomial motion to each Gaussian~ li2024spacetime , or treat each primitive as a 4D Gaussian in space-time whose conditional is a 3D Gaussian at each instant~ yang2024real . We build on the last of these, 4DGS~ yang2024real , because a 4D Gaussian has an explicit time centre and temporal extent. A time-stamped point therefore maps directly onto it. All of these methods start from either random points or a first-frame SfM/MVS cloud. Our contribution is to the starting point, not to the representation. Initialisation of Gaussian splatting. For static scenes, 3DGS is sensitive to its SfM initialisation: random initialisation loses quality, especially on unbounded backgrounds~ kerbl3Dgaussians . This has motivated strategies that relax the dependence on accurate points~ jung2024relaxing or replace SfM with learned dense geometry~ fan2024instantsplat . For dynamic scenes the question has received less attention. Standard practice is a frame-0 COLMAP cloud for multi-view video~ li2022neural,yang2024real . We give the dynamic part of the scene its own spatio-temporal initialisation and keep a static branch for the rest. Structure from motion. Incremental~ snavely2006photo,schoenberger2016sfm and global~ pan2024glomap SfM recover poses and sparse structure from 2D features~ lowe2004distinctive , with robust estimation~ fischler1981random,torr2000mlesac and multi-view triangulation~ hartley2003multiple . They assume a static scene, and moving points are treated as outliers. We assume the opposite regime: poses and intrinsics are known (as in all multi-view video benchmarks), and the goal is the structure, including the moving part. Reconstructing moving points from non-simultaneous views is classical trajectory triangulation~ avidan2000trajectory,park20103d . Sparse dynamic reconstruction has also been addressed for unsynchronised cameras~ zheng2015sparse . With synchronised cameras, the dynamic problem reduces to triangulating correspondences that are simultaneous, provided one can find them. Space-time interest points. Laptev~ laptev2005space extended the Harris detector to the video volume. Dollár ~ dollar2005behavior used separable temporal Gabor filters for denser responses, and Willems ~ willems2008efficient a scale-invariant Hessian detector. 3D SIFT~ scovanner20073 and HOG3D~ klaser2008spatio describe the surrounding cuboid with histograms of 3D gradient orientations. These tools were developed to recognise actions from a single view. To our knowledge they have not been used as cross-view correspondences for metric 4D reconstruction, which is how we use them. Method sec:method Setting. We are given synchronised videos , , , with known intrinsics and poses , projection matrices and pairwise fundamental matrices . This is the setting of multi-view video benchmarks such as Neural 3D Video (N3DV)~ li2022neural , whose poses come from COLMAP. We output a static point set and a dynamic set , each point with its multi-view observations, and convert both into a 4D Gaussian initialisation. Dynamic branch: space-time interest points sec:dynamic Detection. Each video is converted to a grey-level volume and smoothed with separable 3D Gaussians at scales , isotropic in space and time. Candidates are local extrema of the difference-of-Gaussians stack over the spatio-temporal neighbourhood and the adjacent scales, with . The extremum test is a max pool3d comparison on the GPU, and the volume is processed in temporal chunks with a halo. Following Lowe~ lowe2004distinctive , we refine every extremum by fitting a quadratic to , giving sub-pixel and sub-frame . We also reject edge-like responses with the spatial Hessian ratio test ( ). Motion gate. A DoG extremum in is not necessarily motion: static corners under flicker or noise also respond. We keep a candidate only if the temporal share of its gradient energy over a cuboid is large enough: Description. Each STIP is described with HOG3D~ klaser2008spatio : a grid of -voxel cells, with 3D gradient orientations quantised onto the 20 faces of an icosahedron, giving 540 dimensions. In a preliminary descriptor study, HOG3D separated true from false correspondences better than 3D SIFT variants~ scovanner20073 , at about a quarter of the cost. Static branch sec:static A static surface has almost no temporal structure, so most static texture never becomes an extremum. We detect it in 2D instead. For each camera we compute the per-pixel temporal median over all frames, which votes out moving foreground, and run SIFT~ lowe2004distinctive on . A keypoint can still lie on something that is static only most of the time, such as a person standing still. We compare its zero-mean patch in every frame with the zero-mean median patch, and count the frame as changed if they differ by more than 12 grey levels. The keypoint is kept only if at most 5 of frames are changed. Removing the mean makes the test insensitive to global exposure drift. As a proxy for points on movers, we count kept static keypoints with at least 50 STIPs within 15\,px. Across the five N3DV scenes this proxy is 0.15--1.51 ( ). Calibrated, time-guided matching sec:matching Generic SfM matching compares descriptors first and checks geometry afterwards. With known calibration we reverse the order. For a camera pair and keypoints , let be the symmetric point-to-epipolar-line distance in pixels. A pair is a candidate if , and, for STIPs, if in sub-frame time. We use \,px for static points and \,px for STIPs, and frame. Lowe's ratio test (0.8 static, 0.9 dynamic), a maximum descriptor distance and a mutual nearest-neighbour check are then applied among candidates only. Because the epipolar and temporal gates remove almost every wrong candidate before descriptors are compared, the ratio test has little left to do. The thresholds are robust as a result ( ). All camera pairs are matched on the GPU; the static branch is matched once, not once per frame. Consistent multi-view tracks sec:tracks Pairwise triangulation, as in our earlier two-view prototype, turns a point seen by cameras into up to slightly different points. We instead build tracks with a union-find over (camera, keypoint) nodes. Pairwise matches are merged greedily in order of descriptor distance. A merge is refused if the resulting track would contain two keypoints from the same camera, which no single 3D point can explain. For dynamic tracks, a merge is also refused if the track would span more than 1.5 frames, which stops chains of matches from drifting in time. Robust n-view triangulation sec:triangulation Each track is triangulated in four steps, vectorised over all tracks with the same length. (i) Hypotheses: a two-view DLT~ hartley2003multiple in normalised camera coordinates for every pair of the track's observations, each scored by MSAC~ torr2000mlesac on pixel reprojection error over all of the track's views (inlier threshold 3\,px). (ii) Refit: an n-view DLT on the best hypothesis' inliers. (iii) Refine: Gauss--Newton on pixel reprojection error, followed by re-classification of inliers. title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.

Introduction Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and reach a target location in an unseen environment based on visual observations~ r2r,rxr,VLN-CE . Recent approaches use pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to predict navigation actions from the instruction, the current observation, and the interaction history~ zhu2026navida,cheng2024navila,zhang2024uni-navid,Liu2025navid-4D . Yet long-horizon navigation remains vulnerable to action errors. A single wrong action can take the agent off the intended route, even leading to task failure. Reliable navigation agents need to recover from route deviations. Most existing methods collect additional off-route trajectories and use imitation or reinforcement learning to teach navigation policies how to recover during training~ an2024etpnav, activevln, dual-anchoring . Others guide recovery with explicit reasoning capability~ AwareVLN, Adanav . Despite these advances, route deviations can still lead to navigation failures in unseen environments. In this work, we investigate why agents fail to recover from route deviations by examining their instruction progress, which is the attention distribution over sub-instructions at the prefill action token of the VLN agent. This distribution reveals which sub-instruction the agent relies on when taking the next move during the navigation. Through an empirical analysis of 100 failed trajectories generated by NaVIDA~ zhu2026navida , we find that VLN agents tend to misinterpret the off-route observations as evidence of task progress. As a result, their instruction progress advances beyond the actual task stage, preventing them from making recovery decisions based on the appropriate earlier sub-instructions. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:progress_hallucination , ambiguity in the landmark description ``tan couch'' causes the agent to deviate from the intended route. It then mistakes subsequently observed, visually similar indoor scenes for evidence of completing the sub-instruction ``go through the dining room'', causing its instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage. Consequently, the agent prematurely stops based on ``Wait outside the house'' while still indoors. We term this recovery failure progress hallucination: The agent treats off-route observations as visual evidence of task progress, causing its instruction progress to diverge from the actual task stage and preventing it from making recovery decisions based on earlier sub-instruction. Progress hallucination substantially reduces the reliability of VLN agents in unseen environments. This raises two research questions: How can we detect navigation failure, and how can we recover from progress hallucination at test time? To answer the questions above, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework that detects navigation failure and steers instruction progress to recover from progress hallucination. For failure detection, we observe that progress hallucination can cause a mismatch between instruction progress and the visual observations. As shown in Fig.~ fig:progress_hallucination , the agent proposes to stop based on the instruction ``Wait outside the house'' even though its current visual observation shows that it is still indoors. Motivated by this observation, we design a temporal probe that examines residual-stream representations at the prefill action token before termination. The probe detects navigation failure by assessing the consistency of the cross-modal evidence accumulated along the trajectory. We use split conformal prediction~ CP to calibrate the detection threshold and control false alarms. For recovery, when the probe detects navigation failure, we steer instruction progress toward an earlier stage to help the agent recover from progress hallucination. To enable the model to initiate recovery based on the appropriate earlier sub-instructions, we predefine steering actions that rewind instruction progress to varying degrees and formulate action selection as a contextual bandit problem. We use the Linear Upper Confidence Bound (LinUCB)~ LinUCB to refine steering action selection online using verifier feedback, aiming to minimize cumulative recovery regret at test time. Overall, our contributions are threefold: We identify progress hallucination, a failure mode in which the agent's internal instruction progress advances beyond the actual task stage, hindering recovery from route deviations. We propose PHAR, a test-time self-recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier probes residual-stream representations to identify navigation failure, while the adaptive progress steering module rewinds instruction progress to an appropriate earlier stage to support online recovery. We integrate PHAR with multiple state-of-the-art VLN methods and evaluate them on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, demonstrating consistent improvements in navigation reliability at test time. Related Work Vision-and-Language Navigation Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE)~ Hong_2021_CVPR,VLN-CE requires an agent to follow natural-language instructions to reach a target using egocentric observations. Recent methods leverage vision-language models (VLMs) for end-to-end navigation action prediction~ zhang2024navid,cheng2024navila,activevln,zhu2026navida . To improve navigation reliability, these methods take different approaches to correcting route deviations during training. Some expose the policy to off-route states and use imitation learning to teach it to return to the instructed route~ zhu2026navida,DecoVLN . Others sample trajectories during reinforcement learning to promote recovery from deviations~ activevln . Another approach trains the model to acquire self-aware reasoning capabilities that guide self-recovery~ AwareVLN . Despite these advances, many off-route trajectories still end in failure at test time. We investigate this limitation through instruction progress and identify progress hallucination as a failure mode that hinders recovery. Our framework PHAR addresses it at test time with a verify-then-steer paradigm. Progress Estimation and Grounding in VLN Progress estimation and grounding help navigation agents relate instructions to their observations and execution history. Most existing methods strengthen progress tracking during training through auxiliary supervision or progress-aware reasoning. The Self-Monitoring Agent~ ma2019selfmonitoring combines visual-textual co-grounding with auxiliary progress estimation, while the Regretful Agent~ ma2019regretful uses progress estimates to guide backtracking. RCM~ Wang_2019_CVPR encourages instruction--trajectory alignment through a cross-modal matching critic. More recently, AwareVLN~ AwareVLN trains agents to explicitly assess task progress through self-aware reasoning, while SeekVLN~ wang2026seek learns to acquire supplementary visual evidence when available observations are insufficient for progress grounding. Progress supervision and grounding-oriented training aim to align instruction progress with the actual task stage, but this alignment can still break down at test time and lead to failure. Our work targets recovery after such drift has occurred. Progress Hallucination in VLN Agents sec:progress_analysis In this section, we first introduce the instruction progress of the VLN agents. title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
summary: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.
full_text: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence. Introduction sec:intro World models~ team2026dreamx, wang2026matrix, zhu2026sana, team2026advancing, gao2026infinite aim to predict future states from current observations conditioned on actions, playing an increasingly important role in robotics~ li2026causal,yang2025physworld and autonomous driving~ li2026drivevla,wang2024drivedreamer . A prevalent paradigm generates future videos via diffusion models~ blattmann2023align,peebles2023scalable,yang2025cogvideox,wan2025wan , guided by textual prompts alongside camera trajectories or discrete motion signals, as demonstrated by LingBot-World~ team2026advancing,gao2026infinite and Matrix-Game 3.0~ wang2026matrix . Despite demonstrating compelling visual fidelity through large-scale training, these models fundamentally struggle to maintain object persistence in dynamic scenes. When the viewpoint shifts away and subsequently returns, out-of-view objects fail to evolve plausibly in the latent space. As a result, their visual consistency and motion continuity break down, even causing returning entities to mutate or vanish entirely. We attribute this limitation to both training data biases and fundamental modeling bottlenecks. On the data side, current training data for dynamic scenes heavily favor continuous tracking, rarely featuring scenarios where moving entities exit and subsequently re-enter the camera's field of view (FoV). On the modeling side, vanilla diffusion models are inherently limited in preserving out-of-view dynamics without dedicated constraints and priors. Recent works have recognized this challenge and sought to mitigate it mainly from two perspectives. Some methods utilize retrieval frames~ chen2026hybrid and compressed implicit contexts~ yu2026memlearner as memory. Others attempt to predict dynamics of specific entity through auxiliary generative models~ duan2026liveworld and LLMs~ wang2026worlddirector . However, the former often recall static appearance cues that fail to reflect continuous natural motion, while the latter introduce heavy system complexity and scale poorly to multi-entity scenarios. Furthermore, these methods are designed primarily for object consistency across temporal chunks. In fact, even within a single video chunk, combining intra-window bidirectional attention with advanced camera control approaches ( , UCPE~ zhang2026ucpe ) remains insufficient to sustain out-of-view dynamic evolution. To address this problem, we propose modeling scene evolution in panoramic space, leveraging complete spatial context to improve the persistence of dynamic world models. This paradigm offers two distinct advantages. First, conceptually, the omnidirectional nature of panoramic space ensures that when an object leaves the camera view, its continuous motion can still be explicitly predicted on a global canvas. Moreover, this formulation naturally supports multiple moving objects and inherently preserves background memory, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Second, practically, panoramic scenes can be represented as standard 2D frames via equirectangular projection (ERP), allowing existing video diffusion foundation models to adapt seamlessly to panoramic data while fully capitalizing on their strong pretrained priors. Specifically, we propose OmniPersist, which jointly models the perspective camera view and its panoramic counterpart within a single video diffusion model. This unified framework achieves persistent dynamic world modeling in an end-to-end manner, without relying on auxiliary models or additional input. Since generating a dense panorama for every perspective frame introduces heavy computational overhead, we propose to design the panoramic stream to operate at a lower frame rate. To effectively bridge these two representations across space and time, we introduce two complementary modules, , Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp). In particular, GeoAnch establishes explicit geometric correspondences between the perspective and panoramic views, enabling direct feature exchange at synchronized timestamps. Meanwhile, TemComp aggregates features across neighboring frames, effectively compensating for the temporal discrepancy caused by the differing frame rates. Concurrently, AlayaVista~ tan2026alayavista (within the past two months) also explores panoramic representations, but relies on a multi-stage pipeline of panoramic initialization, state evolution, and perspective refinement. In contrast, OmniPersist avoids generating redundant full-rate panoramas, establishing a single-stage, unified framework for persistent dynamic world modeling. To ensure broad applicability, OmniPersist is designed to be agnostic to underlying camera-control architectures. We integrate our framework with two representative paradigms, , latent-level trajectory injection via CameraCtrl~ he2025cameractrl and attention-level pose conditioning via UCPE~ zhang2026ucpe . Furthermore, to benchmark dynamic persistence under complex camera movements, we construct a paired panoramic--perspective dataset featuring diverse trajectory patterns. We systematically evaluate OmniPersist under two settings, namely image-to-video (I2V) generation and video continuation. Extensive experiments across visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence demonstrate that our coupled panoramic evolution yields consistent gains across both control mechanisms. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We propose OmniPersist, a single-stage unified framework that jointly generates perspective video and temporally sparse panoramic evolution to improve out-of-view dynamic persistence. We introduce GeoAnch and TemComp to couple dense perspective and sparse panoramic streams through synchronized geometric exchange and neighboring-time feature aggregation. We construct a paired panoramic--perspective dynamic dataset and demonstrate consistent gains in dynamic persistence and revisit consistency across diverse camera-control mechanisms. Related Work sec:related -Controlled Video Generation. Camera trajectory control has become an essential capability for interactive world models~ team2026dreamx,wang2026matrix,zhu2026sana,team2026advancing,gao2026infinite . Existing efforts encompass text-to-video~ wang2024motionctrl,bahmani2025vd3d , image-to-video~ li2025realcam,ren2025gen3c,zheng2026versecrafter , and video re-shooting~ bai2025recammaster,yu2025trajectorycrafter,team2026inspatio , and roughly divide into two paradigms. (1) Camera-parameter conditioning directly encodes viewpoints as extrinsic matrices~ wang2024motionctrl , Pl\"ucker rays~ he2025cameractrl,bahmani2025vd3d , or relative positional embeddings~ li2026rerope,zhang2026ucpe,yin2026scope . These representations are used to modulate feature latents via auxiliary branches~ he2025cameractrl,bahmani2025vd3d or inject geometric biases into attention mechanisms~ zhang2026ucpe,yin2026scope,li2026rerope . These methods operate strictly within the visible frustum, offering no spatial substrate to sustain the evolution of out-of-view dynamic entities. (2) Explicit 3D reprojection grounds camera trajectories by warping reconstructed 3D geometry into target image or latent spaces. For instance, ViewCrafter~ viewcrafter and GEN3C~ ren2025gen3c condition diffusion on rendered point clouds with iterative scene expansion or 3D caching. MosaicMem~ yu2026mosaicmem retrieves 3D-lifted patches from spatial memory, whereas LSM-World~ wang2026latent caches 3D latent tokens directly to bypass RGB rendering and re-encoding. However, these approaches rely heavily on external depth estimators and are predominantly restricted to static scenes. In contrast, OmniPersist bypasses 3D reconstruction and provides an omnidirectional canvas that naturally sustains unseen dynamic evolution. It acts as an orthogonal, plug-and-play spatial substrate, seamlessly integrating with the camera-parameter conditioning paradigm. Dynamic World Modeling. World models simulate future states conditioned on current observations and actions. A prevalent paradigm generates future videos guided by text and camera trajectories~ wang2026matrix,zhu2026sana,team2026advancing,gao2026infinite . However, maintaining the evolving states of dynamic out-of-view entities remains an unresolved challenge. Existing approaches broadly follow three directions. (1) Memory-based modeling. HyDRA~ chen2026hybrid and MemLearner~ yu2026memlearner query or compress historical observations to preserve generation consistency. ReMind~ xu2026teaching employs a node-structured curriculum that compels the model to retrieve relevant historical states. While historical memory provides informative anchors, these methods inherently infer unobserved evolution from past evidence, often struggling to sustain continuous visual transitions. (2) Auxiliary entity tracking. LiveWorld~ duan2026liveworld uses multiple generative monitors to advance unseen entity states within a persistent scene, while WorldDirector~ wang2026worlddirector employs an LLM to predict object trajectories prior to visual generation. However, relying on external entity-level monitors or LLM planners introduces heavy system overhead, causes pipeline brittleness, and scales poorly to dense, multi-entity interactive scenarios. (3) Panoramic world-state modeling. In concurrent work, AlayaVista~ tan2026alayavista first evolves panoramic latent states and then synthesizes perspective observations through viewport rendering and refinement stages. However, it relies on a separate panorama initialization stage and incurs high computational costs by predicting full-rate panoramas. In contrast, OmniPersist derives its panoramic conditions directly from the observed perspective prefix and predicts panoramic states at a lower temporal rate, establishing a single-stage joint diffusion framework. Video Generation. Panoramic video generation aims to synthesize temporally coherent content, typically achieved by adapting pretrained perspective video diffusion models. Therein, perspective-to-panorama methods expand input videos while preserving their content and dynamics~ luo2025beyond,li2026cubecomposer,wu2026360anything,xie2025videopanda , whereas text- and image-conditioned approaches synthesize omnidirectional scenes and motion~ wang2024dvd,zhang2025panodit,fang2026panoramic,xia2026panowan,xie2025videopanda . Recent methods further extend panoramic synthesis to camera-controlled exploration~ li2026panoworld,tan2026mugen and 3D world construction~ wang2025evoworld,yang2025matrix,chen2026pantheon360 . Technically, these methods address spherical distortion and boundary seams through ERP-aware designs~ xia2026panowan,wu2026360anything,tan2026mugen , cross-view coherence via multi-view attention~ fang2026pan

title: GeoVLDrive: Geometry-Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) planners inherit semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models, but their reasoning is rarely grounded in 3D scene structure and its evolution over time. We introduce GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework for 3D spatiotemporal reasoning and planning. Multi-layer features from a 3D foundation model augment the vision-language backbone through gated cross-attention. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions into ordered, separately supervised latent states. An action expert generates trajectory proposals from these states and multi-layer scene features, and ranks them using scene-grounded, interacting score tokens. We also introduce NAVSIM 3DQA to train and evaluate metric 3D spatial and motion understanding. GeoVLDrive achieves 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. On NAVSIM 3DQA, the geometry-grounded backbone scores 89.2% overall, 4.6 percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. On LingoQA, the backbone achieves 68.6% Lingo-Judge accuracy.

Introduction sec:intro End-to-end autonomous driving has advanced through joint optimization of perception, prediction, and planning~ st-p3,uniad,vad,vadv2 . Building on the semantic knowledge of pretrained vision-language models, vision-language-action (VLA) frameworks use visual observations and language inputs to support driving trajectory generation~ orion,emma,drivevlm,opendrivevla,autovla . Driving requires reasoning about traffic participants, scene geometry, and future scene evolution~ uniad,vadv2,transfuser,navsim . This motivates grounding such reasoning in 3D geometry and scene semantics to connect current spatial relationships and their future evolution with ego planning. Representative approaches differ in how they incorporate semantic reasoning and geometric representations into trajectory planning (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). VLA policies (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)) build on pretrained vision-language models for scene understanding and reasoning to guide trajectory generation~ orion,emma,opendrivevla . Geometry world action models (Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)) encode current scene geometry and predict its future evolution, conditioning planning on geometric representations of the observed and anticipated scene~ geoworldad . Geometry-grounded VLAs (Fig.~ fig:teaser (c)) use observed-scene 3D geometric features or reconstruction supervision to support spatial understanding and trajectory planning~ vggdrive,vlga . A central challenge is to connect scene-wide geometric forecasts with agent-specific motion reasoning and ego maneuvers. Recent VLAs incorporate geometric and dynamic knowledge into latent representations used for planning~ lastvla,coworldvla,driveworldvla . We focus on structuring this connection through distinct, separately supervised latent groups for future scene geometry, the motion of a selected key agent, and meta action. Directed dependencies link scene forecasts to agent motion and maneuver selection. We propose GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework for 3D spatiotemporal reasoning and planning (Fig.~ fig:teaser (d)). Multi-layer geometric features augment the vision-language backbone with 3D spatial information. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta action into separately supervised latent states. Its attention mask lets future-motion states read future-geometry states and meta-action states read both. An action expert uses the latent CoT and geometric and semantic features to jointly generate and score trajectory proposals. Dedicated score tokens incorporate scene and reasoning context and exchange information across proposals, allowing each candidate to be evaluated in relation to the alternatives. We construct NAVSIM~3DQA to train and evaluate box-conditioned metric 3D and motion understanding on NAVSIM scenes. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework with a structured latent CoT that connects future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta action through separately supervised latent states. With the same action-expert architecture, the latent CoT and geometry injection raise NAVSIM~v1 PDMS from to . We develop an action expert that jointly generates and scores trajectory proposals conditioned on the latent CoT and multi-depth scene features. Dedicated score tokens attend to scene context and to one another. This scoring design improves PDMS by over an MLP readout of max-pooled action states. We construct NAVSIM~3DQA, a dataset of M box-conditioned questions on object category, metric position, vehicle dimensions, and motion in NAVSIM scenes. With geometry injection and spatial alignment, our backbone scores overall, percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models for Driving =100000 VLA models use pretrained semantic knowledge for trajectory planning. DriveLM~ drivelm frames driving understanding as graph-structured question answering, and EMMA~ emma incorporates textual reasoning into action generation. Textual chains of thought~ cot expose intermediate reasoning but add autoregressive decoding overhead. ~ autovla and AdaThinkDrive~ adathinkdrive adapt the use of such reasoning to driving scenarios. Geometry-grounded models add 3D information. VGGDrive~ vggdrive injects features from a frozen geometry backbone via multi-layer cross-attention. VLGA~ vlga supervises a geometry expert with dense pointmap reconstruction, and DVGT-2~ dvgt2 jointly reconstructs current geometry and predicts trajectories. Selection-based planners, including Hydra-MDP~ hydramdp , WoTE~ wote , and iPad~ ipad , use learned scores to select candidate trajectories. GeoVLDrive combines geometric grounding with structured reasoning about future scene evolution for ego planning. It uses iPad's proposal formulation with dedicated score tokens. Latent Reasoning and World Modeling =100000 Latent CoT methods replace explicit reasoning traces with continuous intermediate states. Coconut~ coconut recurrently propagates hidden states, CCoT~ ccot learns compressed traces, CODI~ codi uses hidden-state self-distillation, and SIM-CoT~ simcot adds step-level supervision through an auxiliary decoder. In driving, LaST-VLA~ lastvla and CoWorld-VLA~ coworldvla transfer geometric and dynamic priors into separately supervised latent groups. PerceptDrive~ perceptdrive routes distilled perception priors into world-action modeling; DriveWorld-VLA~ driveworldvla shares latent features between world modeling and planning. It supervises scene, agent, and goal queries in a VLM with occupancy, safety-critical agents, and a -s goal pose, learning geometry through occupancy supervision, and a block-wise mask keeps the three groups from attending to one another. title: Completion-Aware Compression for Progressive 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 23 pages, 6 main-paper figures and 4 supplementary figures
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality novel-view rendering, but its large scene representations are costly to transmit. Pruning and compression reduce file sizes, yet progressive delivery also requires usable reconstructions before the full scene arrives. Existing progressive representations provide partial scenes, but level-based updates are limited by predefined coding boundaries. This paper presents a progressive 3DGS codec that balances attribute fidelity with the image benefit of making Gaussians available earlier. Its single compact stream supports partial 3D reconstruction and adds newly decoded Gaussians as more bytes arrive. The stream supports fine-grained updates at arbitrary received-byte budgets, without separate encodings or later attribute refinement. At matched complete-file sizes and received bytes, completion-aware allocation improves 1/8 PSNR over attribute-only allocation by 0.48-1.43 dB. The proposed codec compresses original 3DGS representations by 62-88 times while retaining near-reference Full PSNR. Under the evaluated 50-Mbps delivery model, partial reconstruction becomes available in approximately 0.2 s.

This paper presents a progressive 3DGS codec that balances attribute fidelity with the image benefit of making Gaussians available earlier. Its single compact stream supports partial 3D reconstruction and adds newly decoded Gaussians as more bytes arrive. The stream supports fine-grained updates at arbitrary received-byte budgets, without separate encodings or later attribute refinement. At matched complete-file sizes and received bytes, completion-aware allocation improves 1/8 PSNR over attribute-only allocation by 0.48--1.43 dB. The proposed codec compresses original 3DGS representations by 62--88 times while retaining near-reference Full PSNR. Under the evaluated 50-Mbps delivery model, partial reconstruction becomes available in approximately 0.2~s. In a layered stream, further bytes may not expose a new reconstruction until the next coding unit is complete. To support finer updates, the proposed codec encodes each retained Gaussian as a complete record within one causal stream. Each completed Gaussian can then be added without waiting for a predefined layer boundary. This granularity couples attribute precision to subsequent availability: more bits improve an early Gaussian's fidelity but can postpone later Gaussians at the same received-byte budget. title: Knocked Off Course: Tracing Uncommanded Motion from Perception to Action in Embodied VLAs
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable simultaneous processing of egocentric video and textual target descriptions to produce action commands for embodied tracking platforms. However, these platforms rarely move exactly as commanded, in part due to unexpected environmental disturbances such as wind, unleveled terrain, and road bumps. Here we study how such models handle uncommanded egomotion. First, we explore performance across diverse disturbances by benchmarking three tracking VLAs on three datasets. We find that models differ in which environmental disturbances hurt them most, but all are sensitive to sudden target loss. Tracing egomotion from pixels to emitted actions, we identify two gaps. In representation, motion is reliably recovered through explicit relations between frames, but aggressive compression of past frames weakens small-motion readouts. In action, large rotations do reach the decision state, yet the decoded direction carries only a few percent of a mirrored rotation's effect on the turn. Targeting both gaps, we fine-tune one model, Uni-NaVid, on data amounting to just 1.7% of its original training set in a ladder of analysis-motivated variants. These gain 5-22 points after target-loss without degrading clean success; after a smooth loss, the best one improves success by 72% (relative), recovering 76% of its gap to clean. We also show that targeted fine-tuning improves recovery partly via a text-mediated action dependency, without new architecture, large-scale data collection or training from scratch.

Introduction sec:intro Target tracking has been a core problem of computer vision for decades yilmaz2006tracking, marvastizadeh2022deeptracking , evolving from estimating inter-frame motion lucas1981iterative to matching a learned target template bertinetto2016siamfc and, more recently, to following a target specified in natural language li2017trackinglanguage . As large language models matured, integrating them into visual and embodied architectures enabled merging of perception and action, forming Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,ma2024vlasurvey , which can be applied as embodied visual trackers. As such, these models no longer merely report where a described target appears: they generate the navigation actions that determine the platform's motion and, consequently, its future observations zhang2025uninavid,wang2025trackvla . As tracking systems move toward real-world deployment, they must be evaluated beyond clean, controlled benchmarks. A physical platform rarely executes a command exactly as planned: external forces add uncommanded motion as the platform moves through real world environments. The affected observations are not nuisance noise but a record of the platform's actual movement, which is most useful when the platform loses sight of the target and must react from its memory of earlier frames ( ). It is unclear, however, how well tracking VLAs distinguish commanded motion from these uncommanded residuals when processing visual inputs. Existing studies mostly measure the resulting loss in task performance or train compensatory policies; they do not examine whether, and where, the discrepancy is represented inside the policy. To operate reliably outside controlled conditions, a VLA must detect the departure of its realized motion from commanded actions, and use that information to inform subsequent decisions. We address this at three levels, starting with an evaluation of three tracking VLAs on three scene datasets in closed-loop simulation, under three environmental disturbances and two target-loss profiles, each along a controlled severity ladder. While success falls with severity in every model, each model fails in its own way, and all three fail worst when the target instantly leaves the view. We then look deeper, into each model's internal representations, tracing uncommanded motion from visual encoding to action, to ask whether failures arise because the signal is unavailable, discarded or ignored, and whether knowing it would let each policy recover. Our analysis finds the motion in every policy's visual features, and two gaps en route to the action. A representation gap: we find that small motions become hard to read when historical frames are compressed. An action gap: large rotations do reach the decision state, and we show that knowing their direction would let each policy recover with its own actions, yet the decoded direction barely affects their turn, which follows the target, turning back barely more often than chance after a target is abruptly lost. At the intervention level, we target both gaps with a model adaptation rather than a new architecture. We fine-tune Uni-NaVid on data amounting to of its original training set in a ladder of variants that improves success, most after target-loss, by up to points from the frozen model's state at the loss, without losing clean success; the most complete variant gains most. Beyond performance recovery, fine-tuning changes what drives the turn: out of view the fine-tuned models correct the rotation more often, and those that state their motion act on what they state. contributions are: A systematic closed-loop robustness benchmark of three tracking VLAs under environmental disturbances and target-loss, on 2 , 102 episodes in three scene datasets. A pixels-to-actions model internal analysis of uncommanded motion inside VLAs, following the signal through model layers up to the decision state. A laddered fine-tuning of Uni-NaVid on minimal data that improves success, most after target-loss, and makes the model use its own motion more to correct its turns. Related Work sec:related_work VLA Robustness sec:related_robustness Robustness of embodied policies was studied in navigation, where RobustNav perturbs RGB observations and transition dynamics chattopadhyay2021robustnav . For manipulation VLAs, LIBERO-Plus varies scene, viewpoint, sensor, language and initial conditions fei2025liberoplus , and RobustVLA adds action noise and external forces, finding action execution the most fragile modality guo2025vlarobustness . These studies largely assume static goals; none tests whether a mobile VLA keeps tracking a moving target when its body, and with it the camera, is displaced relative to its commands ( ; details: ). Representation of Motion sec:related_motion_representation Standard trackers localize targets in image coordinates, conflating target and camera motion wu2013benchmark,yan2021stark , whereas embodied trackers wang2025trackvla must separate the two because the policy moves the camera. Frozen visual features encode patch correspondence across nearby views elbanani2024probe3d ; vision-language models (VLMs) answer poorly about camera and egomotion in video lin2025camerabench,schaefer2026egodyn , although ego speed winter2026speedblindspot and the direction of object motion lee2026modirect are decodable from their hidden states. Navigation VLAs likewise encode collisions they do not avoid salsa2026 and signal their own path deviation in a few attention heads navheads2026 . These studies probe or monitor; none tests causally whether a decodable motion signal drives a closed-loop policy's action. NaVid-style VLAs are known to compress historical frames far more than the current one zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,wang2025trackvla , and some works add flow-supervised, video-predictive or frame-difference history yang2026temporalflowvla,miao2026jepavla,na2026evomemvla , but none models the gap between commanded and realized motion, which we trace from pixels to actions. Mitigating Physical Disturbances sec:related_mitigation RobustVLA fine-tunes against worst-case action deviations guo2025vlarobustness , and Self-Adaptive VLA learns a context from earlier rollouts to compensate persistent hardware errors zhang2026selfadaptivevla . Pace-and-Path Correction zhang2026ppc and VLA-Corrector pan2026vlacorrector adjust action chunks from outside the backbone. In navigation, visual odometry replaces GPS and compass under actuation noise zhao2021visualodometry , and TIC-VLA re-anchors decisions with measured egomotion huang2026ticvla . None targets a mobile VLA following a moving target or chooses its change by locating where the policy loses the signal; we adapt a released model where our experiments locate the loss, showing that disturbance fine-tuning benefits from attending to the motion signal and its effect on the action. Benchmark sec:benchmark The benchmark is designed around four key aspects: disturbances displace the robot, never the pixels, so the camera records realized motion and evidence needed to correct it stays observable; one physical severity ladder, in units of the robot's step, applies to every model; every episode receives the same seeded disturbance in every run and is paired with its own clean run; and two separately tested failure modes: persistent displacement of the body, which the policy can correct while it still sees the target, and disturbance-induced loss of the target from view. Complete protocols and parameters are in . Models and Datasets sec:benchmark_models . We use released weights, greedy decoding and the authors' EVT-Bench interfaces. Uni-NaVid zhang2025uninavid : a 7B NaVid-style policy zhang2024navid that compresses each recent historical frame to four tokens and emits discrete commands. LightNav-0 lightnav0 : a 4B generalist whose released vision tower encodes its two latest frames jointly, as one two-frame patch, and which emits short-horizon trajectories. OmTrackVLA omtrackvla2025 : a 0.6B TrackVLA-style policy wang2025trackvla with compressed history and continuous waypoints. Uni-NaVid moves \,m or turns per step; the waypoint models take smaller steps and never turn more than . Task and datasets. EVT-Bench wang2025trackvla requires a robot in Habitat savva2019habitat to follow a language-specified target. We evaluate all models on the complete EVT-Bench validation splits of Matterport3D (MP3D; 721 episodes) chang2017matterport3d and Habitat-Matterport 3D (HM3D; 684) ramakrishnan2021hm3d , and on 697 episodes in the Habitat Synthetic Scenes Dataset (HSSD) khanna2024hssd , which EVT-Bench does not cover; we build them from the EVT-Bench validation episodes ( ). Episodes. Episodes last at most 300 steps and end on target collision or prolonged separation. These continuously alter realized motion: Current: constant world-frame translation in one episode-specific direction, as on a slope, a moving floor or in a stream. Veer: fixed-sign body rotation on each translating step, a drive-train bias such as a worn wheel. Gust: zero-mean correlated translation from an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process uhlenbeck1930theory , as from wind or uneven terrain. title: AnyPrune: Optimization-Free Pruning for Any Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Pipeline
summary: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines reconstruct a scene from images in a single forward pass, representing it as real-time-renderable 3D Gaussians. However, the resulting representations contain far more Gaussians than are needed to render the scene faithfully, especially when there are many input views. This drastically increases memory and storage requirements. Existing pruning methods either require costly re-optimization, which defeats the purpose of a single forward pass, or rely on simple strategies that do not exploit all the available information. We present AnyPrune, a transformer-based, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. To remove unnecessary Gaussians, AnyPrune learns and exploits pipeline-specific redundancy patterns through a short single-GPU training on the frozen target feedforward pipeline. AnyPrune achieves better rendering quality than existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings and generalizes to unseen datasets, as shown through extensive experiments across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input view counts. It prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ on a consumer GPU, faster than every method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. It can also be combined with the pruning built into feedforward pipelines, pruning further at moderate ratios while preserving or improving rendering quality. Finally, it can even suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that retains most of the quality.
full_text: AnyPrune prunes the output of a frozen feedforward 3DGS pipeline. Left: the pipeline uses the input images to predict a redundant set of 3D Gaussians. AnyPrune, the only trained component, takes as input these Gaussians, the input images and their camera poses, scores the importance of every Gaussian and adjusts their parameters. The user can either retain the top- most important Gaussians by importance score to reach a specific pruning ratio or let the network pick a ratio. Right: a RealEstate10K test view reconstructed by F4Splat~ f4splat from 16 input images with its own internal pruning dial set to 50 (524k Gaussians), pruned to 70 (367k) and 50 (262k) of its Gaussians.
