Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl-3DGS achieves high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis by representing a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians. While the original formulation optimizes the parameters of the Gaussians for each scene by minimizing a rendering loss, feedforward pipelines~ pixelsplat,anysplat,yonosplat,zipsplat leverage 3D priors learned from large-scale training to construct a set of splats in a few seconds, avoiding costly iterative optimization. In both cases, the resulting representation is redundant~ compact-3dgs,lightgaussian,pup-3dgs,splatt3rfusion,salon3r , with far more Gaussians than are needed to render a scene faithfully. This increases memory and storage requirements and slows rendering. It also hinders deployment on resource-constrained hardware and makes scenes costlier to transmit. Redundancy can be reduced by removing unnecessary Gaussians from the field predicted by the 3DGS reconstruction while preserving rendering quality~ lightgaussian,radsplat,minigs,nanogs . However, most pruning methods need to perform re-optimization steps on the Gaussian parameters to recover the rendering quality lost through pruning, which prevents their use in a feedforward scenario without defeating its very purpose of reconstructing a scene in a single forward pass. While it is possible to use these methods without the optimization steps, we show that their results have room for improvement . Optimization-free methods~ rap,pointsplat,nanogs have therefore been proposed to avoid per-scene re-optimization, but they do not exploit all the available information, such as the input images. Another approach is to predict fewer Gaussians directly~ resplat,ecosplat or to move away from pixel alignment, in which one or more Gaussians are predicted for every pixel of every input view, to voxels, anchors, or tokens~ learning-compact-3d-repr,volsplat,anchorsplat,tokengs . However, these solutions are often designed to target the redundancies produced by a specific model, such as low-frequency regions~ compactsplat,adaptivesplat or overlapping views~ ggn,freesplat . In short, there are no generic pruning methods competitive when used in conjunction with arbitrary feedforward 3DGS pipelines without requiring an expensive post-processing stage. To bridge this gap, we introduce AnyPrune: a trainable, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. Our key insight is that a learned module running on top of a frozen 3DGS pipeline learns to fix the pipeline's specific redundancy patterns without being explicitly programmed to target them. To this end, given the Gaussians predicted by the pipeline and the input images they were produced from, a transformer-based network predicts (i) per-Gaussian importance scores that make it possible to prune the scene at any desired ratio, (ii) a scene-specific pruning ratio that aims to remove a large fraction of Gaussians with little to no loss in rendering quality, and (iii) parameter adjustments that let the kept Gaussians compensate for the removed ones. illustrates our proposed pipeline. While being particularly well suited to the feedforward setting, AnyPrune makes no assumption about the architecture of the pipeline producing 3D Gaussians, because the feedforward pipeline is treated as a black box that takes images as input and outputs Gaussians that can be rendered from the input images' viewpoints, without making any further assumptions. Supporting a new pipeline does not require designing a new pruning method, but only a short training run of AnyPrune on the frozen pipeline's output. We train AnyPrune separately on each one of several state-of-the-art feedforward 3DGS pipelines on DL3DV~ dl3dv and evaluate the trained modules zero-shot on RealEstate10K~ realestate10k and ACID~ acid . AnyPrune consistently outperforms existing pruning methods across pruning ratios and datasets. Keeping 50 of the Gaussians, AnyPrune improves novel-view PSNR by 1.8\,dB over the best competing method, averaged over all pipelines, datasets and 2 to 32 input views. AnyPrune prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about 5\,s on a single consumer-grade GPU, faster than every competing method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. AnyPrune outperforms existing general optimization-free pruning methods, giving the best novel-view PSNR in all 112 DL3DV settings from 2 to 16 views with 20--70 of the Gaussians kept. In summary, we make the following contributions: We introduce AnyPrune, a transformer-based network that scores the importance of each Gaussian predicted by a feedforward 3DGS pipeline, suggests a scene-specific pruning ratio, and adjusts the surviving Gaussians to preserve rendering quality, all without per-scene optimization. By training it on the outputs of several feedforward 3DGS pipelines, we show that AnyPrune learns the redundancy patterns of a pipeline while generalizing zero-shot to unseen datasets. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that AnyPrune outperforms existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings, including those built into feedforward 3DGS pipelines. It trains in a short run on a single GPU and is much faster than optimization-based baselines. Related Work Feedforward 3DGS and its redundancy. Pixel-aligned feedforward pipelines~ pixelsplat,mvsplat,depthsplat,noposplat predict one or more Gaussians for every pixel of every input view, so the number of Gaussians grows with the number of views and their resolution, and overlapping views produce duplicate primitives~ long-lrm,splatt3rfusion . Several architectures are designed to tackle this problem. Some pipelines decouple Gaussian prediction from pixels, predicting them from learnable tokens~ tokengs,learning-compact-3d-repr,globalsplat , from image-patch tokens merged across views~ zipsplat , from anchors or voxels in 3D space~ anchorsplat,volsplat , or exploiting detected keypoints~ off-the-grid . Some allocate primitives according to image complexity~ compactsplat,pixelgaussian,sparsesplat,f4splat or predict them in a subsampled space and refine them recurrently~ resplat . Others try to reduce the field after it has been predicted: by fusing Gaussians across views~ ggn,freesplat,splatt3rfusion , within voxels~ anysplat or into anchors~ salon3r ; by pooling them along a Z-order curve~ z-order-transformer ; by regularizing opacity so that transparent Gaussians can be discarded~ yonosplat,long-lrm ; by learning to rank them for a target count~ ecosplat . These mechanisms are designed for a specific architecture and trained with it, so there is often no obvious way to transfer them to other pipelines. They also target, in their design, only specific types of redundancy. AnyPrune's core design idea is instead to treat the 3DGS pipeline as a black box to make it compatible with every pipeline, possibly stacking AnyPrune's pruning on top of the existing pruning solutions that a pipeline deploys. Pruning per-scene optimized 3DGS. In the classic setting of 3DGS with per-scene optimization~ kerbl-3DGS , most pruning methods compute an importance score for each Gaussian, such as its contribution to the rendered training views~ lightgaussian,radsplat,mesongs , a weighted combination of its projected position, distance to other Gaussians and opacity~ minigs , or the sensitivity of the reconstruction error to its parameters~ pup-3dgs . They then remove the Gaussians below a threshold or sample them in proportion to their score~ minisplatting , and fine-tune the survivors to recover rendering quality. The threshold or ratio is set by hand, and a poor choice can collapse rendering quality~ safeguardgs . Learned masks avoid this by letting the ratio emerge from a sparsity loss during optimization, and the resulting ratios may differ across scenes and datasets~ compact-3dgs,lp3dgs,maskgaussian . Few methods compensate for the removed Gaussians with a learned module rather than by fine-tuning the survivors alone: SUNDAE~ sundae adds a neural rendering head, and FlexGS~ flexgs pairs a learned selector, which keeps Gaussians for any given ratio, with a transform field that adjusts the selected ones. All methods above are optimized per scene, which defeats the purpose of feedforward reconstruction. Optimization-free and general feedforward pruning. Some recent methods are designed to prune per-scene optimized 3DGS without requiring per-scene optimization. Most derive importance analytically, from an approximate Hessian~ refine , from the effect of removing each Gaussian on the rendered training views, computed exactly~ potr or in a single forward pass~ gaussianpop , or by sensitivity sampling with provable guarantees~ coreset-pruning , while NanoGS~ nanogs progressively merges neighboring pairs of Gaussians. RAP~ rap instead learns to predict importance from Gaussian attributes, and PointSplat~ pointsplat ranks Gaussians with a hand-crafted score and refines the survivors with a learned transformer. None of these methods exploits information from the input images to the pipeline, and all of them leave the ratio to the user. Some pruning strategies are designed in a way that makes them applicable, in principle, to any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. AdaptiveSpla

title: First-Hit Photoconsistency for Neural Surface Reconstruction
summary: Recent neural implicit and Gaussian splatting approaches have achieved impressive results in multi-view surface reconstruction. However, jointly optimizing geometry and appearance introduces ambiguities. A parametric appearance model can compensate for geometric errors, reproducing the input images accurately without an accurate surface. We demonstrate accurate neural implicit surface reconstruction using only multi-view patch photoconsistency with geometry-based visibility, without volumetric rendering or parametric appearance models. For each reference ray, sphere tracing computes the first surface intersection. Its position and normal define a local patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across visible neighboring views using colors sampled directly from the input images. For efficient sphere tracing, we use a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron. We use a single photoconsistency loss, without foreground masks or auxiliary geometric regularization. Experiments show that our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BlendedMVS (BMVS) among compared methods and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU.

Introduction Reconstructing a surface from multiple calibrated images is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Multi-view stereo (MVS) has traditionally recovered geometry through image matching and geometric consistency ~ furukawa2010pmvs,schoenberger2016pixelwise . Neural implicit representations have subsequently become a standard tool, providing continuous, resolution-independent representations of geometry. Early methods optimized signed distance or occupancy fields through differentiable surface rendering~ yariv2020idr,niemeyer2020dvr . Later approaches, including NeuS~ wang2021neus and VolSDF~ yariv2021volsdf , adopted volumetric rendering, converting the implicit representation into a density and accumulating colors along camera rays. More recently, 3D Gaussian splatting~ kerbl2023gaussian has enabled efficient rendering using explicit Gaussian primitives. Geometry-oriented variants, including 2DGS~ huang2024_2dgs , PGSR~ chen2025pgsr and AmbiSuR~ li2026ambisur aim to improve surface reconstruction while retaining opacity-based compositing along camera rays. \\ In these methods, photometric supervision is applied to rendered images rather than directly to the reconstructed surface, potentially allowing geometric inaccuracies to persist (Fig.~ fig:vol_vs_ours , top). Moreover, parametric appearance models, such as color MLPs or spherical harmonics, can compensate for geometric errors by adjusting the predicted appearance. Methods such as NeuralWarp darmon2022neuralwarp and Geo-NeuS fu2022geoneus address these limitations by introducing explicit multi-view patch photoconsistency alongside volumetric rendering, improving geometric accuracy. This raises the question of whether patch photoconsistency alone can provide sufficient supervision to optimize a continuous neural surface, without volumetric rendering or a parametric appearance model. \\ To investigate this question, we directly optimize a continuous neural surface through multi-view patch photoconsistency, building on the principle of photometric agreement between corresponding image regions~ faugeras1998complete,vu2012highaccuracy,furukawa2010pmvs . Specifically, we represent the surface as the zero level set of a 1-Lipschitz MLP and use sphere tracing~ hart1996sphere to compute the first surface intersection along each camera ray (Fig.~ fig:vol_vs_ours , bottom). At each intersection, the surface position and normal define a local tangent-plane patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across neighboring views, with visibility explicitly determined from the evolving surface geometry. Colors are sampled directly from the input images through differentiable interpolation, without a parametric appearance network. Since patch photoconsistency relies on sufficiently accurate initial correspondences, existing methods start from a sparse set of matched keypoints~ furukawa2010pmvs or refine an existing reconstruction~ vu2012highaccuracy,darmon2022neuralwarp . Similarly, we initialize the implicit field from a coarse geometric proxy obtained by classical MVS from the same input images, then refine its zero level set using only multi-view patch photoconsistency. \\ Our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BMVS and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU. \\ The main contributions of this paper are: A geometry-only optimization formulation of neural surface reconstruction based solely on multi-view patch photoconsistency, without volumetric rendering, a parametric appearance model or auxiliary geometric regularization. A differentiable first-hit optimization framework that explicitly evaluates source-view visibility against the evolving neural surface. Related Work -view stereo and variational refinement. Classical MVS recovers geometry by enforcing photometric consistency across calibrated views together with explicit visibility reasoning, whether by expanding and filtering patches from matched seeds~ furukawa2010pmvs or estimating per-view depth maps and fusing geometrically consistent estimates~ merrell2007realtime,galliani2015massively,schoenberger2016pixelwise,xu2022acmmp . Variational approaches optimize surfaces directly through multi-view photoconsistency, evolving level sets on volumetric grids~ faugeras1998complete,pons2007multi or refining triangular meshes through photometric reprojection error~ vu2012highaccuracy,delaunoy2014photometric , typically with smoothness regularization. Like these methods, we optimize the surface directly through multi-view photoconsistency, but represent it as a continuous neural field rather than a grid or mesh, explicitly determine visibility using first-hit intersections and require no auxiliary geometric regularization. surface reconstruction. Neural implicit methods represent geometry as the level set of a signed distance or occupancy field and optimize it by comparing rendered colors with observed images, typically using a parametric appearance model. Colors are evaluated either at the first surface intersection~ yariv2020idr,niemeyer2020dvr or, following NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf , integrated along camera rays~ wang2021neus,yariv2021volsdf . Later work improves geometric detail and representation capacity~ li2023neuralangelo . To address the geometric ambiguity of photometric rendering, several methods introduce additional constraints. MVSDF incorporates stereo-derived depth and feature consistency~ zhang2021mvsdf , while NeuralWarp and Geo-NeuS combine volumetric rendering with patch photoconsistency~ darmon2022neuralwarp,fu2022geoneus . Geometry-oriented Gaussian splatting methods~ huang2024_2dgs,chen2025pgsr,li2026ambisur similarly add geometric constraints to opacity-based rendering. surface rendering. Optimizing implicit surfaces through ray intersections requires both differentiating the intersection points and computing them reliably. Differentiable surface rendering methods propagate gradients through these intersections using implicit differentiation~ yariv2020idr,niemeyer2020dvr or approximate sphere-tracing gradients~ liu2020dist . Other approaches address visibility discontinuities through reparameterization~ vicini2022differentiable,bangaru2022differentiable . Sphere tracing~ hart1996sphere finds the first surface intersection along a ray using steps bounded by the distance to the surface. Eikonal regularization encourages SDF behavior~ gropp2020igr but does not guarantee such bounds, and its optimization can exhibit instabilities~ yang2023steik . neural networks. A 1-Lipschitz field guarantees that sphere-tracing steps do not exceed the distance to the surface. Expressive 1-Lipschitz architectures include GroupSort~ anil2019groupsort , which uses norm-preserving activations, and convex potential layers (CPL)~ meunier2022cpl,prach2024layers . Lenain et al.~ lenain2026surface fit 1-Lipschitz neural fields to range scans using first-hit depth regression and Coiffier and Béthune~ coiffier2024lipschitz fit such fields to point clouds or triangle soups. While we also use a 1-Lipschitz architecture, we address surface reconstruction from calibrated RGB images through multi-view patch photoconsistency with explicit cross-view visibility. title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
summary: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.
full_text: 1 0 0 A A A A Scene types sec:supp-scene-types shows the number of scenes per type in . Dataset creation details sec:supp-creation Scene authoring. Artists compose the scenes from the asset library, starting from a brief for a given type of space, so that layout, object placement, scale, and material use follow real-world logic rather than procedural rules. A reviewer checks each concept against architectural criteria and follows the scene through detailing. Each scene also receives traces of human presence, based on a short scenario of the life that could take place there, so that it does not look artificially clean. A final technical check verifies every scene against the specification. Each scene is stored as a single GLB file with a semantic object hierarchy and PBR textures, in which every object is a separate mesh at metric scale. Simulation-ready processing. We extract the assets and the scene shell ( , walls and ceilings) from each scene and compose a scene graph of the physical relations between assets, such as support and attachment. We classify the assets into categories with a vision-language model (VLM) and have human annotators verify the categorization. To make the scenes physically simulatable, we compute collision hulls for the assets and the scene shell with CoACD~ wei2022approximate . Using the per-part material annotations of the artist meshes, we assign physical properties ( , density) to each part, from which we derive the mass and inertia of each asset. We also use the artists' annotations of emitter materials to define the explicit lighting of each scene, which, combined with the full PBR textures, enables photorealistic rendering. The result is a set of simulation-ready scenes for robotic manipulation and other physics-based tasks. Dataset comparison details sec:supp-comparison We compute the statistics in on the data each dataset releases, which can be smaller than what its paper describes. SpatialGen releases 48 of the 57K rooms in its paper, and GRUtopia releases 99 scenes of a collection that its paper puts at about 100K. Rooms. We count distinct rooms, so a room shipped in several styles counts once. RoboCasa365 ships 2,500 kitchen scenes that restyle 60 floor plans, so we count 60 rooms and measure the floor area of each plan once. GRUtopia annotates rooms only in the 30 home scenes of its benchmark, so we count its 321 rooms on those scenes. For 3D-FRONT, we use the 18,968 furnished rooms reported in its paper, while its floor area covers the whole houses, including unfurnished rooms. We count each Hypersim scene as one room. For ease of computation, we treat each outdoor scene as a single room. Floor area. Floor area is the area of the modeled floor surfaces, summed over all scenes. For , the residential, public indoor, and outdoor scenes contribute 162K, 459K, and 2.70M\,m , respectively. Outdoor scenes model large ground surfaces, so they account for most of the total. However, even without outdoor scenes, the indoor scenes still cover 621K\,m , which is larger than the floor area of other datasets in . Instances and assets. An instance is a placed object, and an asset is a distinct 3D model behind one or more instances. For 3D-FRONT, we count the placed 3D-FUTURE furniture models, 14,051 in the release, close to the 13,151 reported in its paper. We exclude the per-house fittings, such as kitchen cabinets, doors, and windows, which carry no object category. VLM scores. We rate the scenes with Qwen3.8-27B, with thinking disabled. For each dataset with 3D scenes, we sample 20 scenes per room type and render each scene with the same cameras and lighting. A top-down view from 3.5 times the wall height, with the ceiling removed, shows the layout. An eye-level view at 1.55\,m with a 100 horizontal field of view, taken from the corner that sees the most furniture, shows the objects. For datasets that release only images, we use one released frame per scene. The VLM rates each image from 1 to 5 with the prompts in , giving its reason before the score, and we report the mean over all rated images. Layout realism is rated on the top-down view, and asset fidelity and aesthetics on the eye-level view. Datasets that release only images have no top-down view, so we do not report layout realism for them. Grasp affordance labels sec:supp-affordance shows more objects with affordance labels, in addition to . Each label marks the part of an object that a grasp should contact, , the handle of a teapot, the frame of a pair of glasses, or the holder of a toilet brush. For example, picking up the glasses by the lenses counts as a success but lowers the affordance accuracy. Experiment details sec:supp-experiments Inverse rendering sec:supp-ir-benchmark Benchmark. We provide additional benchmarks for single-view and scene-level inverse rendering methods on the test set, using their released code and weights without fine-tuning. The results are shown in . We intentionally include both day and night lighting, so that the methods face both sunlight through the windows and scenes lit only by lamps. For the single-view methods, we take three views per lighting from each of the indoor test scenes, 1,820 frames in total at 640 480. We skip views that are mostly over- or underexposed, too close to the geometry, or show fewer than three objects. For the scene-level methods, we take 15 test scenes, one per scene type, 8 with day and 7 with night lighting. Each scene has 180 input views and 20 held-out views. We query the recovered materials at the surfaces seen by the held-out views, so the scores measure the materials of the whole scene rather than how well a method fits its input views. Prior scene-level methods, such as FIPT~ wu2023factorized , IRIS~ lin2025iris , and Intrinsic Image Fusion~ kocsis2026intrinsic , evaluate on the four synthetic scenes of FIPT, built from the rendering resources of Bitterli~ bitterli2016resources , so our scene-level benchmark covers almost four times as many scenes and a much wider range of scene types. All methods receive the ground-truth camera poses. FIPT, IRIS, NeILF++, and Intrinsic Image Fusion also assume the ground-truth mesh as input, and we evaluate GenRecon both with and without it. We also use the ground-truth mesh for MVInverse to propagate the prediction to held-out views. We score albedo in sRGB space, and roughness and metallic in linear space, over the pixels that do not show emitters, windows, or transparent surfaces. For si-PSNR, we fit one scale per channel in linear space before computing the PSNR. Even with the ground-truth mesh, the scene-level methods struggle to recover accurate materials, since the complex lighting of the scenes is hard to disentangle from the materials. For example, the lamps of are light sources inside the fixtures rather than emissive surfaces, so FIPT finds no emitter at night and bakes the lamp glow into the albedo. NeILF++, on the other hand, models the lighting as an incident light field that depends on position. We observe that at night, the appearance of the materials is absorbed by the lighting, leaving a mostly uniform albedo. title: Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild
summary: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.
full_text: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments. Introduction sec:intro Spatial reasoning is a foundational capability for Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ alayrac2022flamingo, anthropic2024claude, bai2025qwen25vl, chen2024internvl, guo2025seed15vl, hurst2024gpt4o, li2024llavaonevision, lu2024ovis, radford2021learning, team2023gemini, qwenteam2025qwen3vl, wang2025internvl35, zhang2024llavanext that aspire to perceive, navigate, and interact with the physical world. While recent VLMs have demonstrated remarkable proficiency across a spectrum of visual understanding tasks, a critical question remains: how well can they truly reason about space, particularly in embodied settings where reasoning must translate into action? Prior works have examined complementary slices of spatial reasoning, yet primarily confine their scope to static images or passive scenes~ xu2025spatialbench,yang2025thinking . Recent benchmarks have evolved to incorporate multi-view images to capture viewpoint changes~ gholami2025spatial,wu2025indoor , or video inputs that evaluate spatio-temporal understanding capabilities~ li2025sti . While these efforts advance the evaluation of spatial relationships, they predominantly treat the model as a passive observer. In other words, they assess whether a model can comprehend a spatial problem from isolated visual observations, leaving its ability to act spatially within a continuous environment largely untested. Embodied benchmarks and their associated simulators provide interactive environments to address this problem, but they concentrate overwhelmingly on indoor scenes (e.g., Habitat~ savva2019habitat , AI2-THOR~ kolve2017ai2 ). However, indoor settings inherently exhibit high semantic density within spatially constrained layouts. In such environments, models can often avoid authentic spatial reasoning by exploiting structural priors or semantic shortcuts, relying on conceptual associations and semantic pattern matching (e.g., locating a refrigerator implies proximity to a kitchen) rather than actual geometric understanding. While semantically sparse outdoor scenes help decouple the evaluation of spatial reasoning, existing benchmarks still lack realism or continuity. For instance, synthetic platforms like EmbodiedCity~ gao2024embodiedcity fail to capture real-world fidelity, while street-view datasets such as Touchdown~ chen2019touchdown are restricted to discrete topological graphs that preclude continuous actions and fine-grained geometric reasoning. Consequently, a unified evaluation that tightly couples egocentric spatial perception with embodied interaction in realistic and continuous environments remains absent. To fill this gap, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments. As shown in Figure~ fig:framework , we reconstruct diverse regions of a university campus using Octree-based Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233dgs,ren2025octree , yielding a photorealistic, view-consistent and continuously navigable simulation platform. It supports long-horizon closed-loop interaction with high-fidelity egocentric observations for embodied evaluation in real-world open spaces. Built on this environment, we introduce a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework for VLMs, consisting of two complementary paradigms. First, Closed-Loop Interactive Navigation evaluates reasoning in action, aiming to assess whether VLMs can effectively translate spatial observations and reasoning into coherent embodied behavior. We further evaluate navigation under three distinct forms of spatial instruction to probe VLMs' spatial reasoning ability in action. Second, diagnostic QA evaluates spatial reasoning in isolation through six diagnostic tasks targeting different aspects of ESR. Unlike traditional spatial QA on static and disconnected images, our diagnostic protocol is automatically generated from the navigation rollouts across models. Grounded in embodied context, it maps end-to-end task execution back to underlying ESR capabilities, enabling fine-grained evaluation. We summarize our contributions as follows. Outdoor real-world evaluation environment. We construct a photorealistic and continuous outdoor 3DGS campus environment for embodied VLM evaluation, supporting high-fidelity rendering and long-horizon interactive navigation. Unified reasoning-action evaluation framework. We evaluate VLMs through closed-loop interactive navigation and diagnostic QA, combining reasoning in isolation with reasoning in action for fine-grained analysis of ESR capabilities. Empirical findings on outdoor ESR. We comprehensively benchmark representative open- and closed-source VLMs, show that outdoor ESR remains under-solved, identify spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization as primary bottlenecks for embodied navigation. Related Work sec:related Spatial reasoning evaluation for VLMs. Early evaluations of VLM spatial reasoning focused on reasoning within static single-image scenes, bounding the assessment to qualitative relational understanding~ dongfang2025are, johnson2017clevr, liu2025can, ramakrishnan2025does, shiri2024empirical, stogiannidis2025mind, tang2024sparkle, wang2025spatial457, yao2025lens . Recent benchmarks have extended spatial evaluation with multi-view images, videos, and 3D annotations~ gholami2025spatial, yang2025mmsi, yeh2026seeing,gong2025space, yang2025thinking, zhang2025do, zhou2025vlm4d . These efforts introduce richer spatial cues, including viewpoint changes, temporal continuity, depth and 3D geometry across indoor scenes, autonomous-driving scenarios, object-centric 3D datasets and outdoor stereo videos. Such designs substantially broaden the scope of VLM spatial evaluation beyond single images~ gholami2025spatial,li2025sti . However, they still largely evaluate models as passive observers over pre-collected visual inputs or annotated geometric cues~ yang2025thinking,gholami2025spatial . The model is asked to answer spatial questions, but its judgments are not coupled with embodied decisions or evaluated through their consequences in navigation. In contrast, our trajectory-grounded QA acts as a diagnostic probe generated from navigation trajectories in a large-scale outdoor environment. It situates spatial understanding within closed-loop embodied behavior. Embodied navigation benchmarks. Planning and navigating through unknown environments remain fundamental challenges for embodied agents. Recent benchmarks evaluate VLMs as high-level decision makers tasked with interpreting egocentric observations and following instructions~ gao2025octonav,miao2025towards . As summarized in Table~ tab:comparison , most existing efforts~ khanna2024goat, song2025towards,miao2025towards,qiao2026navbench,yang2025navspace,gao2024embodiedcity primarily focus on increasing instruction complexity. Although these tasks have driven progress in instruction-following, they concentrate on benchmarking the multimodal understanding of language and visual semantics, without systematically assessing spatial perception and reasoning~ gao2025octonav,miao2025towards . Several recent efforts have advanced toward spatial evaluation. For instance, NavBench~ qiao2026navbench assesses action consequences in spatial understanding; however, it operates within discrete environments, precluding the evaluation of fine-grained egocentric control. Other efforts, such as NavSpace~ yang2025navspace , advance toward quantitative spatial evaluation in indoor scenes. However, such scenes are limited in spatial scale, semantic diversity and visual variability, hindering evaluation from accurately reflecting real-world conditions. 3D reconstruction and image-based rendering for embodied simulation. Simulation environments are central to embodied AI, supporting evaluation and scalable training. Indoor environment datasets and simulators~ chang2017matterport3d,savva2019habitat have provided important foundations for embodied reasoning benchmarks. However, many existing environments are primarily built upon mesh-based scene representations and may lack the visual fidelity needed for fine-grained perception and motion cues. Meanwhile, existing outdoor environments either rely on discrete panorama graphs~ chen2019touchdown or synthetic rendering engines~ gao2024embodiedcity , leaving realistic and continuous outdoor embodied evaluation less explored. Recent progress in large-scale 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis, particularly 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs , introduces promising solutions to create photorealistic replicas from video captures. However, large-scale reconstructed environments that combine photorealistic appearance, metric consistency, and continuous outdoor interaction remain limited. Such environments can complement existing indoor and synthetic or graph-based outdoor platforms, and support broader evaluation of VLMs under realistic egocentric perception and embodied interaction. The 3D Outdoor Environment sec:environment Data Collection. The Lost on Campus environment is constructed from real-world, large-scale campus captures using Insta360 X4 cameras. The collected panorama frames are split into four perspective images, each with a field of view (FoV). These four frames together cover the horizontal FoV around the camera. Overall, this dataset contains over 50k calibrated video frames on fifteen academic halls and road intersections, covering an area of approximately . While frames within a single video are easier to calibrate, frames between videos introduce challenges, e.g., through inconsistent lighting, visual ambiguities, etc. To achieve accurate metric-scale camera calibration across 50k video frames, we use a mobile RTK device to capture centimeter-accurate GPS coordinates for each image. This allows us to (1) perform dense 3D reconstruction on regions where multiple videos overlap, and (2) introduce consistent metric-scale reconstruction, which is strictly required for evaluating VLMs on distance-aware spatial understanding. Photorealistic 3D Reconstruction. For photorealistic 3D reconstruction and rendering, we employ a modified Octree-GS~ ren2025octree with (1) appearance and transient embeddings to account for lighting and transient variations and (2) a triangle primitive~ held2025triangle for better geometry recovery and collision detection
